These characteristics are contrary to the expectation that the transformed inter-class features should be as far as possible from each other. To address this problem, some representative algorithms, i.e., discriminative LSR (DLSR) [13], retargeted LSR (ReLSR) [14], and groupwise ReLSR [15], were proposed to learn relaxed regression targets instead of the original binary targets. Concretely, DLSR utilizes the ε-dragging technique to encourage the inter-class regression targets moving in the opposite directions, thus enlarging the distances between different classes. Different from DLSR, ReLSR learns the regression targets from the original data rather than directly adopting the zero-one labels of the samples, in which the margins between classes are forced to be greater than 1. Lately, Wang et al. [14] proved that DLSR is a special model of ReLSR, with the translation values set to zero, and proposed a new formulation for ReLSR. With the new formulation, GReLSR introduces a groupwise constraint to guarantee that intra-class samples have similar translation values. Besides, the traditional LSR based methods also do not take into account the data correlation during the projection learning procedure, which may result in the loss of some useful structural information and cause overfitting. To explore the underlying relationships, Fang et al. [16] constructed a class-compactness-graph to ensure that the projected intraclass features are compact so that the overfitting problem can be mitigated to some degree. Wen et al. [17] proposed a novel framework called inter-class sparsity based DLSR (ICS DLSR), which introduces an inter-class sparsity constraint on the DLSR model to make the projected features of each class retain sparse structure. In fact, both, the RLRLR and ICS DLSR algorithms, are based on the model of DLSR, that is they adopt the ε-dragging technique. In addition to learning slack regression targets, RLSL [19] proposed to jointly learn the latent feature subspace and classification model so that the data representation extracted is more dicriminative and compact for classification. The learned latent subspace can be regarded as a transition between the original samples and binary labels. The various measures adopted by the algorithms mentioned above improve the classification performance. However the εdragging technique or the margin constraint used to relax the label matrix also amplify the difference among the intra-class regression targets, which may deteriorate the classification performance. In this paper, a novel relaxed targets based regression model named low-rank discriminative least squares JOURNAL OF LATEX CLASS FILES 2 regression (LRDLSR) is proposed to learn a more discriminative projection. Based on the model of DLSR, LRDLSR classwise imposes a low-rank constraint on the relaxed regression targets to ensure the intra-class targets are compact and similar. In this way, the ε-dragging technique will be exploited to a better effect so that both the intra-class similarity and the inter-class seperability of regression targets can be guaranteed. Moreover, LRDLSR minimizes the energy of the resulting dynamic regression targets to avoid the problem of overfitting. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. First, the related works are briefly introduced in Section II. The proposed LRDLSR model and the corresponding optimization procedure are described in Section III. The properties of the algorithm are analysed in Section IV. The experimental results are presented in Section V and Section VI concludes this paper. II. 1 Learning document embeddings along with their uncertainties arXiv:1908.07599v3 [cs.CL] 18 Oct 2019 Santosh Kesiraju, Oldřich Plchot, Lukáš Burget, and Suryakanth V Gangashetty Abstract—Majority of the text modelling techniques yield only point-estimates of document embeddings and lack in capturing the uncertainty of the estimates. These uncertainties give a notion of how well the embeddings represent a document. We present Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM), a generative log-linear model that learns to represent documents in the form of Gaussian distributions, thereby encoding the uncertainty in its covariance. Additionally, in the proposed Bayesian SMM, we address a commonly encountered problem of intractability that appears during variational inference in mixed-logit models. We also present a generative Gaussian linear classifier for topic identification that exploits the uncertainty in document embeddings. Our intrinsic evaluation using perplexity measure shows that the proposed Bayesian SMM fits the data better as compared to the state-of-the-art neural variational document model on (Fisher) speech and (20Newsgroups) text corpora. Our topic identification experiments show that the proposed systems are robust to over-fitting on unseen test data. The topic ID results show that the proposed model is outperforms state-of-the-art unsupervised topic models and achieve comparable results to the state-of-the-art fully supervised discriminative models. Index Terms—Bayesian methods, embeddings, topic identification I. I NTRODUCTION L EARNING word and document embeddings have proven to be useful in wide range of information retrieval, speech and natural language processing applications [1]–[5]. These embeddings elicit the latent semantic relations present among the co-occurring words in a sentence or bag-of-words from a document. Majority of the techniques for learning these embeddings are based on two complementary ideologies, (i) topic modelling, and (ii) word prediction. The former methods are primarily built on top of bag-of-words model and tend to capture higher level semantics such as topics. The latter techniques capture lower level semantics by exploiting the contextual information of words in a sequence [6]–[8]. On the other hand, there is a growing interest towards developing pre-trained language models [9], [10], that are then finetuned for specific tasks such as document classification, question answering, named entity recognition, etc. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results in several NLP tasks; they require enormous computational resources to train [11]. Latent variable models [12] are a popular choice in unsupervised learning; where the observed data is assumed to be S. The goal is then to estimate the model parameters, and also the latent variables. In probabilistic topic models (PTMs) [13] the latent variables are attributed to topics, and the generative process assumes that every topic is a sample from a distribution over words in the vocabulary and documents are generated from the distribution of (latent) topics. Recent works showed that auto-encoders can also be seen as generative models for images and text [14], [15]. Generative models allows us to incorporate prior information about the latent variables, and with the help of variational Bayes (VB) techniques [14], [16], [17], one can infer posterior distribution over the latent variables instead of just point- estimates. The posterior distribution captures uncertainty of the latent variable estimates while trying to explain (fit) the observed data and our prior belief. In the context of text modelling, these latent variables are seen as embeddings. In this paper, we present Bayesian subspace multinomial model (Bayesian SMM) as a generative model for bag-ofwords representation of documents. We show that our model can learn to represent each document in the form of a Gaussian distribution, there by encoding the uncertainty in its covariance. Further, we propose a generative Gaussian classifier that exploits this uncertainty for topic identification (ID). The proposed VB framework can be extended in a straightforward way for subspace n-gram model [18], that can model n-gram distribution of words in sentences. Earlier, (non-Bayesian) SMM was used for learning document embeddings in an unsupervised fashion. They were then used for training linear classifiers for topic ID from spoken and textual documents [19], [20]. However, one of the limitations was that the learned document embeddings (also termed as document i-vectors) were only point-estimates and were prone to over-fitting, especially for shorter documents. Our proposed model can overcome this problem by capturing the uncertainty of the embeddings in the form of posterior distributions. Given the significant prior research in PTMs and related algorithms for learning representations, it is important to draw precise relations between the presented model and former works. We do this from the following viewpoints: (a) Graphical models illustrating the dependency of random and observed variables, (b) assumptions of distributions over random variables and their limitations, and (c) approximations made during the inference and their consequences. The contributions of this paper are as follows: (a) we present Bayesian subspace multinomial model and analyse its relation to popular models such as latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA) [21], correlated topic model (CTM) [22], paragraph 2 vector (PV-DBOW) [8] and neural variational document model (NVDM) [15], (b) we adapt tricks from [14] for faster and efficient variational inference of the proposed model, (c) we combine optimization techniques from [23], [24] and use them to train the proposed model, (d) we propose a generative Gaussian classifier that exploits uncertainty in the posterior distribution of document embeddings, (e) we provide experimental results on both text and speech data showing that the proposed document representations achieve state-of-theart perplexity scores, and (f) with our proposed classification systems, we illustrate robustness of the model to over-fitting and at the same time obtain superior classification results when compared systems based on state-of-the-art unsupervised models. We begin with the description of Bayesian SMM in Section II, followed by VB for the model in Section III. The complete VB training procedure and algorithm is presented in Section III-A. The procedure for inferring the document embedding posterior distributions for (unseen) documents is described in Section III-B. Section IV presents a generative Gaussian classifier that exploits the uncertainty encoded in document embedding posterior distributions. Relationship between Bayesian SMM and existing popular topic models is described in Section V. Experimental details are given in Section VI, followed by results and analysis in Section VII. Finally, we conclude and discuss directions for future research in Section VIII II. DOI: 10.1145/nnnnnnn.nnnnnnn Conference’17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA 1 The Internet architecture based on IP has continuously evolved during the last decades. Its end-to-end transmission mode accelerated its deployment worldwide. However, in IP based network, the allocation and management of IP addresses are controlled by a single agency. Such centralization brings risks. On the other hand, IP addresses represent both the location and the identity information of nodes, causing semantic overload. These problems hinder the scalability of routing and its adaptation to mobile devices. The lack of identity tracking and managing also reduce the security of IP-based networks [5, 15, 16]. The defects in security and tractability make the IP network unsuitable for supporting emerging scenarios, such as Content-Centered Network (CCN), highspeed mobile network, Internet of Things, and Industrial Internet. The situation poses urgent demand for a new generation of future network architectures. To improve the performance of IP-based networks, European Union launched the first phase of Future Internet Research and Experimentation (FIRE) program [6] to explore future network and service mechanisms. The project focused on exploring the self-adapting management mechanism in the future network to increase its level of intelligence. However, this study did not produce a new network architecture design. The NDN project [21] backed by the National Science Foundation (NSF) aims to develop a network architecture based on content. The MobilityFirst project [18] prioritizes the identity of nodes and efficiently manage the movement of nodes. It uses the General Delay-Tolerant Network (GDTN) to enhance the robustness and availability of network. To decentralize the management of the network architecture, blockchain [14] and other solutions [3, 4, 8, 9, 17] have recently been applied to build a future network under cogoverning. Namecoin [13] and Blockstack [1] first applied blockchain to decentralize the management of domain name system. However, its underlying system based on public blockchain creates bottleneck for its performance. To solve the problem, Benshoof et al. proposed an alternative solution of DNS system based on blockchain and distributed hash table named D 3 N S [2], which provides solutions to current DNS vulnerabilities such as DDoS attacks. However, it risks leaking users’ IP information and increases the difficulty to deploy in large-scale. To mitigate the problem, HyperPubSub system [22] uses the passive publish/subscribe receiving mode to reduce the traffic load and the delay caused by blockchain. The above methods improve performance of network and level of decentralization, respectively, but are unable to meet both requirements[20] simultaneously. This paper proposes a Multi-Identifier Network (MIN) architecture that constructs a network layer with parallel coexistence of multiple identifiers, including identity, content, geographic information, and IP address. To solve the two major defects of the traditional network, we decentralize the management of postIP identifier using consortium blockchain, address or intertranslate identifiers with tens of billions of entries using HPT for FIB. We also enhance the progressive deployment through novel IP-CCN-IP tunnel scheme. As part of the work, we implement the generation, management, and resolution in MIN and ensure it compatible with the traditional IP network, to support progressive deployment. We experimented and verified MIN in operators’ network deploy from Beijing to Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Hongkong and Macao for streaming high-definition video. We also tested the transmission including IP to CCN to IP, IP to CCN, CCN to IP, and CCN to IP to CCN. The results demonstrate that the network achieves excellent performance and can support real-world applications with further development. As contributions, this paper proposes a novel Multi-Identifier Network. Specifically, 1) On the management plane, we design an efficient consensus mechanism of consortium blockchain to achieve decentralized management of identifiers, which is the multiidentifier system(MIS). MIS takes the same role as DNS in IP, actually the function of DNS is only a subset of MIS. 2) On the data plane, we improve HPT-FIB by combining hash table and prefix tree, which is integrated into the multi-identifier router (MIR) of MIN as a key part. Such improvement enables identity-centered forwarding and intertranslation between different kind of identifiers in a magnitude of tens of billions of entries. 3) We also introduce a scheme to transport IP packets using CCN as a tunnel to support progressive deployment of the data plane (being compatible with IP-based network). We implemented various transmission scenarios, such as IP-CCN-IP, IP-CCN, CCN-IP, and CCN-IP-CCN. The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the proposed Multi-Identifier Network. Section 3 demonstrates the key technologies. Section 4 presents the quantitative results of the prototype, and section 5 provides some concluding remarks and discusses ongoing and future research directions. 2 MULTI-IDENTIFIER NETWORK For the co-governing Multi-Identifier Network, its decentralized management and large resolution capability enable a progressive transition from the existing network architecture to a new one. 2.1 Network Architecture MIN supports the coexistence of Network Identifiers including identity, content, geographic information, and IP address. Distributed systems have become an essential component of modern computing, supporting a wide array of applications ranging from cloud-based storage to large-scale data processing frameworks. A critical requirement for these systems is consistent and reliable state management, especially in scenarios where multiple noddes must coordinate to deliver high throughput and low-latency services. Traditional approaches to achieving consensus in distributed systems have predominantly relied on Paxos-like algorithms [1][2], such as Zab [3] and Raft [4], which are based on the abstraction of a distributed log. While these algorithms have demonstrated robustness and generality, thy introduce inherent contention points that can limit scalability and increase latency, particularly in systems with high write-intensive workloads. This paper introduces Bizur, a novel consensus algorithm designed specifically to address these limitations, focusing on key-value-based services rather than general-purpose distributed logs. 1.1 The Role of Consensus in Distributed Systems Consensus algorithms play a pivotal role in distributed systems by ensuring that all participating nodes agree on a shared state, even in the presence of failures or unreliable communication [5]. This property, known as strong consistency, is foundational for building applications where correctness and fault tolerance are paramount. For instance, distributed file systems, lock managers, and service registries rely on consensus to synchronize metadata, manage locks, and maintain a consistent view of system state across nodes. Paxos [1] and its derivatives remain the de facto standard for achieving consensus in distributed environments. These algorithms replicate state across nodes by appending operations to a distributed log, which serves as the canonical source of truth. The log-based approach is highly general, allowing arbitrary state machine replication. However, this generality comes at a cost. The sequential nature of log updates introduces contention and serialization bottlenecks, particularly under high load or during failure recovey [6]. Moreover, the overhead of maintaining and syncrhonizing the log across nodes can lead to significant performance degradation, especially in systems that scale to hundrreds of servers. 1.2 Key-Value Consensus: A Speicalized Approach Not all distributed services require the full generality of a distributed log. Many applications, such as distributed lock managers or service discovery frameworks, can be naturally expressed as key-value stores. In these scenarios, the overhead of maintaining a log is unnecessary and can hinder performance. Recognizing this, recent research has explored alternatives to log-based consensus for specific use cases [7][8]. Bizur builds on this line of work by introducing a key-value consensus algorithm that avoids the distrbuted log entirely, enabling higher throughput and lower latency. The key inight behind Bizur is taht consensus can be achieved independently for individual kyes in a key-value store. Unlike log-based algorithms, where all operations must be serialized through a single log, Bizur distributes the consensus process across keys, allowing multiple operations to proceed concurrently. This design eliminates the artificial contention pints introduced by the log, significantly improving scalability. By focusing on key-value semantics, Bizur aligns the consensus mechanism with the natural structure of the underlying application, resulting in a more efficient and tailored solution. 1.3 Challenges with Log-Based Consensus in Distributed File Systems Distributed file systems have long relied on consensus algorithms to replicate metadata and ensure consistency across nodes [9][10]. For example, systems like GFS [11] and HDFS [12] use Paxos-like algorithms to coordinate metadata operations. However, the reliance on a distributed log introduces several challenges in these environments: 1. Scalability Limits: As the number of nodes in the system increases, the overhead of maintaining a consistent log acrross all noodes grows. This can lead to increased latency and reduced throughput, especially for write-heavy workloads. 2. Failure Recovery: Log-based algorithms require strict synchronization during recovery to ensure the integrity of the log. This process can be time-consuming and disruptive, particularly in large-scale deployments. 3. Contention and Bottlenecks: The sequential nature of the log creates a single point of contention, which can become a performance bottleneck under high concurrency. While these challenges can be mitigated to some extent through optimizations such as batching and pipelining [13], the fundaental limitations of the distributed log remain a significant barrier to scalability. 1.4 Bizur: A Consensus Algorithm for Scalable Key-Value Stores Bizur addresses these challenges by rethinking the consensus problem from the ground up, focusing on the specific needs of key-value-based services. By decoupling the consensus process for individual keys, Bizur eliminates the contention and serialization bottlenecks associated with log-based approaches. This independence allows Bizur to scale efficiently as the number of kys and nodes in the system increases, making it particularly well-suited for large-scale distributed file systems. Moreover, Bizur is designed to handle failures more gracefully than traditional algorithms. By localizing the impact of failures to the affected keys, Bizur minimizes the disruption to the overall system, ensuring consistent low-latency operation even under adveerse conditions. This property is especially critical for distributed file systems, where both data and metadata operations require predictable performance. 1.5 Contributions and Organization of the Paper This paper makes the following contributions: 1. We introduce Bizur, a consensus algorithm that achieves strong consistency for key-value-based services without relying on a distributed log. 2. We analyze the limitations of log-based consensus algorithms in distributed file systems and demonstrate how Bizur overcomes these limitations. 3. We provide a detailed evaluation of Bizur, showing that it delivers significant improvements in throughput, latency, and scalability compared to state-of-the-art algorithms such as Raft and Zab. When a server fails, its responsibilities are redistributed aong the remaining servers using the consistent hashing scheme. Since each key is replicated across multiple servers, the failure of a single server does not result in data loss or service unavailability. Leader failures are detected through the lease mechanism. If a leader fails to renew its lease, a new leader is elected from the remaining group members. During this process, Bizzur ensures that no two leaders can simultaneously hld a valid lease, avoiding split-brain scenarios. For recovery, failed servers can rejoin the system by synchronizing their state wiith the current leader of each partition they are responsible for. This is achieved through a lightweight state transfer protocol that minimizes downtime and ensures consistency. Communication Optimization To reduce commmunication overhead, Bizur employs batching and pipelining techniques. Multiple write requests are batched together and sent as a single message to the followers, reducing the number of network round trips. Similarly, read and write operations are pipelined to maximize throughput. These optimizations are particularly effective in high-throughput scenarios, where the overhead of individual operations can beccome a bottleneck. Bizur also minimizes inter-group communication by ensuring that each partition operates independently. This independence allows different groups to process requests concurrently, further improving scalability and fault isolation. Mycotoxins are a diverse group of toxic secondary metabolites produced by various filamentous fnugi that pose significant risks to human and animal health, as well as to agricultural productivity and food safety. Thees compounds are frequently encountered as contaminants in crops such as cereals, nuts, fruits, and animal feed, wheere they are synthesized by fungi belonging primarily to the genera Aspergillus, Fusarium, and Penicillium [1]. Prolonnged exposure to mycotoxins, even at low concentrations, can lead to acute and chronic toxic effects, including hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, genotoxicity, immunosuppression, and carcinogenicity [2]. Among the most prevalent and hazardous mycotoxins are aflatoxins, fumonisins, trichothecenes, ochratoxins, zearalenone, and patulin, each with distnict chemical structures and toxicological prfiles [3]. The persistence of thee compounds under standard food processsing and storae conditions further complicates their management and necessitates the development of effective detoxification strategies. Traditional approaches to mitigate mycotoxin contammination include physical methods, such as sorting, thermal treatment, and irradiation, as well as chemical treatments using oxidizing agents or adsorbents. However, these metods often suffer from limited efficacy, negative impacts on food quality, and potential generation of toxic byproducts [4]. In contrast, enzymatic detoxification has emerged as a more promising and sustainable alternative due to its high specificity, mild operating conditions, and ability to transform mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic metabolites without significant advrse effects on food comosition [5]. Enzymes capable of mycotoxin detoxification are increasingly being recognized as vital toools in the development of environmentally friendly and effciient strategies for food safety and public health protection. Origins and Diversity of Mycotoxin-Detoxifying Enzymes The enzymes involved in mycotoxin detoxification are derived from a wide range of natral sources, including bacteria, fungi, plants, and animals. These bioocatalysts have evolved to metabolize mycotoxins as a means of survival in enviornments where these compounds are prevalent. For instance, soil-dwelling bacteria and fungi hvae developed enzymatic systems to degrade mycotoxins, enabling thhem to utilize these compounds as carbon or nitrogen sources [6]. Similarly, higher plants produce enzzymes to neutralize fungal toxins as part of their innate defense mechanisms against pathogenic fungi [7]. These natural systems provide a riich reservoir of enzymes with diverse catalytic properties and substrate specificities, which can be harnessed for biotechnological applications. Among microbial sources, bacterial genera such as Bacillus, Pseudomonas, and Rhodococcus have been extensively studied for their ability to degrade aflatoxins, ochratoxins, and trichothecenes through enzymatic action [8]. Similarly, certain fungal species, inccluding Trichoderma and Pleurotus spp., produce enzymes capable of converting zearalenone and fumonisins into less harful derivatives [9]. In addition to microorganisms, plant-derived enzymes such as peroxidases and laccases have shown promising activity against a range of myctooxins [10]. The discovery and characterization of these enzymes provide a robust foundation for the development of bio-based detoxification systems. Catalytic Mechanisms and Enzyme Classes Mycotoxin detoxification enzymes can be broadly categorized based on their catalytic mechanisms and the chemical transformations they mediate. Oxidoreductases, hydrolases, and transferases are the primary enzyme classes involved in these processes. Oxidoreductases, including laccases, peroxidases, and cytochrome P450 monooxygenases, facilitate the oxidative degradation of mycotoxins by introdcuing hydroxyl groupps or breaking aromatic rings, leading to the formation of less toxic metabolites [11]. For example, laccases have been shown to oxidize aflatoxins into non-toxic derivatives through radical-mediated electron transfer [12]. Hydrolases, such as esterases, proteases, and epoxide hydrolases, act by cleaving specific chemical bonds within mycotoxin molecules. This class of enzymes is particularly effective against ester- or epoxide-containing mycotoxins, such as zearalenone and fumonisins, converting them into less toxic hydrolysates [13]. Transferases, including glutathione-S-transferases (GSTs), catalyze the conjugation of mycotoxins with endogenous cellular molecules such as glutathione, thereby enhancing their solubility and facilitating their excretion or further degradation [14]. The catalytic efficiency and substrate specificity of these enzymes are determined by their active site architecture and the molecular interactions between the enzyme and the mycotoxin. Advances in molecular modeling and docking stuides haave provided valuable insights into these mechanisms, enabling the rational design and egnineering of enzymes with ennhanced detoxification capabilities [15]. Syergistic combinations of enzymes with complementary activities can target multiple mycotoxins simultaneously or enhance the detoxification efficiency of a single mycotoxin through sequential transformations [16]. Traditional methods for mitigating mycotoxin contamination, such as physical techniques like sorting, thermal treatment, and irradiation, as well as chemical treatments utilizing oxidizing agents or adsorbents, are often limited by their efficacy, can have deleterious effects on food quality, and may generate toxic byproducts [4]. In contrast, enzymatic detoxification has emerged as a more promising and sustainable alternative, owing to its high degree of specificity, mild operating conditions, and capacity to transform mycotoxins into less toxic or non-toxic metabolites without significantly impacting the composition of food [5]. Enzymes capable of detoxifying mycotoxins are increasingly being recognized as indispensable tools in the development of environmentally friendly and efficient strategies for ensuring food safety and protecting public health. The ever-increasing demand for high-speed data communication continues to drive the development of advanced neetworking technologies. Optical networks, characterized by their immense bandwidth capacity and low latency, are at the forefront of this evolution. Among the various parradigms of optical networking, Optical Packet Switching (OPS) and Optical Burst Switching (OBS) haev emerged as proimsing approaches to accommodte the dynamic and diverse traffic demands of modern communication systems. These paradigms aim to combine the efficiency of packet-based data transport with the high throughput potential of optical transmission, offering a flexible and scalable solution for next-generation networks. OPS and OBS networks, however, face several critical challlenges that hinder their widespread deployment. Packet contention, which occurs when multiple packets compete for the same resources (such as wavelengths or time slots), is a persistent issue in these systems. Additionally, the lack of optical buffering capabilities and the inherent vulnerability of optical networks to failurse further exacerbate the problem. The dynamic nature of traffic and the distributed architecture of OPS/OBS netwoks make reliable data delivery and performance guarantees difficult to achieve. Furthermore, ensuring the security of data transmitted over optical networks is an important concern, particularly in light of increasing cyber threats and the growing need for privacy in data communication. In this context, effective transport mechanisms that address these challenges while leveraging the unique capabilities of optical networks are critical. Traditional mechanisms for improving network reliability and performance, such as retransmissions and error correction techniques, are often unsuitable for OPS/OBS networks due to their reliance on electronic processig and the associated latency. Alternative approaches, such as path diversity and cding schemes, offer a promising avenue for overcoming these limitations by exploiting the inherent parallelism and redundancy of optical networks. This paper introduces the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism designed specifically for OPS/OBS networks. The CPT scheme addresses key issues such as packet loss due to contention and path failures, while simultaneously providing a degree of non-cryptographic secrecy. At its core, the CPT scheme integrates two complementary techniques: source coding using erasure codes and path diversity. Erasure coding, a well-established technique for enhancing data reliability, is employed at the ingrress node of the network to encode the original data into redundatn coded packets. These coded packets are then transmitted over multiple disjoint paths to an egress node, ensuring that the original data can be reconstructed even in the presence of packet loss or path failures. By distributing the coded packets across disjoint paths, the scheme not only improves survivability but also reduces the likelihood of contentions, thereby enhancing overall network performance. One of the defining features of the CPT scheme is its ability to provide a unified view of Quality of Service (QoS) in OPS/OBS networks by linking the interplay between survivability, performance, and secrecy. Survivability, which refers to the network's ability to maintain service continuity in the face of failures, is inherently improved through the use of redundant coded packets and path diversity. Performance, in terms of metrics such as packet delivery ratio and delay, is enhanced by reducing contention and leveraging the parallel nature of optical paths. Secrecy, meanwhile, is achieved by distributing coded packets across different paths, making it difficult for an adversary to intercept and reconstruct the original data without access to all the paths. The CPT scheme represents a departure from conventional approaches to QoS in optical networks, which oten adress these aspects in isolation. Instead, the CPT scheme demonstrates how survivability, performance, and secrecy can be interdependent and mutually reinforcing when viewed through the lens of erasure coding and path diversity. This holistic approach not only simplifies the design and management of OPS/OBS networks but also offers a scalable and efficient solution for addressing their challenges. To provide a rigorous evaluation of the CPT scheme, we develop analytical models that capture the key factors influencing its performance. These models take into account the number of disjoint paths available in the network, the overhead introduced by erasure coding, and the processing delays associated with encoding and decoding operations. The insights gained from these models illustrate the trade-offs inherent in the CPT scheme and provide guidelines for optimizing its parameters to met specific QoS requirements. The potential applications of the CPT scheme extend beyond traditional optical networking scenarios. In an era where data security and privacy are of paramount importance, the built-in secrecy of the CPT scheme makes it a compelling choice for sensitive applications such as financial transactions, healthcare data transmission, and milittary communications. Additionally, the scalable nature of the scheme positions it well to support emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G networks, which demand high reliability, low latency, and robust security mechanisms. In summary, the Coded Packet Transport scheme represents a significant advancement in the design of transport mechanisms for OPS/OBS networks. By leveraging the synergy between erasure coding and path diversity, the CPT scheme addresses the dual challenges of packet loss and network security while providing a unified framework for QoS. The network control plane dynamically monitors the status of the disjoint paths and updates the path assignments in response to failures or congestion. The insatiable demand for rapid data exchange has fueled the advancement of innovative networking solutions, with optical networks standing at the vanguard of this revolution. These networks boast an extraordinary capacity for bandwidth and minimal latency, making them an appealing option for contemporary communication systems. Among the diverse array of optical networking architectures, Optical Packet Switching (OPS) and Optical Burst Switching (OBS) have garnered significant attention as viable approaches to accommodating the dynamic and varied traffic requirements of modern communication systems [1]. By harmoniously integrating the efficiency of packet-based data transmission with the high throughput potential of optical signals, these architectures offer a flexible and scalable solution for next-generation networks. Nonetheless, OPS and OBS networks are not without their complexities. The issue of packet contention, wherein multiple packets vie for the same resources, such as wavelengths or time slots, poses a persistent challenge in these systems [2]. Furthermore, the absence of optical buffering capabilities and the inherent susceptibility of optical networks to failures exacerbate the problem, rendering reliable data delivery and performance guarantees difficult to attain [3]. The dynamic nature of traffic patterns and the distributed topology of OPS/OBS networks further complicate the situation, underscoring the need for effective transport mechanisms that can address these challenges while leveraging the unique attributes of optical networks. In addition to concerns regarding reliability and performance, ensuring the security of data transmitted over optical networks has become an increasingly pressing consideration, particularly in light of the evolving threat landscape and the need for confidentiality in data communication [4]. Traditional mechanisms for enhancing network reliability and performance, such as retransmissions and error correction techniques, are often ill-suited for OPS/OBS networks due to their reliance on electronic processing and the attendant latency [5]. Alternative approaches, such as path diversity and coding schemes, offer a promising avenue for overcoming these limitations by exploiting the inherent parallelism and redundancy of optical networks [6]. This paper presents the Coded Packet Transport (CPT) scheme, a novel transport mechanism specifically designed for OPS/OBS networks. The CPT scheme tackles key issues such as packet loss due to contention and path failures, while simultaneously providing a degree of non-cryptographic secrecy [7]. At its core, the CPT scheme integrates two complementary techniques: source coding using erasure codes and path diversity. Erasure coding, a well-established method for enhancing data reliability, is employed at the network's ingress point to encode the original data into redundant coded packets [8]. These coded packets are then transmitted over multiple disjoint paths to an egress point, ensuring that the original data can be reconstructed even in the presence of packet loss or path failures. By distributing the coded packets across disjoint paths, the scheme not only enhances survivability but also reduces the likelihood of contentions, thereby improving overall network performance [9]. One of the defining characteristics of the CPT scheme is its ability to provide a unified perspective on Quality of Service (QoS) in OPS/OBS networks by linking the interplay between survivability, performance, and secrecy [10]. Survivability, which refers to the network's capacity to maintain service continuity in the face of failures, is inherently enhanced through the use of redundant coded packets and path diversity. Performance, in terms of metrics such as packet delivery ratio and delay, is improved by reducing contention and leveraging the parallel nature of optical paths. Secrecy, meanwhile, is achieved by distributing coded packets across different paths, rendering it challenging for an adversary to intercept and reconstruct the original data without access to all the paths [11]. The CPT scheme represents a departure from conventional approaches to QoS in optical networks, which often address these aspects in isolation [12]. Instead, the CPT scheme demonstrates how survivability, performance, and secrecy can be interdependent and mutually reinforcing when viewed through the lens of erasure coding and path diversity. This holistic approach not only simplifies the design and management of OPS/OBS networks but also offers a scalable and efficient solution for addressing their challenges [13]. To provide a rigorous evaluation of the CPT scheme, we develop analytical models that capture the key factors influencing its performance [14]. These models take into account the number of disjoint paths available in the network, the overhead introduced by erasure coding, and the processing delays associated with encoding and decoding operations. The insights gained from these models illustrate the trade-offs inherent in the CPT scheme and provide guidelines for optimizing its parameters to meet specific QoS requirements [15]. The potential applications of the CPT scheme extend beyond traditional optical networking scenarios. In an era where data security and privacy are of paramount importance, the built-in secrecy of the CPT scheme makes it a compelling choice for sensitive applications such as financial transactions, healthcare data transmission, and military communications [16]. Furthermore, the scalable nature of the scheme positions it well to support emerging technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing, which require high-bandwidth, low-latency, and secure data transmission [17]. The CPT scheme's ability to provide a unified view of QoS, combining survivability, performance, and secrecy, makes it an attractive solution for these applications, where data security and reliability are paramount [18]. Additionally, the CPT scheme's use of erasure coding and path diversity can be applied to other areas of networking, such as wireless communication systems, to improve their reliability and security [19]. The CPT scheme's potential impact on the field of optical networking is significant, as it offers a novel approach to addressing the challenges of packet contention, path failures, and data security [20]. By providing a scalable and efficient solution for OPS/OBS networks, the CPT scheme can help enable the widespread adoption of these technologies, leading to faster and more reliable data transmission [21]. In conclusion, the CPT scheme is a promising transport mechanism for OPS/OBS networks, offering a unified view of QoS, combining survivability, performance, and secrecy [22]. The CPT scheme is specifically designed to tackle several pivotal challenges inherent to OPS/OBS networks. Firstly, the loss of packets poses a significant threat to network performance, as the disappearance of even a single packet can lead to substantial performance degradation. Secondly, the failure of paths, which can be attributed to a variety of factors including network congestion, link failures, or node failures, can precipitate considerable disruptions within the network. Lastly, the provision of non-cryptographic secrecy is indispensable in OPS/OBS networks to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive information. The CPT scheme addresses these challenges by utilizing erasure coding at the point of entry into the OPS/OBS network, where data is encoded into redundant packets to enhance survivability and secrecy. The erasure coding process is a fundamental component of the CPT scheme. Consider a data block comprising \( k \) original packets. By employing an erasure code, such as Reed-Solomon or Fountain codes, these \( k \) original packets are transformed into \( n \) coded packets, where \( n \geq k \) [2]. The erasure code guarantees that any \( k \) out of \( n \) coded packets are sufficient to reconstruct the original data block, thereby providing resilience against packet loss during transmission. The redundancy factor, defined as \( r = n/k \), is a crucial parameter in the CPT scheme, as it strikes a balance between the level of robustness and the associated overhead. A higher redundancy factor affords greater protection against packet loss but also increases the overhead associated with the transmission of redundant packets. At the entry point of the network, the encoding process unfolds in the following manner: 1) the data block is segmented into \( k \) packets of equal size; 2) the erasure coding algorithm is applied to generate \( n \) coded packets, introducing redundancy by combining data from the original packets; and 3) each coded packet is assigned a unique identifier and metadata, including coding parameters and sequence information, to facilitate decoding at the exit point of the network. The computational complexity of the encoding process is directly related to the values of \( k \) and \( n \), with higher values resulting in increased computational demands [5]. Furthermore, the CPT scheme incorporates path diversity to enhance the survivability and secrecy of data transmission. By transmitting coded packets over diverse paths, the scheme mitigates the risk of path failures and unauthorized access to sensitive data [9]. The synergy between erasure coding and path diversity enables the CPT scheme to provide a unified framework for addressing the challenges of survivability, performance, and secrecy in OPS/OBS networks. The results of the performance evaluation demonstrate the practical viability of the CPT scheme and its potential for adoption in next-generation optical networks. In conclusion, the CPT scheme represents a substantial advancement in the design of transport mechanisms for OPS/OBS networks, offering a unified approach to addressing the challenges of survivability, performance, and secrecy in these systems. The scheme's ability to harness the combined strengths of erasure coding and path diversity makes it an attractive solution for ensuring the reliable and secure transmission of data in OPS/OBS networks. The allocation of resources to explore and engage with communities is a fundamental problem that arises in numerous real-world settings, ranging from online advertising campaigns to public health outreach and social network growth. Effectively distributing a limited budget to maximize the impact of exploration is a critical challenge faced by practitioners in these domains. For instance, in online advertising, advertisers often seek to identify and engage diverse audience groups by allocating their budget across multiple demographic or interest-based communities, while balancing trade-offs between exploratory and exploitative strategies. Similarly, in the context of social networks, community managers aim to expand their influence by interacting with various subgroups, often without complete prior knowledge of their size or engagement potential. This work introduces the community exploration problem, a framework that captures the essence of such scenarios. The problem can be described as follows: given a limited budget, an explorer must allocate resources across multiple communities to maximize the number of members encountered. The challenge lies in devising strategies that are both efficient and effective, particularly when the underlying characteristics of the communities, such as theiir sizes, may be unknown or uncertain. This setting spans two paradigms: the offline setting, in which the community sizes are fully known beforehand, and the online setting, where community sizes msut be laerned through repeated interactions over time. The offline version of the problem serves as a baseline for understanidng the optimal allocation strtaegies when complete information is available. Thsi scenario allows for the derivation of optimal policies under deterministic conditions, providing a fundamental benchmark for evaluating solutions in more complex settings. In contrast, the online version of the problem introduces significant challenges due to the inherent uncertainty in community sizes. Here, the explorer must balance the dual objectives of learning and optimization: on the one hand, allocating resources to explore communities and gather information about their sizes; on the other hand, leveraging this information to maximize engagement. This dynamic interplay between exploration and exploitation is central to many real-world problems, making the online community exploration problem a particularly compelling area of study. Existing literature has addressed related problems in various forms. The offline allocation problem can be seen as a combinatorial optimization problem, which has a long history of study in operations reserch and resource allocation [1, 2]. Greedy algorithms, in particular, have been shown to perform well in such contexts, often yielding near-optimal or even optimal results under certain conditions [3]. On the other hand, the online setting is cloosely related to the rich body of work on multi-armed bandit (MAB) problems, which model sequential decision-making under uncertainty [4]. Algorithms in this domain, such as Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) methods and their variants, have been widley studied for their ability to achieve sublinear regret in learning environments [5, 6]. However, while these techniques address soem aspects of online resource allocation, they do not directly account for the specific structure and constraints of the community exploration problem. Thsi paper provides a systematic study of the community exploration problem, bridging the gap between the offline and online settings. For the offline setting, we analyze two modes of exploration: non-adaptive exploration, where the allocation of resources is determined upfront, and adaptive exploration, where allocation decisions can be adjusted based on intermediate outcomes. We prove that in both cases, greedy methods yield optimal solutions, offering computationally efficient strategies for resource allocation. These results not only establish the theoretical foundation for offline community exploration but also provide practical guidelines for implementing exploration policies in real-world scenarios with known community sizes. For the online setting, we propose an algorithm inspired by the UCB framework that is tailored to the community exploration problem. This algorithm accounts for the unique structure of the problem, including the need to allocate resources across multiple communities while simultaneously learning their sizes. We prove that this approach achieves logarithmic regret bounds, demonstrating its efficiency in balancing exploration and exploitation over multiple rounds. Furthermore, by incorporating feedback from different rounds, we show that it is possible to achieve a constant regret bound, significantly improving long-term performance. These results highlight the potential for leveraging online learning techniques to optimize resource allocation in dynamic and uncertain environments. The contributions of tihs work are threefold. First, we formalize the community exploration problem, providing a unified framework that encompasses both offline and online settings. Second, we establish optimality results for greedy algorithms in the offlie setting, offering theoretical guarantees and practical insights for resource allocation. Third, we develop and analyze an online learning algorithm tht achieves strong performance guarantees, including logarithmic and constant regret bounds, depending on the feedback structure. Together, these contributions advance the state of the art in resource allocation and online learning, with implications for a wide range of applications. Section 3 focuses on the offline setting, presentting our analysis of optimal strategies for both non-adaptive and adaptive exploration. In Seciton 4, we addess the online setting, detailing the proposed algorithm and its theoretical properties. Section 5 discusses related work, situating our contributions within the broader literature. Finally, in Section 6, we conclude with a summary of our findings and directions for future research. Through this study, we aim to provide a comprehensive understanding of the community exploration problem, along with practical tools and techniques to address its challenges in both offline and online contexts. --- References [1] Nemhauser, G. Offline Optimization The offline setting assumes that the sizes of all communities are known a priori. Under this assumption, we consider two exploration strategies: non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration. Non-Adaptive Exploration: In the non-adaptive setting, the explorer allocates the budget across all communities in advnce and does not adjust allocations based on feedback during the exploration process. Formally, let there be \( n \) communities, each with a known size \( si \) (where \( i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\} \)), and let \( B \) denote the total exploration budget. The gooal is to allocate the budget \( bi \) to each community \( i \) such that \( \sum{i=1}^n bi \leq B \), thereby maximizing the expected number of members met. The expected number of members met in community \( i \) is modeled as a concave function \( fi(bi) \), reflecting diminishing returns with increased allocation. We prove that a greedy algorithm is optimal for this problem. The algorithm iteratively allocates one unit of budget to the community with the largest marginal gain in the number of members met, i.e., it selects the community \( j \) that maximizes \( fj(bj + 1) - fj(bj) \). This process continues until the budget \( B \) is exhausted. The optimality of the greedy algoritm is ensured by the concavity of \( fi(bi) \), which guarantees that the problem satisfies the properties of submodular optimization [1]. Adaptive Exploration: In the adaptive setting, the explorer can adjust the allocation dynamically based on real-time feedback during the exploration process. Feedback is modeled as the observed number of members met after allocating \( bi \) units of budget to community \( i \). The adaptive strategy also employs a greedy approach, but decisions are made sequentially, incorporating observations from previous allocations. We demonstrate that the adaptive greedy algorithm achieves optimality by leveraging the same sbmodular prperties as the non-adaptive case. Importantly, the adaptive strategy is particularly advantageous in scenarios where real-time observation can significantly refine allocation decisions. Online Lerning The online setting introduces an additional layer of complexity: the sizes of communities are initially unknown and must be learned over multiple rounds of exploration. Let \( T \) denote the total number of rounds, with each round involving a budget \( B \) to be allocated across \( n \) communities. The objective is to minimize regret, defined as the difference between the cumulative reward of the optimal offline strategy and that of the online algorithm. To address this, we propose an algorithm inspired by the upper confidence bound (UCB) framework, which balances exploration (learning the sizes of communities) and exploitation (allocating budget based on current knowledge). Algorithm Description: At the start of round \( t \), the algorithm maintains an estimate \( \hat{s}i(t) \) for the size of each community \( i \) based on past observations. The estimates are initialized with a prior assumption, and the algorithm updates them iteratively as new data becomes available. To account for uncertainty, an upper confidence bound \( Ui(t) \) is computed for each community, defined as: \[ Ui(t) = \hat{s}i(t) + c \sqrt{\frac{\log t}{ni(t)}}, \] where \( c \) is a tunable exploration parameter, \( ni(t) \) is the number of times community \( i \) has been explored up to round \( t \), and \( \log t \) encourages exploration of less-sampled communities. During each round \( t \), the algorithm allocates the budget \( B \) to communities greedily, using the upper confidence bounds \( Ui(t) \) in place of the true sizes \( si \). Specifically, the budget is allocated to maximize the expected reward based on \( Ui(t) \), following the same submodular framework as in the offline setting. Theoretical Guarantee: We prove that the proposed algorithm achieves logarithmic regrret bounds, i.e., the regret \( R(T) \) grows as \( O(\log T) \). This result is derived using the properties of UCB-based algorithms, which ensure that the algorithm gradually focuses on the optimal allcation as the estimates \( \hat{s}i(t) \) converge to the true sizes \( si \) [2]. Constant Regret with Feedback Aggregation: To further improve performance, we incorporate feedback aggregation acorss rounds. By combining observations from multiple rounds, we refine the size estimates \( \hat{s}i(t) \) more rapidly, enabling the algorithm to converge faster. Specifically, after each round, the feedback from all explored communities is agrgegated and used to update a global estimate of community sizes. This refinement reduces uncertainty and improves allocation decisions in subsequent rounds. We show that incorporating feedback aggregation can reduce the regret to a costant value, independent of \( T \), under certain conditions. This improvement highlights the importance of leveraging cumulative informtion in online learning scenarios. Implementation and Complexity Both the offline and online algorithms are computationally efficient. The greedy algorithm for offline optimization has a time complexity of \( O(B \cdot n) \), as it involves iterating oveer all communities at each step of budget allocation. The online algorithm, with its UCB-inspired framework, has a per-round complexity of \( O(n \log T) \), dominated by the computation of confidence bounds and the greedy allocation step. These complexities make the methods scalable to large-scale problems with numerous communities and rounds. The offline greedy algorithms are provably optimal due to submodular properties of the problem, while the online UCB-based algorithm achieves logarithmic regret and can further be enhanced with feedback aggregation. The offline setting assumes that the sizes of all communities are known a priori, allowing us to consider two exploration strategies: non-adaptive exploration and adaptive exploration. In the non-adaptive setting, the explorer allocates the budget across all communities in advance, without adjusting allocations based on feedback during the exploration process. Formally, let there be $n$ communities, each with a known size $si$ (where $i \in \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$), and let $B$ denote the total exploration budget. The goal is to allocate the budget $bi$ to each community $i$ such that $\sum{i=1}^n bi \leq B$, thereby maximizing the expected number of members met. The expected number of members met in community $i$ is modeled as a concave function $fi(bi)$, reflecting diminishing returns with increased allocation. This is a common phenomenon in many real-world scenarios, where the marginal gain of allocating additional resources to a community decreases as the allocation increases. We prove that a greedy algorithm is optimal for this problem, which iteratively allocates one unit of budget to the community with the largest marginal gain in the number of members met. This process continues until the budget $B$ is exhausted. The optimality of the greedy algorithm is ensured by the concavity of $fi(bi)$, which guarantees that the problem satisfies the properties of submodular optimization, as discussed in [1]. In contrast, the adaptive setting allows the explorer to adjust the allocation dynamically based on real-time feedback during the exploration process. Feedback is modeled as the observed number of members met after allocating $bi$ units of budget to community $i$. The adaptive strategy also employs a greedy approach, but decisions are made sequentially, incorporating observations from previous allocations. We demonstrate that the adaptive greedy algorithm achieves optimality by leveraging the same submodular properties as the non-adaptive case. Importantly, the adaptive strategy is particularly advantageous in scenarios where real-time observation can significantly refine allocation decisions. The online setting introduces an additional layer of complexity, where the sizes of communities are initially unknown and must be learned over multiple rounds of exploration. Let $T$ denote the total number of rounds, with each round involving a budget $B$ to be allocated across $n$ communities. The objective is to minimize regret, defined as the difference between the cumulative reward of the optimal offline strategy and that of the online algorithm. This is a classic problem in online learning, where the algorithm must balance exploration (learning the sizes of communities) and exploitation (allocating budget based on current knowledge). To address this, we propose an algorithm inspired by the upper confidence bound (UCB) framework, which has been extensively studied in the context of multi-armed bandit problems [4, 5, 6]. At the start of round $t$, the algorithm maintains an estimate $\hat{s}i(t)$ for the size of each community $i$ based on past observations. The estimates are initialized with a prior assumption, and the algorithm updates these estimates as new observations become available. The algorithm then allocates the budget $B$ to the communities based on the estimated sizes and the UCB principle, which balances exploration and exploitation. We analyze the performance of the algorithm and derive bounds on the regret, including logarithmic and constant regret bounds, depending on the feedback structure. In contrast, LAA stroke is caused by atherothrombotic occlusion or stenosis of major extracranial or intracranial arteries. These two etiologies differ not oly in their underlying mechanisms but also in theiir response to therapeutic interventions, with cardioembolic strooke often requiring long-term anticoagulation therapy and LAA stroke being more amenable to antiplatelet therapy and management of atherosclerotic risk factors. Consequently, accurate differentiation between these subtypes is critical for optimizing patient care. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has emerged as a cornerstone in the evaluation of acute stroke, offering unparalleled detail in vsualizing brain anatomy and pathology. Among the various MRI techniques, perfusion imaging provides valuable insights into cerebral hemodynamics by measuring parameters such as cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, mean transit time, and time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax). These parameters enable the identification of ischemic penumbra and infarct core, which are vital for therapeutic decision-making in the acute phase of stroke. Beyond its conventional applications, perfusion MRI holds the potential to reveal distinct hemodynamic patterns associated wih different stroke subtypes, particularly cardioembolic stroke and LAA stroke. Cardioembolic stroke is often characterized by a sudden and severe reduction in blood flow due to the abrupt occlusion of a major cereral artery by an embolus. This results in larger infarct volumes and more severe clinical presentations compared to LAA stroke, which typically involves more gradual vessel occluusion and better collateral circulation. Perfusion MRI parameters, particularly Tmax, can provide indirect evidence of these differences by reflecting the degree and distribution of perfusion deficits. Specifically, the ratio of Tmax volumes at diifferent thresholds may serve as a surroate marker for the extent of collateral circulation, with lower collateral flow hypothesized to be a hallmark of cardioembolic stroke. Moreover, the clinical application of these findings has been limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneity in study populations, and variability in imaging protocols. This prospective study was designed to assess the utility of perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in distinguishing cardioembolic stroke from large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) stroke. The study population included patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke who were admitted to our institution within 24 hurs of symptom onset. Eligible patients were classified into cardioembolic or LAA stroke subtypes according to the Triaal of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification system. Patients with evidence of other stroke mechanisms, such as small-vessel disease or an undetermined etiology, were excluded from the study. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal representatives, and the study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Seventeen patients with cardioembolic stroke and 22 with LAA stroke were recruited. The diagnosis of cardioembolic stroke was based on the presence of a high-risk cardioembolic source, such as atrial fibrillation, left ventricular thrombus, or valvular heart disease, in the absence of significant large atery stenosis. LAA stroke was diagnosed in patients with significant stenosis (≥50%) or occlusion of a major extracranial or intracranial artery attributable to atherosclerosis, accompanied by clinical and imaging evidence of infarction in the corresponding vascular territory. All enrolled patients underwent a comprehensive evaluation, including clinical assessment, laboratory investigations, electrocardiography, echocardiography, and vascular imaging (e.g., carotid ultrasound, computed tomography angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography). Stroke severity at presentation was assessed using the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS). Demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, vascular risk factors, and comorbidities, were collected for all participants. Perfusion MRI was performed on a 3.0T magnetic resonance scanner using standard imaging protocols. The imaging protocol included diffusion-weighted imagnig (DWI), fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and dynamic susceptibility contrast-enhanced perfusion imaging. A gadolinium-based contrast agent was administered intravenously for perfusion imaging. The perfusion data were analyzed using automated postprocessing software to generate perfusion parameter maps, including time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax), mean transit time (MTT), cerebral blood flow (CBF), and cerebral blood volume (CBV). To quantify perfusion abnormalities, volumes of ischemic tissue were calculated for predefined Tmax thresholds. Specifically, ischemic volumes were calculated for Tmax delays of >2 seconds, >3 seconds, >4 seconds, >5 seconds, and >8 seconds. The rattio of ischemic volume at each threshold (Tmax > 2s, Tmax > 3s, Tmax > 4s, and Tmax > 5s) to the ischemic volume at Tmax > 8s was calculated for each patient. The Tmax > 8s volume was considered representative of the core infarct volume, while lower Tmax thresholds were used to assesss the extent of hypoperfused tissue. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the ability of the Tmax volume ratios to differentiate between cardioembolic and LAA stroke. The area under the cuve (AUC) was calculated for each ratio, and optimal thresholds for distinguishing cardioembolic stroke were determined based on maximizing sensitivity and specificity. Logistic regression analysis was used to adjust for potential confounders, including initial stroke severity as measured by the NIHSS. Odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated to quantify the strength of association betwen perfuion imaging parameters and cardioembolic stroke. To assess infarct progression, follow-up imaging was performed 3 to 7 days after the initial MRI or earlier in cases of clinical deterioration. Final infarct volumes were measured on follow-up DWI or FLAIR images, and the relationship between initial Tmax volumes and final infarct volumes was examined. Statistical analysis was performed using SPS software, version 25.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were compared between groups using the independent-samples t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables wee compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The primary outcoem measure was the ability of perfusin MRI-derived Tmax volume ratios to differentiate cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. Secondary outcome measures included the relationship between perfusion imaging parameters and initial stroke severity, as well as the association between initial perfusion abnormalities and final infarct volumes. All imaging analyses were performed by two experienced neuroradiologists who were blinded to the clinical and etiological classification of stroke. Discrepancies between the two readers were resolved by consensus. Interobserver agreement for perfusion parameter measurements was assessed using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). This methodological approach enabled a comprehensive evaluation of the potential of perfusion MRI to serve as a diagnostic tool for distinguishing cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke, while controlling for confounding variables and ensuring robust statistical analysis. A thorough understanding of the underlying cause of an ischemic stroke is essential for informing treatment decisions, minimizing the risk of subsequent events, and optimizing patient outcomes [2]. Despite significant advances in diagnostic technologies and imaging modalities, the etiology of ischemic stroke remains elusive in approximately one-quarter of cases, even after exhaustive evaluation [3]. This enigmatic subset of strokes, commonly referred to as cryptogenic strokes, underscores the pressing need for more sophisticated diagnostic tools to elucidate the underlying mechanisms and refine the classification of stroke subtypes [4]. Among the established etiologies of ischemic stroke, cardioembolic stroke and large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) are two prevalent subtypes characterized by distinct pathophysiological processes and therapeutic approaches [5]. Cardioembolic stroke typically arises from emboli originating from the heart, often as a consequence of conditions such as atrial fibrillation, recent myocardial infarction, or valvular heart disease [6]. In contrast, LAA stroke is caused by atherothrombotic occlusion or stenosis of major extracranial or intracranial arteries [7]. These two etiologies not only differ in their underlying mechanisms but also in their response to therapeutic interventions, with cardioembolic stroke frequently necessitating long-term anticoagulation therapy and LAA stroke being more responsive to antiplatelet therapy and management of atherosclerotic risk factors [8]. Consequently, accurate differentiation between these subtypes is crucial for optimizing patient care and outcomes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has emerged as a pivotal modality in the evaluation of acute stroke, providing unparalleled resolution in visualizing brain anatomy and pathology [9]. Among the various MRI techniques, perfusion imaging offers valuable insights into cerebral hemodynamics by quantifying parameters such as cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, mean transit time, and time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax) [10]. These parameters enable the identification of the ischemic penumbra and infarct core, which are vital for informing therapeutic decisions in the acute phase of stroke [11]. Beyond its conventional applications, perfusion MRI holds the potential to reveal distinct hemodynamic patterns associated with different stroke subtypes, particularly cardioembolic stroke and LAA stroke [12]. Cardioembolic stroke is often characterized by a sudden and severe reduction in blood flow due to the abrupt occlusion of a major cerebral artery by an embolus [13]. This results in larger infarct volumes and more severe clinical presentations compared to LAA stroke, which typically involves more gradual vessel occlusion and better collateral circulation [14]. Perfusion MRI parameters, particularly Tmax, can provide indirect evidence of these differences by reflecting the degree and distribution of perfusion deficits [15]. Specifically, the ratio of Tmax volumes at different thresholds may serve as a surrogate marker for the extent of collateral circulation, with lower collateral flow hypothesized to be a hallmark of cardioembolic stroke [16]. This hypothesis forms the basis for exploring the utility of perfusion MRI in differentiating cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke. Several studies have underscored the potential of perfusion imaging in the evaluation of stroke subtype-specific characteristics [17]. However, few have systematically investigated the role of quantitative perfusion parameters in distinguishing cardioembolic stroke from other etiologies [18]. Moreover, the clinical application of these findings has been limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneity in study populations, and variability in imaging protocols [19]. To address these gaps, we conducted a prospective study to evaluate the utility of perfusion MRI in differentiating cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke [20]. By examining the relationship between perfusion parameters and stroke etiology, we aimed to identify reliable imaging biomarkers that could aid in the accurate classification of ischemic stroke. In this study, we recruited patients with cardioembolic and LAA stroke, classified according to the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) criteria [21], and performed perfusion MRI within 24 hours of stroke onset. Our findings demonstrate that patients with cardioembolic stroke exhibit more severe initial stroke severity, larger infarct volumes, and distinct perfusion patterns compared to those with LAA stroke [22]. Notably, the ratio of Tmax volumes at specific thresholds emerged as a highly sensitive and specific marker for predicting cardioembolic stroke [23]. These results suggest that perfusion MRI not only provides critical information about the extent and severity of ischemic injury but also serves as a valuable tool for uncovering the underlying mechanism of stroke. The ability to accurately identify cardioembolic stroke using perfusion MRI has significant clinical implications [24]. Early recognition of this subtype enables timely initiation of anticoagulation therapy, which is essential for preventing recurrent embolic events [25]. Moreover, perfusion imaging could complement existing diagnostic approaches, such as echocardiography and prolonged cardiac monitoring, by providing supportive evidence for cardioembolism in cases where the etiology is uncertain [26]. This is particularly relevant in cryptogenic strokes, where perfusion MRI may help identify subtle hemodynamic patterns that point to an underlying cardioembolic source [27]. By leveraging the capabilities of perfusion MRI, clinicians may be able to refine their diagnostic algorithms and improve the management of ischemic stroke, ultimately leading to better patient outcomes. In conclusion, this study highlights the potential of perfusion MRI as a reliable and non-invasive tool for differentiating cardioembolic stroke from LAA stroke, thereby underscoring its utility in the clinical management of ischemic stroke. The implications of these findings are far-reaching, with potential applications in the development of more personalized and effective treatment strategies for patients with ischemic stroke.
