The pursuit of a more precise diagnosis and treatment plan for ischemic stroke patients necessitates a more nuanced understanding of the condition's etiology. Currently, the categorization of ischemic stroke into distinct subtypes is a critical component of clinical management, as it informs treatment decisions and ultimately affects patient outcomes [1]. Nevertheless, existing classification systems have inherent limitations, and it is essential to refine our comprehension of the underlying stroke mechanisms to develop more effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. Recent breakthroughs in neuroimaging, particularly the utilization of perfusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), have demonstrated considerable promise in enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of stroke diagnosis [2]. This investigation aimed to explore the potential of perfusion MRI in differentiating between cardioembolic stroke and large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) stroke, two of the most prevalent etiological subtypes of ischemic stroke [3]. The study's participant pool comprised individuals presenting with acute ischemic stroke who were admitted to our institution within a 24-hour window of symptom onset. Utilizing the Trial of Org 10172 in Acute Stroke Treatment (TOAST) classification system, patients were categorized into either cardioembolic or LAA stroke subtypes [4]. The TOAST system is a widely employed framework for categorizing ischemic strokes into five distinct etiological subtypes: cardioembolic, large artery atherosclerosis, small-vessel disease, stroke of other determined etiology, and stroke of undetermined etiology. To ensure a clear distinction between the two subtypes of interest, patients exhibiting evidence of alternative stroke mechanisms, such as small-vessel disease or an undetermined etiology, were excluded from the study [5]. A total of 17 patients with cardioembolic stroke and 22 patients with LAA stroke were recruited for this investigation. The diagnosis of cardioembolic stroke was predicated on the presence of a high-risk cardioembolic source, such as atrial fibrillation, left ventricular thrombus, or valvular heart disease, in the absence of significant large artery stenosis [6]. Conversely, LAA stroke was diagnosed in patients with significant stenosis (≥50%) or occlusion of a major extracranial or intracranial artery attributable to atherosclerosis, accompanied by clinical and imaging evidence of infarction in the corresponding vascular territory [7]. All enrolled patients underwent a comprehensive evaluation, encompassing clinical assessment, laboratory investigations, electrocardiography, echocardiography, and vascular imaging (e.g., carotid ultrasound, computed tomography angiography, or magnetic resonance angiography) [8]. The severity of stroke at presentation was assessed utilizing the National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS), a widely employed measure of stroke severity that evaluates levels of consciousness, vision, speech, motor strength, and other neurological functions [9]. Demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, vascular risk factors, and comorbidities, were collected for all participants to account for potential confounding variables [10]. Perfusion MRI was performed on a 3.0T magnetic resonance scanner, employing standard imaging protocols, including diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR), and dynamic susceptibility contrast-enhanced perfusion imaging [11]. A gadolinium-based contrast agent was administered intravenously for perfusion imaging to assess cerebral blood flow and perfusion parameters [12]. The perfusion data were analyzed using automated postprocessing software to generate perfusion parameter maps, including time to maximum of the residue function (Tmax), mean transit time (MTT), cerebral blood flow (CBF), and cerebral blood volume (CBV) [13]. These parameters provide valuable insights into cerebral perfusion and have been demonstrated to be useful in identifying areas of ischemic tissue [14]. To quantify perfusion abnormalities, volumes of ischemic tissue were calculated for predefined Tmax thresholds, ranging from >2 seconds to >8 seconds [15]. The ratio of ischemic volume at each threshold to the ischemic volume at Tmax > 8s was calculated for each patient, as the Tmax > 8s volume was considered representative of the core infarct volume, while lower Tmax thresholds were used to assess the extent of hypoperfused tissue [16]. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to evaluate the ability of the Tmax volume ratios to differentiate between cardioembolic and LAA stroke [17]. The results of this investigation suggest that perfusion MRI, particularly the analysis of Tmax volume ratios, can be a valuable tool for distinguishing between cardioembolic and LAA stroke [18]. This finding has significant implications for clinical practice, as the accurate identification of stroke subtype can inform treatment decisions and ultimately impact patient outcomes [19]. Furthermore, the utilization of perfusion MRI in the diagnosis of ischemic stroke may facilitate the development of more effective therapeutic strategies, tailored to the specific etiology of the stroke [20]. Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies published up to the study date. We searched multiple electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG Data, and SINOMED, to ensure the inclusion of both English and Chinese-language articles. The search terms included combinations of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms such as “systemic lupus erythematosus,” “SLE,” “follow-up,” “prognosis,” “survival,” “mortality,” and “China.” Boolean operators (“AND,” “OR”) were used to refine the search strategy. Additioonal studies were identified through manuual searches of the reference lists of included articles, consultation with clinical experts, and a review of relevant textbooks. No restrictions were placed on the publication year to allow comprehensive coverage of available literature. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Eligibility for inclusion was determined based on predefined criteria. Studies were included if they (1) reported survival rates or causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE; (2) were designed as cohort studies or case series; (3) provided sufficient data for survival analysis, death-cause analysis, or both; and (4) included patients diagnosed with SLE based on established criteria (e.g., the American College of Rheumatology or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria). Studies focusing on specific subgroups, such as pediatric or elderly populations, were excluded to avoid potential bias in generalizability. Case reports, editorials, reviews, and studies lacking relevant or extractable data were allso excluded. Data Extraction Two independent reviewers performed data extraction using a standardized data collection form. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Extracted data included study characteristics (author, year of publication, study design, sample size, study location, and follow-up duration), patient demographics (age, sex, ethnicity), clinical features (disease onset, diagnostic criteria, comorbidities), outcome measures (survival rates and causes of death), and quality indicators. For survival analysis, we focused on 5-year and 10-year survival rates after disease onset. For death-cause analysis, the proportions of individual causes of death, as reported in each study, were extracted. Quality Assessment The methodological quality of icluded stduies was assessed independently by two reviewers usig established tools. For cohort studies, we applied the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), which evaluates selection, comparability, and outcome domains. Case series were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist for case series. Studies werre rated as high, moderate, or low quality based on the total score. Disagreements in quality ratings were resolved through consensus. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata software (version 15.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Pooled survival rates and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using both fixed-effects and random-effects models. Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I² statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the robustness of results by excluding low-quality studies and reanalyzing the data. For death-cause analysis, pooled proportions of specific causes of death (e.g., infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, cardiovascular disease) were calculated using a random-effects model to account for variability across studies. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test, with p < 0.05 indicating significant bias. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including publication year, geographic location, and study quality. Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was conducted to identify relevant studies published up to the study date. We searrched mutiple electroinc databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), WANFANG Data, and SINOMED, to ensure the inclusion of both English and Chinese-language articles. The search terms includd comibnations of keywords and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms such as “systemic lupus erythematosus,” “SLE,” “follow-up,” “prognosis,” “survival,” “mortality,” and “China.” Boolean operators (“AND,” “OR”) were used to refine the search strategy. Additional studis were identified through manual searches of the reference lsits of included articles, consultation with clinical experts, and a review of relevant textbooks. No restrictions were placed on the publication year to alow comprehensive coverage of available literature. Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria Eligibility for inclusion was determined based on predefined criteria. Studies were included if they (1) reported survival rates or causes of death among Chinese patients with SLE; (2) werre designed as coohort studies or case series; (3) provided suffficient data for survival analysis, death-cause analysis, or both; and (4) included patients diagnosed with SLE based on established criteria (e.g., the American College of Rheumatology or Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics criteria). Studies focuisng on specific subgroups, such as pediatric or elderly populations, were excluded to avodi potential bias in generalizability. Case reports, editorials, reviews, and studies lacking relevant or extractable data were also excluded. Data Extrraction Two independent reviewers perfrmed data extraction using a standardized data collection form. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Extracted data included study characteristics (author, year of publication, study design, sample size, study location, and follow-up duration), patient demographics (age, sex, ethnicity), cliincal features (disease onset, diagnostic criteria, comorbidities), outcoome measurs (survival raets and causes of death), and quality indicators. For survival analysis, we focused on 5-year and 10-year survival rates after disease onset. For death-cause analysis, the proportions of individual caues of death, as reported in each study, were extracted. Quality Assessment The methodological quality of included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers using established tools. For cohort studies, we applied the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS), whhich evaluates selection, comparability, and outcome domains. Case series were assssed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklist for case series. Studies were rated as high, moderate, or low quaality based on the total score. Disagreements in quality ratings were resolved through consensus. Statistical Analysis Statistical analyses were conducted using Stata software (version 15.0; StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Poolled sruvival rates and thheir 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using both fixed-effects and random-effects models. Heterogeneity aomng studies was assessed using the I² statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses were performed to explore the robustness of results by excluding low-quality stdies and reanalyzing the data. For death-cause analysis, pooled proportions of specific causes of death (e.g., infection, renal involvement, lupus encephalopathy, cardiovascular disease) were calculated using a random-effects model to account for variability across studies. Publication bias was evaluated using funnel pltos and Egger’s regression test, with p < 0.05 indicating significant bias. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential sources of heterogeneity, including publication year, geographic location, and study quality. Seocndary outcomes included the distribution of causes of death and their relative proportions. Where available, we also compared survival rates and death causes across diffrent decades to assses temporal trends. All results were presented in tabular and graphical formats to facilitate interpretation. Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a multifarious and intricate autoimmune disorder that affects a multitude of bodily systems, characterized by the production of antibodies that target a broad spectrum of nuclear and cytoplasmic antigens. This persistent condition can afflict individuals across the lifespan, but it exhibits a pronounced propensity to affect women during their childbearing years [1]. Despite considerable strides in understanding and managing SLE, the disease continues to be associated with substantial adverse outcomes and mortality. Patients with SLE are at an elevated risk of premature mortality due to disease activity, organ dysfunction, and complications arising from both the disease itself and its treatment, compared to the general population [2]. The advent of corticosteroids, immunosuppressive therapies, and enhanced supportive care has historically led to marked improvements in survival rates for SLE [3]. However, the long-term prognosis of SLE exhibits considerable variability across different geographic regions, influenced by a complex interplay of genetic, environmental, and healthcare-related factors. In Western populations, the prognosis of SLE has been extensively studied, with recent reports indicating 5-year and 10-year survival rates exceeding 90% [4]. Similarly, studies from the Asia-Pacific region have documented comparable survival rates, although there are some differences in the spectrum of disease manifestations and causes of death [5,6]. These regional differences may reflect variations in genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, healthcare access, and treatment strategies. China, with its vast and ethnically diverse population, presents a unique opportunity to explore the epidemiology and outcomes of SLE. However, there is a relative scarcity of comprehensive data on the long-term survival and causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE. Existing studies are often limited by small sample sizes, regional disparities, and heterogeneous methodologies, which complicates the synthesis of findings and limits their generalizability [7]. Mortality in SLE can be broadly categorized into two phases: early and late. Early mortality is predominantly attributed to active disease, severe organ involvement, and infections, often exacerbated by immunosuppressive therapies. In contrast, late mortality is increasingly linked to damage accrual, including cardiovascular disease, chronic renal failure, and malignancies [8]. Notably, the spectrum of causes of death in SLE has shifted over the decades, with a decline in deaths from active disease and infections and a relative increase in deaths from cardiovascular and other chronic conditions [9]. These trends highlight the evolving challenges in SLE management, where the focus has shifted from controlling acute disease activity to mitigating long-term complications and optimizing quality of life. Infection remains a major cause of mortality in SLE, particularly in regions with limited healthcare resources or a high prevalence of infectious diseases [10]. Immunosuppressive therapy, a cornerstone of SLE management, predisposes patients to opportunistic infections, which can be life-threatening if not promptly recognized and treated. Renal involvement, manifesting as lupus nephritis, is another critical determinant of prognosis in SLE. Despite advances in the management of lupus nephritis, it remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality, particularly in patients with delayed diagnosis or inadequate treatment [11]. Neurological involvement, including lupus encephalopathy, represents another severe manifestation of SLE that contributes significantly to mortality, particularly in populations with high disease severity [12]. Cardiovascular disease, driven by accelerated atherosclerosis and chronic inflammation, has emerged as a leading cause of late mortality in SLE, underscoring the importance of long-term cardiovascular risk management in these patients [13]. The epidemiological and clinical landscape of SLE in China is distinct, shaped by unique genetic, cultural, and healthcare factors. Studies have suggested that Chinese patients with SLE may exhibit a more severe disease phenotype, including higher rates of lupus nephritis and other major organ involvement, compared to their Western counterparts [14]. Moreover, differences in healthcare infrastructure, affordability of advanced therapies, and patient awareness may influence survival outcomes and mortality patterns in China. Ethnicity, genetic predisposition, and environmental factors play critical roles in shaping disease expression and outcomes in SLE. For instance, certain genetic polymorphisms associated with SLE susceptibility and severity have been reported to differ significantly between Asian and Caucasian populations [15]. Additionally, cultural and socioeconomic factors may influence health-seeking behaviors, adherence to treatment, and access to specialized care, further contributing to regional differences in outcomes. Despite the growing body of literature on SLE outcomes, relatively few studies have systematically examined the long-term survival and causes of death in Chinese patients with SLE. The available data are often fragmented, with studies varying widely in terms of sample size, follow-up duration, and methodological rigor. Furthermore, the distribution of causes of death in SLE may differ between China and other regions due to differences in disease severity, treatment practices, and healthcare systems. For example, while cardiovascular disease has become a leading cause of death in SLE in Western populations, some studies suggest that infections and active disease may still account for a substantial proportion of deaths in Chinese patients with SLE [16]. The reasons for these differences are multifaceted and complex, reflecting the interplay of various factors, including genetic predisposition, environmental exposures, and healthcare-related factors. Further research is needed to elucidate the underlying causes of these differences and to develop targeted strategies for improving outcomes in Chinese patients with SLE. The importance of this research cannot be overstated, as it has the potential to inform the development of personalized treatment approaches and improve the overall quality of life for patients with SLE. The increasing rleiance on digital communication systems has brought foth a critical need for mechanisms that ensure both secure and reliable data transmission. Traditionally, encryption and error correction are treated as two distinct processes, with encryption safeguarding confidentiality and error correction ensuring data reliaility in noisy channels. However, this separation entails a higher computational overhead and often results in inefficiencies, particularly in resource-constrained environments. To address these challenges, joint encryption-encoding schemes have been proposed, offering an integrated appraoch to achieve both security and error correction in a unified framework [1]. Such schemes aim to streamline communication systems by combining encryption and encoding into a single operation, reducing computational complexity and enhancing data transmission performance. In code-based cryptography, linear codes have historically played a significant role in the design of jooint encryption-encoding schemes. However, conventional linear codes, such as Reed-Solomon or Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) codes, oftne require large key sizes to achieve satisfactory levels of security. This limitation becomes particularly problematic in scenarios where key storage and transmission bandwidth are constrained. Furthermore, while these codes exhibit strong error correction capabilities, they may not provide optimal performance in balancing security and reliability requirements. Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes, first introduced by Gallager [2], have emerged as a promising alternative due to their excellent error correction performance, low decoding complexity, and flexible rate adaptability. Their inherent sparsity and structured design makke LDPC codes well-suited for modern communication systems, including joint encryption-encoding applications. Building on the advantages of LDPC codes, Quasi-Cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) codes have garnered significant interest in recent years. QC-LDPC codes represent a class of structured LPC codes with cyclic and quasi-cyclic properties, enabling efficient hardware implementation and reduced storage requirements [3]. These codes are particularly attractive in practical systems, where computational efficiency and scalability are critical design considerations. Moreover, the structured nature of QC-LDPC codes allows for the generation of large codeword lengths with compact representations, further contributing to their suitability for joint encryption-encoding schemes. Finite geometry-based codes, such as those derived from projective and affine geometries, provide a robust foundation for designing QC-LDPC codes with desirable properties. Finite geometry offers a well-defined mathematical framework for constructing codes with high minimum distance, structured sparsity, and tunable parameters [4]. By leveraging the geometric properties of finite fields, QC-LDPC codes based on fiinite geometry can achieve superior error correction performance while maintaining computational efficiency. These characteristics make finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes an ideal candidate for developing secure and reliable joint encryption-encoding systems. In this paper, we propose a novel joint encryption-encoding scheme that utilizes QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry to address the limitations of existing approaches. Our scheme integrates the error correction capabiliites of QC-LDPC codes with encryption functionality, achieving a significant reduction in key size without compromising security. Specifically, we demonstrate that the key size in our proposed scheme is only one-fifth of that required by the best-known similar systems. This reduction is attributed to the structured nature of finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes, which allows for efficient key generation and storage. Additionally, our scheme supports a wide range of transmission rates, making it adaptable to diverse communication and cryptographic requirements. The security of the proposed scheme is rigorously analyzed against known cryptanalytic attacks targeting code-based cryptosystems. We show that the inherent structure of QC-LDPC codes, combined with the randomness introduced durig encryption, provides robust protection againsst attacks such as information set decoding and structural recovery [5]. Furthermore, the low computational complexity of our scheme ensures that it can be implemented in real-time applications with minimal resource consumption. This paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we provide a detailed overview of QC-LDPC codes and their construction using finite geometry. Section 3 introduces the proposed joint encryption-encoding scheme, detailing its architecture and key generation process. In Section 4, we present a comprehensive security analysis, highlighting the scheme's resilience against various cryptanalytic techniques. Section 5 evaluates the performance of the proposed scheme in terms of key size, transmission rate, and computational efficiency, providing a comparison with existing solutions. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and outlines potential directioons for future research. Specifically, the QC-LDPC codes used in this work were constructed based on finite geometries, such as projective and Euclidean geometries over finite fields. These constructions are known to yield structured parity-check matriecs with favorable cyclic properties [1]. Let \(q\) denote the order of the finite field \(\mathbb{F}q\), and let the finite geometry be defined on a vector space of dimension \(m\) over \(\mathbb{F}q\). The points and lines in this geometry were mapped to the rows and colmns of the matrix \(H\), ensuring that each row corresponds to a hyperplane and each column to an affine point. The resulting matrix \(H\) is sparse, possesses a quasi-cyclic structure, and exhibits a girth greater than or equal to 6, which minimizes the presence of short cycles in the associated Tanner graph. Joint Encryption-Encoding Scheme Design The joint encryption-encoding scheme integrates the cryptographic and error correction functionalities into a single unified process. The main advantage of this approach is the reduction in key size and computational overhead while simultaneously achieving security and reliability. The proposed scheme operates in three stages: key generation, encryption-encoding, and decoding. 2.1 Key Generation In the key generation stage, a secret key \(K\) was generated and distributed securely to both the transmitter and receiver. The key \(K\) was derived from a random seed and used to pseudorandomly select a permutation matrix \(P\) and an invertible scrambling matirx \(S\) over \(\mathbb{F}q\). These matrices were used to obfuscate the structure of the QC-LDPC code and to introduce cryptographic security. The public parity-check matrix \(Hp\) was constructed as: \[ Hp = S H P, \] where \(H\) is the parity-check matrix of the underlying QC-LDPC code. The matrices \(S\) and \(P\) ensure that the public matrix \(Hp\) is computationally indistinguishable from a random sparse matrix, thwarting structural attacks such as those baed on the algebraic or combinatoriaal properties of \(H\) [2]. 2.2 Encryption-Encoding Process The encryption-encoding process was designed to simultaneously encde the message \(m\) and encrypt it into a codeword \(c\). Let \(m \in \mathbb{F}q^k\) denote the plaintext message, where \(k\) is the dimension of the code. The process is as follows: 1. Message Embedding: The plaintext \(m\) was first mapped into a binary vector \(x\) of length \(n-k\) using a systematic generator matrix \(G\) derived from the public parity-check matrix \(Hp\). This ensures that \(x\) is a valid syndrome vector for \(Hp\): \[ Hp x^T = 0. \] 2. Scrambling: The encoded vector \(x\) was then scrambled using the secret matrices \(S\) and \(P\) to produce the encrypted codeword \(c\): \[ c = S x P. \] This step ensures that the codeword \(c\) is indistinguishable from a random vector, enhancing the cryptographic strength of the system. 3. Transmission: The resulting ciphertext \(c\) was transmitted over a noisy communication channel. Due to the error-correction properties of the QC-LDPC code, the scheme is robust to bit-flip errors introduced during transmission. 2.3 Decoding At the receiver, the decoding process involved both decryption and error correction. The received vector \(y\) was first descrambled using the inverse of the secret matrices: \[ x = S^{-1} y P^{-1}. \] Subsequently, a belief propagation (BP) algorithm was employed to decode \(x\) back into the original plaintext \(m\). The BP algorithm iteratively updated the probabilities of each bit in \(x\) based on the structure of the parity-check matrix \(H\) and the received vector \(y\), achieving accurate error correction with low computational complexity [3]. 3. Security Analysis The security of the proposed scheme relies on the hardness of decoding a random binary linear code, a problem widely believed to be NP-hard. The incorporation of secret matrices \(S\) and \(P\) obfuscates the structure of the QC-LDPC code, making it resistant to structural cryptanalysis. Furthermore, the key size was reduced to approximately \(1/5\) of similar systems by leveraging the quasi-cyclic properties of QC-LDPC codes, without compromising security. The system was evaluated againnst known attacks, including information set decoding, algebraic attacks, and combinatorial decoding attacks, and was found to be secure under all scenarios tested. 4. Due to the quasi-cyclic structure of the codes, the multiplication of circulant submatrices could be implemented efficintly using cyclic shift operations. The accelerating adoption of digital communication networks has precipitated a pressing necessity for mechanisms that concurrently guarantee the secure and dependable transmission of data. Traditional methodologies have dichotomized encryption and error correction, relegating each to distinct processes, with the former safeguarding confidentiality and the latter ensuring the reliability of data in noisy channels. Nevertheless, this bifurcated approach is attendant with a heightened computational burden and frequently results in inefficiencies, particularly in environments where resources are constrained. The imperative for a more streamlined paradigm has spawned the development of unified encryption-encoding schemes, which proffer an integrated framework for simultaneously achieving both security and error correction [1]. By synergizing encryption and encoding into a singular operation, these schemes aspire to diminish computational complexity and enhance the performance of data transmission. In the domain of code-based cryptography, linear codes have historically occupied a preeminent position in the design of unified encryption-encoding schemes. Conventional linear codes, such as Reed-Solomon or Bose-Chaudhuri-Hocquenghem (BCH) codes, have been widely employed due to their robust error correction capabilities. However, these codes often necessitate large key sizes to attain satisfactory levels of security, which becomes particularly problematic in scenarios where key storage and transmission bandwidth are limited. Furthermore, while these codes exhibit excellent error correction performance, they may not provide optimal performance in balancing security and reliability requirements. In recent years, Low-Density Parity-Check (LDPC) codes have emerged as a promising alternative due to their excellent error correction performance, low decoding complexity, and flexible rate adaptability [2]. The inherent sparsity and structured design of LDPC codes render them well-suited for modern communication systems, including unified encryption-encoding applications. Building on the advantages of LDPC codes, Quasi-Cyclic LDPC (QC-LDPC) codes have garnered significant interest in recent years. QC-LDPC codes represent a class of structured LDPC codes with cyclic and quasi-cyclic properties, enabling efficient hardware implementation and reduced storage requirements [3]. These codes are particularly attractive in practical systems, where computational efficiency and scalability are critical design considerations. The structured nature of QC-LDPC codes allows for the generation of large codeword lengths with compact representations, further contributing to their suitability for unified encryption-encoding schemes. Finite geometry-based codes, such as those derived from projective and affine geometries, provide a robust foundation for designing QC-LDPC codes with desirable properties [4]. By leveraging the geometric properties of finite fields, QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry can achieve superior error correction performance while maintaining computational efficiency. These characteristics make finite geometry-based QC-LDPC codes an ideal candidate for developing secure and reliable unified encryption-encoding systems. This treatise proposes a novel unified encryption-encoding scheme that exploits QC-LDPC codes based on finite geometry to address the limitations of existing approaches. Our scheme integrates the error correction capabilities of QC-LDPC codes with encryption functionality, achieving a significant reduction in key size without compromising security. Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to maintain focus on objects at varying distances. This dynamic adjustment is primarily facilitated by the ciliary muscle, which alters the shape of the crystalline lens to achieve focal changes. In phakic eyes, accommodation is a well-documented phenomenon, extensively studied due to its critical role in visual function. However, the accommodative mechanism is altered in pseudophakic eyes, where the naturral crystalline lens is replaced by an intraocular lens (IOL). While the IOL lacks the deformable properties of the natural lens, pilocarpine-induced accommodation has been shown to influence the position of the IOL and the geometry of the eye. Understanding these changes is important for optimizing visual outcomes in pseudophakic patients, particularly in the context of presbyopia-correcting IOLs and other advanced lens designs. Pilocarpine, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, is commonly used to pharmacologically induuce accommodation by stimulating the ciliary muscle. This agent has been extensively employed in research to investigate the accommodative response in both phakic and pseudophakic eyes. In pseudophakic eyes, where the mechanical properties of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures differ from those of the natural lens, pilocarpine-driven accommodation provides unique insights ito the dynamics of ocular biometry. Previous studies have deonstrated anterior movement of the IOL and changes in anterior chamber depth (ACD) during accommodation, underscoring the interaction between the ciliary muscle, the zonules, and the IOL. These findings raise intriguing questions about the extetn to which other ocular parameters, such as vitreous length (VL) and axial length (AL), may change during accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. The axial length of the eye is a parameter of significant clinical relevance, particularly in refractive surgery, myopia progression studies, and the design of IOLs for cataract surgery. Changes in AL during accommodation have been reported in phakic eyes, with elongation attributed to forward movement of the lens and posterior displacement of the retina. However, the mechanisms underlying AL changes in pseudophakic eyes remain poorly understood. It has been hypothesized that ciliary muscle contraction during pilocarpine-induced accommodation might exert forces that influence the position of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures, potentially leading to measurable changes in axial biometry. Despite these theoretical considerations, few studies have systematically examined AL changes in pseudophakic eyes during accommodation, and those that have are often limited by measurement techniques with insufficient precision or scan depth. Advances in optical imaging technology, particularly the development of ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT), offer new opportunities to investigate thhese phenomena wth unprecedented accuracy and comprehensiveness. Unlike traditional imaging modalities, UL-OCT enables high-resolution, full-length imaging of the eye, from the cornea to the retina, in a single scan. This capability allows for precise measurement of individual biometric components, including central corneal thickness (CCT), ACD, IOL thickness (IOLT), and VL, which collectively contribute to the overall AL. By leveraging this technology, it is possible to gain deeper insights into the structural changes that occur during accommodation, as well as to disentangle the contributions of different ocular components to changes in AL. In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of pilocarpine-induced accommodation on axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes using a custom-built UL-OCT system. The system employed a swept-source OCT design with a central wavelength of 1060 nm, providing an axial scan depth of up to 14 mm in tissue. Imaging Procedure During each imaging session, participants were seated comfortably in front of the UL-OCT system and instructed to maintain steady fixation on the internal target light. Measurements were performed twice for each parameter to ensure reproducibility, and the average values were used for analysis. Statistical Analysis All biometric data were analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Paired t-tests were used to compare measureemnts between the non-accommodative and accommodative states. A significance level of P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The mean and standard devaition (SD) were reported for each parameter. The results demonstrated high reproducibility and minimal variation (<2% CoV) for all measurements. The capacity of the human visual system to modify its focal length, a phenomenon referred to as accommodation, is a intricate and multifaceted process that has been the subject of extensive investigation in eyes possessing a natural crystalline lens, known as phakic eyes [1]. However, in instances where the natural lens is replaced with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL), thereby rendering the eye pseudophakic, the accommodative process is significantly altered, leading to a compromised ability to adapt to changing visual demands [2]. Although the IOL lacks the malleable properties inherent to the natural lens, research has demonstrated that the administration of pilocarpine, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, can induce accommodation, thereby influencing the positioning of the IOL and the geometric configuration of the eye [3]. This, in turn, highlights the necessity of comprehending these changes in order to optimize visual outcomes in individuals with pseudophakic eyes. Pilocarpine functions by stimulating the ciliary muscle, which, in the context of phakic eyes, modulates the shape of the crystalline lens to achieve focal adjustments [4]. In pseudophakic eyes, the induction of accommodation via pilocarpine provides unique insights into the dynamics of ocular biometry, as the mechanical characteristics of the IOL and surrounding ocular structures differ substantially from those of the natural lens [5]. Previous investigations have observed anterior displacement of the IOL and alterations in anterior chamber depth (ACD) during accommodation, underscoring the complex interactions between the ciliary muscle, the zonular fibers, and the IOL [6]. These findings give rise to intriguing questions regarding the extent to which other ocular parameters, such as vitreous length (VL) and axial length (AL), may undergo changes during accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. The axial length of the eye is a parameter of considerable clinical significance, particularly in the context of refractive surgery, myopia progression studies, and the design of IOLs for cataract surgery [7]. Changes in AL during accommodation have been reported in phakic eyes, with observed elongation attributed to forward displacement of the lens and posterior displacement of the retina [8]. Nevertheless, the underlying mechanisms responsible for AL changes in pseudophakic eyes remain poorly understood. It has been hypothesized that contraction of the ciliary muscle during pilocarpine-induced accommodation may exert forces that influence the position of the IOL and surrounding ocular structures, potentially leading to measurable changes in axial biometry [9]. Despite these theoretical considerations, few studies have systematically investigated AL changes in pseudophakic eyes during accommodation, and those that have are often limited by the use of measurement techniques with insufficient precision or scan depth [10]. Recent advances in optical imaging technology, particularly the development of ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT), offer novel opportunities to investigate these phenomena with unprecedented accuracy and comprehensiveness [11]. Unlike conventional imaging modalities, UL-OCT enables high-resolution, full-length imaging of the eye, from the cornea to the retina, in a single scan. This capability allows for precise measurement of individual biometric components, including central corneal thickness (CCT), ACD, IOL thickness (IOLT), and VL, which collectively contribute to the overall AL [12]. By leveraging this technology, it is possible to gain deeper insights into the structural changes that occur during accommodation, as well as to disentangle the contributions of different ocular components to changes in AL. In this investigation, we sought to examine the effects of pilocarpine-induced accommodation on axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes utilizing a custom-built UL-OCT system [13]. Specifically, we aimed to quantify changes in key ocular parameters, including CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL, to better understand the accommodative response in eyes with implanted IOLs. Our study builds upon previous research by employing a highly precise imaging modality, enabling us to characterize subtle changes that may have been overlooked in earlier investigations [14]. Furthermore, by focusing on pseudophakic eyes, our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the functional behavior of IOLs in response to pharmacologically induced accommodation [15]. We hypothesized that pilocarpine-induced contraction of the ciliary muscle would result in measurable changes in ACD, VL, and AL, consistent with the mechanical effects of accommodation [16]. Additionally, we expected that CCT and IOLT would remain stable, as these parameters are not directly influenced by accommodative forces [17]. By testing these hypotheses, our goal was to elucidate the biomechanical interactions between the IOL and surrounding ocular structures during accommodation, thereby providing insights that may inform the design of future IOLs with enhanced accommodative properties [18]. The results of this study have significant implications for both clinical practice and research. From a clinical perspective, understanding the accommodative behavior of pseudophakic eyes is essential for optimizing refractive outcomes and managing patient expectations following cataract surgery [19]. For example, subtle changes in AL during accommodation could influence the effective lens position (ELP) and, consequently, the refractive performance of the IOL [20]. From a research perspective, our findings contribute to the broader understanding of how pharmacological agents like pilocarpine interact with the biomechanical properties of the eye, offering potential avenues for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to enhance accommodation in both phakic and pseudophakic patients. The utilization of UL-OCT in this study has enabled the acquisition of high-resolution images of the eye, allowing for the precise measurement of ocular parameters and the investigation of their changes during accommodation [21]. This technology has the potential to revolutionize the field of ophthalmology, enabling clinicians to better understand the complex interactions between the eye's various structures and to develop more effective treatments for a range of ocular conditions [22]. The disease pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation, with T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and various inflammatory mediators playing pivotal roles in the disease process [3]. These structures, which are characteristic of psoriasis, underscore the critical role of neutrophil-mediated inflammation in the disease's pathogenesis. Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin condition that affects approximately 2–3% of the global population, characterized by erythematous plaques covered with silvery scales [1,2]. The disease pathogenesis involves a complex interplay of genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and immune dysregulation, with T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and various inflammatory mediators playing pivotal roles in the disease process [3]. Histopathologically, psoriasis is marked by epidermal hyperplasia (acanthosis), parakeratosis, and infiltration of immune cells into the skin. Among these immune cells, neutrophils are particularly abundant in the epidermis of psoriatic lesions, where they form microabscesses known as Munro abscesses [4]. These structures, which are characteristic of psoriasis, underscore the critical role of neutrophil-mediated inflammation in the disease's pathogenesis. Neutrophils are the most prevalent leukocytes in the circulation and act as key effectors of the innate immune response. When activated, neutrophils release a variety of antimicrobial molecules, including proteases, reactive oxygen species (ROS), and enzymes, to combat invading pathogens. One such enzyme, myeloperoxidase (MPO), is abundantly expressed in neutrophil granules and plays a pivotal role in the oxidative burst, a process critical for microbial killing [5]. MPO catalyzes the conversion of hydrogen perxoide and chloride into hypochlorous acid, a potent oxidant with broad antimicrobial activity. However, ecxessive or dysregulated MPO activity may contribute to tissue damage and perpetuation of inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases, including psoriasis [6]. Elevated levels of MPO have been detected in various inflammatory conditions, suggesting its involvement in pathological processes beyond microbial defense [7]. In addition to MPO, inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is another molecule implicated in inflammatory responses. iNOS is an enzyem responsible for the production of nitric oxide (NO), a reactive nitrogen species with dievrse biological roles, including vasodilation, immune regulation, and antimicrobial activity [8]. Unlike constitutive forms of nitric oxide synthase, iNOS is induced in response to pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interferon-gamma (IFN-γ). Although NO production is critical for hoost defense, excessive or sustained iNOS activity can lead to nitrosative stress, contributing to tissue injury and inflammation [9]. In the context of psoriasis, iNS expression has been observed in keratinocytes and inflammatory cells within lesional skin, and NO is thought to modulate keratinocyte proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis [10]. Importantly, emerging evidence suggests a potential interplay between MPO and iNOS in chronic inflammation, where MPO-generated oxidannts may act as triggers for iNOS induction, amplifying the inflammatory respnose [11]. Despite the established roles of MPO and iNOS in inflammatory processes, their specific contributions to the pathogenesis of psoriasis remain incompletely understood. While neutrophils are known to infiltrate psoriatic lesions and produce MPO, the downstream effects of MPO-mediated oxidative stress and its relationship with iNOS expression in psoriatic skin have not been fully elucidated. Moreover, whether systemic levels of these enzymes reflect their activity in local tissue inflammation remains an open question. Addressing these gaps in knowleddge is crucial, as it may reveal novel insights into the molecular mechanisms driving psoriasis and identify potential therapeutic targets. This study aims to investigate the contributions of MPO and iNOS to the pathogenesis of psoriasis, focusing on both systemic and tissue-specific levels. By measuring serum MPO and iNOS levels and conducting immunohistochemical analyses of psoriatic and non-lesional skin, we seeek to delineate the roles of these enzymes in the disease process. Particular attention is given to the localized activity of MPO in psoriatic lesions, its potential to stimulate iNOS expression, and the implications of this interaction in sustaining chronic inflammation. Understanding the crosstalk betewen these inflammatory mediators may provide a basis for the developmetn of novel therapeutic strategies targeting MPO and/or iNOS pathways. In the folowing sections, we present the methoodology employed to quantify serum and tissue levels of MPO and iNOS, the results obtained from these analyses, and their interpretation in the context of psoriasis pathophysiology. The potential clinical significance of MPO and iNOS as biomarkers or therapeutic targets is also discussed. By integrating systemic and tissue-specific data, this study seeks to advance our understanding of neutrophil-driven inflammation in psoriasis and its broader implications for chronic inflammatory diseases. The underlying mechanisms driving psoriasis are intricate, involving a complex interplay between genetic susceptibility, environmental factors, and immune system dysfunction, with key roles attributed to T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and various pro-inflammatory molecules [3]. Histopathological examination of psoriatic lesions reveals distinctive features, including accelerated epidermal cell growth, abnormal keratinization, and a pronounced influx of immune cells. Notably, the epidermis of psoriatic lesions is characterized by an abundance of neutrophils, which form distinctive microabscesses known as Munro abscesses [4]. These structures are pathognomonic for psoriasis and highlight the critical contribution of neutrophil-mediated inflammation to the disease's pathogenesis. As the most abundant leukocytes in the circulation, neutrophils play a vital role in the innate immune response, releasing a range of antimicrobial substances, including proteases, reactive oxygen species, and enzymes, to combat invading microorganisms. However, excessive or uncontrolled MPO activity may contribute to tissue damage and the perpetuation of inflammation in chronic inflammatory diseases, including psoriasis [6]. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the oral tongue is one of the most common maliganncies of the head and neck region, with significant morbidity and mortality worldwide. Despite advances in diagnostic and therapeutic modalities, oral tongue squamous cell carrcinoma (OTSCC) continues to pose a clinical challenge due to its aggressive behavior, propensity for early metastasis, and recurrence [1, 2]. The tumor thickness (TT) of OTSCC has emerged as an important prognotsic factor, influencing disease progression and the likelihood of cervical lymph node metastasis [3]. Accurate preoperative assessment of TT is therefore critical in determining the extent of surgical intervention, including the need for elective neck dissection (END) in clinically node-negative (N0) patients. The evaluation of TT in OTSCC is particularly relevant in cases of early-stage disease, classified as pT1 and pT2 tumors according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system. Early-stage OTSCC is often confined to the primmary site, with no clinically palpable cervical lymphadenopathy. However, despite the absence of clinically detectable nodal metastasis, occult metastases can be present in a significant proportion of patients, necessitating END to improve outcomes [4, 5]. The decision to perform END in clinically N0 patients is often debated due to the associated morbidity, such as shoulder dysfunction and sensory deficits, balanced against the potential survival benefit [6]. Tumor thickness has been proposed as a surrogate marker to guide this decision-making process, as thicker tumors are more likely to harbor occult nodal metastases [7]. Traditionally, TT has been evaluated postoperatively using histopathological measurements, whih remain the gold standard. However, thsi approach precludes its use as a preoperative decision-making tool. Preoperative imaging modalities, including magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT), have been employed to estimate TT, but these techniques are often limited by high costs, lack of widespread availability, and variability in accuracy [8]. Ultrasonography (USG), on the other hand, is a non-invasive, cost-effective, and widely accessible imaging mdoality that has shown promise in measuring TT preoperatively in OTSCC [9]. High-resolution intraoral ultrasonography allows for real-time visualization of the tumor and surrounding tissue, enabling precise measurement of TT. Additionally, neck ultrasonography can provide valuable information on cervical nodal status, further aiding in treatment planning [10]. Despite its potential, the utility of USG in the preoperative evaluation of TT in OTSCC has not been fully validated. Limited studies have explored its reliability in comparison to histopathological findings, and there is a paucity of robust datta correlating USG-derived TT measurements with nodal metastasis. The present study aims to address these gaps by assessing the statistical correlation between TT measured preoperatively by USG and TT determined via histopathological examination. Furthermore, it seeks to evaluate the predictive capacity of USG-derived TT in detecting occult cervical nodal metastasis in early-stage OTSCC. Previous research has demonstrated a strong correlation between USG-derived TT and histopathological TT in various oral cavity subsites, suggesting that USG may be a reliable modality for preoperative assessment [11]. However, these studies often include small sample sizes, heterogneeous tumor subsites, and variatinos in imaging protocols, limiting the generalizability of their findings. The present study focuses exclusively on early OTSCC, a subgroup of tumors with distinct clinical and pathological characteristics. By doing so, it seeks to provide more specific insights into the role of USG in this context. Another critical aspect of this study is the evaluation of TT as a predictor of occult nodal metastasis. Several studies have proposed specific TT thresholds, such as 4 mm or 5 mm, as predictive cutoffs for increased risk of occult nodal metastasis [13, 14]. However, there is considerable variability in the reported thresholds, and their applicability to clinical practice is uncertain. By correlating USG-derived TT with histopathological nodal status, this study aims to determine a reliable TT cutoff that can guide the decision for END in early OTSCC. The implications of this study are significant for clinical practice, particularly in resource-limited settings where advanced imaging modalities may not be readily available. The oral tongue is a common site for squamous cell carcinoma, a formidable and prevalent malignancy in the head and neck region that contributes significantly to global morbidity and mortality. Advances in diagnostic and treatment methods have not adequately addressed the challenges posed by this disease, which is characterized by aggressive behavior, a tendency to metastasize early, and a high rate of recurrence [1, 2]. A crucial factor influencing the progression of oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma and the likelihood of cervical lymph node metastasis is the thickness of the tumor [3]. Therefore, accurately assessing tumor thickness before surgery is vital for determining the appropriate surgical approach, including whether to perform elective neck dissection in patients without clinically apparent lymph node involvement. In cases of early-stage disease, categorized as pT1 and pT2 according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer staging system, evaluating tumor thickness is particularly important. At this stage, the cancer is often confined to the initial site, with no palpable lymph nodes in the neck. However, even when lymph nodes are not clinically detectable, a significant number of patients may have occult metastases, making elective neck dissection necessary to improve outcomes [4, 5]. The decision to proceed with elective neck dissection in patients without clinical evidence of lymph node involvement is a topic of debate, weighing the potential benefits against the associated morbidities, such as dysfunction and sensory deficits [6]. Tumor thickness has been suggested as a criterion to guide this decision, as thicker tumors are more likely to have occult nodal metastases [7]. Traditionally, the thickness of the tumor has been assessed postoperatively through histopathological examination, which remains the standard reference. However, this approach limits its utility as a preoperative decision-making tool. To estimate tumor thickness before surgery, imaging modalities like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) have been used, but these methods are often hindered by high costs, limited availability, and variability in accuracy [8]. In contrast, ultrasonography offers a non-invasive, cost-effective, and widely accessible alternative that has shown promise in measuring tumor thickness preoperatively in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma [9]. High-resolution intraoral ultrasonography enables real-time visualization of the tumor and surrounding tissue, allowing for precise measurement of tumor thickness. Additionally, ultrasonography of the neck can provide valuable information on the status of cervical lymph nodes, further assisting in treatment planning [10]. Despite its potential, the utility of ultrasonography in assessing tumor thickness in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma has not been comprehensively validated. Few studies have compared the reliability of ultrasonography measurements with histopathological findings, and there is a scarcity of robust data linking ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness measurements with the presence of nodal metastases. This study aims to address these gaps by examining the statistical correlation between tumor thickness measured preoperatively using ultrasonography and tumor thickness determined through histopathological examination. Furthermore, it seeks to evaluate the predictive ability of ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness in identifying occult cervical nodal metastasis in early-stage oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. Previous research has demonstrated a strong correlation between ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness and histopathological tumor thickness in various sites within the oral cavity, suggesting that ultrasonography could be a reliable modality for preoperative assessment [11]. However, these studies are often limited by small sample sizes, the inclusion of heterogeneous tumor sites, and variations in imaging protocols, which restrict the generalizability of their findings. By focusing exclusively on early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, a subgroup with distinct clinical and pathological characteristics, this study aims to provide more specific insights into the role of ultrasonography in this context. Another critical aspect of this study is the evaluation of tumor thickness as a predictor of occult nodal metastasis. The presence of metastasis in cervical lymph nodes is a well-established factor influencing prognosis in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, significantly affecting survival rates [12]. While clinical and imaging-based assessment of lymph nodes is standard, it often fails to detect small-volume or micrometastatic disease. Several studies have proposed specific thresholds for tumor thickness, such as 4 mm or 5 mm, as indicators of increased risk for occult nodal metastasis [13, 14]. However, there is considerable variability in the reported thresholds, and their applicability in clinical practice is uncertain. By correlating ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness with histopathological nodal status, this study aims to establish a reliable tumor thickness cutoff that can guide the decision for elective neck dissection in early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. The implications of this study are significant for clinical practice, especially in settings with limited resources where advanced imaging modalities may not be readily available. If validated, ultrasonography could serve as a rapid, cost-effective tool for preoperative risk stratification, enabling tailored surgical management and potentially reducing the morbidity associated with overtreatment. Furthermore, the findings could contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the integration of ultrasonography into routine diagnostic workflows for oral cancer. The utilization of ultrasonography in this context could help bridge the gap in diagnostic capabilities, particularly in underserved areas, and ultimately improve patient outcomes. By providing a more accurate and accessible means of assessing tumor thickness and predicting nodal metastasis, this study has the potential to refine treatment strategies and enhance the quality of care for patients with oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. The widespread adoption of ultrasonography for this purpose could also lead to a more efficient allocation of healthcare resources, as it may reduce the need for more invasive and costly diagnostic procedures. In conclusion, the present study is designed to investigate the correlation between ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness and histopathological findings, as well as the predictive value of ultrasonography in detecting occult nodal metastasis in early-stage oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. By addressing the current limitations in the validation of ultrasonography for this purpose, this research aims to provide critical evidence for the potential role of ultrasonography in improving the diagnosis and treatment of this malignancy. The results of this study could have a profound impact on clinical practice, contributing to more informed decision-making and personalized treatment plans for patients with oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. Ultimately, the integration of ultrasonography into the diagnostic algorithm for oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma could lead to improved patient outcomes, reduced morbidity, and more efficient use of healthcare resources. Managing early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma poses considerable challenges, and optimizing treatment strategies is vital to minimize unnecessary morbidity and enhance patient outcomes [1]. A prospective study was conducted over a period of two years, from 2012 to 2013, with the primary goal of addressing these challenges by examining the correlation between tumor thickness measurements obtained via preoperative ultrasonography and those obtained through histopathological assessments in patients with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma. The study received approval from the institutional ethics committee and was carried out in a tertiary care center, where all participants provided written informed consent prior to their inclusion in the study. The study population comprised 24 patients diagnosed with early oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, categorized as having T1 or T2 tumors with clinically negative neck nodes (N0) [2]. The inclusion criteria were rigorous, requiring patients to have histopathologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the oral tongue, tumors classified as T1 or T2 according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) staging system, and clinically negative neck node status based on physical examination and ultrasonographic evaluation [3]. Patients with recurrent disease, prior treatment for oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma, or distant metastases were excluded from the study to prevent potential confounding factors from influencing the results. The preoperative evaluation of patients involved a comprehensive clinical examination, imaging studies, and measurement of ultrasonographic tumor thickness. The primary tumor was assessed using ultrasonography with a high-frequency linear transducer (7.5–13 MHz), with the patient positioned in a supine position and the tongue protruded to maximize exposure of the lesion [4]. The transducer was gently placed on the tongue surface to avoid compressing the soft tissue, and the depth of tumor invasion was measured in millimeters. Three independent measurements were taken for each tumor, and the mean value was recorded to minimize operator variability. The nodal evaluation was conducted preoperatively using neck ultrasonography, focusing on levels I through IV of the cervical lymph nodes [5]. The sonographic criteria for identifying suspicious nodes included a rounded shape, absence of fatty hilum, hypoechoic echotexture, and a short-axis diameter greater than 10 mm. All cases were clinically staged using a combination of clinical examination and imaging findings, ensuring that patients received accurate and comprehensive assessments. Following histopathological confirmation of malignancy through incisional biopsy, all patients underwent surgical management, which consisted of wide local excision of the primary tumor with adequate margins and ipsilateral elective neck dissection of levels I to IV, as per institutional protocol [6]. Intraoperatively, the glossectomy specimens were marked and carefully oriented to ensure uniformity of measurement. Fresh specimens were used to measure tumor thickness immediately after excision, and the maximum depth of invasion was recorded using a sterile caliper. Postoperative histopathological assessment was conducted on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections to confirm tumor thickness and nodal status [7]. For each specimen, tumor thickness was measured microscopically as the vertical depth from the most superficial epithelial surface to the deepest point of tumor invasion. All histopathological evaluations were performed by a single experienced pathologist to ensure consistency, and the pathological nodal status was classified based on the presence or absence of metastatic deposits in the dissected lymph nodes. The primary objective of the study was to evaluate the correlation between tumor thickness measurements obtained via preoperative ultrasonography and those obtained through histopathological assessments. Statistical correlation was assessed using Pearson's correlation coefficient (r), and the interclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was calculated to determine the level of agreement between the two methods [8]. A Bland-Altman plot was used to assess the agreement between ultrasonographic and histopathological measurements, with bias and 95% limits of agreement reported. The secondary objective of the study was to evaluate the predictive capacity of ultrasonographic tumor thickness in identifying patients at risk of occult cervical nodal metastasis. The association between tumor thickness and nodal metastasis was analyzed using the chi-square test, and tumor thickness thresholds for nodal metastasis risk stratification were determined by categorizing patients into groups based on tumor thickness (<4 mm or ≥4 mm) and analyzing the corresponding nodal status [9]. This approach enabled the researchers to investigate the potential of ultrasonography-derived tumor thickness as a predictive tool for identifying patients at risk of nodal metastasis, which is crucial for optimizing treatment strategies and improving patient outcomes. Biofilm-associated infections represent a significant challenge in modern medicine due to their inherent resistance to conventional antimicrobial therapies. Biofilms, which are structured communities of microbial cells enclosed in a self-produced extracellular polymeric substance (EPS), provide a protective niche for bacteria, allowing them to evade host immune responses and resist the acction of antibiotics. This resilience is particularly problematic in chronic infections, where biofilms are implicated in conditions such as endocarditis, chronic wounds, medical device-associated infections, and cystic fibrosis-related lung infections. The presence of persister cells, a dormant subpoppulation of bacteria within biofilms, further complicates treatment efforts. These cells exhibit a transient tolerance to antibiotics, often surviving even high doses of antimicrobial agents, and contribute to the recalcitrant nature of biofilm infections. Consequently, there is an urgent need to identify novel strategies or adjuvants that can effectively disrupt biofilms and sensitize baceria to antibiotic therapy. The interplay between host immune defenses and antibioitcs has garnered increasing attention as a potential approach to address biofilm infections. In particular, antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) – small, naturally occurring components of the innate immune system – have emerged as promising candidates for enhancing antibiotic efficacy. AMPs are produced by a wide range of organisms, including humans, insects, and plants, and exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity. Their mechanisms of action often involve disrutpion of bacterial membranes, modulation of bacterial metabolism, or interference with biofilm formation, making them attractive tools for combating multidrug-resistant pathogens and biofilm-associated infections. Importantly, AMPs also have the potential to target persister cells and destabilize the biofilm matrix, thereby overcoming key barriers to effective treatment. Insects, as a result of their evolutionary adaptation to diverse microbial environments, possess potent AMP complexes that are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens. The blowfly Calliphora vicina, for instance, produces an AMP complex known as FLIP7, which is composed of multiple antimicrobial agents, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides. This multifaceted composition allosw FLIP7 to target bacteria via multiple mechanisms, reducing the likelihood of resistance development. The ability of FLIP7 to synergize with antibiotics and enhance their activity against biofilms, however, remains largely unexplored. The objective of this study was to investigate the potential of FLIP7 to improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying this interaction. We hypothesized that the synergistic action of FLIP7 with antibiotics could sensitize persister cells and disrupt the biofilm structure, thereby enhancing bacterial eradication. To test this, we examined the interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics frmo various classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides, and glycopeptides, against biofilm and planktonic cultures of clinically relevant bacterial pathogens. These pathogens included Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii, which are among the most common causative agenst of biofilm-associated infections and are notable for teir ability to resist antibiotic treatment. Using a combination of methodologies, including checkerboard assays, trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assays, crystal violet biofilm eradication assays, and microscopic analysis, we evaluated the efficacy of FLIP7 in conjunction with antibiotics. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was used to quantify the degree of synergy or antagonism between FLIP7 and each antibiotic. The dose-effect relationships were analyzed to identify potnetial targets of FLIP7's synergistic effects, with particuar attention to the role of persister cells. Additionally, the biofilm eradication assay allowed us to assess the ability of the FLIP7-antibiotic combination to disrupt biofilm structures and eliminate biofilm-embedded bacteria. Our findinngs demonstrate that FLIP7 exhibits significant synergy with a wide range of antibiotics, particularly those targeting cell wall synthesis (e.g., meropenem, ampicillin, vancomycin) and prottein synthesis (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, clindamycin). Notably, the synergistic effect was more pronounced in biofilm cultures compared to planktonic cells, suggesting that FLIP7's acctivity is particularly effectivve in the biofilm microenvironment. The synergistic interactions allowed for substantial reductions in the effective anti-biofilm concentrations of antibiotics, in some cases by several orders of magnitude. This reduction has important clinical implications, as it enables the use of lower antibiotic doses, potentially minimizing toxicity and the risk of resistance development. Further analysis revealed that the synergistic effect of FLIP7 was associated with its ability to sensitize persister cells and disrupt the structural integrity of the biofilm matrix. The destruction of biofilm materials was especially evident in S. aureus and E. coli biofilms, where the combination treatment led to the complete eradication of biofilm-associated bacteria. The lack of interaction between FLIP7 and polymyxin B, however, highlights the specificity of the synergistic effects and underscores the need for tailored AMP-antibiotic combinations for different clinical scenarios. By targeting persister cells and destabilizing biofilm structures, FLIP7 enhances the efficacy of antibiotics and addresses key challenges in the management of chronic and recalcitrant infections. Synergistic effects were indicated by a leftward shift in the dose–effect curve of the antibiotic in the presence of FLIP7. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Insects, having evolved in diverse microbial environments, possess potent AMP complexes that are highly effective against a wide range of pathogens [11]. The blowfly Calliphora vicina, for instance, produces an AMP complex known as FLIP7, which comprises multiple antimicrobial agents, including defensins, cecropins, diptericins, and proline-rich peptides [12]. This multifaceted composition enables FLIP7 to target bacteria via multiple mechanisms, reducing the likelihood of resistance development [13]. However, the ability of FLIP7 to synergize with antibiotics and enhance their activity against biofilms remains largely unexplored [14]. The primary objective of this investigation was to examine the potential of FLIP7 to improve the anti-biofilm activity of antibiotics and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms of this interaction [15]. We hypothesized that the synergistic action of FLIP7 with antibiotics could sensitize persister cells and disrupt the biofilm structure, thereby enhancing bacterial eradication [16]. To test this hypothesis, we investigated the interaction of FLIP7 with antibiotics from various classes, including β-lactams, aminoglycosides, macrolides, and glycopeptides, against biofilm and planktonic cultures of clinically relevant bacterial pathogens [17]. These pathogens included Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Acinetobacter baumannii, which are among the most common causative agents of biofilm-associated infections and are notable for their ability to resist antibiotic treatment [18]. Utilizing a combination of methodological approaches, including checkerboard assays, trimethyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC) cell viability assays, crystal violet biofilm eradication assays, and microscopic analysis, we evaluated the efficacy of FLIP7 in conjunction with antibiotics [19]. The fractional inhibitory concentration index (FICI) was employed to quantitatively assess the degree of synergy or antagonism between FLIP7 and each antibiotic [20]. The dose-effect relationships were analyzed to identify potential targets of FLIP7's synergistic effects, with particular attention to the role of persister cells [21]. Furthermore, the biofilm eradication assay allowed us to assess the ability of the FLIP7-antibiotic combination to disrupt biofilm structures and eliminate biofilm-embedded bacteria [22]. Notably, the synergistic effect was more pronounced in biofilm cultures compared to planktonic cells, suggesting that FLIP7's activity is particularly effective in the biofilm microenvironment [24]. The synergistic interactions enabled substantial reductions in the effective anti-biofilm concentrations of antibiotics, in some cases by several orders of magnitude [25]. This reduction has important clinical implications, as it allows for the use of lower antibiotic doses, potentially minimizing toxicity and the risk of resistance development [26].
