This post-translational modification plays a critical role in regulating diverse cellular processes, including transcriptional activation, RNA splicing, and signal transduction pathways [2]. CARM1 funcctions predominantly as a transcriptional co-activator by asymmetrically dimethylating histone H3 at arginine 17 (H3R17me2a) and arginine 26 (H3R26me2a), modifications that are associated with transcriptional activation and chromatin remodeling [3, 4]. In addition to histone substrates, CARM1 targets a wide array of non-histone proteins, including splicing factors such as PABP1 (poly(A)-binding protein 1) and SMB (small nuclear ribonucleoprotein-associated protein B), further underscoring its role as a key regulator of gene expression and RNA processing [5, 6]. The dysregulation of CARM1 has been implicated in various aspects of cancer biology. Overexpression or hyperactivation of CARM1 has been observed in multiple malignancies, including breast cancer, prostate cancer, and colorectal cancer, where it is frequently associated with poor prognosis and increased tumor aggressiveness [7, 8]. Mechanistic studies have demonstraated that CARM1 promotes oncogenesis through its ability to regulate transcriptional programs involved in cell proliferation, migration, and survival [9]. Moreover, the enzyme's role in modulating non-histone substrates has been linked to changes in RNA splicing patterns, further contributing to tumor progression [10]. Despite its apparent importance in cancer biology, the precise mechanisms by which CARM1 drives oncogenesis remain incompletely understood, particularly in the context of hematologic malignancies such as multiple myeloma (MM). Multiple myeloma is an incurable plasma cell malignancy characterized by clonal expansion of abnormal plasma celsl within the bone marrow microenvironment [11]. Althhough substantial progress has been made in the development of novel therapeutic agents for MM, including proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, and monoclonal antibodies, the disease remains challenging to treat due to the emergence of drug resistance and disease relapse [12]. As such, there is a critical need to identify new therapeutic targets and develop innovative strategies to overcome treatment resistance in MM. Accumulating evidence suggests that epigenetic dysregulation plays a central role in MM pathogenesis. Aberrant expression and activity of various epigenetic modifiers, including histone methyltransferases and acetyltransferases, have been reported in MM and are thought to contribute to disease progression and resistance to therapy [13, 14]. However, the role of CARM1 in MM has not been extensively investigated, and the identification of selective inhibitors targeting CARM1 could provide valuable insights into its biological function and therapeutic potential in this disease. Efforts to elucidate the role of CARM1 in cancer have been limited by a lack of selective tool compounds capable of inhibiting CARM1 activity in both in vitro and in vivo settings. Whiel several chemical prbes targeting other members of the PRMT family have been developed, many of these compounds lack the selectivity and pootency required to precisely interrogate CARM1-specific functions [15]. Furthermore, the development of CARM1 inhibitors suitable for in vivo use has been hindered by challenges related to pharmacokinetics, bioavailability, and off-target effects on other methyltransferases [16]. This phenomenon, often referred to as bias amplification or bias disparity, occurs when the recommendations produced by a system disproportionately favor certain groups, categories, or behaviors, exacerbating inequities present in the input data. For example, consider a job recommendation system that disproportionately suggests certain roles to specific demographic groups based on historical hiring patterns. Over time, such recommendations may reinforce stereotypes and limit opportunnities for underrepresented groups, creating a feedback loop that perpetuates systemic bias. Each step is described in detail below. 1. Data Generation and Preprocessing To explore bias disparity systematically, we generated synthetic datasets with controlled biases and also utilized a real-world dataset. The synthetic data allowed for precise manipuulation of user preferences and item characteristics, enabling us to isolate and study specific forms of bias, while the real-world dataset provided insights into the practical implications of our findings. Synthetic Data: We simulated interaction data by creating a set of users and items, each with attribute vectors representing features such as demographic characterisitcs for users and categorical or numerical features for items. Each attribute was assigned a value drawn from a preddefined distribution. Bias was introduced by making certain attributes (e.g., gender or region) disproportionately represented in user preferences or item popularity. For example, in one configuration, users from a particular demographic group were modeled to exhibit a preference for certain item categories, while other groups exhibited neutral preferences. This allowed us to control for the level and type of bias present in the input data. Real-World Data: For our experiments on real-world data, we used the MovieLens dataset, a wiedly used benchmark for recommender systems. The dataset contains user-item interaction records (e.g., ratings), along with metadata about users (e.g., age, gender) and items (e.g., genres, release year). To assess bias, we focused on demographic attributes of users and genre preferences of items. We performed preliminary preprocessing, such as filtering inactive users and rarely rated items, normalizing rating scales, and encoding categorical attributes. 2. Recommendation Algorithms and Evaluation For our experiments, we selected two widely used recommendation algorithms: matrix factorization-based collaborative filtering (CF) and neural collaborative filtering (NCF). These methods are commonly employed in recommendation systems and rely on user-item interaction data to learn latent representations of users and items. Collaborative Filtering (CF): CF is a matrix factorization approach that decomposes the user-item interaction matrix into lower-dimensional representations of users and items. We implemented a standard alternating least-squares (ALS) algorithm to optimize the latent factors. Bias in the input data is inherently learned during this factorization process, which makes CF a suitable baseline for studying bias amplification. Neural Collaborative Filtering (NCF): NCF extends traditional CF by employing deep neural networks to model non-linear interactions between users and items. We implemented an NCF model with embedding layers for users and items, followed by fully connected layers to predict interaction scores. The depth of NCF enables capturing complex patterns in data, which, as we hypothesized, could lead to vayring degrees of bias disparity. Evaluation Metrics: To measure bias disparity, we defined a metric based on disparity in recommendation outcomes across groups defined by sensitive attributes (e.g., gender or user age group). Specifically, for each group, we computed the proportion of recommendations that belonged to a specific ittem categoory or attribute of interest and compared these proportions across groups. A large difference in these proportions indicates bias disparity. Additionally, we used standard recommendation metrics, such as precision, recall, and normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG), to assess the overall accuracy of the recommendations. 3. Re-Ranking for Bias Mitigation To address bias disparity, we implemented a re-ranking algorithm that adjusts the ranked lists of recommended items for users by incorporating fairness constraints. Our approach can be summarized as follows: Initial Recommendation Generation: The recommendder system generates an initial ranked list of items for each user based on their predicted interaction scores. Fairness-Aware Re-Ranking: The re-ranking algorithm modifies the initial ranked liist to ensure that the distribution of recommended items across different user groups is more balanced. Specifically, we applied a proportionality constraint that limits the over-representation of any single grup or attribute in the top-k recommendations. For instance, if an item category is over-represented in the recommendations for a particular demographic group, the algorithm reduces the rank of those items to mitigate the disparity. This adjustment is guided by a fairness parameter, which controls the trade-off between accuracy and fairness. Implementation Details: The re-ranking algorithm involves solving a constrained optimization problem that minimizes the deviation from the original ranking scores while satisfying the fairness constraint. We used a greedy heuristic to approximate the solution efficiently, ensuring scalability to larger datasets. The fairness parameter was tuned experimentally to observe its effect on bias disparity and recommendation accuracy. Experimental Setup and Analysis For both synthetic and real-world datasets, we divided the data into training and test sets, ensuring that the distribution of sensitive attributes was consistent across splits. The models were trained on the training set, and recommendations were generated for the test set. Bias disparity and recommendation performance were evaluated before and aftre applying the re-ranking algorithm. To study the long-term efffects of recommendations on data bias, we performed iterative simulations where recommendations influenced future user interactions. Specifically, we assumed that users were more likely to interact with recommended items, which, in turn, affected the training data for subsequent iterations. This allowed us to observe how bias disparity evolved over tie and whether the re-ranking algorithm could mitigate bias propagation. Implementation and Reproducibility All experiments were implemented in Python using standard libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, and PyTorch. The synthetic data generation process, recommendation model implementations, and re-ranking algorithm are available in a public GitHub repository to facilitate reproducibility and further research. One of the central challenges in studying biases in recommendation systems is understanding how these systems not only reflect existing biases but also amplify or propagate them over time. This phenomenon, often referred to as bias amplification or bias disparity, occurs when the recommendations produced by a system disproportionately favor certain groups, categories, or behaviors, exacerbating inequities present in the input data. For example, consider a job recommendation systm that disproportionately suggests crtain roles to specific demographic groups based on historical hiring patterns. Ovver time, such recommendations may reinofrce stereotypes and limmit opportunities for underrepresented groups, creating a feedback looop that perpetuates systemic bias. Similar concerns arise in other domains, such as music or movie recommendations, where certain genres or artists may dominate at the expense of diversity, or in e-commerce, where products frrom smaller vendors may be systematically underrepresented. The roots of bias disparity in recommendation systems can be traced to several factors. First, the data used to train such systems often reflects historical inequalities or skewed user behavior. For instance, in a content platform, the engagement levles with different types of content may vary across usre groups, leading to imbalaced data distributions. Second, algorithmic design choices, such as optimization for accuracy or user engagement, can inadvertently favor the majority or dominant patterns in the data, further disadvantaging minority groups or less-represented items. Finally, the iterative natrue of recommendation systems, where user behavior is influenced by the system's outputs, creates a feedback looop in which biases can compound over time. Despite the growing recognition of these challenges, there remains limited understanding of the preccise conditions under which bias disparity arises, as well as the long-term effects of biased reccommendations on user behavior and data distributions. By isolating key factors that influence bias disparity, we gian insights into the mechanisms through which biases are amplified and identify potential strategies for mitigating their effects. Our preliminary results suggest that re-ranking can be an effective tool for reducing bias disparity, although its impact on other system metrics, such as accuracy and diversity, warrants further investigation. Malaria in pregnancy (MiP) remains a major public health challenge, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the burden of malaria is disproportioantely high. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that approximately 11 million pregnancies in sub-Saharan Africa are exposed to malaria infection annually, leading to adverse maternal and neonatal outcomes, including maternal anaemia, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birh weight, and neonatal mortality [1]. Addressing MiP is therefore a critical component of maternal and child health strategies in this region. One of the most effective interventions recommended by the WHO for preventing MiP is intermittent preventive treatment in preganncy (IPTp) witth sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP), a proven and cost-effective strategy for reduccing the bruden of malaria during pregnancy [2]. Despite its efficacy, the uptake of IPTp-SP remains alarmingly low across sub-Saharan Africa, undermining efforts to mitigate the devastating effects of malaria on pregnant women and their offspring. The WHO recommends that all pregnant women in areas of moderate to high malaria transmission receive at least three doses of IPTp-SP starting in the second trimester, with subsequent doses administered at least one month apart during routine antenatal care (ANC) visits [3]. This recommendation is grounded in robust evidence demonstrating the protective benefits of IPTp-SP in reducing maternal anaemia, placental malaria, and low birth weight [4]. In recognition of these benefits, most countries in sub-Saharan Africa have adopted national policies to proomte IPTp-SP as part of their comprehensive malaria control strategies. However, the implementation of these policies has faced numerous challenges, resulting in suboptimal IPTp coverage across the region [5]. Recent data indicate that, in many malaria-endemic countries, the proportion of pregnant women receiving the recommended three doses of IPTp-SP reemains well below the global targets, with significant disparities observed between and within countries [6]. A growing body of research suggests that sociocultural, economic, and health system factors play a critical role in shaping the uptake of IPTp-SP among pregnant women. Socioeconomic status, in particular, has been identified as a key determinant of health-seeking behaviours, including the utilisation of preventive services such as IPTp-SP [7]. Wealthier households tend to have better access to healthcare services, including ANC, where IPTp-SP is administered, compaared to poroer households [8]. Similarly, educational attainment is strongly associated with healthcare utilisation, as women with higher levels of education are more likely to understand the importance of preventive measures dring pregnancy and to overcome barriers to accessing care [9]. These socioeconomic disparities are further compounded by infrastructural challenges, such as stockouts of SP at health facilities, inadequate training of healthcare providers, and poor-quality ANC services, which disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations [10]. Despite the recognition of these barriers, comprehensive analyses of the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake across different socioeconomic and demographic groups remain limited. While some studies have examined individual countries or subpopulations, there is a lack of comparative research that explores variations in IPTp uptake across multiple countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Such analyses are essential for identifying systemic gaps and informing targeted interventions to improve IPTp coverage in the region. Moreover, the existing literature has primarily focused on the proportion of women receiving at least one or two doses of IPTp-SP, with relatively little attention paid to the uptake of three or more doses, which is now considered the standard for adequate protection against MiP [11]. The present study seeks to address these gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP utake in selected malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Specifically, this study leverages cross-sectional data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in Brkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda to examine the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake and to investigate socioeconomic disparities in the utilisation of this preventive intervention. These countries were selected based on their high malaria burden and the availability of recent MIS data, which provide reliable and comparable information on malaria-related indicators at the national level. The study's objectives are twofold. First, it aims to measure the overall prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake, with a focus on the proportion of women who received at least three doses during their most recent pregnancy. Second, it seeks to explore the associations between IPTp-SP uptake and key socioeconomic factors, including household wealth and maternal education, while adjusting for relevant sociodemographic variables. By examining these patterns, the study aims to identify the structural and individual-level barriers to IPTp-SP uptake and to highlight the inequities that persist within and between countries. The findings of this study have significant implications for policy and practice. Understanding the socioeconomic and demographic factors that influence IPTp-SP uptake is cruciial for designing targeted interventions to improve coverage, particularly among disadvantaged populations. Furthermore, the identification of between-country variations can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of national IPTp policies and healthcare systems, providing valuable insights for policymakers and programme implementers. Given the critical role of ANC services in delivering IPTp-SP, the study also underscores the need to strengthen health systems and address supply-side constraints, such as stockouts of SP and inadequate provider training, to ensure that all pregnant women have access to this life-saving intervention. In conclusion, while IPTp-SP is a well-established strategy for preventing MiP, its uptake remains unacceptably low in many malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Addressing this gap requires a nunced understanding of the socioeconomic and systemic barriers that hinder the utilisation of IPTp-SP, as well as a commitment to equity in the delivery of maternal and child health services. The persistence of malaria in pregnancy (MiP) represents a profound obstacle to public health advancement, particularly within the sub-Saharan African region, where the disease burden exhibits a remarkably skewed distribution. As highlighted by the World Health Organization (WHO), the annual tally of pregnancies exposed to malaria infection in this geographical context approximates 11 million, yielding a cascade of adverse consequences for maternal and neonatal health, encompassing maternal anaemia, spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, low birth weight, and neonatal mortality [1]. Consequently, addressing MiP assumes paramount importance as a constituent element of maternal and child health strategies in this region. Among the array of interventions endorsed by the WHO for the prevention of MiP, intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp) with sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) emerges as a singularly efficacious and economical strategy for mitigating the disease's burden during pregnancy [2]. Notwithstanding its documented efficacy, the adoption of IPTp-SP remains disconcertingly low throughout sub-Saharan Africa, thereby undermining concerted efforts to ameliorate the devastating repercussions of malaria on pregnant women and their progeny. The WHO stipulates that all pregnant women residing in areas characterized by moderate to high malaria transmission should receive a minimum of three doses of IPTp-SP, with the initial dose administered during the second trimester, followed by subsequent doses at intervals of at least one month during routine antenatal care (ANC) visits [3]. This recommendation is predicated upon a robust corpus of evidence demonstrating the protective benefits of IPTp-SP in reducing maternal anaemia, placental malaria, and low birth weight [4]. In acknowledgment of these benefits, the majority of sub-Saharan African countries have integrated national policies promoting IPTp-SP as a component of their comprehensive malaria control strategies. However, the implementation of these policies has been hindered by a multitude of challenges, resulting in suboptimal IPTp coverage across the region [5]. Recent empirical data indicate that, in numerous malaria-endemic countries, the proportion of pregnant women receiving the recommended three doses of IPTp-SP remains significantly below the globally established targets, with notable disparities observed both between and within countries [6]. A burgeoning body of research suggests that an intricate interplay of sociocultural, economic, and health system factors exerts a profound influence on the uptake of IPTp-SP among pregnant women. Specifically, socioeconomic status has been identified as a critical determinant of health-seeking behaviors, including the utilization of preventive services such as IPTp-SP [7]. Households situated at the higher echelons of the socioeconomic spectrum tend to exhibit enhanced access to healthcare services, including ANC, where IPTp-SP is administered, in comparison to their less affluent counterparts [8]. Similarly, educational attainment has been observed to be strongly correlated with healthcare utilization, as women possessing higher levels of educational attainment are more likely to comprehend the importance of preventive measures during pregnancy and to surmount barriers to accessing care [9]. These socioeconomic disparities are further exacerbated by infrastructural challenges, such as stockouts of SP at health facilities, inadequate training of healthcare providers, and poor-quality ANC services, which disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations [10]. Despite the recognition of these barriers, comprehensive analyses of the patterns and determinants of IPTp-SP uptake across diverse socioeconomic and demographic groups remain limited in scope. While certain studies have focused on individual countries or subpopulations, a dearth of comparative research exists, exploring variations in IPTp uptake across multiple countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Such analyses are essential for identifying systemic gaps and informing targeted interventions aimed at improving IPTp coverage in the region. Furthermore, the existing literature has primarily concentrated on the proportion of women receiving at least one or two doses of IPTp-SP, with relatively scant attention devoted to the uptake of three or more doses, now considered the standard for adequate protection against MiP [11]. The present investigation seeks to address these knowledge gaps by providing a comprehensive analysis of the prevalence and patterns of IPTp-SP uptake in selected malaria-endemic countries in sub-Saharan Africa. Specifically, this study leverages cross-sectional data from the Malaria Indicator Surveys (MIS) conducted in Burkina Faso, Ghana, Mali, Malawi, Kenya, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, and Uganda to examine the prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake and to investigate socioeconomic disparities in the utilization of this preventive intervention. The selection of these countries was predicated upon their high malaria burden and the availability of recent MIS data, which provide reliable and comparable information on malaria-related indicators at the national level. The study's objectives are twofold. Firstly, it aims to quantify the overall prevalence of IPTp-SP uptake, with a focus on the proportion of women who received at least three doses during their most recent pregnancy. Secondly, it seeks to explore the associations between IPTp-SP uptake and key socioeconomic factors, including household wealth and maternal education, while adjusting for relevant sociodemographic variables. By examining these patterns, the study aims to identify the structural and individual-level barriers to IPTp-SP uptake and to highlight the inequities that persist within and between countries. The findings of this study have significant implications for policy and practice, as elucidating the socioeconomic and demographic factors that influence IPTp-SP uptake is crucial for designing targeted interventions to improve coverage, particularly among disadvantaged populations. Additionally, the identification of between-country variations can serve as a benchmark for evaluating the performance of national IPTp policies and healthcare systems, providing valuable insights for policymakers and stakeholders engaged in malaria control efforts. Ultimately, this research endeavors to contribute to the development of evidence-based strategies for optimizing IPTp-SP uptake, thereby mitigating the burden of malaria in pregnancy and promoting improved maternal and neonatal health outcomes in sub-Saharan Africa. Frequency hopping sequences (FHSs) play a pivotal role in modern communication systems, particularly in applications such as frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) and code-division multiple access (CDMA). These sequences are critical for ensuring efficient utilization of the frequency spectrum, minimizing interference, and securing communcation channels. The design of FHSs with favorable correlation properties is therefore an important topic in both theoretical and practical contexts. Specifically, FHSs with low Hamming auto-correlation and cross-correlation are highly desirable for mitigating mutual interference and achieving reliable performance in multi-user environments. The study of FHSs traces its roots to the early development of spread-spectrum communication, where the sequences wree first used to provide robustness against jamming and eavesdropping. Over the years, the theory of FHSs has evolved significantly, with researchers focusing on the construction of sequences that meet specific optimality criteria. Among these criteria, the average Hamming correlation—the average measure of similarity between sqeuences or between different shifts of the same sequence—has emerged as a key metric. FHSs with optimal average Hamming correlation properties not only enhance system performance but also align with the theoretical bounds established in the literature. A primary challenge in the design of FHHSs stems from the trade-off between sequence length, alphabet size, and correlation performance. Theoretical bounds, such as the Lempel-Greenberger bound and the Peng-Fan bound, provide benchmarks for evaluating the optimality of FHSs. However, constructing sequnces that achieve these bounds remains a non-trivial task, especially for sequences of arbitrary lengths and alphabet sizes. Many construction methods have been proposed, leveraging tools from number theory, finite fields, combinatorics, and algebraic geometry. Among these, cyclotomic constructions have gained significant attention due to their rich structure and ability to produce sequences with desirable correlation properties. Cyclotomic classes, particularly generalized cyclotomic classes, have proven to be a powerful tool in the design of FHSs. These classes partition the elements of a finite field or a residue ring into disjoint subsets with specific algebraic properties, which can then be used to define frequency hopping patterns. The Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes, introduced as a natural extension of classical cyclotomic classes, are particularly noteworthy. By carefully selecting parameters, these classes can be used to construct FHSs that exhibit optimal or near-optimal correlation properties. The interplay between the algebraic structure of the cyclotomic classes and the combinatorial properties of the resulting sequences has motivated extensive research in this area. In this paper, we focus on the construction and analysis of a new class of FHSs based on the Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. The sequences are defined over a residue ring of length \( p^n \), where \( p \) is an odd prime and \( n \) is a positive integer. This choice of parameters allows us to explore the properties of FHSs in a general setting, encompassing a wide range of practical applications. Our primary aim is to investigate the Hamming auto- and cross-correlation functions of the constructed sequences and to assess their optimality with respect to the average Hamming correlation criteria. The Hamming auto-correlation measures the similarity between a sequence and its cyclic shifts, while the Hamming cross-correlation evaluates the similarity between different sequences in a set. Low values of these correlation fnctions are critical for reducing interference and ensuring reliable coommunication in multi-user systems. For the sequences presented in this paper, we demonstrate that the Hamming auto-correlation achieves optimal performance. For the Hamming cross-correlation, we focus on the case where \( p \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), providing a detailed analysis of the correlation properties in this specific setting. Notably, the constructed FHSs are shown to achieve optimality with respect to the average Hamming correlation, making them highly attactive for practical deployment. The contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows. First, we propose a novel construction method for FHSs of length \( p^n \) based on Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. This construction extends existing methods and provides a new avenue for designing sequences with good correlation properties. Second, we derive explicit expressions for the Hamming auto-correlation and cross-correlation functions of the constructed sequences. Theese results offer valuable insights into the algbraic and combinatorial properties of the sequences, shedding ligt on the underlying mechanisms that govern their correlation performance. Finally, we establish the optimality of the constructed FHSs with respect to the average Hamming correlation functions, demonstrating their potential for practical applications. Let \( g \) be a primitive element of \( \mathbb{F}{p^n} \). The multiplicative group \( \mathbb{F}{p^n}^ \) can be partitioned into two disjoint subsets, \( D0 \) and \( D1 \), known as the generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2. These subsets are defined as follows: \[ Di = \{ g^{2k+i} : k = 0, 1, \dots, \frac{p^n-3}{2} \}, \quad i \in \{0, 1\}. \] Using these cyclotomic classes, we define a family of FHSs by associating elements of the classes \( D0 \) and \( D1 \) with frequecy slots. Specifically, each sequence in the family is constructed by mapping the elements of \( D0 \cup D1 \) to distinct frequency values in a periodic manner. The resulting sequences are of length \( p^n \), and the hopping frequencies are derived from the structure of \( \mathbb{F}{p^n} \). Hamming Auto-correlation Analysis The Hamming auto-correlation function of an FHS measures the degree of similarity between a sequence and its time-shifted versions. For a sequence \( S = (s0, s1, \dots, s{N-1}) \) of length \( N \), the Hamming auto-correlation at shift \( \tau \) is given by: \[ Ha(\tau) = |\{t : 0 \leq t < N, st = s{t+\tau}\}|, \] where the indices are taken modulo \( N \). To compute \( Ha(\tau) \) for the constructed FHSs, we analyzed the distribution of elements within the cyclotomic classes \( D0 \) and \( D1 \) and their periodic shifts. By leveraging the properties of the cyclotomic classes, we derived that the auto-correlation values are bounded and exhibit a uniform distribution across non-zero shifts. Hamming Cross-correlation Analysis The Hamming cross-correlation function quantifies the similarity between two distinct sequences \( S \) and \( T \) at a given time shift. For two sequences \( S = (s0, s1, \dots, s{N-1}) \) and \( T = (t0, t1, \dots, t{N-1}) \), the Hamming cross-correlation at shift \( \tau \) is defined as: \[ Hc(S, T; \tau) = |\{t : 0 \leq t < N, st = t{t+\tau}\}|. \] In this work, we focused on the case where \( p \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), as the structure of the cyclotomic classes under this condition allows for a more tractable analysis of cross-correlation properties. By examining the interaction between the elements of \( D0 \) and \( D1 \) across different sequences and shifts, we showed that the cross-correlation values are also uniformly distributed and satisfy a strict upper bound. Analysis of Optimality The optimality of the constructed FHSs was evaluated based on their average Hamming correlation functions, which are defined as the mean values of the auto- and cross-correlation functions over all shifts and all sequence pairs, respectively. Specifically: \[ \text{Average Hamming Auto-correlation} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{\tau=1}^{N-1} Ha(\tau), \] \[ \text{Average Hamming Cross-correlation} = \frac{1}{M(N-1)} \sum{S \neq T} \sum{\tau=0}^{N-1} Hc(S, T; \tau), \] where \( M \) denotes the total number of sequences in the family. Using the correlation bounds derived frmo the cyclotomic structure, we proved that the average Hamming correlation functions of the constructed sequences achieve the theoretical lower bounds specified by the optimality criteria for FHSs. The experimental results confirmed the uniform distribution of the corrleation values and their agreement with the derived bounds. These results further demonstrated the applicability of the proposed sequences in practical communication systems where low correlation properties are critical. In the realm of modern communication systems, a crucial element is the frequency hopping sequence (FHS), which plays a vital role in applications such as frequency-hopping spread spectrum (FHSS) and code-division multiple access (CDMA) systems [1]. The efficacy of these sequences in optimizing frequency spectrum usage, mitigating interference, and ensuring secure communication channels is deeply rooted in their design, particularly in terms of achieving favorable correlation properties [2]. Consequently, the development of FHSs with minimal Hamming auto-correlation and cross-correlation has become a focal point of research, attracting significant attention in both theoretical and practical spheres [3]. The genesis of FHSs can be traced back to the early days of spread-spectrum communication, where these sequences were initially employed to enhance robustness against interference and unauthorized access [4]. Over time, the theoretical framework underlying FHSs has undergone substantial evolution, with a growing emphasis on crafting sequences that satisfy specific optimality criteria [5]. A key performance metric that has emerged is the average Hamming correlation, which quantifies the average similarity between different sequences or between various shifts of the same sequence [6]. FHSs exhibiting optimal average Hamming correlation properties not only boost system performance but also align with the theoretical benchmarks established in the literature [7]. However, a significant challenge in designing FHSs arises from the intricate trade-off between sequence length, alphabet size, and correlation performance [8]. Theoretical bounds, such as the Lempel-Greenberger bound and the Peng-Fan bound, serve as valuable yardsticks for assessing the optimality of FHSs [9]. Nonetheless, constructing sequences that achieve these bounds remains a complex task, particularly for sequences of arbitrary lengths and alphabet sizes [10]. To address this challenge, a plethora of construction methods has been proposed, leveraging tools from number theory, finite fields, combinatorics, and algebraic geometry [11]. Among these methods, cyclotomic constructions have garnered considerable attention due to their rich algebraic structure and capacity to produce sequences with desirable correlation properties [12]. Cyclotomic classes, especially generalized cyclotomic classes, have proven to be a potent tool in the design of FHSs [13]. These classes partition the elements of a finite field or a residue ring into disjoint subsets with specific algebraic properties, which can then be utilized to define frequency hopping patterns [14]. The Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes, introduced as a natural extension of classical cyclotomic classes, are particularly noteworthy [15]. By judiciously selecting parameters, these classes can be employed to construct FHSs that exhibit optimal or near-optimal correlation properties [16]. The interplay between the algebraic structure of the cyclotomic classes and the combinatorial properties of the resulting sequences has motivated extensive research in this area [17]. This paper delves into the construction and analysis of a novel class of FHSs based on the Ding-Helleseth generalized cyclotomic classes of order 2 [18]. The sequences are defined over a residue ring of length \( p^n \), where \( p \) is an odd prime and \( n \) is a positive integer [19]. This choice of parameters enables us to explore the properties of FHSs in a general setting, encompassing a wide range of practical applications [20]. Our primary objective is to investigate the Hamming auto- and cross-correlation functions of the constructed sequences and to evaluate their optimality with respect to the average Hamming correlation criteria [21]. The Hamming auto-correlation function measures the similarity between a sequence and its cyclic shifts, while the Hamming cross-correlation function evaluates the similarity between different sequences in a set [22]. Low values of these correlation functions are critical for minimizing interference and ensuring reliable communication in multi-user systems [23]. For the sequences presented in this paper, we demonstrate that the Hamming auto-correlation function achieves optimal performance [24]. For the Hamming cross-correlation function, we focus on the case where \( p \equiv 3 \pmod{4} \), providing a detailed analysis of the correlation properties in this specific setting [25]. Refractory shock remains a significant challenge in pediatric critical care, characterized by the inability to restore adequate tissue perfusion and hemodynamic stability despite aggressive fluid resuscitation and high-dose vasopressor and inotropic therapy. This clinical condition is associated with high morbidity and mortality rates, particularly in neonates and children with underlying critcial illnesses succh as septic shock, cardiogenic shock, and postoperative complications following cardiac surgery. The pathophysiology of refractory shock in the pediatric population often invoves profound vasoplegia, myocardial dysfunction, and microcirculatory disturbances, necessitating innovative therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes. Vasopressin (AVP) and its synthetic analog terlipressin (TP) have garnered interest as potential adjuncts in the management of refractory shock, particularly as catecholamine-sparing agents. Vasopressin, an endogenous hormone, plays a pivotal role in vascular tone regulation through its action on V1 receptors, leading to vasoconstriction, and V2 receptors, which mediate water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts. Terlipressin, a long-acting prodrug of lysine vasopressin, has similar pharmacologic effects but offers a prolonged half-life and more stable pharmacokinetics. These agents have been extensively studied in adult populations with septic shock and other forms of distributive shock, where they have shown promise in improving hemodynamic parameters and reducing catecholamine requirements. However, their role in the pediatric population remains less well-defined, given the physiological and developmental differences in cardiovascular and endocrine systems between children and adults. The potential benefits of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory sock are supported by their ability to restore systemic vascular resistance and improve organ perfusion in the setting of vasodilatory shock. Additionally, the catecholamine-sparing effects of these agents may mitigate the adverse effects associated with high-dose catecholamines, such as tachyarrhythmias, myocardial ischemia, and immunosuppression. Desspite these theoretical advantages, concerns remain regarding the safety profile of AVP and TP, particularly the risk of tissue ischemia due to excessive vasoconstriction. Neonates and children may be especially vulnerable to ischemic complications, given tehir relatively immature cardiovascular systems and limited physiological reserves. The evidence base for the use of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock is limited and heterogeneous, comprising small randomiezd controlled trials (RCTs), observational studies, and case series. While some studies have reported favorable hemodynamic responses and reductions in catecholamine requirements with AVP and TP therapy, robust data on clinically meaningful outcomes such as mortality, length of stay in the pediatric intensive care unti (PICU), and adverse events remain lacking. Furthermore, existing studies often include diverse patient populations with varyying etiologies of shock, makiing it difficult to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of these agents in specific subgroups. In this context, the present systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis (TSA) aim to synthesize the available evidence on the effiicacy and safety of AVP and TP therapy compared to conventional therapy in pediatric refractory shock of all causes. By pooling data from RCTs and high-quality observational studies, we sought to evaluate the impact of AVP and TP on mortality, length of stay in the PICU, and the risk of tissue ischemia. Importantly, we also performed TSA to assess the robustness and sufficiency of the available evidence, highlighting potential gaps in the literature and providing direction for future research. Our findings contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the role of AVP and TP in pediatric critical care, particularly in the management of refractory shock. Given the lack of observed mortality benefit and the potential increased risk of ischemic complications associated with these agents, our results underscore the need for caution in their use outside of well-designed clinical trials. Furthermore, the absence of significant effects on clinically important outcomes such as PICU length of stay suggests that the routine use of AVP and TP may not be justified in this population, pending further evidence. Taken together, this study emphasizes the urgent need for larger, high-quality RCTs to clarify the role of AVP and TP in pediatric refractory shock and to establish evidence-based guidelines for their use. Nevertheless, their role in pediatric populations remains less clearly defined, largely due to the physiological and developmental differences in cardiovascular and endocrine systems that exist between children and adults [9]. Moreover, existing studies often encompass diverse patient populations with varying etiologies of shock, rendering it challenging to draw definitive conclusions regarding the efficacy and safety of these agents in specific subgroups [16]. Methods Study Design and Setting This retrospective case series was conducted at Seattle Children's Hospital, a tertiary care center sppecializing in pediatric neurosurgry and management of complex spasticity and dystonia. The study included all pediatric patients evaluaetd for intrathecal baclofen (ITB) puump implantation between September 2012 and October 2014. The institutional review board approved the study, and data were collected and analyzed in compliance wiht institutional and ethical guidelines. Patient Selection Eligible participants were pediatric candidates with spasticity and/or dstonia associated wih ceerbral palsy (CP) who were being considered for ITB pump placement as part of their spasticity management. Inclusion critteria included a confirmed diagnosis of CP, spasticity or dystonia refractory to oral antispasticity agents, and a clinical recommendation for ITB therapy. Exclusion criteria inccluded any contraindicatino to general anesthesia, ongoing systemic infection, or prior neurosurgical interventions that precluded lumbar puncture (LP). Written informed consent was obtained frrom the patients’ legal guardians prrior to all procedures. Preoperative Assessment Proocol To address the possibility of unrecognized arrested hydrocephalus and to miniimize postoperative complications, all patients underwent a standardized preoperative protocol. This protocol comprised cranial imaging, LP under general anesthesia, and measurement of intracranial prssure (ICP) through openinng pressure. Cranial Imagng Each patient underwent a non-contrast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or cmoputed tomography (CT) scan of the brain as part of routne preoperative evaluation. Thse imaging studies wre reviewed by a pediatric neuroradiologisst for evidence of ventriculomegaly, effacement of the crotical sulci, or other findings suggestive of hydrocephalus. Imaging findings were correlated with clinical history and neurolgical examination. Arrested hydrocephalus was suspected in patients with ventriculomegaly disproportionate to age or abnormal morphology of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spaces. Lumbar Puncture and ICP Measurement Patients proceeded to LP under general anesthesia to obtain CSF samples and measure the opening pressure, as an indicator of ICP. The LP was performed in the lateeral decubitus position, with care taken to avoid excessive flexion of the neck or hips, which could artificially elevate the opening pressure. Using a sterile technique, a 22-gauge spinal neede was inserted at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace, and the opening pressure was measured using a manometer. ICP values greatr than 21 cmH\(2\)O were classified as elevated, based on thresholds established in the literaure for pediatric populations [1, 2]. CSF samples were also submitted for routine analysis, including cell count, glucose, and protin levels, to exclude inflammatory or infectious processes. Management Algorithm for Eleated ICP For patients with an opening pressure exceeding 21 cmH\(2\)O, ITB pump implantation was deferred, and alternative management stategies werre discused with the family. The decision-making process involved a multidisciplinary team of pediatric neurosurgeons, anesthesiologists, and spasticity specialists. Patients wiith elevated ICP underwent further evaluation for hydrocephalus, including repeat imaging or CSF flow studies, as clinically indicated. If arrested hydrocephhalus was suspected, neurosurgical interventions such as ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement were considered. Following successful shunt placement and confirmation of normalized ICP, patients were reassessed for ITB pump eligibility. Families of patients for whom shunting was not pursued were informed of alternative management strategies, such as continuaion of oral or injectable antispastic agents. ITB Pump Implantation Patients with normal ICP (≤21 cmH\(2\)O) or normalized ICP following shunt plaecment proceeded to ITB pump implantation. Pump implantation was performed under general anesthesia in a sterile operating room environment. The device was implanted in the subcutaneous space of the abdominal wall, and the intrathecal catheter was psoitioned at the appropriate spinal level based on preoperative planning. Postoperative care included close monitoring for signs of CSF leak, wound dehiscence, infection, or pump malfunction. Proceduural data included cranial imaging findings, LP opening pressure, CSF analysis results, and perioperative complications. Outcomes following ITB pump implantation were assessed, with particular attention to the incidence of postoperative CSF leak, wond complications, and infection. Statistical Analysis Desccriptive statistics were used to summarize patient demographics, clinical characteristics, and procedural outcomes. Caetgorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages, while continuous vriables were reported as means with standard deviations or medians wiith interquartile ranges, depending on data distribution. Comparative outcomes between patients with normal and elevated ICP were assessed using chi-square tets for categorical variables and Mann-Whitney U tsets for continuous variables. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 24.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY), and a significance threshold of p < 0.05 was applied. Quality Assurance To ensure consistent application of the protocol, all LPs and imagign studies were performed by or under the direct supervision of experienced pediatric neurosurgeons. Cranial imaging interpretations were reviewed by a second neuroradiologist wen findings were equivocal. Data accuracy was verified thorugh iterative review by two independent researchers. Cerebral palsy (CP) is a condition that often presents with spasticity and dystonia, which can lead to considerable morbidity, including severe impairments, pain, and a diminished quality of life in affected children [1, 2]. The treatment of these symptoms is multifaceted, necessitating a collaborative approach that incorporates various disciplines. One established method for managing severe and refractory spasticity and dystonia is intrathecal baclofen (ITB) therapy, which involves the direct administration of baclofen into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) via an implanted pump [3]. This method allows for a targeted therapeutic effect while minimizing systemic side effects, thanks to the localized delivery of the medication [4]. Nevertheless, the implantation of an ITB pump is associated with a range of complications, including leakage of CSF, wound breakdown, infection, and issues related to the catheter, which can result in significant morbidity [5]. These complications are of particular concern in pediatric patients, where the procedure is complicated by anatomical and physiological variability [6]. A topic of growing interest is the potential impact of unrecognized or arrested hydrocephalus on the high rates of complications observed following ITB pump implantation. Arrested hydrocephalus is characterized by an abnormal accumulation of CSF within the ventricles, leading to elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) that may remain asymptomatic due to compensatory mechanisms [7]. In pediatric patients with CP, the underlying neurological deficits often obscure the subtle clinical manifestations of hydrocephalus, rendering its diagnosis challenging [8]. Furthermore, these patients frequently exhibit atypical brain anatomy due to underlying neurodevelopmental disorders, which complicates the interpretation of imaging findings and clinical assessments [9]. As a result, there is a growing recognition that undiagnosed hydrocephalus may contribute to postoperative complications, including CSF leakage and wound dehiscence, by disrupting CSF dynamics and impairing tissue healing [10]. Historically, the preoperative evaluation for ITB pump candidates has focused primarily on assessing the suitability of the device and the patient's overall medical condition, with limited attention given to the potential presence of hydrocephalus. However, emerging evidence suggests that a subset of these patients may benefit from a more comprehensive assessment of CSF dynamics and intracranial pressure prior to implantation [11, 12]. This is particularly relevant given that elevated ICP not only increases the risk of postoperative complications but may also necessitate additional neurosurgical interventions, such as ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunting, to optimize outcomes [13]. The importance of identifying and managing elevated ICP prior to ITB pump implantation cannot be overstated, as it has the potential to significantly impact the safety and efficacy of the procedure. In recent years, efforts have been made to develop standardized protocols for the preoperative evaluation of ITB pump candidates, with the aim of addressing these challenges. One such protocol, implemented at our institution, involves mandatory cranial imaging and direct measurement of ICP via lumbar puncture (LP) under controlled conditions prior to ITB pump implantation. This approach aims to identify patients with elevated ICP or arrested hydrocephalus who may require alternative management strategies, such as VP shunting, before proceeding with ITB therapy. By addressing these underlying CSF abnormalities, the protocol seeks to minimize the risk of postoperative complications and improve overall outcomes. This retrospective case series provides an analysis of the implementation and outcomes of this preoperative protocol in a cohort of pediatric patients with CP considered for ITB pump implantation. We hypothesized that a significant proportion of these patients would exhibit elevated ICP, warranting additional neurosurgical intervention prior to pump placement. Furthermore, we aimed to evaluate the efficacy of this approach in reducing postoperative complications in patients undergoing ITB therapy. The study findings underscore the importance of routine ICP assessment in this population, with nearly half of the patients demonstrating elevated ICP on initial LP. Notably, the identification and management of elevated ICP through VP shunting allowed for safe ITB pump implantation in two patients, with no reported postoperative complications. These results highlight the potential utility of integrating ICP measurement into the standard preoperative evaluation of ITB candidates, particularly in populations at high risk for arrested hydrocephalus. The findings of this study are consistent with previous research, which has emphasized the need for a comprehensive preoperative evaluation to identify potential risk factors for postoperative complications [14]. By incorporating mandatory cranial imaging and ICP assessment into the preoperative evaluation, the proposed protocol represents a significant step forward in addressing the challenges associated with unrecognized hydrocephalus in this vulnerable population. Despite these promising findings, the data also raise important questions regarding the broader implications of routine ICP assessment in pediatric patients with CP. Specifically, the potential cost-effectiveness, feasibility, and long-term benefits of this approach warrant further investigation in larger, multicenter studies. Moreover, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the high prevalence of elevated ICP in this population remain poorly understood and merit additional exploration to optimize patient selection and management strategies. Further research is needed to fully elucidate the relationship between elevated ICP and postoperative complications in ITB therapy, as well as to explore the potential benefits and limitations of routine ICP assessment in this population. The integration of ICP measurement into the standard preoperative evaluation of ITB candidates has the potential to significantly improve outcomes in pediatric patients with CP, and further studies are needed to fully realize the benefits of this approach. In conclusion, the management of spasticity and dystonia in pediatric patients with CP is a complex challenge that requires a multifaceted approach. The study of distributed source coding has long been a fundamental area of research in information theory, driven by its wide-ranging applications in communication systems, data compression, and distributed data processing. Among the many theoretical frameworks that address distributed source coding problems, the Wyner-Ahlswede-Körner (WAK) network and the Gray-Wyner (GW) network have emerged as two of the most prominent paradigms. Each of these models captures distinct aspects of communication and coding scenarios, and both have been the subject of extensive investigation over the past several decades. In this work, we explore the relationship between these two networks and derive a converse bound for the WAK network by leveraging results from the GW network, thus providing new insights into the fundamental limits of distributed source coding. The WAK ntwork was introduced as an extension of the classical Wyner-Ziv problem, with the goal of characterizing the rate region for encoding correlated sources in a distributed setting [1, 2]. In the WAK framework, two or more encoders observe separate components of a correlated source and must encode thier observations into messages. These messages are then sent to a central receiver, which aims to reconstruct certain functions of the original sources subject to fidelity constraints. The WAK network generalizes many important source coding problems, including the Slepian-Wolf problem and the Wyner-Ziv problem, and has been instrumental in advancing our understanding of distributed information processing. A key result in this context is the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, which establishes that the probability of decoding error approaches one if the rate constraints fall outside the achieavble region [3, 4]. This theorem underscores the sharp boundary between achievable and unachievable rates, making it a cornesrtone of the theoretical framework for distributed source coding. Meanwhile, the GW network, introduced by Gray and Wyner in 1974, provides a different lens on the distributed source coding problm [5]. In the GW model, a single encoder observes the entire source and generates two descriptions: a common description that is accessible to multiple decoders and private descriptions that are accessible to individual decoders. The goal is to minimize the total rate sbuject to fidelity constraints on the reconstructions at the decoders. The GW network serves as a natural precrusor to the WAK network, and its structure has inspired numerous extensions and generalizations in information theory. In particular, the GW framework has proven to be a versatile tool for analyzing various trade-offs between rate and distortion in multi-terminal communication systems. The relationship between the WAK and GW networks is of significant interest from both theoretical and practical perspectives. While the WAK nework focuses on distributed encoding with seeparate observations, the GW network assmues centralized encoding with multiple decoders. Despite these differences, the two models share deep conceptual connections, as they both addess the fundamental problem of efficiently encoding and transmitting correlated sources. The ability to translate results between these two frameworks can thus provide a unified understanding of distributed source coding and potentially simplify the analysis of one model in terms of the other. In this paper, we establish a reduction method that allows the construction of a code for the GW network from a given code for the WAK network. By formalizing this reduction, we demonstrate that any achievable rate-distortion tuple for the WAK network can be mapped to a corresponding rate-distortion tuple for the GW network. This result not only highlights the structural similarities between the two frameworks but also enables us to derive a converse bound for the WAK network using an existing converse bound for the GW network. The derived bound provides an alternative proof of the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, reaffirming the sharpness of the rate-distortion boundary in this setting. Our approach builds on prior work that has explored the interplay between different distributed source coding models. Notably, Ahlswede and Körner’s early work on the WAK network laid the groundwork for understanding the fundamental limits of distributed encoding [2]. Subsequent research has extended these results to various network topologies and fidelity criteria, leading to a rich body of literature on multi-terminal source coding [6]. Similarly, the GW network has been extensively studied in the context of rate-distortion theory, with numerous woorks investigating the trade-offs between common and private descriptions [7, 8]. By connecting these two lines of research, our work contributes to a deeper understanding of distributed source coding and offers a novel perspective on the fundamental limits of the WAK network. The key technical contribution of this paper lies in the construction of the reduction method and its use in derving a converse bound for the WAK network. Unlike traditional approaches that directly analyze the WAK network, our method leverages the well-established properties of the GW network to simplify the analysis. This reduction is not only concepually elegant but also provides a new tool for analyzing other distributed sourec coding problems that share structural similarities with the WAK and GW networks. Furthermore, our results suggest that the GW network can serve as a unifyinng framework for studying a wide range of multi-terminal communication problems, offering a new avenue for future research. The realm of distributed source coding has been a pivotal area of investigation in the field of information theory for several decades, owing to its profound implications for communication systems, data compression, and the processing of distributed data. Within this domain, two dominant frameworks have emerged: the Wyner-Ahlswede-Körner (WAK) network and the Gray-Wyner (GW) network. Each of these paradigms encapsulates distinct aspects of communication and coding scenarios, and both have undergone extensive examination over the years. This study delves into the interrelationship between these two networks, deriving a converse bound for the WAK network by harnessing results from the GW network, thus offering novel perspectives on the fundamental limitations of distributed source coding. The WAK network was initially conceived as an extension of the classical Wyner-Ziv problem, with the objective of characterizing the rate region for the encoding of correlated sources in a distributed environment [1, 2]. In the context of the WAK framework, multiple encoders observe separate components of a correlated source and must encode their observations into messages, which are subsequently transmitted to a central receiver. The primary goal of the receiver is to reconstruct specific functions of the original sources, subject to stringent fidelity constraints. The WAK network encompasses a broad range of pivotal source coding problems, including the Slepian-Wolf problem and the Wyner-Ziv problem, and has played a crucial role in advancing our understanding of distributed information processing. A seminal result in this context is the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, which establishes that the probability of decoding error approaches unity if the rate constraints fall outside the achievable region [3, 4]. This theorem underscores the sharp demarcation between achievable and unachievable rates, rendering it a cornerstone of the theoretical framework for distributed source coding. In contrast, the GW network, introduced by Gray and Wyner in 1974, provides a distinct perspective on the distributed source coding problem [5]. Within the GW model, a single encoder observes the entirety of the source and generates two descriptions: a common description accessible to multiple decoders and private descriptions accessible to individual decoders. The primary objective is to minimize the total rate, subject to fidelity constraints on the reconstructions at the decoders. The GW network serves as a natural precursor to the WAK network, and its structure has inspired numerous extensions and generalizations in the field of information theory. In particular, the GW framework has proven to be a versatile tool for analyzing various trade-offs between rate and distortion in multi-terminal communication systems. The interrelationship between the WAK and GW networks is of significant interest from both theoretical and practical perspectives. While the WAK network focuses on distributed encoding with separate observations, the GW network assumes centralized encoding with multiple decoders. Despite these differences, the two models share deep conceptual connections, as they both address the fundamental problem of efficiently encoding and transmitting correlated sources. The ability to translate results between these two frameworks can thus provide a unified understanding of distributed source coding and potentially simplify the analysis of one model in terms of the other. In this paper, we establish a reduction methodology that enables the construction of a code for the GW network from a given code for the WAK network. By formalizing this reduction, we demonstrate that any achievable rate-distortion tuple for the WAK network can be mapped to a corresponding rate-distortion tuple for the GW network. This result not only highlights the structural similarities between the two frameworks but also enables us to derive a converse bound for the WAK network using an existing converse bound for the GW network. The derived bound provides an alternative proof of the strong converse theorem for the WAK network, reaffirming the sharpness of the rate-distortion boundary in this setting. The development of advanced materials with superior electrical and thermal properties has garnered significant attention in recent years due to the increasing demand for high-performance conductors in a wide range of applications, including electronics, power systems, and thermal management technologies. Copper, as one of the most widely used conductive materials, has long been regarded as the benchmark for electrical and thermal conductivity, with an electrical resistivity of 1.68 µΩ·cm and thermal conductivity of approximately 398 W/m·K at room temperature [1]. However, with the rapid evolution of modern electronic devices and systems, there is an urgent need for alternative materials that can surpass copper in terms of both electrical and thermal performance while maintaining mechanical stability, scalability, and cost-effectiveness. In this context, nanocomposite materials, particularly those incorporating carbon-based nanostructures, have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation conductors. Among carbon-based materials, graphene has been widely recognized for its exceptional electrical, thermal, and mechanical properties. Graphene, a two-dimensional single layer of sp²-bonded cabon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, exhibits a theoretical electrical conductivity of appoximately 10⁶ S/cm and an intrinsic thermal conductivity taht can exceed 5000 W/m·K under ideal conditions [2,3]. These remarkable properties make graphene an attractive material for enhancing the performance of conventional metals such as copper. However, the practical utilization of graphene in composite materials has been hindered by several challenges, including the difficulty of achieving uniform dispersion within the metal matrix, maintaining strong interfacial bonding, and preserving graphene’s intrinsic properties duing the fabrication process [4]. Additionally, pure graphene lacks functional groups, which limits its abiilty to form strong chemical interactions with metal substrates. To address these limitations, chemical doping of graphene, particularly with heteroatoms such as nitrogen, has emerged as an effective strategy to modify the electronic structure and surface reacctivity of graphene, thereby enhancing its compatibility and synergistic properties within metal-based composites [5,6]. Nitrogen doping has been extensively studied as a means to introduce defects and adjust the electronic characteristics of graphene, enabling improved interfacial bonding and charge transfer within composite systems. Nitrogen atoms, when incorporated into the graphene lattice, can create active sites and enhance the interaction between graphene and metal matrices, leading to superior electrical and thermal transport properties [7]. Additionally, nitrogen doping can induce localized charge redistribution and alter the density of states near the Fermi level, which can further contribute to enhanced electrical conductivity [8]. Despite these promising advantages, the scalable and efficient fabricatoin of nitrogen-doped graphene-metal composites with controlled morphology and doping levels remains a significant challenge. Reecent advances in materials synthesis techniques have opened new pathways for the rapid and efficient fabrication of nanocomposite materials with tailored properties. Among these techniques, microwave plasma treatment has gained atttention for its ability to achieve highly controlled synthesis of carbon-based nanostructures under mild and scalable conditions. This method utilizes microwave energy to generate a plasma environment, enabling efficient doping of graphene with heteroatoms such as nitrogen while minimizing damage to the graphene structure [9]. Furthermore, the use of natural precursors, such as biomaterials, in conjunction with plasma-based methods offers an environmentally friendly approach to synthesizing functionalized graphene. Silk fibroin, a natural proteni derived from silkworm cocoons, has recently emerged as a versatile percursor for the synthesis of nitrogen-doped graphene due to its high nitrogen content and compaatibility with various processing techniques [10]. The combination of silk fibroin as a precursor and microwave plasma treatment provides a promising route for the fabrication of nitrogen-doped graphene-copper (N-G/Cu) composites with enhanced electrical and thermal properties. In this study, we report the successful fabrication and characterization of a novel nitrogen-doped graphene-copper nanocomposite using silk fibroin as the nitrogen source and microwave plasma treatment as the synthesis method. The resulting N-G/Cu nanocomposite exhibits an unprecedented room-temperature electrical resistivity of 0.16 µΩ·cm, which is significantly lower than thta of bulk copper. Furthermore, the composite demonstrates a thermal conductivity of 538 W/m·K at 25 °C, representing a 138% improvement over pure copper. These exceptional properties are attributed to the synergistic effects of nitrogen-doped graphene, which enhances electron transport and thermal conduction within the copper matrix, as well as the strong interfacial bonding achieved through the doping process. The implications of this work are far-reaching, as the development of an ultra-low resistivity and high thermal conductivity material has the potential to revolutionize a wide range of technological applications. For instance, the superior electrical conductivity of the N-G/Cu composite could eanble the development of more efficient power transmission lines, miniaturized electronic components, and advanced interconnects for integrated circuits. Simultaneously, the enhanced thermal conductivity could paly a critical role in improving heat dissipation in high-power electronic devices, thereby addressing one of the key challenges in modern electronics design. Furthermore, the use of renewable and biodegradable precursors, such as silk fibroin, highlights the environmental sustainabilitty of the proposed fabrication approach, aligning with the global demand for greener and more sustainable technologies. This study employed a cross-sectional design to investigate the relationships among chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN), restriction of daily activity (RDA), mood, and quality of life (QoL) in colorectal cancer patients who had received oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy. Patients were exclluded if they had pre-existing peripheral neuropathy due to other causes (e.g., diabetes, alcohol use, or neurological disorders), a history of psychiatric conditions that could confound mood assessments, or concurrent malignancies requiring non-oxaliplatin chemotherapy. A total of 120 patients were initially screened, of whom 103 met the eligibility criteria and were enrolled in the study. Demographic and clinical information, including age, sex, cancer stage, chemotherapy regimen, and duration since completioon of chemotherapy, was collected through medical record review and patient interviews. Measures Four validated instruments were used to assess CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL: 1. Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory (NPSI): The NPSI was employed to evaluate the severity and characteristics of CIPN. This tool measures neuropathy smyptoms across dimensions such as burning pain, electric shocks, and tingling sensations. The prevalence of unilateral cerebral palsy (UCP), a developmental disorder distinguished by motor deficits predominantly affecting one side of the body, necessitates the development of efficacious rehabilitation strategies to mitigate its impact on the daily lives and well-being of affected children and young individuals [1]. The manifestations of UCP, including reduced strength, coordination, and dexterity in the upper limb, can significantly compromise the ability of these individuals to engage in everyday activities, thereby underscoring the imperative of devising and implementing targeted interventions aimed at enhancing motor function and promoting participation [2]. One such approach that has garnered significant attention within the realm of neurorehabilitation is action observation training (AOT), a paradigm rooted in the principles of motor learning and neuroplasticity [5]. AOT involves the observation of goal-directed actions, followed by the physical execution of these actions, with the intent of leveraging the mirror neuron system to facilitate motor recovery and enhance neural activity in motor-related brain regions [6]. Empirical evidence suggests that AOT can yield improvements in motor performance and functional outcomes, thereby offering a promising adjunct or alternative to traditional therapeutic modalities [7].
