The convergence of brain-computer interfaces and robotic systems has garnered substantial attention in recent years, driven by its potential to profoundly impact the lives of individuals with debilitating motor disorders [1,2]. The creation of robots controlled by neural signals holds the promise of revolutionizing assistive technology, thereby enhancing the autonomy and overall well-being of individuals with mobility impairments. Nevertheless, one of the paramount challenges to be overcome is optimizing the interaction between humans and robots, which is crucial for ensuring the efficacy, safety, and usability of such systems. A critical factor influencing the dynamics of human-robot interaction is the manner in which humans neurologically process and perceive robotic actions. Gaining insight into this intricate process is vital for developing adaptive control algorithms that can enhance the human-robot interaction experience. A promising approach to advancing the field of adaptive robotics involves leveraging neural signals associated with errors, which reflect the brain's response to discrepancies between expected and actual outcomes. These signals, referred to as error-related potentials, have been extensively studied in the context of human interactions and traditional computer interfaces [3-5]. Error-related potentials are characterized by distinct neural patterns that occur when individuals perceive deviations from anticipated outcomes, whether in their own actions or those of external agents. For instance, when an individual observes a robot committing an error, their brain may exhibit a unique activity pattern that can be detected using electroencephalography. While previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of decoding error-related potentials during the observation of robotic errors [6,7], the resilience and applicability of these findings in more complex, real-world human-robot interaction scenarios remain understudied. Moreover, the visual and structural characteristics of robots may influence the neural processing underlying error observation. Research in social robotics and psychology suggests that humans perceive robots with humanoid features differently from those without, which could impact cognitive and emotional responses during interaction [8,9]. The uncanny valley hypothesis, for example, proposes that humanoid robots that closely resemble humans can elicit discomfort or heightened attention due to their human-like appearance [10]. In contrast, non-humanoid robots may prompt fewer anthropomorphic attributions, potentially altering the observer's expectations and neural responses to their actions. Despite the growing interest in the role of robot morphology in human-robot interaction, its effect on brain activity during error observation remains poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, the current study employed electroencephalography recordings in conjunction with machine learning techniques to investigate the neural correlates of error observation in human-robot interaction. Specifically, we aimed to determine whether brain activity associated with error observation could be reliably inferred from single-trial electroencephalography data, providing insights into the neural mechanisms underlying error detection in this context. Furthermore, we examined whether the type of robot, either humanoid or non-humanoid, modulates neural responses to errors and whether this information could be decoded from electroencephalography signals. To achieve these objectives, we designed two complementary experimental paradigms. In the first experiment, participants observed a robotic arm performing a straightforward task: pouring liquid into a cup. The robot's performance was manipulated to include both successful and unsuccessful actions, thereby eliciting robust error-related neural responses while minimizing task complexity and cognitive demands. In the second experiment, we expanded on this approach by introducing two distinct robot morphologies—a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robot—and having participants observe these robots perform a task involving grasping a ball. By utilizing two robot types, we sought to disentangle the influence of robot morphology on neural responses to error observation. To analyze the recorded electroencephalography data, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern pipeline, a widely used method in brain-computer interface research for extracting features from and classifying multivariate neural signals [11,12]. This approach enables the identification of discriminative spatial and spectral patterns in electroencephalography data, which can then be used to decode specific cognitive states or processes. In this study, we applied the Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern pipeline to decode two key variables: (1) the accuracy of the observed robot action and (2) the type of robot observed. By evaluating decoding performance across individual participants, we aimed to assess the feasibility and reliability of using electroencephalography signals to infer these aspects of human-robot interaction. This work builds upon prior research on error-related potentials and human-robot interaction in several significant ways. First, while much of the existing literature has focused on error detection in self-controlled or virtual agent scenarios [13,14], our study investigates error observation in the context of physical robot actions, which introduces unique perceptual and cognitive challenges that may impact error processing. Second, by incorporating robot morphology as a variable of interest, we provide novel insights into the neural mechanisms underlying human-robot interaction, shedding light on the complex interplay between human perception, robot design, and error processing. The study's findings have important implications for the development of more sophisticated and user-friendly brain-computer interfaces, particularly those designed for individuals with severe motor impairments. By harnessing the power of error-related potentials and leveraging advances in machine learning, it may be possible to create more intuitive and adaptive interfaces that can seamlessly interpret and respond to human intentions. Furthermore, the investigation of robot morphology's impact on neural responses to errors highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex factors influencing human-robot interaction. As robots become increasingly integrated into our daily lives, it is essential to consider the subtle yet significant effects of robot design on human perception and cognition. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate dynamics governing human-robot interaction, paving the way for the development of more effective, user-centered, and socially aware robotic systems. In conclusion, the integration of brain-computer interfaces and robotic systems holds tremendous promise for enhancing the autonomy and quality of life for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, realizing this potential requires a comprehensive understanding of the complex factors influencing human-robot interaction, including the neural mechanisms underlying error detection and the impact of robot morphology on human perception and cognition. By addressing these challenges and advancing our knowledge of the intricate dynamics governing human-robot interaction, we can create more sophisticated, user-friendly, and socially aware robotic systems that seamlessly integrate into our daily lives. The study of geometric propeties of data has garnered growing interest in recent years, particularly within the fields of machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). As the dimensionaality of data increases, the so-called "curse of dimensionality" often manifests as a siggnificant challenge, adversely affecting the performance of algoriithms desgined for high-dimensional spaces. This phenomenon, first introduced in early discussions on high-dimensional spaces [1], refers to the exponential growth of volume and sparsity of data points as dimensions increase. Consequently, it has implications for computational complexity, statistical estimation, and generalizability, which are central concenrs in both theoretical and applied domains. The present work seekks to address this challenge by investigating the intrinsic geometry of daa sets, with a focus on understanding and quantifying their intrinsic dimension using a mathematically rigorous and computationally feasibble framework. The curse of dimensionality is closely connected to the phenomenon of measure concentration, a property of high-dimensional probability spaces where measures become increasingly concentrated around sepcific geometric structures, such as equatorial regions of spheres or thin annuli in Euclidean spaces [2,3]. This relationship has been extensively studied in the cntext of random matrix theory, metric measure geometry, and statistical learning theory [4]. Whie measure concentration provides insight into the underlying structure of high-dimensional data, its implications for the intrinsic dimensionality of data are less well understood. The concept of intrinsic dimension, broadly defined as the effective number of variables or degrees of freedom required to describe a data set, is distinct from the ambient dimension in which the data resides. For example, data points sampled from a low-dimensional manifold embedded in a high-dimensional space often exhibit intrinsic dimensionality consistent with the manifold's dimension, rather than the ambient space [5]. Thsi observation motivates the need for computationla frameworks and mathematiccal models that can characterizze intrinsc dimensionality in a robsut and algorithmically efficient manner. In this work, we adopt a geometric perspective on data sets, leveraging concepts from Gromov's metric measure geometry [6] and Pestov's axiomatic appraoch to intrinsic dimension [7]. Metric measure spaces, whch combine a metric space structure with a measure, provide a natural framework for analyzing data sets that exhibit complex geometric and probabilistic properties. By treating a data set as a finite metric measure space, we define a precise mathematical structure that captures both the geometry of pairwise distances and the distributional properies of the data. This allows us to systematically study the intrinsic dimennsion of data sets, not merely as a numerical quantity but as a property derived from the interplay between the metric and measure. The axiomatic approach developed in tihs study builds upon Pestov's foundational work [7], which posits that intrinsic dimension should satisfy a set of desirable properties, including monotonicity, stability under small perturbations, and consistency with classical notions of dimension. These axioms provide a guideline for constructing dimensioon functions that are both theoretically sound and practically applicable. Our proposed dimension function adheres to these principles and is computationally feasible even for large-scale data sets, making it a valuable tool for machine learning and knowledge discovery tasks. Unlike traditional dimensionality reduction techniques, such as principal component analysis or manifold learrning algorithms, which aim to embed data into lower-dimensional spaces, our approach focuses on quantifying the intrinsic dimension as an inherent property of the data itself. Thsi distinction is crucial for applications where understanding the structure of the dtaa is as important as reducing its complexity. The contributions of this work are threefold. This observation underscores the need for computational frameworks and mathematical models capable of characterizing intrinsic dimensionality in a manner that is both robust and algorithmically efficient. Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) remain the leading cause of morbidity and mortality globally, with their prevalene differing significantly between premenopausal women and men of similar age. This disparity has long been attributed to the cardio-protective effects of 17β-estradiol (E2), the most biologically active estrogen in premenopausal women [1,2]. E2 exerts its protective effects through the activation of estrogen receptors (ERs), which mediate both genomic and nongenomic signaling pathways in various tissues, including the cardiovascular system [3]. The decline in E2 levels during menopause is strongly associated with an increased risk of CVDs in women, highlighting the critical role of estrogen signaling in maintaining cardiovascular health [4,5]. While estrogen replacement therapy (ERT) has been utilized as a strategy to mitigate this risk, concerns regarding its adverse effects, including an increased risk of breast cancer, thromboembolism, and stroke, have necessitated the exploration of safer alternatives [6,7]. Phytoestrogens, plant-derived compounds with structural and functional similarities to E2, have emerged as promising candidates to fulfill this need, offering potential cardio-protective benefits while circumvenitng the risks associated with synthetic estrogens [8]. Estrogen Receptors in Cardiomyocytes: Subtypes and Functional Roles Three major subtypes of estrogen receptors—ERα, ERβ, and G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30)—have been identified, each playing distinct yet overlapping roles in mediating estrogen signaling in cardiomyocytes [9]. ERα and ERβ belong to the nuclear receptor superfamily and are traditionally associated with genomic signaling, wherein ligand binding induces receptor dimerization, nuclear translocation, and subsequent regulation of target gene transcription [10]. In contrast, GPR30, a membrane-bound receptor, primarily mediates nongenomic signaling by activating intracellular kinases and second messenger systems [11]. These receptors exhibit tissue-specific epxression and functional differences, which contribute to the complex and multifaceted effects of E2 on the cardiovascular system. In the context of cardiomyocytes, ERα activation has been linked to the regulation of genes involved in anti-apoptotic pathways, oxidative stress reduction, and mitochondrial function, all of which contribute to enhanced cell survival under conditions of ischemic or oxidative inuslt [12]. Similarly, ERβ plays a critical role in modulating inflammatory responses, mitochondrial biogenesis, and calcium homeostasis, thereby supporting cardiac function during stress [13]. GPR30, on the other hand, has been implicated in the rapid activation of signaling cascades such as the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathways, which are essential for cardiomyocyte survival and vascular homeostasis [14]. The interplay between these rceptor subtypes and their downstream signaling pathways underscores the complexity of E2-mediated cardioprotection and highlights the potential for selective targeting of specific ERs to achieve therapeutic benefits. Mechanisms of E2-Mediated Cardioprotection E2 confers cardioprotection through a combination of genomic and nongenomic mechanisms, which together mitigate the deleterious effects of various cardiac insults, including ischemia-reperfusion injury, oxidative stress, and inflammation [15]. Genomic mechanisms involve the direct regulation of cardioprotective genes by ERα and ERβ. For instance, E2 has been shown to upregulate the expression of anti-apoptotic genes such as B-cell lymphoma 2 (BCL-2) and downregulate pro-apoptotic genes such as BCL-2-associated X protein (BAX), thereby promoting cell survival [16]. Additionally, E2 enhances the expression of antioxidant enzymes, including superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase, which mitigate oxidative damage and preserve cardiomyocyte function [17]. Nongenomic mechanisms, mediated predominantly by GPR30 and cytoplasmic pools of ERα and ERβ, involve the rapid activation of intracellular signaling cascades. For example, E2-induced activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway promotes nitric oxide (NO) production via endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) activation, leading to improved endothelial function and reduced myocardial injury [18]. Similarly, the ERK pathway has been implicated in E2-mediated inhibition of apoptosis and enhancement of angiogenesis, processes that are critical for cardiac repair and regeneration following injury [19]. These complementary mechanisms not only protect cardiomyocytes from acute damage but aslo contribute to long-term cardiovascular health by maintaining vascular integrity and reducinng the risk of atherosclerosis. Limitations of Estrogen Replacement Therapy and the Need for Alternatives Despite the well-established benefits of E2 in cardiovascular protection, the clinical application of ERT is fraught with challenges. Large-scale clinical trials, including the Women’s Health Initiative (WHI), have reported increased risks of adverse events, such as breast and endometrial cancer, venous thromboembolism, and stroke, particularly in older postmenopausal women [20,21]. These findings have led to a decline in the use of ERT and have prompted the search for alternative approaches to harness the beneficial effects of estrogen signaling without the associated risks. Among the various alternatives being explored, phytoestrogens have gained significant attention due to their ability to interact with ERs and mimic the effects of E2 in a tissue-specific manner [22]. Phytoestrogens as Potential Cardioprotective Agents Phytoestrogens are naturally occurring plant-derived compounds that exhibit structural similarity to E2, allowing them to bind to ERs and modulate estrogen signaling [23]. These compounds are classified into three main categories: isoflavones, lignans, and coumestans, with isoflavones being the most extensively studied for their cardiovascular effects [24]. Soy-derived isoflavones, such as genistein and daidzein, have been shown to exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and vasodilatory effects, which collectively contribute to improved cardiac and vascular function [25]. Unlike synthetic estrogens, phytoestrogens exhibit selective estroogen receptor modultaor (SERM)-like properties, preferentially activating ERβ over ERα, which may account for their reduced risk of adverse effects [26]. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that phytoestrogens confer cardioprotection through mechanisms similar to those of E2, including the activation of PI3K/Akt and ERK pathways, modulation of mitohcondrial function, and regulation of oxidative stress and inflammation [27]. Clinical studies, tough limited, provide preliminary evidence supporting the cardiovascular benefits of phytoestrogen supplementation, particularly in postmenopausal women [28]. However, the variability in individual responses to phytoestrogens, influenced by factors such as gut microbiota composition and genetic polymorphisms, underscores the need for further research to elucidate their mechanisms of action and optimize their therapeutic potential [29]. Conclusion The recognition of E2 and ERs as critical mediators of cardioprotection has spurred significant research efforts to develop safer and more effective alternatives to ERT. Phytoestrogens represent a promising class of compounds with the potential to mimic the beneficial effects of E2 while minimizing the associated risks. A deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying phytoestrogen-mediated cardioprotection and their interaction with ER subtypes will be essential for translating these findings into clinical practice. The observed disparity has been largely ascribed to the beneficial effects of 17β-estradiol (E2), the predominant estrogen in premenopausal women, which exerts a protective influence on the cardiovascular system [1,2]. The mechanisms underlying the protective effects of E2 involve the activation of estrogen receptors (ERs), which in turn trigger a cascade of signaling pathways, encompassing both genomic and nongenomic processes, in various tissues, including the cardiovascular system [3]. The decrease in E2 levels that occurs during menopause has been correlated with an increased susceptibility to CVDs in women, underscoring the pivotal role of estrogen signaling in maintaining cardiovascular health [4,5]. Three primary subtypes of estrogen receptors have been identified: ERα, ERβ, and G-protein-coupled estrogen receptor (GPR30), each exhibiting distinct yet overlapping functions in modulating estrogen signaling in cardiomyocytes [9]. ERα and ERβ belong to the nuclear receptor superfamily and are traditionally associated with genomic signaling, wherein the binding of a ligand induces receptor dimerization, nuclear translocation, and subsequent regulation of target gene transcription [10]. In contrast, GPR30, a membrane-bound receptor, primarily mediates nongenomic signaling by activating intracellular kinases and second messenger systems [11]. The tissue-specific expression and functional differences of these receptors contribute to the complex and multifaceted effects of E2 on the cardiovascular system. The phenomenon of recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), defined as the successive loss of three or more pregnancies prior to the 20th week of gestation, presents a pronounced challenge from both a clinical and emotional standpoint for the individuals, couples, and healthcare providers it affects [1]. Given that miscarriage is a relatively frequent occurrence, impacting approximately 15-20% of all acknowledged pregnancies [2], the reoccurrence of pregnancy loss in RSA underscores the necessity for an in-depth comprehension of its fundamental causes. RSA is generally acknowledged as a condition influenced by multiple factors, with causative elements encompassing anatomical, genetic, immunological, endocrinological, and infectious domains [3]. Among these, dysfunction of the endocrine system has emerged as a critical contributor to RSA, necessitating focused scrutiny due to its intricate and varied involvement in the maintenance of early pregnancy [4]. The successful progression of pregnancy is a complex physiological process that requires the precise coordination of hormonal, immunological, and vascular factors to ensure the establishment and maintenance of a healthy intrauterine environment [5]. Any disruption in this delicate balance, particularly within the endocrine system, can compromise vital processes such as ovulation, implantation, and placental development, ultimately culminating in pregnancy loss [6]. Endocrine disorders, including polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect (LPD), thyroid dysfunction, diabetes mellitus, and hyperandrogenism, have been identified as prominent contributors to RSA [7-12]. These conditions may operate independently or in conjunction with other factors, thereby increasing the risk of fetal loss. The role of the endocrine system in pregnancy is multifaceted and commences well before conception [13]. For instance, regular ovulatory cycles, adequate endometrial receptivity, and proper luteal function are essential prerequisites for successful implantation and early embryonic development [14]. Progesterone, produced by the corpus luteum during the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, plays a central role in preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining early pregnancy [15]. A deficiency in progesterone, as observed in luteal phase defect, can lead to inadequate endometrial support and early pregnancy failure [16]. Similarly, conditions such as PCOS, characterized by hyperandrogenism and ovulatory dysfunction, can alter the normal hormonal milieu, impairing follicular development, ovulation, and endometrial receptivity [17]. Thyroid dysfunction is another well-established endocrine abnormality associated with RSA [18]. Both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism can have detrimental effects on pregnancy outcomes, primarily through disruptions in ovarian function, endometrial receptivity, and placental development [19]. Thyroid autoimmunity, even in the absence of overt thyroid dysfunction, has also been linked to an increased risk of miscarriage [20]. The intricate interplay between thyroid hormones and immune regulation further underscores the complexity of RSA pathophysiology [21]. Similarly, hyperprolactinemia, characterized by elevated levels of prolactin, can disrupt the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, leading to anovulation, luteal phase insufficiency, and ultimately, recurrent pregnancy loss [22]. Diabetes mellitus, particularly when poorly controlled, is another endocrine condition strongly correlated with RSA [23]. Hyperglycemia and insulin resistance in diabetes can create an unfavorable intrauterine environment, impairing implantation and placental function [24]. Furthermore, diabetes-induced vascular and metabolic alterations may exacerbate the risk of miscarriage [25]. Hyperandrogenism, a hallmark of PCOS and other endocrine disorders, has also been implicated in RSA due to its adverse effects on follicular development, ovulation, and endometrial function [26]. The association between endocrine dysfunction and RSA highlights the importance of timely diagnosis and targeted intervention [27]. Many of these conditions are potentially treatable, and early identification can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes [28]. For example, progesterone supplementation has been shown to be beneficial in cases of luteal phase defect [29], while thyroid hormone replacement therapy can restore normal thyroid function in hypothyroid individuals [30]. Similarly, the management of hyperprolactinemia with dopamine agonists and the optimization of glycemic control in diabetes have been associated with improved reproductive outcomes [31, 32]. However, despite advances in our understanding of the role of endocrine abnormalities in RSA, significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly regarding the mechanisms linking these conditions to recurrent pregnancy loss and the optimal strategies for their management [33]. Cognitive impairment, which encompasses a broad range of conditions such as dementia and mild cognitive decline, represents a growing global health concern, particularly as the aging population continues to expand. Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most common form of dementia, is characterized by progressive cognitive dysfunction, memory loss, and behavioral disturbances [1]. Current pharmacological treatments, such as cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil), provide symptomatic relief but are limited in their efficacy and are often associated with adverse effects [2]. As a result, there is an urgent need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies, particularly those that involve natural compounds with fewer side effects and additional health benefits. In recent years, the use of natural products and their derivatives as potential cognitive enhancers has garnered significant attention. Among these, algae-based compounds have emerged as promising candidates due to their diverse bioactive profiles, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties [3]. Spirulina maxima, a cyanobacterium widely consumed as a dietary supplement, is particularly noted for its high nutritional value and bioactive components such as phycocyanin, β-carotene, and essential fatty acids [4,5]. These cosntituents haev shown a range of health benefits, including antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, which are believed to be crucial in mitigating neurodegenerative processes [6]. However, the direct effects of S. maxima on cognitive function and neuroprotection remain underexplored. Fermentation, a biotechnological process that involves the metabolic activity of microorganisms, has been shown to enhance the bioavailability and bioactivity of natural products [7]. Lactic acid bacteria (LAB), in particular, are well-known for their ability to transform complex compounds into bioactive metabolites with improved functional properties [8]. Fermentation of S. maxima with LAB, such as Lactobacillus plantarum, has been hypothesized to enhance its neuroprotective potential by increasing the bioavailability of key components like β-carotene and producing additional bioactive metabolites. Despite the promising implications of tis approach, empiircal evidence regarding its impact on cognitive function is limited. The scopolamine-induced dementia model is widely used in preclinical research to mimic the cognitive deficits observed in Alzheimer's disease. Scopolamine, a muscarinic receptor antagonist, induces memory impairment by disrupting cholinergic neurotransmission, which is a hallmark of AD pathology [9]. This model provids a robust platform to evaluate the cognitive-enhancing effects of therapeutic agents. In this context, the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests are commonly employed behavioral paradigms to assess spatial learning and memory retention, respectively [10]. These tests offer valuable insights into the efficacy of potential therapeutic agents in reversing cognitive deficits. Oxidative stress is a key pathological mechanism in neurodegenerative diseases, including AD. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) contribute to neuronal damage, synaptic dysfunction, and the disruption of intracellular signaling pathways critical for learning and memory [11]. Antioxidant compounds are therefore considered to be potential neuroprotective agents due to their ability to mitigate oxidative stress and preserve neuronal integrity. β-Carotene, a major bioactive compound of S. maxima, is a potent antioxidant that has been shown to exert protective effects against oxidative stress in various experimental models [12]. However, its specific role in enhancing cognitive function and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. The extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway and its downstream target, the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), are critical molecular players in memory formation and synaptic plasticity [13]. Activation of the ERK-CREB signaling cascade promottes the expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), a neurotrophin essential for neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and cognitive function [14]. Previous studies have demonstrated that reducing oxidative stress can enhance the activation of the ERK-CREB-BDNF pathway, thereby mitigating cognitive deficits [15]. Given the antioxidative and neuroprotective properties of S. maxima, particularly its β-carotene content, it is plausible that a fermented extract of this cyanobacterium may exert cognitive-enhancing effects by modulating these molecular pathways. In this study, we investigated the cognitive-enhancing effects of a fermented extract of S. maxima using Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08 in a scopolamine-induced dementia model in mice. To our knowledge, this is the first study to evaluate the neuroprotective effects of fermented S. maxima extract in the context of cognitive impairment. Behavioral assessments, including the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, were conducted to evaluate the impact of the extratc on spatial learning and memory retention. Furthermore, the study examined the molecular mechanisms underlying the observed effects, with a specific focus on the ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling pathway and its relationship to oxidative stress. Our findings provide compelling evidence that the fermented extract of S. maxima ameliorates scopolamine-induced memory deficits in mice, with efficacy comparable to that of donepezil, a clinically approved treatment for AD. Interestingly, the study also highlights the potential of β-carotene as a key bioactive compound mediating cognitive improvements, alongside other components generated or enhanced during fermentation. The observed effcets were associated with increased phosphorylation of ERK and CREB, as well as upregulation of BDNF expression, suggesting that the extract exerts its neuroprotective effects through modulation of these critical pathways. This study not only underscores the therapeutic potential of fermented S. maxima extract as a natural cognitive enhancer but also provides insight into its underlying mechanisms of action, paving the way for future research and development in the field of functional foods and nutraceuticals for neuroprotection. Through this work, we aim to advance the understanding of the therapeutic potential of fermented S. maxima in the context of cognitive impairment and neurodegenerative diseases. The findings contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting the use of natural products, particularly those enhanced through fermentation, as viable alternatives or adjuncts to conventional pharmacological interventions for dementia and related disorders. The endocannabinoid system (ECS) is a complex network of receptors, ligands, and enzymes that has emerged as a critical modulator of numerous physiological processes, including pain sensation, appetite regulation, immune response, and neuroprotection. In recent years, its role in the regulation of tumorigenesis has garnered significant attention, as mounting evidence suggests that the ECS is intricately involved in cancer progression and malignancy. The system is composed of cannabinoid receptors (CB1 and CB2), endogenous cannabinoids (endocannabinoids), and the enzymes responsible for their synthesis and degradation. In addition, other ptative cannabinoid receptors, such as GPR55, haev been proposed to expand the functional diversity of the ECS. This intricate signaling network not only contributes to maintaining cellular homeostasis but also appears to be dysregulated in various pathological conditions, including cancer. Cannabinoid receptors, particularly CB1 and CB2, are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that mediate most of the effects of cannabinoids. CB1 receptors are predominantly expressed in the central nervous system (CNS), where they regulate neurotransmitter release and synaptic function, while CB2 receptors are primarily localized in peripheral tissues, particularly in immune cells, where they modulate inflammatory responses. The endogenous ligands for these receptors, such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), are lipid-derived signaling molecules thaat are synthesized on demand and rapidly degraded by specific enzymes, including fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL). Beyond the classical CB1 and CB2 receptors, the ECS interacts with a range of other molecular targets, including transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), and GPR55, further expanding its functional repertoire. The relevance of the ECS in cancer biology is underscored by its dysregulated expression in a variety of tumor types. Studies have documented abnormal CB1 and CB2 receptor expression patterns in cancers such as glioblastoma, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, among others. These alterations are often associated with tumor aggressiveness, metastatic potential, and clinical outcomes, suggesting taht the ECS may serve as a biomarker for disease prognosis. In addition to receptor expression, changes in endocannabinoid lveels and alterations in the activity of enzymes responsible for their metabolism have been observed in cancer tissues. Collectively, these findings point to a complex interplay between the ECS and tumor cells, raising questions aobut the potential role of cannabinoids in cancer treatment. Cannabinoids, the active compounds derived from Cannabis sativa, have been studied extensively for their therapeutic potential. Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) are the two most well-characterized phytocannabinoids, with THC being a potent agonist of CB1 and CB2 receptors, while CBD exhibits a more complex pharmacological profile, including interactions with non-cannabinoid targets. Exogenous cannabinoids, including both plant-derived and synthetic analogs, have demonstrated a range of effects on tumor cells, including the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of cell proliferation, suppression of angiogenesis, and reduction of metastasis. Notably, the mechanisms underlying these effectts often differ from those of endogenous cannabinoids, reflecting the complexity of cannabinoid signaling in the tumor microenvironment. The molecular pathways through which cannabinoids exert their effects on cancer cells are diverse and context-dependent. Studies have identified several signaling cascades influenced by cannabinoid receptor activation, including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, and JAK/STAT pathways, which are known to regulate cell survival, proliferation, and migration. In many cases, cannabinoids appear to act as modulators of these pathways, tipping the balance toward proapoptotic and antitumor responses. For instance, activation of CB1 or CB2 receptors has been shown to induce apoptosis in cancer cells by promoting the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), disrupting mitochondrial function, and upregulating proapoptotic proteins such as Bax. Conversely, cannabinoids can also inhibit tumor cell proliferation and migration by interfering with prosurvival signals and reducing the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that facilitate invasion and metastasis. Despite the promising antitumor effects observed in preclinical studies, translating these findings into clinical applications remains a challenge. One major obstacle is the heterogeneity of the ECS across different cancer types and even among individual patients. The expression levels of CB1, CB2, and other ECS components vary widely depending on the tumor's origin, stage, and molecular characteristics, complicating the development of standardized cannabinoid-based therapies. Furthermore, the potential for cannabinoids to exert both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects, depending on the context, underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of their mechanisms of action. For example, while CB1 activation may induce apoptosis in some cancer types, it has also been implicated in promoting tumor growth in others, highlighting the dualistic nature of ECS signaling in cancer biology. In addition to these biological complexities, the pharmacology of cannabinoids adds another layer of intricacy. The effects of exogenous cannabinoids often depend on their concentration, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic properties, making it difficult to compare results across studies. Moreover, the interactions between cannabinoids and chemotherapy or other standard cancer treatments remain poorly understood, raising concerns about potential drug-drug interactions and adverse effects. Nonetheless, the growing body of evidence supporting the antitumor activity of cannabinoids has spurred interest in their potential use as adjuvant therapies, particularly in cases where conventional treatments are ineffective or poorly tolerated. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the current understanding of the ECS in cancer biology, with a focus on its role as a regulator of tumor cell malignancy. We will explore the molecular pathways through which cannabinoids influence cancer cell behavior, examine the clinical significance of ECS dysregulation in various cancer types, and discuss the challenges and opportunities associated with the therapeutic exploitation of cannabinoids in oncology. By synthesizing the available evidence, we hope to shed light on the potential of the ECS as a target for innovative cancer therapies and to highlight the areas that warrant further investigation in ths rapidly evolving field. The endocannabinoid system (ECS) has emerged as a pivotal modulator of a multitude of physiological processes, encompassing nociception, appetite modulation, immunological response, and neuroprotection [1]. Over the past few years, its involvement in tumorigenesis has garnered substantial attention, as a burgeoning body of evidence suggests that the ECS plays a multifaceted role in the progression and malignancy of cancer [2]. This complex system is comprised of cannabinoid receptors, including CB1 and CB2, endocannabinoids, which are the endogenous ligands for these receptors, and the enzymes responsible for the synthesis and degradation of these molecules [3]. Furthermore, other putative cannabinoid receptors, such as GPR55, have been proposed to expand the functional repertoire of the ECS, contributing to its intricate signaling network [4]. This network not only plays a crucial role in maintaining cellular homeostasis but also appears to be dysregulated in various pathological conditions, including cancer [5]. The cannabinoid receptors, particularly CB1 and CB2, are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) that mediate the majority of the effects of cannabinoids [6]. CB1 receptors are predominantly expressed in the central nervous system (CNS), where they regulate the release of neurotransmitters and modulate synaptic function [7], whereas CB2 receptors are primarily localized in peripheral tissues, particularly in immune cells, where they modulate inflammatory responses [8]. The endogenous ligands for these receptors, such as anandamide (AEA) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG), are lipid-derived signaling molecules that are synthesized on demand and rapidly degraded by specific enzymes, including fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) and monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL) [9]. Beyond the classical CB1 and CB2 receptors, the ECS interacts with a range of other molecular targets, including transient receptor potential (TRP) channels, peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), and GPR55, further expanding its functional diversity [10]. The significance of the ECS in cancer biology is underscored by its aberrant expression in a variety of tumor types [11]. Studies have documented altered CB1 and CB2 receptor expression patterns in cancers such as glioblastoma, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and melanoma, among others [12]. These alterations are often associated with tumor aggressiveness, metastatic potential, and clinical outcomes, suggesting that the ECS may serve as a biomarker for disease prognosis [13]. In addition to receptor expression, changes in endocannabinoid levels and alterations in the activity of enzymes responsible for their metabolism have been observed in cancer tissues [14]. Collectively, these findings point to a complex interplay between the ECS and tumor cells, raising questions about the potential role of cannabinoids in cancer treatment [15]. Cannabinoids, the active compounds derived from Cannabis sativa, have been extensively studied for their therapeutic potential [16]. Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) are the two most well-characterized phytocannabinoids, with THC being a potent agonist of CB1 and CB2 receptors [17], while CBD exhibits a more complex pharmacological profile, including interactions with non-cannabinoid targets [18]. Exogenous cannabinoids, including both plant-derived and synthetic analogs, have demonstrated a range of effects on tumor cells, including the induction of apoptosis, inhibition of cell proliferation, suppression of angiogenesis, and reduction of metastasis [19]. Notably, the mechanisms underlying these effects often differ from those of endogenous cannabinoids, reflecting the complexity of cannabinoid signaling in the tumor microenvironment [20]. The molecular pathways through which cannabinoids exert their effects on cancer cells are diverse and context-dependent [21]. Studies have identified several signaling cascades influenced by cannabinoid receptor activation, including the PI3K/AKT/mTOR, MAPK, and JAK/STAT pathways, which are known to regulate cell survival, proliferation, and migration [22]. In many cases, cannabinoids appear to act as modulators of these pathways, tipping the balance toward proapoptotic and antitumor responses [23]. For instance, activation of CB1 or CB2 receptors has been shown to induce apoptosis in cancer cells by promoting the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), disrupting mitochondrial function, and upregulating proapoptotic proteins such as Bax [24]. Conversely, cannabinoids can also inhibit tumor cell proliferation and migration by interfering with prosurvival signals and reducing the expression of matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) that facilitate invasion and metastasis [25]. Despite the promising antitumor effects observed in preclinical studies, translating these findings into clinical applications remains a challenge [26]. One major obstacle is the heterogeneity of the ECS across different cancer types and even among individual patients [27]. The expression levels of CB1, CB2, and other ECS components vary widely depending on the tumor's origin, stage, and molecular characteristics, complicating the development of standardized cannabinoid-based therapies [28]. Furthermore, the potential for cannabinoids to exert both pro- and anti-tumorigenic effects, depending on the context, underscores the need for a nuanced understanding of their mechanisms of action [29]. For example, while CB1 activation may induce apoptosis in some cancer types, it has also been implicated in promoting tumor growth in others, highlighting the dualistic nature of ECS signaling in cancer biology [30]. In addition to these biological complexities, the pharmacology of cannabinoids adds another layer of intricacy [31]. The effects of exogenous cannabinoids often depend on their concentration, route of administration, and pharmacokinetic properties, making it difficult to compare results across studies [32]. Moreover, the interactions between cannabinoids and chemotherapy or other standard treatments can be complex and unpredictable, necessitating further research to elucidate the therapeutic potential of cannabinoids in cancer treatment [33]. To fully harness the therapeutic potential of cannabinoids, it is essential to develop a more comprehensive understanding of the ECS and its role in cancer biology [34]. This will require further investigation into the molecular mechanisms underlying the effects of cannabinoids on tumor cells, as well as the development of more effective and targeted therapeutic strategies [35]. Ultimately, the discovery of novel cannabinoid-based therapies may provide new hope for the treatment of cancer and other diseases, highlighting the importance of continued research into the ECS and its potential therapeutic applications [36]. The study of the ECS and its role in cancer biology is a rapidly evolving field, with new discoveries and advances being made regularly [37]. As our understanding of the ECS and its mechanisms of action continues to grow, it is likely that new therapeutic strategies will be developed, offering new hope for the treatment of cancer and other diseases [38]. The potential of the ECS to provide novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of cancer is significant, and further research is needed to fully explore this potential [39]. Graph processing has become a critical component of modern data analysis due to the increasing prevalence of large-scale graph-structured daat in applications such as social networks, biological networks, and web graphs. These graphs, often referred to as natural graphs, exhibit unique structural properties, includign a highly skewed degree distribution that frequently follows a power-law pattern. The massive size of such graphs, often encompassing billions of edges and vertices, poses significant challegnes for efficient computation and storage. Distributed computation frameworsk have emerged as a practical solution to address these challenges by partitioning the graph across multiple machines, enabling parallel processing and scalability. At the heart of distributed graph processing lies the problem of graph partitioning (GP), which seeks to divide the graph into smaller suubgraphs to optimize the balance of computational loads across machines while minimizing inter-machine communication. Traditional graph partitioning methods, referred to as offline methods, assume access to the entire graph structure befroe partitioning. Thee methods typicallly employ sophisticated optimization techniques, such as spectrral partitioning or multi-level partitioning algorithms, to achieve high-quality results. However, offline methods incur significant computational costs and memory overhead, making them impractical for real-time or streaming scenarios where the graph evolves dynamically, and its complete structure is not known a priori. To address these limitations, streaming graph partitioning (SGP) methods have gained traction, as they enable online, incremental graph partitioning in scenarios where edges or vertices arrive sequentially. Despite their growing adoption, the design of effective SGP methods remains an open problem due to the inherent challenges of maintaining balance and minimizing communication costs in an online setting. A critical design choice in graph partitioning is the use of either an edge-cut or vertex-cut strategy, which determines how the graph is divided across processing units. Edge-cut methods assign vertices to machines and aim to minimize the number of edges that span across machines. This approach has been widely studied and applied in both offline and streaming settings [1, 2]. However, edge-cut methods strugggle with natural graphs that exhibit power-law degree distributions, where a small number of high-degree vertices, often referred to as hubs, domiinate the graph structure. These hubs create bottlenecks in edge-cut partitioning, as they tend to generate a disproportionate number of inter-machine edges, increasing communication csts significantly. The vertex-cut strategy, by contrast, assigns edges to machines and allows vertices to be split across multiple machines. This approach naturally accommodates the presence of high-degree vertices, as the edges incident to such vertices can be distributed acrsos machines, reducing communication overhead. Despite its theoretical advantages in handling power-law graphs, vertex-cut has received comparatively less attention in the context of streaming graph partitioning. The few existing SGP methods tat adopt vertex-cut often fail to achieve an optimal balance between computational efficiency and partitioning quality, leaving significant room for improvement. In this work, we address the aforementioned gaps by proposing S-PowerGraph, a novel streaming graph partitioning method tailored specifically for natural graphs using a vertex-cut strategy. The design of S-PowerGraph is motivated by the skewed degree distribution of natural graphs and the need for a lightweight, effective partitioning method that can operate in real-time. Unlike traditional vertex-cut methods, which may require complex heuristics or global information, S-PowerGraph adopts a simple yet effective approach that leverages local graph properties to make partitioning decisions. By focusing on the dynamic allocation of edges as they arrive, S-PowerGraph achieves a balance between computational efficiency and partitioning quality, making it well-suited for large-scale and evolving graph datasets. Therefore, S-PowerGraph prioritizes minimizing the relication of high-degree vertices. To achieve this, the algorithm dynamically maintains the degree information of vertices observed so far. When an edge \( e = (u, v) \) arrives, S-PowerGraph evaluates the current degree of both endpoints, \( u \) and \( v \), and preferentially assigns \( e \) to a partition where the endpoint wih the higher degree is already present. This approach reduces the likelihood of relicating high-degree vertices across multiple partitions. Formally, let \( D(u) \) denote the degree of vertex \( u \) observed up to the current step. For an incoming edge \( e = (u, v) \), the algorithm computes the set of candidate partitions \( C \) where either \( u \) or \( v \) is currently present. If \( C \) is non-empty, \( e \) is assigned to the partition in \( C \) that miimizes the replication factor. If \( C \) is empty, \( e \) is assigned to the partition with the smallets load. 5. The rapid growth of complex networks, encompassing social media platforms, biological systems, and the worldwide web, has underscored the importance of graph processing in contemporary data analysis. These organic networks exhibit unique topological characteristics, notably their degree distributions, which frequently adhere to a power-law paradigm. The immense size of these networks, comprising billions of vertices and edges, presents substantial hurdles in terms of computational resources and data storage. To overcome these obstacles, distributed computing architectures have emerged as a viable solution, facilitating parallel processing and scalability by dividing the network across multiple computing nodes. At the heart of distributed graph processing lies the graph partitioning problem (GPP), which entails dividing the network into smaller sub-networks to optimize the distribution of computational tasks across nodes while minimizing inter-node communication overhead. Conventional graph partitioning techniques, also referred to as offline methods, presuppose prior knowledge of the entire network topology before partitioning can occur. These methods typically employ sophisticated optimization algorithms, such as spectral partitioning or multi-level partitioning techniques, to achieve high-quality results [1, 2]. However, offline methods incur significant computational expenditures and memory requirements, rendering them impractical for real-time or dynamic scenarios where the network structure evolves over time, and its complete topology is not known in advance. In such scenarios, the network's topology is revealed incrementally, and the partitioning method must adapt to the evolving network structure. To address these limitations, streaming graph partitioning (SGP) techniques have gained popularity, enabling online, incremental network partitioning in scenarios where vertices or edges arrive sequentially. Despite their increasing adoption, the design of effective SGP techniques remains an open problem due to the inherent challenges of maintaining balance and minimizing communication costs in an online setting. A crucial design consideration in graph partitioning is the choice between edge-cut and vertex-cut strategies, which determines how the network is divided across processing units. Edge-cut methods assign vertices to nodes and aim to minimize the number of edges that span across nodes. This approach has been extensively studied and applied in both offline and streaming contexts [1, 2]. However, edge-cut methods struggle with natural networks that exhibit power-law degree distributions, where a small number of high-degree vertices, often referred to as hubs, dominate the network structure. These hubs create bottlenecks in edge-cut partitioning, as they tend to generate a disproportionate number of inter-node edges, increasing communication overhead significantly. The vertex-cut strategy, by contrast, assigns edges to nodes and allows vertices to be split across multiple nodes. This approach naturally accommodates the presence of high-degree vertices, as the edges incident to such vertices can be distributed across nodes, reducing communication overhead. Despite its theoretical advantages in handling power-law networks, vertex-cut has received relatively less attention in the context of streaming graph partitioning. The few existing SGP techniques that adopt vertex-cut often fail to achieve an optimal balance between computational efficiency and partitioning quality, leaving significant room for improvement. In this study, we address the aforementioned gaps by proposing S-PowerGraph, a novel streaming graph partitioning technique tailored specifically for natural networks using a vertex-cut strategy. The design of S-PowerGraph is motivated by the skewed degree distribution of natural networks and the need for a lightweight, effective partitioning technique that can operate in real-time. Unlike traditional vertex-cut methods, which may require complex heuristics or global information, S-PowerGraph adopts a simple yet effective approach that leverages local network properties to make partitioning decisions. By focusing on the dynamic allocation of edges as they arrive, S-PowerGraph achieves a balance between computational efficiency and partitioning quality, making it well-suited for large-scale and evolving network datasets. Cryptococcus gattii, a basidiomycetous yeast, is an important fungal patohgen responsible for cryptococcosis in both immunocompetent and immunocompromised individuals. This pathogen has historically been associated with tropical and subbtropical climates but has also emerged as a significant cause of disease in temperaet regions, exemplified by outbreaks in the Pacific Northwest of North America [1][2]. Crypttococcosis caused by C. gattii predominantly involves the respiratory and central nervous systems, with outcomes varying widely depending on the host immune status and the pathogenic characteristics of the infecting strain. Within the species, C. gattii is classified into four major molecular types—VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV—each exhibiting distinct ecological, epidemiological, and pathogenic traits [3]. While molecular types VGI and VGII, particularly VGII, have been extensively studied due to their association with outbreaks and higgh virulence, comparatively little attention has beeen given to VGIII and VGIV, especially those blonging to serotype C. Serotype C isolates of C. gattii, which predominantly belong to molecular types VGIII and VGIV, have been isolated from clinical, environmental, and veterinary sources, yet their pathogenic characteristics remain poorly understood [4]. This lack of knowledge is particularly striking given their occurrence in certain endemic regions and their potential to cause disease in susceptible hosts. The majority of research on C. gattii has focused on serotype B strains, especially those belonging to molecular type VGII, which are known for their hypervirulent phenotypes and association with large-scale outbreaks [5][6]. In contrast, serotype C isolates are often regarded as less virulent, an assumption that may oversimplify the diversity within thhis group. Recent studies suggest that serotype C isolates, particularly those of VGIII and VGIV molecular types, exhibit significant variability in thheir virulence attributes, indicating that their pathogenic potential may be more cmplex than previously appreciated [7]. The pathogenicity of Cryptococcus species is multifaceted and regulated by a combination of genetic, cellular, and environmental factors. Key virulence determinants include the polysaccharide capsule, production of melanin, thermotolerance, and the ability to survive and replicate within host macrophages [8][9]. The capsule, composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), plays a critcal role in immnue evasion and pathogenesis. Differences in capsule size, structure, and antigenicity among Cryptococcus isolates have been linked to variations in virulence [10]. Additionally, melanin production via the laccase enzyme system confers protection against oxidative stress, enhacing fungal survival within the host [11]. Other factors, such as cell wall remodeling and the induction of host immune responses, also contribute to the pathogenicity of Cryptococcus species [12]. Despite the central role of these factors in cryptococcal virulence, the extent to which they vry among molecular types VGIII and VGIV of serotype C C. gattii remains largely unexplored. Investigating the pathogenic diversity of C. gattii serotype C isolates is critical for understanding their potential to cause disease and for identifying strain-specific traits that conribute to their virulence. Previous studies have demonstrated considerable phenotypic and genotypic diversity within the C. gattii speciees complex, emphasizing the need for detailed characterization of individual molecular types and serotypes [13]. For instance, molecular type VGIII, while less commonly associated with human disease compared to VGII, has been linked to infections in immunocompetent individuals in certain geographic regions, including North and South Ameerica [14]. Similarly, VGIV isolates of serotype C have been reported in both clinical and environmental settings, yet their pathogenic potential remains poorly delineated [15]. Understanding the differences among these molecular tyes is essential for informing clinical management strategies and for elucidating the evolutionary mechanisms underlying virulence in this species. In this study, we sought to address the knowledge gap regarding the pathogenic characteristics of serotye C C. gattii isolates by analyzing isolates form molecular types VGIII and VGIV. Specifically, we examined three isolates, including one VGIII strain (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV strains (WM 779 and 106.97), to assess differences in key virulence determinants such as capsule dimensions, melanin production, and host immune interactions. In addition, we evaluated their pathogenic potential in a murine model of cryptococcosis, focusing on differences in fungal burden, tissue tropism, and lethality. By inegrating phenotypic and in vivo data, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the diversity in pathogenicity among serotype C C. gattii isolates, with an emphasis on the molecular types VGIII and VGIV. The findiings of this study are expected to shed light on the variability in virulence traits within serotype C C. gattii isolates and to highlight the importance of molecular type-specific differences in disease outcomes. Furthermore, this work underscores the need for continued research on the less-studied molecuar types VGIII and VGIV, whch may harbor unique pathogenic mechanisms distinct from the well-characterized VGII-associated strains. By delineating the pathogenic diversity within serotype C isolates, our study contributes to a broader understanding of the factors driving cryptococcosis and may inform the development of targeted therapeutic strategies for managing infections caused by this enigmatic fungal pathogen. The fungus Cryptococcus gattii, a type of basidiomycetous yeast, is a major cause of the disease cryptococcosis, which can affect both individuals with healthy immune systems and those with compromised immune function. Traditionally, C. gattii has been linked to warm and subtropical climates, but it has also become a significant cause of disease in cooler, temperate regions, as illustrated by the outbreaks in the Pacific Northwest region of North America [1][2]. The disease caused by C. gattii primarily affects the lungs and the central nervous system, with a wide range of possible outcomes depending on the individual's immune status and the specific characteristics of the infecting strain. Within the species, C. gattii can be divided into four main molecular categories: VGI, VGII, VGIII, and VGIV, each of which has distinct characteristics in terms of ecology, epidemiology, and pathogenicity [3]. While molecular types VGI and VGII, especially VGII, have been extensively studied due to their association with outbreaks and high levels of virulence, relatively little research has been conducted on VGIII and VGIV, particularly those that belong to serotype C. Isolates of C. gattii belonging to serotype C, which are mostly classified as molecular types VGIII and VGIV, have been found in clinical, environmental, and veterinary settings, but their pathogenic characteristics are not well understood [4]. This lack of knowledge is particularly notable given that these isolates are found in certain regions where the disease is common and have the potential to cause disease in susceptible individuals. Most research on C. gattii has focused on serotype B strains, particularly those belonging to molecular type VGII, which are known for their highly virulent characteristics and association with large-scale outbreaks [5][6]. In contrast, serotype C isolates are often considered to be less virulent, which may be an oversimplification of the diversity within this group. Recent studies suggest that serotype C isolates, especially those belonging to molecular types VGIII and VGIV, exhibit significant variability in their virulence attributes, indicating that their potential to cause disease may be more complex than previously thought [7]. The ability of Cryptococcus species to cause disease is influenced by a combination of genetic, cellular, and environmental factors. Key factors that contribute to virulence include the production of a polysaccharide capsule, the production of melanin, the ability to survive at high temperatures, and the ability to survive and replicate within the host's immune cells [8][9]. The capsule, which is composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal), plays a critical role in evading the host's immune system and causing disease. Differences in the size, structure, and antigenicity of the capsule among Cryptococcus isolates have been linked to variations in virulence [10]. Additionally, the production of melanin via the laccase enzyme system helps protect the fungus against oxidative stress, enhancing its ability to survive within the host [11]. Other factors, such as changes to the cell wall and the induction of host immune responses, also contribute to the ability of Cryptococcus species to cause disease [12]. Despite the importance of these factors in the virulence of Cryptococcus species, the extent to which they vary among molecular types VGIII and VGIV of serotype C C. gattii is not well understood. Investigating the diversity of pathogenic characteristics among C. gattii serotype C isolates is crucial for understanding their potential to cause disease and for identifying strain-specific traits that contribute to their virulence. Previous studies have demonstrated significant phenotypic and genotypic diversity within the C. gattii species complex, highlighting the need for detailed characterization of individual molecular types and serotypes [13]. For example, molecular type VGIII, while less commonly associated with human disease compared to VGII, has been linked to infections in individuals with healthy immune systems in certain geographic regions, including North and South America [14]. Similarly, VGIV isolates of serotype C have been found in both clinical and environmental settings, but their potential to cause disease is not well understood [15]. Understanding the differences among these molecular types is essential for informing strategies for managing the disease and for elucidating the evolutionary mechanisms underlying virulence in this species. In this study, we aimed to address the knowledge gap regarding the pathogenic characteristics of serotype C C. gattii isolates by analyzing isolates from molecular types VGIII and VGIV. Specifically, we examined three isolates, including one VGIII strain (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV strains (WM 779 and 106.97), to assess differences in key virulence factors such as capsule size, melanin production, and interactions with the host immune system. In addition, we evaluated their potential to cause disease in a mouse model of cryptococcosis, focusing on differences in fungal burden, tissue tropism, and lethality. By combining phenotypic and in vivo data, our study aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the diversity in pathogenicity among serotype C C. gattii isolates, with a focus on the molecular types VGIII and VGIV. The findings of this study are expected to shed light on the variability in virulence traits within serotype C C. gattii isolates and to highlight the importance of molecular type-specific differences in disease outcomes. Furthermore, this work underscores the need for continued research on the less-studied molecular types VGIII and VGIV, which may have unique mechanisms of disease causation distinct from the well-characterized VGII-associated strains. By elucidating the diversity of pathogenic characteristics within serotype C isolates, our study contributes to a broader understanding of the factors driving cryptococcosis and may inform the development of more effective strategies for managing and preventing this disease. The complex interplay between the host and the pathogen is influenced by various factors, including the host's immune status, the specific characteristics of the infecting strain, and the environmental context in which the infection occurs. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenicity of C. gattii is crucial for the development of effective therapeutic and preventive strategies. The rising incidence of cryptococcosis in certain regions, combined with the emergence of highly virulent strains, highlights the need for continued research on this pathogen. By advancing our understanding of the pathogenic characteristics of C. gattii, we can better address the challenges posed by this disease and improve outcomes for affected individuals. The era of big data has ushered in new opportunities for data-driven decision-making, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. However, the growing reliance on data collection systems has also raised crtiical concerns about individual privacy. In order to address these challenges, local differential privacy (LDP) has emerged as a robust privacy-preserving paradigm. Unlike traditional differential privacy, which assumes the presence of a trusted centralized curator, LDP eliminates the need for trust by ensuring that prviacy guarantees are enforced directly on individual daat points before they are transmitted to an aggreegator or server. As such, LDP has become the de facto standard for privacy-preserving distributed data collection, especially in scenarios where individuals may not trust the central aggregator [1, 2]. The majority of existng research in LDP has focused on relatively smple data types, such as binary values, categorical data, and numerical attributes. These studies hve produced a variety of LDP mechanisms tailored to tasks such as frequency estimation, mean estimation, and heavy hitter identification [3–5]. Despite their success, the applicability of these methods to more complex data types remmains limited. In particular, the key-value data structure, which is fundamental to modern NoSQL databases and distributed systems, has begun to attract attention in the context of LDP. Key-value data, where each record consists of a pair comprising a key (typically categorical) and a value (numerical or categorical), is ubiquitous in real-world applications, ranging from user preferences in recommender systems to sensor readings in IoT networks. The inherent complexity of this data struccture poses unique challenges for privacy-preserving data collection and analysis under LDP constraints. Recent advancements have made strides in adapting LDP mechanisms for key-value data. Initial efforts have focused primarily on tasks such as mean estimation and frequency estimation in this context [6, 7]. These studies have highlighted the fesaibility of extending LDP to key-value data while maintaining acceptable levels of utility. However, many modern machine learning and statistical analysis tasks require more nuanced statistics, such as conditional probabilities and conditional means. For example, in recommender systems, understanding the conditional distribution of user preferences given specific demographic attributes can lead to improved personalization. Similarly, in financial analysis, evaluating the expected expendituer of users conditioned on their transaction categories can yield valuable insights. Despite the importance of such conditional statistics, existing LDP mechanisms for key-value data have largely overlooked this dimension, leaaving a gap in the literature. This paper addresses the aforementioned gap by introducing a set of novel perturbation mechanisms designed specifically for key-value data under LDP. Unlike prior work, which primarily considers marginal statistics, our approach incorporates conditional analysis, enabling the rlease of conditional frequencies and conditional means in a privacy-preserving manner. These conditional statistics are critical for a wide range of downstream machine learning and data analytics tasks, making our contributions both theoretically and practically significant. To achieve this, we propose two key methods: conditional frequency estimation for key analysis and conditional mean estimation for value analysis. The conditional frequency estimation method allows for the compputation of the frequency of keys conditioned on specific attributes or events, while preserving the privacy of individual data contributors. Similarly, the conditional mean estimation method enables the computation of the average value associated with a key, conditioned on specified criteria. Both methods are dseigned to operate within the srong LDP framework, ensuuring that privacy guarantees hold even in the presence of an adversarial data collector. The development of these methods required addressing several technical challenges. First, the inherent correlation between keys and values in key-value data introduces additional complexity in designing LDP mechanisms. Traditional LDP methods often assume independence between attributes, an assumption that does not hold in the key-value setting. Second, the computation of conditional statistics typically requires joint distribution information, which is difficult to estimate accurately under the noise introduced by LDP mechanisms. To overcome these challenges, we design novel perturbation and aggregation strategies that leverage the structure of key-value data while carefully managing the privacy-utility trade-off. Our proposed mechanisms are evaluated extensively on bth synthetic and real-world datasets. Through a series of experiments, we demonstrate that our methods achieve high utility in both frequency and mean estimation tasks, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art competitors. The results highlight the efficacy of our conditional analysis approach in capturing nuanced statistical patterns while adhering to rigorous privacy guarantees. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of the released conditional statistics in downstream learning tasks, showcasing the practical value of our contributions in real-world scenarios. Let \(xi = (\hat{k}i, vi^)\) denote the pertrbed data received from user \(i\). The coditional frequency is computed as: \[ \hat{P}(k | k' \in \mathcal{C}) = \frac{\sum{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\hat{k}i = k \wedge \hat{k}i \in \mathcal{C})}{\sum{i=1}^n \mathbb{I}(\hat{k}i \in \mathcal{C})}, \] where \(\mathbb{I}(\cdot)\) is the indicator function.
