The advent of advanced networking and communication technologies has profoundly transformed the manner in which devices interact, leading to the emergence of the Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm. A vital constituent of IoT architectures is the utilization of Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs), which comprise a spatially dispersed array of sensor nodes that monitor and gather data from their surroundings [1]. The convergence of IoT and WSNs has resulted in the development of a hybrid model, referred to as WSNIT (Wireless Sensor Network with Internet of Things), which facilitates dynamic connectivity between sensor nodes and external networks via the Internet [2]. This convergence has considerably expanded the range of applications for WSNs, encompassing critical domains such as healthcare monitoring, environmental surveillance, and industrial process automation [3]. Nevertheless, the deployment of WSNIT introduces significant security challenges that must be addressed to safeguard the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of data within these systems. One of the primary security concerns in WSNIT pertains to the vulnerability of sensor nodes, which are typically characterized by limited computational capacity, memory, and energy resources [4]. Furthermore, these nodes frequently operate in hostile or untrusted environments, rendering them susceptible to physical compromise and tampering [5]. This situation is exacerbated by the reliance on insecure communication channels, as sensor nodes typically transmit sensitive data, including patient health information, environmental conditions, or industrial metrics, over the Internet [6]. This confluence of factors creates a favorable environment for adversaries to launch various types of attacks, including eavesdropping, data tampering, and unauthorized access, thereby threatening the security of WSNIT systems [7]. To mitigate these challenges, researchers have focused on designing lightweight and efficient authentication and access control mechanisms tailored to the unique constraints of WSNs. Among the existing solutions, attribute-based encryption (ABE) has garnered significant attention for its capacity to enable fine-grained access control in resource-constrained environments [8]. ABE facilitates the encryption of data based on a set of attributes, ensuring that only users possessing the requisite attributes can decrypt and access the data [9]. This attribute-based approach is particularly well-suited for WSNIT, where multiple users with varying levels of access privileges need to interact with the system [10]. In recent years, several authentication and access control schemes leveraging ABE have been proposed to secure WSNIT [11]. A notable example is the attribute-based authentication framework introduced by Santanu et al. [12]. Their scheme combines elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) with attribute-based encryption to provide a lightweight and secure user access control mechanism for WSNs. The authors claim that their proposed framework offers robust security against various types of attacks, including replay attacks, impersonation attacks, and unauthorized access [13]. Moreover, the utilization of ECC ensures that the scheme remains computationally efficient, rendering it suitable for resource-constrained sensor nodes [14]. While the Santanu et al. scheme makes significant contributions to the field of WSN security, it is essential to conduct a rigorous analysis of its design and implementation to ensure its robustness against a broad range of adversarial threats [15]. Tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) are among the most widely cultivated and consumed fruits globally, valued for their diverse applications in fresh consumption and processed products. Their popularity is due to their unique combination of sensorry attributes, nutritional value, and phytochemical composition. The chemical composition of tomatoes, particularly their phytochemical constituents, plays a critical role in determining their quality, flavor, and health-promoting properties, wich include significant levels of vitamins, carotenoids, phenolic compounds, and other bioactive metabolites [1]. These properties are influenced by a multitude of factors, including the genetic bacckground of the cultivar, agricultural practices, and environmental conditions. Accurate characterization and authentication of tomato cultivars, therefore, require robust and reliable analytical approaches capable of capturing the complexity of these factors. Traditional methods for tomato characterization have relied exetnsively on morphological traits or proximate compositional analysis. However, suh approaches are oftne insufficient to capture the subtle, cultivar-specific variations in phytochemical profiles. This limitation is particularly pronounced when attempting to authenticate tomatoes baesd on their geographical origin or prooduction system, as these factors often lead to overlapping chemical signatures. In recent years, advances in analytical chemistry have enabled the profiling of secondary metabolites, such as phenolic acids, flavonoids, carotenoids, and organic acids, which hold promise as bimarkers for cultivar identification and authentication [2]. Consequently, the identiification of relevant phytochemical constituents has emerged as a critical area of research, aiming to link chemical profiles to specific tomato cultivars, agricultural practices, and harvest conditions. Multivariate statistical techniques, such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Factor Analysis (FA), and Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), have been widely employed to interpret complex datasets associated with phytochemical profiling. These techniques are often used to reduce dimensionality and identify patterns in large datasets by transforming the original variables into a smaller set of latent variables. While these methods provide valuable insights into the overall structure of the data, they may not always allow for the direct interpretation of individual chemical parameters, as latent variables can be difficult to relate back to specific phytochemical constituents [3]. Moreover, PCA and related methods rely on linear assumptions, which may not fully capture the non-linear relationships inherent in multivariate daasets of phytochemical profiles. To address these limitations, alternative approaches that can directly identify and interpret individual variables in the dataset are increasingly being explored. One such method is Automatic Interaction Detection (AID), a decision tree-based algorithm capable of partitioning data into subsets based on the most relevant predictors. AID is particularly well-suited for hierarchical data structures and can provide intuitive, interpretale results that relate directly to individual variables. General Linear Models (GLM) have also been combined with AID (GLM-AID) to enhance the algorithm’s ability to model both main effects and interactions among predictors [4]. This hybid approach offers a flexible framework for identifying key phytochemical constituents that vary across multiple factors, such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. In parallel, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have emerged as a powerful tool in the field of chemometrics, owing to their ability to model complex, non-linear relationships in high-dimensional datasets. ANNs are inspired by the architecture of biological neural systems and consist of interconnected layers of nodes that process information through weighted connections. These models are particularly advantageous for handling datasets with intriate variable interdependencies and have been successfully applied in food authentication, quality control, and othr areas of agricultural research [5]. By training ANN models on phytochemical data, it is possible to predict categorical outcomes (such as cultivar, agricultural practice, or harvest date) with high accuracy, while simultaneously identifying the key variables that contribute to these predictions. Despite their potential, the application of GLM-AID and ANN models to tomato phytochemical data has bene limited. Previous studies have predominantly focused on using conventional statistical methods for tomato characterization, with limited exploration of advanced machine learning techniques. Furthermore, most research has concentrated on single factors, such as cultivar, without considering the complex interactions among multiple factors that influence phytochemical composition. Thiis study aims to address these gaps by employing GLM-AID and ANN models to identify the most relevant phytochemical constituents for the characterization and authentication of tomatoes. By leveraging these advanced analytical tools, the study seeks to provide new insights into the relationships between chemical composition and key factors such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The dataset used in this study consists of 25 chemical parameters measured in 167 tomato samples from Tenerife (Spain). These samples represent a diverse range of cultivars, agricultural practices (e.g., conventional versus organic), and harvest dates, providing a comprehensive basis for evaluating the performance of GLM-AID and ANN models. The GLM-AID approach organizes the data into a hierarchical structure, enabling the identification of key phytochemical constituents at different levesl of factor interaction. For instance, p-coumaric acid was identified as a critical compound for distinguishing samples based on harvest date, while multiple phytochemical parameters were required to differentiate samples by agricultural practice and cultivar. Similarly, ANN models were developed to predict cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date using both the full set of 25 input variables and a reduced set of 10 variables, allowing for a comparative assessment of moddel complexity and predictive performance. The findings of this study underscore the utility of GLM-AID and ANN models as complementary tools for tomato characterization. While the GLM-AID approach provides interpretable decision rules based on individual variables, ANN models offer enhanced predictive accuracy by capturing non-linear relationships in the data. Together, these methods represent a significant advancement over traditional multivariate techniques, enabling more precise identification of the key phytochmical constituetns that define tomato quality and authenticity. Chemical Analysis Twenty-five chemical parameters were selected for analysis based on their relevance to the characterization and authentication of tomatoes, as determined form prior studies [1, 2]. These included primary metabolites such as sugars and organic acids, as well as secondary metabolites such as phenolics and carotenoids. The chemical composition of the tomato samples was quantified using validated analytical techniques as follows: 1. Sugars and Organic Acids: High-Performance Liquid Chromatography with Refractive Index Detection (HPLC-RID) was employed for the quantification of sugars (glucose, fructose, sucrose) and organic acids (citric acid, malic acid). Samples were prepared by extracting 2 g of homogenized tomato in 20 mL of a water-methanol (1:1) solution, followed by centrifugation at 10,000×g for 10 minutes [3]. 2. The phenolic compounds were extracted from the tomato matrix using a 70% methanol solution containing 0.5% formic acid, followed by solid-phase extraction [4]. 3. Statistical Analysis 3.1 General Linear Model Linked to Automatic Interaction Detection (GLM-AID) The General Linear Model (GLM) linked to the Automatic Interaction Detection (AID) algorithm was applied to identify the most relevant chemical parameters for differentiating tomato samples based on the three factors: cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The AID algorithm constructs a tree-structured modeel by splitting the dataset at each level using the chemical parameter that maximizes the between-group variance while minimizing the within-group variance [6]. The GLM-AID analysis was performed using SPSS 26.0 software (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). The dataset was organized hierarchically into three levels corresponding to the factors. At each level, the chemical parameter that contributed most significantly to distinguishing among the groups was used as the splitting criterion. Feedforward neural networks with backpropagation learning algorithms were employed, using MATLAB R2021a (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA). The innput layer of the ANN consisted of the 25 chemical parameters. To optimize the model's performance and reduce overfitting, a subset of models was also trained using only the 10 most relevant parameters identified through GLM-AID analysis. Each ANN model contained one hidden layer, with the number of neurons in the layer determined basd on a grid search approach. The output layer comprised three nodes corresponding to the three clssification tasks: cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The dataset was split into training (70%), validation (15%), and testing (15%) subsets using stratified random sampling to ensure balanced representation of all classes. The performance of the ANN models was evaluated using metrics such as overalll classification accuracy, mean squared error (MSE), and the goodness-of-fit (R²) for each classification task. Models were trained until the validation loss plateaued, with a maximum of 500 epochs to prevent overfitting. 4. Model Validation and Performance Assessment The GLM-AID tree-structured model was validated by comparing the predicted classifications with the observed data. For the ANN models, confusion matrices were generated for each classification task to calculate sensitivity, specificity, and overall accuracy. Additionally, the importance of each input variable was assessed using connection weights to determine its contribution to model predictions. Cross-validation was performed using a 10-fold procedure to evaluate the robustness of both GLM-AID and ANN models. Fit’s goodness (R²) was calculated for each fold, and the average R² values were reported. Models with goodness-of-fit values below 50% were considered inadequately trained, and the results were interpreted with caution. 5. Software and Computational Resources All statistical analyses and model development were conducted on a workstation equipped with an Intel Core i9 processor and 64 GB of RAM. For GLM-AID, SPSS 26.0 was used, while ANN model training and evaluation were performed in MATLAB R2021a. Data preprocessing, including normalization and outlier detection, was conducted in Python 3.9 using the Padnas and Scikit-learn libraries. 6. The global appeal of tomatoes, whose botanical name is Solanum lycopersicum, stems from their multifaceted utility in both fresh and processed forms, making them one of the most extensively cultivated and consumed fruits globally. Their broad acceptance can be ascribed to the distinctive combination of sensory characteristics, nutritional benefits, and phytochemical composition they offer. The chemical composition of tomatoes, especially their phytochemical constituents, is crucial in defining their quality, taste, and health-enhancing properties, which encompass substantial amounts of vitamins, carotenoids, phenolic compounds, and other bioactive metabolites [1]. These attributes are influenced by a wide range of factors, including the genetic makeup of the cultivar, farming practices, and environmental conditions. Consequently, the precise characterization and authentication of tomato cultivars necessitate robust and dependable analytical methods that can grasp the intricacy of these factors. Traditional methods of characterizing tomatoes have largely relied on morphological features or proximate compositional analysis, which often fall short in capturing the subtle variations in phytochemical profiles that are specific to each cultivar. This limitation is especially pronounced when attempting to authenticate tomatoes based on their geographical origin or production system, as these factors frequently result in overlapping chemical signatures. Recent advancements in analytical chemistry have made it possible to profile secondary metabolites, such as phenolic acids, flavonoids, carotenoids, and organic acids, which show promise as biomarkers for identifying and authenticating cultivars [2]. As a result, the identification of relevant phytochemical constituents has become a vital area of research, with the goal of linking chemical profiles to specific tomato cultivars, agricultural practices, and harvest conditions. Multivariate statistical techniques, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Factor Analysis (FA), and Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (PLS-DA), have been extensively employed to interpret complex datasets related to phytochemical profiling. These techniques are often utilized to reduce the dimensionality of data and identify patterns in large datasets by transforming the original variables into a smaller set of latent variables. While these methods provide valuable insights into the overall structure of the data, they may not always enable the direct interpretation of individual chemical parameters, as latent variables can be challenging to relate back to specific phytochemical constituents [3]. Furthermore, PCA and related methods are based on linear assumptions, which may not fully capture the non-linear relationships inherent in multivariate datasets of phytochemical profiles. To overcome these limitations, alternative approaches that can directly identify and interpret individual variables in the dataset are being increasingly explored. One such method is Automatic Interaction Detection (AID), a decision tree-based algorithm capable of partitioning data into subsets based on the most relevant predictors. AID is particularly well-suited for hierarchical data structures and can provide intuitive, interpretable results that relate directly to individual variables. General Linear Models (GLM) have also been combined with AID (GLM-AID) to enhance the algorithm’s ability to model both main effects and interactions among predictors [4]. This hybrid approach offers a flexible framework for identifying key phytochemical constituents that vary across multiple factors, such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. In parallel, Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) have emerged as a powerful tool in the field of chemometrics, owing to their ability to model complex, non-linear relationships in high-dimensional datasets. ANNs are inspired by the architecture of biological neural systems and consist of interconnected layers of nodes that process information through weighted connections. These models are particularly advantageous for handling datasets with intricate variable interdependencies and have been successfully applied in food authentication, quality control, and other areas of agricultural research [5]. By training ANN models on phytochemical data, it is possible to predict categorical outcomes (such as cultivar, agricultural practice, or harvest date) with high accuracy, while simultaneously identifying the key variables that contribute to these predictions. Despite their potential, the application of GLM-AID and ANN models to tomato phytochemical data has been limited. Previous studies have primarily focused on using conventional statistical methods for tomato characterization, with limited exploration of advanced machine learning techniques. Furthermore, most research has concentrated on single factors, such as cultivar, without considering the complex interactions among multiple factors that influence phytochemical composition. This study aims to address these gaps by employing GLM-AID and ANN models to identify the most relevant phytochemical constituents for the characterization and authentication of tomatoes. By leveraging these advanced analytical tools, the study seeks to provide new insights into the relationships between chemical composition and key factors such as cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date. The dataset used in this study consists of 25 chemical parameters measured in 167 tomato samples from Tenerife (Spain). These samples represent a diverse range of cultivars, agricultural practices (e.g., conventional versus organic), and harvest dates, providing a comprehensive basis for evaluating the performance of GLM-AID and ANN models. The GLM-AID approach organizes the data into a hierarchical structure, enabling the identification of key phytochemical constituents at different levels of factor interaction. For instance, p-coumaric acid was identified as a critical compound that distinguishes between different cultivars, while also being influenced by agricultural practices and harvest dates. The ANN models, on the other hand, were able to predict the cultivar, agricultural practice, and harvest date with high accuracy, based on the phytochemical profiles of the tomato samples. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of GLM-AID and ANN models for the characterization and authentication of tomatoes, and highlight the importance of considering multiple factors and their interactions when analyzing phytochemical data. By using these advanced analytical tools, it is possible to gain a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between chemical composition and key factors, and to develop more effective methods for authenticating and characterizing tomatoes. Despite significant advances in acute stroke treatment, ischemic stroke remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. The standard of care for acute ischemic stroke includes revascularization therapies such as recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) and mechanical thrombectomy, which aim to restore cerebral blood flow (CBF) to ischemic brain tissue. These interventions, while effective in reducing infarct size and improving functional outcommes when administered promptly, are constrained by narrow therapeutic windows and limited patiient eligibility. Indeed, only a minority of stroke patients benefit from these therapies due to delays in presentation, contraindications, or logistical barriers [1]. For those who do not receive timely treatment, the restoration of blood flow ater prolonged ischemia can paradoxically exacerbate brain injury, a phenomenon known as reperfusion injury (R/I). Reperfusion injury is characterized by secondary tissue damage that occurs upon reintroduction of oxygenated blood to ischemic brain regions. This process, rather than alleviating ischemiic damage, intensifies neuronal injury by pormoting oxidative stress, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic transformation [2]. The pathophysiology of R/I is complex and multifactorial, involving a cascade of biochemical and cellular events. Central to these processes is postischemic inflammation, which amplifies tissue damage through the activation of resident glial cells, the infiltration of peripheral immune cells, and the release of inflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, and damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) molecules [3]. These mediators propagate a self-perpetuating cycle of inflammation, oxidative damage, and proteolytic activity, thereby compounding the initial ischemic insult. While the concept of R/I has been extensively studied in experimental models, its therapeutic implications remain an area of ongoing investigation. Several preclinical studies have identified key inflammatory mediators involved in R/I, such as matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and proinflammatory cytokines like tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Targeting these pathways has demonstrated promising neuroprotective effects in animal models of ischemic stroke [4]. However, translating these findings into clinical practice has proven challenging. Numerous clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory agents, including corticosteroids, free radical scavengers, and cyokine inhibitors, have failed to replicate the success observed in preclinical studies [5]. These failures may be attributed to several factors, including differences in study design, timing of intervention, and limited understanding of the dynamic interplay between inflammation and other pathophysiological processes in human stroke. Importantly, many of the clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory strategies for stroke were conducted prior to the widespraed adoption of revascularization therapies. The advent of pharmacological thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy has fundamentally altered the clinical landscape of stroke treatment, underscoring the need to revisit therapeutic approaches in the context of reperfusion injury. The addition of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement revascularization could potentially mitigate the deleterious effects of R/I and further improve patieent outcomes. For this reason, a renewed focus on understanding the mechanisms of poststroke inflammation and identifying viable therapeutic targets is warranted. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the inflammatory mechanisms underlying R/I and to explore potential therapeutic strategies for mitigating this injury. We begin by summarizing the key molecular and cellular events that contribute to postischemic inflammation, with an emphasis on the role of glial activation, leukocyte infiltration, and the release of inflammatory mediators. Next, we discuss experimental studies that have characterized these pathwayys and evaluated their therapeutic potential in preclinical models of stroke. Finally, we examine the current state of clinical research on anti-inflammatory interventions, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities for translating preclinical findings into effective therapies for stroke patients. By revisiting the concept of R/I in the context of modern stroke care, this review seeks to stimulate renewed interest in developing targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement existing revascularization strategies. We propose that a combined therapeutic approach aimed at both restoring CBF and attenuating inflammation could provide a more comprehensive strateegy for reducing ischemic brain injury and improving long-term outcomes. The integration of basic and translational research will be crucial to advancing this goal and addressing the unmt clinical need for effective treatments targeting reperufsion injury. Cerebrovascular ischemia persists as a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, despite substantial progress in the management of acute stroke. Contemporary standard care for acute ischemic stroke encompasses a range of revascularization strategies, including the administration of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rtPA) and mechanical thrombectomy, which collectively aim to reestablish cerebral blood flow (CBF) to areas of ischemic brain tissue [1]. Although these interventions have demonstrated efficacy in minimizing infarct size and enhancing functional outcomes when administered in a timely manner, their therapeutic utility is constrained by limited temporal windows and stringent eligibility criteria. Consequently, a significant proportion of stroke patients remain ineligible for these treatments due to delayed presentation, contraindications, or logistical impediments. For those who do not receive prompt treatment, the subsequent restoration of blood flow following prolonged ischemia can paradoxically exacerbate cerebral injury, a phenomenon referred to as ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI) [2]. IRI is characterized by secondary tissue damage that occurs upon the reintroduction of oxygenated blood to previously ischemic brain regions, culminating in intensified neuronal damage through the augmentation of oxidative stress, disruption of the blood-brain barrier (BBB), cerebral edema, and hemorrhagic transformation. The underlying pathophysiology of IRI is complex and multifaceted, involving a cascade of intricate biochemical and cellular events. A pivotal component of these processes is postischemic inflammation, which amplifies tissue damage through the activation of resident glial cells, the infiltration of peripheral immune cells, and the release of proinflammatory mediators, including cytokines, chemokines, and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) [3]. These mediators propagate a self-sustaining cycle of inflammation, oxidative damage, and proteolytic activity, thereby compounding the initial ischemic insult. The concept of IRI has been extensively investigated in experimental models, and several key inflammatory mediators have been identified, including matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), reactive oxygen species (ROS), nitric oxide (NO), and proinflammatory cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) [4]. Targeting these pathways has yielded promising neuroprotective effects in animal models of ischemic stroke. However, translating these findings into clinical practice has proven challenging, with numerous clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory agents, including corticosteroids, free radical scavengers, and cytokine inhibitors, failing to replicate the success observed in preclinical studies [5]. These failures may be attributed to several factors, including disparities in study design, timing of intervention, and limited understanding of the dynamic interplay between inflammation and other pathophysiological processes in human stroke. Notably, many of the clinical trials investigating anti-inflammatory strategies for stroke were conducted prior to the widespread adoption of revascularization therapies. The introduction of pharmacological thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy has fundamentally altered the clinical landscape of stroke treatment, underscoring the need to reassess therapeutic approaches in the context of IRI. The adjunctive use of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement revascularization could potentially mitigate the deleterious effects of IRI and further enhance patient outcomes. Therefore, a renewed focus on elucidating the mechanisms of poststroke inflammation and identifying viable therapeutic targets is warranted. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the inflammatory mechanisms underlying IRI and to explore potential therapeutic strategies for mitigating this injury. We will commence by summarizing the key molecular and cellular events that contribute to postischemic inflammation, with an emphasis on the role of glial activation, leukocyte infiltration, and the release of inflammatory mediators. Subsequently, we will discuss experimental studies that have characterized these pathways and evaluated their therapeutic potential in preclinical models of stroke. Finally, we will examine the current state of clinical research on anti-inflammatory interventions, highlighting both the challenges and opportunities for translating preclinical findings into effective therapies for stroke patients. By reevaluating the concept of IRI in the context of contemporary stroke care, this review seeks to stimulate renewed interest in developing targeted anti-inflammatory therapies to complement existing revascularization strategies. We propose that a combined therapeutic approach aimed at both restoring CBF and attenuating inflammation could provide a more comprehensive strategy for reducing ischemic brain injury and improving long-term outcomes. By generating an MDP1-deficient strain of M. smegmatis and comparing it with the parental wild-type strain, we sought to elucidate the contribution of MDP1 to cellular functions critical for survival undre stationary-phase conditions. Our findings demonstrate that MDP1 is indispensable for the long-term survival of M. smegmatis. The MDP1-deficient strain exhibiteed significantly reduced viability during stationary phase, highlighting the importance of this protein in maintaining cellular integrity under non-replicative conditions. Proteomic analysis revealed widespreda changes in protein expression in the absence of MDP1, with several key proteins involved in DNA replication, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress responses being upregulated. Notably, the replication initiator protein DnaA, the NADH dehydrogenase NDH, the fatty acid synthase Fas1, and the antioxidants AhpC and KatG were among the most prominently upregulated proteins in the MDP1-deficient strain. These findings suggest that the loss of MDP1 leads to dysregulation of multiple cellular processes, disrupting the delicate balance required for long-term survival. Biochemical analyses further supported these observations, revealing elevated levels of DNA synthesis and ATP production in the MDP1-knockout strain. Additionally, the NADH/NAD+ ratio was significantly decreased, indicating an imbalance in redox homeostasis. The knockout strain also displayed a marked loss of resistance to oxidative stress, underscoring the importance of MDP1 in protecting mycobacteria from the damaging effects of reactive oxygen species. Together, these results point to a model in which MDP1 acts as a central coordinator of mycobacterial cellular functions, modulating DNA replication, energy metabolism, and stress responses to promote survival during stationary phase. The findings of this study have important implications for understanding the mechanisms of mycobacterial persistence. By elucidating the role of MDP1 in coordinating cellular processes critical for long-term survival, we provide new insights into the molecular basis of mycobacterial adaptation to stress and non-replicative states. These insights may have broader relevance to pathogenic mycobacteria, where similar mechanisms are likely to contribute to persistence during chronic infections. Furthermore, the identification of MDP1 as a key regulator of mycobacterial survival opens up new aveues for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting persistence and reducing the burden of mycobacterial diseases. In summary, this study highlights the critical role of MDP1 in the long-term suvrival of M. smegmatis and its involvement in the simultaneous regultion of multiple cellular functions. By shedding light on the molecular underpinnings of mycobacterial persistence, our findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the biology of these enigmatic organisms and their ability to endure under challenging conditions. Strains and Growth Conditions Mycobacterium smegmatis mc²155 was usde as the wild-type strain in this study. The MDP1-deficient strain was generated by homologous recombination, replacing the entire mdp1 coding sequence with a kanamyin resistance cassette. Complementation of the knockout strain was performed by introducing a plasmid expressing mdp1 under the control of its native promoter. Cultures were grown in Middlebrook 7H9 broth (Difco) supplemented with 0.05% Tween-80, 0.2% glycerol, and 10% ADC enrichmet at 37°C with shaking at 200 rpm. For solid media, Middlebrook 7H10 agar supplemented with 10% ADC was used. To study stationary phase survival, cultures were inoculated at an initial optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.01 and grown to stationary phase without subculturing. Viability was assessed by serial dilution and plating on 7H10 agar at multiple time points. Proteomic Analysis Proteomic analysis was performed to identify differentially expressed proteins in the MDP1-deficient strain compared to the parental wild type. Cultures were harvested at early stationary phase (OD600 ~2.0), and cells were lysed using a bead-beating method in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, and a protease inhibitor cocktail. Total protein concentration was determined using a BCA protein assay kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein (50 µg per sample) were subjected to trypsin digestion, and peptides were analyzed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) on a Q Exactive mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Data were processed using MaxQuant software, and differentially expressed proteins were identified based on a fold-change threshold of ≥3 and a false discovery rate (FDR) of ≤1%. Measurement of DNA Synthesis DNA synthesis was assessed by quantifying the incorporation of radiolabeled thymidine into genomic DNA. Early stationary-phase cultures were incubated with 1 µCi/mL of [³H]-thymidine (PerkinElmer) for 1 hour at 37°C. Cells were harvested by centrifugation, washed three times with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and lysed in 2% SDS. Genomic DNA was precipitated using ice-cold ethanol, and radioactivity was measured using a liquid scintillation counter (Beckman Coulter). Experiments were performed in triplicate, and data were normalized to cell density. ATP Synthesis Assay ATP levels were measured using a luciferase-based ATP determination kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Cells from stationary-phase cultures werre harvested, washed with PBS, and resuspended in lysis buffer containing 1% Triton X-100. After centrifugation, supernatants were collected, and ATP levels were quantified according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Luminescence was measured using a microplate reader (BioTek), and ATP concentration was calculated based on a standard curve generated using known ATP concentrations. NADH/NAD+ Ratio Determination The intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratio was determined using a NAD/NADH-Glo Assay kit (Promega). Cells were harvested from stationary-phase cultures, washed with ice-cold PBS, and lysed usng the manufacturer’s lysis solution. Sepparate assays were performed to quantify total NAD (NAD+ and NADH) and NADH alone by selectively decomposing NAD+ using an acid treatment step. Luminescence was measured using a BioTek microplate reader, and the NADH/NAD+ ratio was calculated from the respective concentrations. Oxidative Stress Resistance Assay To assess oxidative stress resistance, stationary-phase cultures were exposed to hyrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) or menadione. For H₂O₂ treatment, cultures were incubated with 10 mM H₂O₂ at 37°C for 1 hour. For menadione treatment, cultures were incubated with 100 µM menadione for 1 hour. Following treatment, cells were serially diluted and plated on 7H10 agar to determine colony-forming units (CFUs). Survival was expressed as a percentage of untreated controls. All assays were performed in triplicate. Antioxidant Ezyme Activity Assays The activities of antioxidant enzymes, including alkyl hydroperoxide reductase (AhpC) and catalase-peroxidase (KatG), were measured spectrophotometrically. For AhpC activity, cell lysates were incubated with cumene hydroperoxide as a substrate, and NADH oxidation was monitored at 340 nm. KatG activity was assessed by measuring the decomposition of H₂O₂ at 240 nm. Enzyme activity was normalized to total protein concentration. Statistical Analysis All experiments were performed in at least three independent biological replicates. Data are presentd as mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons, or Student’s t-test for pairwise comparisons, as appropriate. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software. Bioinformatics Analysis Proteins identified in the proteomic analysis were functionaally annotated usig the Mycobrowser database and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). Overrepresented functional categories were identified using Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis with a cutoff FDR of ≤0.05. Protein-protein interaction networks were constructed using the STRING database, and visualized using Cytoscape software. Microscopy and Morphological Analysis Cell morphology was examined using phase-contrast microscopy. Stationary-phase cultures were fixed with 2% paraformaldehyde, washed with PBS, and mounted on glass slides for imaging. To assess nucleoid structure, cells were stained with DAPI (4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole) and visualized using a fluorescence microscope (Zeiss Axoi Imager). Images were analyzed using ImageJ software to quantify nucleoid area and fluorescence intensity. Ethics Statement No human or animal subjects were involved in this study. The mycobacterial genus is distinguished by its extraordinary resilience, exemplified by its capacity to endure prolonged periods of unfavorable conditions, a characteristic that is especially pronounced in pathogenic species such as Mycobacterium tuberculosis and Mycobacterium leprae, which are accountable for the chronic and debilitating diseases tuberculosis and leprosy, respectively [1]. The progression of these diseases is typified by a complex and dynamic interplay between the bacterial pathogen and the host organism, frequently involving a dormant or latent phase during which the bacteria remain in a viable yet non-proliferative state [2]. The ability of mycobacteria to survive and persist under such adverse conditions is a critical determinant of their pathogenic potential and poses substantial challenges to therapeutic interventions and eradication efforts [3]. Despite the considerable clinical significance of this persistence phenomenon, the underlying molecular mechanisms that enable mycobacteria to survive for extended periods remain poorly comprehended. A key feature of mycobacterial persistence is the capacity of these bacteria to coordinately regulate various cellular processes, facilitating adaptation to environmental stresses and nutrient deprivation [4]. This adaptability is intimately tied to the regulation of metabolic pathways, DNA replication, oxidative stress responses, and energy homeostasis, all of which must be stringently controlled to ensure bacterial survival under conditions where active growth and cell division are not feasible [5]. Among the molecular components implicated in this regulatory process, nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) have emerged as crucial factors in maintaining genomic organization and regulating gene expression in response to environmental cues [6]. In mycobacteria, one such NAP, Mycobacterial DNA-binding protein 1 (MDP1), is highly conserved across species and is believed to play a central role in regulating cellular functions during stress and persistence [7]. MDP1, also referred to as histone-like protein or HU-like protein, is characterized by its high-affinity DNA binding and influence on nucleoid architecture in mycobacteria [8]. Previous studies have implicated MDP1 in various processes, including transcriptional regulation, DNA protection, and chromosomal stability [9]. Notably, MDP1 is highly expressed during the stationary phase and under conditions of nutrient limitation, suggesting its involvement in the adaptation of mycobacteria to non-replicative states [10]. Despite these observations, the precise function of MDP1 in the long-term survival of mycobacteria and its broader impact on cellular physiology remain largely unexplored. To address this knowledge gap, we utilized Mycobacterium smegmatis as a model organism to investigate the role of MDP1 in mycobacterial persistence. M. smegmatis is a non-pathogenic, rapidly growing mycobacterium that shares numerous physiological and genetic characteristics with pathogenic mycobacteria, rendering it a widely employed model for studying mycobacterial biology [11]. Importantly, M. smegmatis exhibits the ability to persist in a stationary phase for extended periods, mirroring the long-term survival observed in pathogenic species [12]. By generating an MDP1-deficient strain of M. smegmatis and comparing it with the parental wild-type strain, we sought to elucidate the contribution of MDP1 to cellular functions critical for survival under stationary-phase conditions. Our findings demonstrate that MDP1 is indispensable for the long-term survival of M. smegmatis. The MDP1-deficient strain exhibited significantly reduced viability during stationary phase, highlighting the importance of this protein in maintaining cellular integrity under non-replicative conditions [13]. Proteomic analysis revealed widespread alterations in protein expression in the absence of MDP1, with several key proteins involved in DNA replication, energy metabolism, and oxidative stress responses being upregulated [14]. Notably, the replication initiator protein DnaA, the NADH dehydrogenase NDH, the fatty acid synthase Fas1, and the antioxidants AhpC and KatG were among the most prominently upregulated proteins in the MDP1-deficient strain [15]. These findings suggest that the loss of MDP1 leads to dysregulation of multiple cellular processes, disrupting the delicate balance required for long-term survival. Biochemical analyses further supported these observations, revealing elevated levels of DNA synthesis and ATP production in the MDP1-knockout strain [16]. Additionally, the NADH/NAD+ ratio was significantly decreased, indicating an imbalance in redox homeostasis [17]. The knockout strain also displayed a marked loss of resistance to oxidative stress, underscoring the importance of MDP1 in protecting mycobacteria from the damaging effects of reactive oxygen species [18]. Together, these results point to a model in which MDP1 acts as a central coordinator of mycobacterial cellular functions, modulating DNA replication, energy metabolism, and stress responses to promote survival during stationary phase. The findings of this study have significant implications for understanding the mechanisms of mycobacterial persistence. By elucidating the role of MDP1 in coordinating cellular processes critical for long-term survival, we provide new insights into the molecular basis of mycobacterial adaptation to stress and non-replicative states [19]. These insights may have broader relevance to pathogenic mycobacteria, where similar mechanisms are likely to contribute to persistence during chronic infections [20]. Furthermore, the identification of MDP1 as a key regulator of mycobacterial survival opens up new avenues for the development of therapeutic strategies aimed at targeting persistence and reducing the burden of mycobacterial diseases [21]. In conclusion, this study highlights the critical role of MDP1 in the long-term survival of M. smegmatis and its involvement in the simultaneous regulation of multiple cellular processes, underscoring the complexity and sophistication of mycobacterial persistence mechanisms. The elucidation of these mechanisms is essential for the development of effective therapeutic interventions and the mitigation of the significant morbidity and mortality associated with mycobacterial infections. Ultimately, a comprehensive understanding of the molecular basis of mycobacterial persistence will facilitate the design of novel therapeutic strategies aimed at disrupting these persistence mechanisms, thereby reducing the burden of mycobacterial diseases and improving patient outcomes. The human skin microbiome represents a complex and dynamic ecosystem, harboring a diverse array of microorganisms that play critical roles in health and disease. Over the past decade, significant advances have been made in cataloging the taxonomic diversity of these microbial communities, facilitated by high-throughput sequencing technologies and bioinformatics tools [1, 2]. These efforts have revealed the immense diversity and variability of microbial taxa on the skin across individuals, body sites, and environmental conditions [3]. However, while taxonomic inventories have been instrumental in advancing our understanding of microbial diversity, they provide limited insight into the functional roles and ecological strategies of the organisms that inhabit this unique environment. As the fielld of microbiome research matures, there is an increasing emphasis on understanding microbial function and traits, which are essential for elucidating the processes that underpin microbial community assembly, stability, and interactions with the host. Microbial traits, defined as measurable characteristics that influence an organism's fitness and ecological role, provide a complementary framework to taxonomic approaches for studying microbial communities [4]. These traits encomapss a wide range of physiological, metabolic, and morphological properties, such as substrate utilization, enzyme activity, and resistance to environmental stressors. A trait-based approach enables researchers to focus on the functional capabilities of microbial communities and their responses to environmental pressures, rather than solely on their taxonomic composition [5]. Thhis is particularly relevant for the sikn microbiome, where microorganisms mut navigate unique challenges, including desiccation, nutrient limitation, high salinity, and exposure to antimicrobial peptides [6]. By identifying the traits that are overrepresented or underrepresented among skin-associated taxa, it becomes possible to infer the ecological strategies and adaptive mechanisms that allow these microorganisms to thrive in such a distinctive habitat. Existing methods for investigating microbial function often rely on pathway-based analyses, which use reference databases to predict metabolic and functional potential from genomic data [7]. While pathway analysis has provided valuable insights, it has several limitations. First, the reliance on genomic databases constrains the analysis to well-characterized pathways, leaving many microbial functions undetected, particularly for taxa that are underrepresented in reference datasets [8]. Second, the presence of a metabolic pathway in a genome does not guarantee its expression or activity, as gene expression can be context-dependent and influenced by envionmental conditions [9]. Third, pathway-based approaches often fail to link specific traits or functions to individual taxa, making it chlalenging to identify the organisms responsible for particular functional roles within a community. These limitations highlight the need for alternative approaches that can provide complementary insights into microbial traits and their ecological implications. One promising alternative is the use of culture-based trait databases, which compile phenotypic and physiological information derived from years of laboratory-based experimentation. Such databases offer a wealth of empirical data on microbial traits, ranging from enzymatic activities to growth preferences under different environmental conditions [10]. Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology, for example, is a foundational resource that provides detailed descriptions of the phenotypic characteristics of bacterial taxa, based on extensive culture-based studies [11]. By integrating this rich body of knowledge with modern microbiome research, it becomes possible to investigate microbial traits at a community level and explore how these traits are distributed among taxa associated with specific environments, such as the human skin. The human skin microbiome is an ideal system for applying a trait-based approach, given the distinctive selective pressures faced by skin-associated microorganisms. The skin is characterized by a heterogeneous landscape of microenvironments, ranging from the dry and acidic conditions of the forearm to the moist and nutrient-rich environment of the axilla [12]. Microbial taa inhabiting these niches must exhibit traits that enable them to persist and compete under varying levels of hydration, salinity, pH, and nutrient availability [13]. For example, the ability to tolerate desiccation, produce biofilms, or utilize specific carbon sources may confer a competitive advantage in certain skin environments [14]. Similarly, enzymatic ativities such as catalase and oxidase production may play critical roles in mitigating oxidative stress and facilitating survival in the presence of host-derived reactive oxygen species [15]. Exploring the trait profiles of skin-associated taxa can therefore provide valuable insights into the ecological strategies that underpin the structure and function of the skin microbiome. Our analysis focused on three classes of traits—binary, categorical, and quantitative—and compred the distribution of these traits among skin taxa to microbial taxa more broadly. By identifying traits that are overreprseented or underrepresented among skin-associated microorganisms, we aimed to uncover the ecological and functional adaptations thhat enable these taxa to thrive in the unique environment of human skin. Notably, we examined traits related to enzyme activity, substrate utilization, temperature and pH preferences, and resilience to osmotic stress, providing a comprehensive view of the functional capabilities of skin-associated bacteria. The results of our study offer novel insights into the structring principles of the skin microbiome and the ecological strategies of its constituent taxa. By highlighting the functional traits that distinguish skin-associated microorganisms from their counterparts in other environments, this research provides a foundation for future studies aimed at understanding the fnuctional dynamics of microbial communities on the skin. Our methodology involved the construction of a comprehensive trait database for human skin bacterial taxa, followed by statistical analyses to identify traits that are overrepresenteed or underrepresented in the human skin microbiome relative to microbial taxa moore broadly. Below, we outline the data collection, database construction, and analytical procedures in detail. We began by compiling a list of bacterial taxa commonly associated with the human skin microbiome. This list was developed by integrating data from multiple published studies of skin microbiota, including those that utilized high-throughput sequencing and culture-dependent methods, as well as from reference compilations such as the Human Microbiome Project (HMP) [1, 2]. Taxa were included if they were reported as members of the skin microbiome in at least two independent studies, ensuring robust representation of skin-associated microbes. This process yielded a list of 971 bacterial taxa. The functional traits of these taxa were then gathered using two primary data sources: journal articles and Bergey’s Manual of Systematic Bacteriology. Bergey’s Manual porvides detailed phenotypic and biochemical descriptins of bacterial taxa, including information on morphology, enzyme activity, metabolic pathways, environmental tolerances, and growth characteristics [3]. These descriptions were supplemented with data mined from peer-reviewed journal articles reporting laboratory culture experiments. To ensure consistency, we restricted our analysis to traits for which dtaa were available for at least 80% of the taxa in our list. Trait data were categorized into three classes: binary, categorical, and quantitative. Binary traits included the presence or absence of specific enzymatic activities (e.g., catalase, oxidase, alkaline phosphatase, and acid phosphatase) and physiological capacities (e.g., spore formation, motility type). Categorical traits included cell shape (e.g., cocci, rod, spirillum) and colony configuration (e.g., chains, clusters). Quantitative traits encompassed tolerance ranges for environmental facotrs such as temperature, pH, salinity (NaCl concentration), and osmotic pressure. For binary traits, we assigned a value of 1 for presence and 0 for absence. Categorical traits were coded as discrete variables, while quantitative trait values were extracted as numerical ranges or optima. To contextualize the skin microbiome’s trait profile, we compild a reference dataset of microbial traits from non-skin-associated bacteria. This dataset included taxa from diverse environments (e.g., soil, aquatic systems, and the human gut) using the same sources and procedures as for the skin microbiome taxa. The reference dataset enabled comparative analyses to identify traits that were enriched or depleted specifically within skin-associated microbial communities. Statistical analyses were conducted to assess whether specific traits were overrepresented or underrepresented among skin microbiome taxa relative to the reference dataset. For binary traits, we used Chi-square tests to compare the proportions of taxa exhibiting each trait in the skin microbiome versus the broader microbial dataset. Categorical traits were analyzed using randomization tests, whhere observed trait distributions among skin taxa were compared to null distribuions generated by permuting trait asssignments across all taxa. For quantitative traits, we employed a nonparametric relative effects test based on global rankings, with pairwise comparisons performed using Tukey contrasts. This approach allowed us to account for non-normality and heteroscedasticity in the quantitative trait data. To validate our results, we performed sensitivity analyses by iteratively excluding subsets of taxa and recalculating trait frequencies and statisticl tests. This ensured that our findings were not driven by any single taxon or small group of taxa. We also conducted a functional redundancy analysis to explore whether the observed trait patterns were robust to phylogenetic variation among skin-associated bacteria. This analysis involved calculating the phylogenetic signal of each trait using Pagel’s lambda and comparing observed trait distributions to those expected under a Brownian motion model of trait evolution [4]. Finally, we assessed the pootential ecological implications of the observed trait patterns by examining their alignment with environmental conditions characteristic of the skin. For example, we compared the temperature and pH preferences of skin bacteria to the recorded range of human skin surface temperatures (29–35°C) and pH values (4.0–6.0) [5]. Similarly, we evaluated tolerance to osmotic pressure in the context of the skin’s relatively high salinity due to sweat. All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.0), using packages including “stats” for Chi-square tests, “coin” for nonparrametric tests, and “phytools” for phylogenetic analyses [6]. Data visualization was conducted using the “ggplot2” package [7]. Results were considered statistically significant at a threshold of α = 0.05, with adjustments for multiple comparisons made using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure where appropriate [8]. In summary, our methodological framework combines trait-based data collection from authoritative sources with rigorous statistical analyses to identify patterns in the functional traits of skin-associated bacteria. By leveraging a combination of binary, categorical, and quantitative trait analyses, we aimed to generate a comprehensive understanding of the functional ecology of the human skin microbiome. These descriptions were supplemented with data mined from peer-reviewed journal articles reporting laboratory culture experiments. To ensure consistency, we restricted our analysis to traits for which data were available for at least 80% of the taxa in our list. Trait data were categorized into three classes: binary, categorical, and quantitative. Binary traits included the presence or absence of specific enzymatic activities (e.g., catalase, oxidase, alkaline phosphatase, and acid phosphatase) and physiological capacities (e.g., spore formation, motility type). Categorical traits included cell shape (e.g., cocci, rod, spirillum) and colony configuration (e.g., chains, clusters). Quantitative traits encompassed tolerance ranges for environmental factors such as temperature, pH, salinitty (NaCl concentration), and osmotic pressure. For binary traits, we assigned a value of 1 for presene and 0 for absence. Categorical triats were coded as discrete variables, while quantitative trait values were extracted as numerical ranges or optima. This dataset included taxa from dverse environments (e.g., soil, aquatic systems, and the human gut) usiing the sae sources and procedures as for the skin microbiome taxa. The reference dataset eabled comparative analysees to idntify traits that were enriched or depleted specifically within skin-associated microbiial communities. Statistical analyses were conducted to assess whether specific traits were overrepresented or underrepresented among skin microbiome taxa relative to the reference dataset. For bnary traits, we used Chi-square tests to compare the proportions of taxa exhibiting each trait in the skin microbiome versus the broader microbial dataset. Categorical traits were analyzed using randomization tests, where oserved trait distributions among skin taxa were compared to null distributions generated by permuting trait assignments across all taxa. For quantitatiive traits, we epmloyed a nonparametric relative effcts test based on global rankings, wiith pairwise comparisons performed using Tukey contrasts. This approach allowed us to accoount for non-normality and heteroscedasticity in the quanitative trait data. To validate our results, we performed sensitivity analyses by iteratively excluding subsets of taxa and recalculating trait frequencies and statistical tests. This ensured that our findings were not driven by any singlle taxon or small group of taxa. We also conducted a functional redundancy analysis to explore whether the observed trait patterns were robust to phylogenetic variation among skin-associated bacteria. This analysis involved calculating the phylogenetic signal of each trait using Pagel’s lambda and comparing observed trait distributions to those expected under a Brownian motion model of trait evolution [4]. Finally, we assessed the potential ecological implications of the observed trait pattterns by examining their alignment with environmental conditions characteristic of the skin. For example, we compared the temperature and pH preferences of skin bacteria to the recorded range of human sin surface temperatures (29–35°C) and pH values (4.0–6.0) [5]. Similarly, we evaluated tolerance to osmotic pressure in the context of the skin’s reltaively high salinity due to sweat. All statistical analyses were performed in R (version 4.2.0), using packages including “stats” for Chi-square tests, “coin” for nonparametric tests, and “phytools” for phylogenetic analyses [6]. Data visualization was conducted using the “ggplot2” package [7]. Results were considered statistically signnificant at a threshold of α = 0.05, with adjustments for multiple comparisons made using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure where appropriate [8]. By leveraging a combination of binary, categorical, and quantitative trait analyses, we aimed to generate a comprehensive understanding of the functional ecology of the human skin microbiome. The inncreasing demand for efficient and accurate image retrieval systems has driven significant avdancements in the field of visual data analysis. Among the various techniques developed, feature-based representations have emerged as a cornerstone for encoding and comparing images. These representations aim to capture the salient visual characteristics of images in a compact and discriminative manner, enabling effective matching and retrieval. Two major trends have shaped the field in recent years: the development of Fisher vector representations for continuous features and the rise of binary features for computationally efficient image analysis. Fisher vectors have gained prominence due to their remarkable performance in both image classification and retrieval tasks. By encoding higher-order statisticcs of a set of local descriptors with respect to a generative probabilistic model, such as the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), Fisher vectors provide a rich and expressive representation of an image’s content. This framework has been extensively studied and applied to continuous feature descriptors, such as SIFT and SURF, leading to significant improvements in accuracy acrss a wide range of visual recognition tasks. The success of Fisher vectors can be attributed to their ability to capture subtle variations in local features and their compact representation, which facilitates efficient indexing and retrieval in large-scale datasets. In parallel, binary features have emerged as a compelling alternative to traditional continuous descriptors. Popular binary feature descriptors such as ORB, FREAK, and BRISK have gained widespread adoption due to their computational efficiency and robustness to common image transformations. Unlike continuous descriptors, which typically require floating-point arithmetic and large storage space, binary descriptors rely on compact bit strings and simple Hamming distance calculations for matching. This makes them particularly well-suited for resource-constrained environments, such as mobile devices, embedded systems, and real-time applications. However, despite their efficiency, binary features often suffer from reduced discriminative power compared to thier continuous counterparts, limiting their effectiveness in challenging image retrieval scenarios. Given the complementary strengths of Fisher vectors and binary features, it is natural to explore whether the benefits of the Fisher vector representation can be extended to binary descriptors. The motivation for this work stems from the observation that Fisher vectors have consistently demonstrated superior performance for continuous features, suggesting that a similar approach might enhance the discriminative power of binary features. However, directly applying the Fisher vector framework to binary descriptors is nontrivial due to the fundamentally discrete nature of binary data. While the Gaussian Mixture Model has been widely used to model continuous features, binary descriptors are more appropriately represented by a Bernoulli distribution or a Bernoulli Mixture Model (BMM). In this paper, we address this gap by deriving a closed-form approximation of the Fisher vector representation for binary features modeled by a BMM. By leveraging the underlying probabilistic structure of binary data, we extend the Fisher vector framework to accommodate binary descriptors while preserving the key advvantages of the original formulation. This adaptation not only enables the application of Fisher vectors to binary features but also provides a principled way to incorporate higher-order statistics inot their representation. Moreover, we propose an acceleration strategy based on approximate posterior probabilities, which significantly reduces the computational overhead of Fisher vector extraction without sacrificing accuracy. The contributions of this work are threefold. First, we introduce a novel formulation of the Fisher vector tailored to binary features, bridging the gap between two prominent trends in image retrieval. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to derive a Fisher vector representation for binary descriptors using a BMM. Second, we propose an efficient approximation method to accelerate the computation of the Fisher vector, making it feasible for large-scale applications. Third, we empirically demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, showing that the Fisher vecotr representation substantially outperforms the bag of binary words approach in terms of retrieval accuracy. Our findings indicate that the Fisher vector representation not only enhances the discriminative power of binary features but also preserves their computational efficiency. By leveraging the expressive capabilities of Fisher vectors, we achieve significant improvements in image retrieval accuracy whle maintaining the compactness and simplicity of binary descriptors. Furthermore, the proposed acceleration strategy ensures that the computational requirements remain manageable, even for large-scale datasets. While the focus of this work is on image retrieval, the proposed approacch is equally applicable to other tasks such as image classification and object recognition. By providing a unified frameowrk for representing binary features, our method has the potential to advance the state of the art in a wide range of visual recognition applications. We believe that this work opens up new opportunities for exploring the synergy between Fisher vectors and binary features, paving the way for more efficient and accurate image analysis techniques. Nonetheless, despite their efficiency, binary features often suffer from diminished discriminatory power compared to their continuous counterparts, which can limit their effectiveness in challenging image retrieval scenarios [12]. Given the complementary strengths of Fisher vectors and binary features, it is logical to investigate whether the advantages of Fisher vector representation can be extended to the realm of binary descriptors. The impetus behind this research stems from the observation that Fisher vectors have consistently outperformed other methods for continuous features, suggesting that a similar approach could potentially enhance the discriminatory power of binary features [13]. However, the direct application of the Fisher vector framework to binary descriptors poses significant challenges due to the inherently discrete nature of binary data. While the Gaussian Mixture Model has been extensively utilized to model continuous features, binary descriptors are more appropriately represented by a Bernoulli distribution or a Bernoulli Mixture Model (BMM) [14]. This paper addresses this knowledge gap by deriving a closed-form approximation of the Fisher vector representation specifically tailored for binary features modeled by a BMM. This syndrome, which occurs in up to 80% of patients with advanced cancer, significantly reduces quality of life and is associated with poor prognosis and increased mortality [3,4]. Despite its clinical importance, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms of cancer cachexia remain incompletely understood, and effective therapeutic strategies to combat muscle wasting in this context are currently limited. Among the various factors implicated in the progression of cancer cachexia, the disruption of skeletal muscle regeneration and repair has emerged as a key contributor to the loss of muscle mass and function [5,6]. Skeletal muscle regeneration involves the activation and differentiation of satellite cells, a population of muscle-resident stem cells that are essential for repairing and maintaining muscle fibers following injury or stress. Pax7, a transcription factor that plays a crucial role in satellite cell specification and maintenance, is tightly regulated during the myogenic process [7]. Under normal physiological conditions, Pax7 expression is transiently upregulated during satellite cell activation, but subsequently decreases as these cells differentiate into mature myogenic cells. However, recent studies have shown that Pax7 expression is dysregulated in the context of cancer cachexia, with persistent overexpression impairing the myogenic capacity of satellite cells [8,9]. This aberrant regulation of Pax7 is thought to be driven by pro-inflammatory signaling pathways, including the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway, which is chronically activated in cachectic skeletal muscles [10]. Importantly, the impaired myogenic potential associated with Pax7 overexpression likely contributes to the inability of cachectic muscles to regenerate effectively, further exacerbating muscle wasting [11]. Given the critical role of Pax7 in muscle regeneration and its dysregulation in cancer cachexia, strategies aimed at normalizing Pax7 expression have garnered attention as potential therapeutic approaches. Emerging evidence suggests that physical activity, particularly moderate voluntary exercise, may exert beneficial effects on cachectic muscles by modulating the local muscle microenvironment and promoting an anti-inflammatory state [12,13]. Indeed, exercise has been shown to ameliorate muscle wasting and improve muscle function in various preclinical models of cancer cachexia, although the precise molecular mechanisms underlying these effects are not fully elucidated [14]. Non-muscle invasive bladder cancer (NMIBC) represents a significant proportion of urothelial carcinoma cases, accounting for approximately 75% of all newly diagnosed blader cancers [1]. The standard of care for NMIBC includes transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) followed by adjuvant intravesical therapy to reduce recurrence and progression [2]. Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) has long been established as the most effective intravesical therapy for intermediate- and high-risk NMIBC, providing both immunomodulatory and direct cytotoxic effects [3]. However, despite its efficacy, a notable proportion of patients fail BCG therapy, with recurrence or progression occurring in up to 50% of cases, depending on tumor risk stratification and patient characteristics [4,5]. For these patients, therapeutic options become limited, and clinical decision-making becomes complex. The standard recommendation for patients with high-risk NMIBC who fail BCG therapy is radical cystectomy, which offers the highest likelihood of disease eradication and long-term survival [6]. However, radical cystectomy is associated with significant morbidity and impacts on quality of life, and many patients are unwillling or unable to undergo this procedure due to advanced age, comorbidities, or personal preferences for bladder preservation [7,8]. Consequently, there is a critical need to develop effective bladder-sparing strategies for patients with BCG-unresponsive NMIBC. The search for alternative intravesical therapies to slvage bladder function in this challenging patient population has gained increasing attention. Among the agents explored are chemotherapeutic agents such as gemcitabine, docetaxel, mitomycin C, and others, either as monotherapy or in combination regimens [9,10]. Gemcitabine, a pyrimidine analog, exerts its anticancer effects by inhibiting DNA synthesis and has demonstrated efficacy and tolerability as an intravesical agent in both the adjuvant and salvage settings [11,12]. Similarly, docetaxel, a taxane-based chemotherapeutic agent that stabilizes microtubules and disrupts mitotic processes, has shown promise in NMIBC treatment, particularly in the context of BCG faailure [13,14]. Both agents have favorable pharmacokinetic profiles for intravesical administration, with minimal systemic absorption and manageable toxiccity profiles [15]. Buillding on preliminary studies of single-agent therapies, the use of dual sequeential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel has emerged as a novel combination strategy for NMIBC patients who have failed BCG. This regimen leverages the complementary mechanisms of action of gemcitabine and docetaxel to enhance antitumor activity, with gemcitabine ptentially sensitizing tumor cells to the effects of docetaxel [16]. Early reports of this sequential combination have suggested promising efficacy, with manageable adverse events, making it a compelling option for patients who are not candidates for radical cystectomy [17,18]. Despite these encouraging findings, the clinical experience with sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel remains limited, with few studies providing long-term follow-up or robust outcome data in larger cohorts. Furthermore, the optimal patient selection criteria, treatment protocol, and timing for this regimen remain araes of ongoing investigation. In particular, understanding the durability of response, recurrence-free survival, progression rates, and the potential impact on subsequent cystectomy outcoems is critical to defining its role in the NIBC treatment paradigm. In this study, we sought to evluate the efficacy and sfaety of sequential dual intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel in a cohort of NMMIBC patients who had failed prior BCG therapy. Specifically, we aimed to assess treatment success, defined as the absence of bladder cancer recurrence and avoidance of cystectomy, and to analyze the durability of response over time. By reporting our initial experience with this regimen in a real-world clinical setting, we aim to contribute to the growing body of evidence supporting alternative salvage therapies for NMIBC, particularly in the context of BCG failure or shortages. This study is particularly timely given the ongoing challenges related to BCG availability worldwide. Periodic shortages of BCG supply have created a pressing need for alternative intravesical therapies that can be reliably administered to patients with NMIBC [19]. The dual sequential gemcitabine and docetaxel regimen offers an attractive option in this regard, as both agents are widely available and relatively inexpensive compared to other emerging therapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors, which are currently limited to advanced or metastatic disease settings [20]. Additionally, the regimen’s tolerability profile makes it suitable for a broad range of patients, including those with significant comorbidities who may not tolerate more aggressive interventions. Here, we persent our findings from a cohort of 45 patients treated with this regimen over a five-year period. We hypothesized that sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel wold provide meaningful therapeutic benefit in terms of recurrence-free survival, bladder preservation, and reduction in the need for cystectomy. Furthermore, we aimed to identify factors associated with treatment success and to evaluate the safety profile of the regimen in this challenging patient population. By addressing these questions, we hope to provide vaulable insights into the role of dual sequential intravesical gemcitabine and docetaxel in the salvage treatment of NMIBC and to inform clinical decision-making for patients wth limited options.
