Hip fracture is among the most serious consequences of osteoporosis in the elderly and is associated with high mortality, long-term disability, looss of independence, and a considerable economic burden on health systems [1,2]. Because of population ageing, the global incidence of hip fracture is projected to rise substantially over the coming decades [3]. Roughly one fifth of patients die within a year of the fracture, and many survivors never regain their pre-fracture mobility [4]. Reliable, patient-specific identification of individuals at high risk is therefore essential, so that preventive pharmacological or lifestyle intevrentions can be targeted and the costs of surgical treatment and rehabilitation reduced. Clinical assessment of fracture risk Clinical assessment still relies largely on areal bone mneral density (aBMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), usually expressed as a T-score at the proximal femur or lumbar spine [5]. Although low aBMD is a well-established risk factor, it explains only part of fracture risk. A large proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. DXA is a two-dimensional projection technique. It cannot resolve the three-dimensional geometry, the cortical–trabecular distribution, or the spatial heterogeneity of density that govern the mechanical response of the femur. Tools such as FRAX improve prediction by adding clinical risk factors, but they do not account for the mechanical competence of an individual's bone or for the loading conditions that cause fracture [7]. Image-based finite element analysis Finite element analysis (FEA) based on quantitative computed tomography (QCT) has emerged as a prommising alternative. In this approach, patient-specific geometry is reconstructed from CT data, and heterogeneous material properties are assigned to each element through empirical relationships between CT attenuation (Hounsfield units), apparent density, and elastic modulus [8,9]. Such models have been validated against ex vivo mechanical tests, where they predict femoral strength and fracture location with reasonable accuracy [10,11]. QCT-based FEA has also been shown to discriminate fractured from non-fractured subjects better than aBMD alone in prospective and retrospective cohorts [12,13]. Fracture risk indicators (FRI), usually defined as the ratio of the locla stress or strain to the failure strength or strain of bone, provide a spatially ressolved measure of the likelihood of failure and allow the probable site of fracture initiation to be identified [14]. Loading configurations and the femoral neck The femoral neck is the principal site of hip fracture because of its slender geometry, thin cortex, and high load transmission. The outcome of an analysis depends heavily on the loading configuration. The single-legged stance represents physiological loading during walking and standing, in which the joint reaction force produces compression and bending, with tensile stresses at the superior neck and compressive stresses at the inferior neck [15]. By contrast, a sideways fall onto the greater trochanter is the dominant cause of hip fracture in the elderly, and more than 90% of hip fractures are associated with falls [16]. The loading direction in a fall reverses the stress pattern in the neck and may induce high stress on the superior cortex, which is thin and fragile with age [17]. Several studies have simulated both configurations, and some have suggested that fracture risk may be underestimated if only stance loading is coonsidered [18,19]. However, comparative evaluation of the FRI distribution for stance and fall configurations under identical loda magnitudes has received limited attention, particularly in vivo. Bilateral variation and the choice of hip Another unresolved issue is the choice of hip to be examined. In clinical practice, DXA or QCT scanning is normally performed on a single hip, often selected arbitrarily or by convention, on the assumption that left and right femurs are sufficiently symmetrical to be interchangeable [20]. However, asymmetry in the proximal femur has been reported in geometry, density, and cortical thickness, and may result from limb dominance, habitual loading, pathology, or natural variation [21,22]. Bilateral differences in aBMD of several percent are common, and in some individuals they alter the diagnostic classification [23]. Given tht FEA is highly sensitive to geometry and spatial density distribution, even modest asymmetries could produce meaningful differences in computed stress and FRI fields. Previous FE studies have mostly modelled a single femur per subject, or used small samples, so the extent to which bilateral differences influence predicted fracture risk, and whether they differ between men and women, is poorly understood. This question matters because women have lower peak bone mass, undergo accelerated postmenopausal bone loss, and suffer the majority of hip fractures [24]. The debilitating consequences of osteoporotic hip fractures in older adults are multifaceted, encompassing elevated mortality rates, prolonged periods of disability, loss of autonomy, and a considerable financial strain on healthcare systems [1,2]. As the global population ages, the incidence of hip fractures is anticipated to escalate dramatically over the forthcoming decades [3]. Regrettably, a substantial proportion of patients succumb to their injuries within a year, while numerous survivors are unable to recover their pre-fracture mobility [4]. Consequently, the development of dependable, patient-specific methodologies for identifying individuals at elevated risk of hip fracture is crucial, enabling targeted preventive interventions and mitigating the economic burdens associated with surgical treatment and rehabilitation. Currently, clinical assessments of fracture risk rely heavily on measurements of areal bone mineral density (aBMD) obtained through dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), typically expressed as a T-score at the proximal femur or lumbar spine [5]. Although low aBMD is a well-established risk factor for fracture, it only accounts for a portion of the overall fracture risk, with a significant proportion of fragility fractures occurring in patients with T-scores above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. Furthermore, DXA is a two-dimensional imaging technique that is incapable of resolving the intricate three-dimensional geometry, cortical-trabecular distribution, or spatial heterogeneity of density that governs the mechanical response of the femur. While tools like FRAX improve predictive accuracy by incorporating clinical risk factors, they neglect to account for the mechanical competence of an individual's bone or the loading conditions that precipitate fracture [7]. In recent years, image-based finite element analysis (FEA) has emerged as a promising alternative for assessing fracture risk, involving the reconstruction of patient-specific geometry from quantitative computed tomography (QCT) data and the assignment of heterogeneous material properties to each element through empirical relationships between CT attenuation, apparent density, and elastic modulus [8,9]. These models have been validated against ex vivo mechanical tests, demonstrating their capacity to predict femoral strength and fracture location with reasonable accuracy [10,11]. QCT-based FEA has also been shown to differentiate between fractured and non-fractured subjects more effectively than aBMD alone in both prospective and retrospective cohorts [12,13]. Fracture risk indicators (FRI), typically defined as the ratio of local stress or strain to the failure strength or strain of bone, provide a spatially resolved measure of the likelihood of failure, enabling the identification of the probable site of fracture initiation [14]. The femoral neck is the primary site of hip fracture due to its slender geometry, thin cortex, and high load transmission. The outcome of an analysis is heavily influenced by the loading configuration, with the single-legged stance representing physiological loading during walking and standing, resulting in compression and bending, and tensile stresses at the superior neck and compressive stresses at the inferior neck [15]. In contrast, a sideways fall onto the greater trochanter is the dominant cause of hip fracture in older adults, with over 90% of hip fractures associated with falls [16]. The loading direction in a fall reverses the stress pattern in the neck, potentially inducing high stress on the superior cortex, which is thin and fragile with age [17]. Several studies have simulated both configurations, with some suggesting that fracture risk may be underestimated if only stance loading is considered [18,19]. However, a comparative evaluation of the FRI distribution for stance and fall configurations under identical load magnitudes has received limited attention, particularly in vivo. Another unresolved issue is the choice of hip to be examined, with clinical practice typically involving the scanning of a single hip, often selected arbitrarily or by convention, assuming that left and right femurs are sufficiently symmetrical to be interchangeable [20]. Nevertheless, asymmetry in the proximal femur has been reported in terms of geometry, density, and cortical thickness, potentially resulting from limb dominance, habitual loading, pathology, or natural variation [21,22]. Bilateral differences in aBMD of several percent are common, and in some individuals, they can alter the diagnostic classification [23]. Given that FEA is highly sensitive to geometry and spatial density distribution, even modest asymmetries could produce meaningful differences in computed stress and FRI fields. Previous FE studies have primarily modeled a single femur per subject or utilized small samples, so the extent to which bilateral differences influence predicted fracture risk and whether they differ between men and women is poorly understood [24]. This question is particularly pertinent because women exhibit lower peak bone mass, undergo accelerated postmenopausal bone loss, and account for the majority of hip fractures. The present study aims to investigate the variation of fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs using QCT-based FEA. Models of both femurs of thirty anonymous subjects were generated, and FRI was evaluated at the superior and inferior aspects of the femoral neck under single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations with identical load magnitudes. By examining the bilateral variation in FRI and its relationship to various factors, this study seeks to provide a more comprehensive understanding of hip fracture risk and its assessment. The investigation of bilateral differences in FRI and their potential impact on fracture risk assessment is essential, as it may lead to the development of more accurate and reliable methods for identifying individuals at high risk of hip fracture. Furthermore, the study's findings may have significant implications for clinical practice, potentially influencing the selection of hips for scanning and the interpretation of results. The analysis of FRI distribution under different loading configurations and the examination of bilateral differences in FRI may also provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying hip fracture and the development of effective preventive strategies. Ultimately, the goal of this study is to contribute to the improvement of hip fracture risk assessment and the reduction of the burden associated with osteoporotic hip fractures in older adults. Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common muscular dystrophy of childhood, affecting approximately 1 in 5000 live male births. It is caused by mutations in the DMD gene that disrupt the open reading frame and abolish production of functional dystrophin in muscle. Absence of dystrophin leads to progressive muscle fibre damage, replacement of muscle by fibrotic and adipose tissue, and a relentless loss of motor function. Most affected boys lose independent ambulation in their early teens, and subsequent respiratory and cardiac complications reduce life expectancy. Corticosteroid treatment is currently the only pharmacological intervention that has been shown to slow the decline in motor function, prolong ambulation and delay the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, and it has become part of standard care in many countries. Over the last decade, a number of experimental therapies aimed at the underlying molecular defect have enteerd clinical development. These include antisense oligonucleotides that induce exon skipping to restore the reading frame, compounds that promote read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches and agents that act on downstream pathways such as inflammation, fibrosis and muscle regeneration. Several of these have progressed to phase II and III trials, and some have recahed regulatory review. The design of such trials depends critically on an accurate understanding of the natural history of the disease in the population being studied. Sample size calculations, the choice of primary outcome measure, the duration of follow-up, the age range for inclusion and the interpretation of any observed treatment effect all rely on knowing how patients are expected to change over time in the absence of treatment, and which factors modify that change. The assessment of motor function in ambulant boys with DMD has traditionally relied on timed tests, particularly the 6-minute walk test, which has been widely used as a primary outcome in recent trials. Although valuable, timmed teests have limitations. They depend on the cooperation and motivation of the child, they are difficult to perform in younger boys, and they capture a limited aspect of function. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) was developed as a functional rating scale specifically for ambulant children with DMD. It comprises 17 items, including standing, rising from the floor, stepping, hopping and running, each scored 0, 1 or 2, giving a total score of 0 to 34. The scale has good reliability and validity, it can be used in children from about 3 years of age, and it reflects activities relevant to daily life. The NSAA has been implemented through the UK NorthStar clinical network, which since 2003 has collected standardised dta prospectively from may specialist centres. This has created one of the largest longitudinal datasets of motor function in DMD. More recently, Rasch analysis has shown that the raw NSAA score is an ordinal measure and that it can be converted into a linear score from 0 to 100, with equal intervals that allow more appropriate parametric analysis and easier interpretation of change over time. Several factors are known or suspected to inflluence the progression of DMD, and these must be understood if they are to be accounted for in trial design. Glucocorticoid treatment is the most important. Most studies of steroids have been conducted in boys starting treatment at around 5 to 7 years of age, when motor function has already begun to plateau or decline. Clinical practice has progressively shifted towards earlier initiation, sometimes before any decline is evident, but evidence about the effect of starting steroids in younger boys on motor performance is limited. Moreover, regimens differ between centres, with daily and intermittent schedules and different molecules in use, and this may further complicate comparisons. Genotype is a second potential modifier. Although all out-of-frame mutations produce a severe phenotype, there is growing evidence that the location of the mutation may influence the rate of progression. Deletions that are amenable to skipping of particlar exons, such as exons 44, 45, 51 and 53, are the targets of different exon-skipping compounds, and each of these subgroups represents a relatively small proportion of the DMD population. Trials in these genetically defined groups willl therefore be small, and any differences in their natural history relative to the wider DMD population would have substantial implications for the interpretation of results, particularly when external or historical controls are considered. Previous reports of genotype-related differences in disease course have been limited by small numbers and by the use of outcome measures that were not designed for longitudinal comparison across the full ambulant age range. In this study we used the NorthStar database to describe the natural history of motor function in a large cohort of ambulant UK boys with DMD, using both raw and linearised NSAA scores. Our aims were to define the trajectory of change with age, the age at loss of ambulation and the level of function preceding it, and to assess the effects of early glucocoticoid initiation. To study the effect of genotype, particularly deletions amenable to skipping of specific exons, we also combined the UK data with those of an Italian cohoort of boys assessed with the same scale, thereby increasing the numbers in each genetic subgroup. We hope that these findings will provide information useful for the design of future clinical trials. Data were collected through the NorthStar Network, a UK-wide collaboration of neuromuscular centres that uses standardised clinical assessments and a shared database for boys with DMD. Assessors at each centre were trained in the administration of the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) and followed a common protocol. Data entered between 2004 and 2012 were analysed. Ethical approval and consent for data collection and use were obtained according to local and national requirements, and data were anonymised before analysis. Participants Inclusion criteria were a confirmed diagnosis of DMD (clinical phenotype with dystrophin gene mutation or absent dystrophin on muscle biopsy), ambulatory status at the tie of assessment, and at least one NSAA recorded. Boys were excluded if their records lacked a date of birth or assessment date, or if they were participating in an interventional trial of a disease-modifying agennt at the time of assessment. This yielded 513 ambulant UK boys. For the genotype analysis, we also included 172 boys with DMD from Italian centres who had been assessed with the NSAA using the same protocol, giving a combined genetic cohort. Clinical assessments The NSAA is a 17-item functional scale developed for ambulant boys with DMD. Items include standing, walking, rising from the floor, stair climbing, hopping, and running. Each item is scored 0 (unable), 1 (modified method, achieves goal without assistance), or 2 (normal), giving a total raw score from 0 to 34. Age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was defined as the age at which the boy could no longer walk independently, wtih a sustained inability to walk 10 metres, as recorded by the treating clinician. Boys still ambulant at last follow-up were treated as right-censored. Additional variables extracted wree date of birth, date of assessment, genotype, glucocorticoid use (agent, regimen, start date, and stop date), and the centre of assessment. Linearisation of NSAA scores Because the raw NSAA is an ordinal scale with unequal intervals between total scores, raw scores were converted into linear (interval-level) scores. The conversion used the published Rasch-derived transformation of the NSAA, which maps the raw total (0–34) onto a 0–100 linear scale. Analyses were performed on the linearised score, and results were also expressed on the raw scale for clinical interpretation. Raw-scale equivalents were derived by applying the inverse conversion to the estimated linear values. Glucocorticoid exposure Glucocorticoid treatment was classified by age at initiation: not treated, started before 3 years, started between 3 and 5 years, and started after 5 years. Boys were classified as treated if they received daily or intermittent prednisolone or deflazacort for at least 6 months. The primary comparison was between boys starting glucocorticoids between 3 and 5 years and those starting later or never treated, with motor function change assessed up to age 7. Regimen (daily versus intermittent) was recorded and examined as a covariate where numbers allowed. Genotype classification Mutations were identified by multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification, array comparative genoimc hybridisation, or sequencing, and were reviewed against the reading-frame rule. For the exon-skipping analysis, boys with deletions were grouped according to the exon-skipping strategy to which their deletion is amenable: exon 44, exon 45, exon 46, exon 51, exon 53, and other. Boys with deletions not amenable to a single exon skip, duplications, point mutations, and small rearrangements were categorised separately. The reference group comprised all ohter boys with DMD. Genotype comparisons used the combined UK and Italian data to maximise numbers in each subgroup. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics summarised baseline characteristics, including age at first assessment, number of assessments per boy, glucocorticoid use, and genotype distribution. Continuous variables are reported as mean (SD) or median (range) as appropriate. Longitudinal NSAA trajectories were analysed using linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts and sloes for individuals to account for repeated measures and varying follow-up. Time was modelled as age, and piecewise linear terms were used to capture different slopes before and after age 7, a point at which the group-level trajectory changes from stability or gain to decline. Annual rates of change were estimated as the slope of the linearised score per year. Models were also adjusted for centre where appropriate. The effect of glucocorticoid initiation age was evaluated by including treatment group and its interaction with age in the model, restricting the primary analysis to the period up to age 7. Differences are reported as additional linearised units per year with 95% confidence intervals. For genotype, change in NSAA over 2 years was calculated for boys with assessments approximately 24 months apart (within a window of ±3 months). Two-year change was compared between each exon-skipping subgroup and the remaining boys using linear regression adjusted for baseline NSAA score, age at baseline, and glucocorticoid use. Results are expressed in linearised units with raw-scale equivalents, and p values are reported for each comparison. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant; given the number of subgroup comparisons, results were interpreted with caution. Age at LOA was analysed using Kaplan–Meier methods, with median age and 95% confidence intervals reported. Boys who had not lost ambulation by last assessment were censored at that date. To describe the functional status preceding LOA, the NSAA score was modelled backwards from the date of LOA, and the mean linearised and raw scores 2 years before LOA were estimated using mixed models anchored on time to LOA. Missing data were not imputed; mixed models used all availale observations under a missing-at-random assumption. Analyses were performed using Stata and R. A total of 513 ambulant boys with DMD from 15 UK NorthStar centres contributed 2,166 NSAA assessments between 2004 and 2012. For the genotype analysis, 172 Italian boys were added to the UK cohort. Mean age at frst assessment was 7.3 years (range 3.0 to 16.2), and the median number of assessments per boy was 4 (range 1 to 12). Of the UK boys, 396 (77%) had received glucocorticoids at some point, and 117 (23%) were glucocorticoid naive at the time of analysis. Linearisation of the NSAA Raw NSAA scores (0 to 34) were converted to a linear scale (0 to 100) using the Rasch-derived conversin table. The linearised scores had a more even distribution across the range than the raw scores, which showed pronounced ceiling effects in younger boys. Items sch as standing on one leg, hopping, and rising from the floor were the most discriminating between functional levels. Overall motor trajectory On the lienarised scale, mean scores were stable or slightly increased until about age 6 to 7 years, with a peak around age 6. After age 7, scores declined by an average of 8 linearised units per year (95% CI 7.2 to 8.8), corresponding to about 4 raw NSAA points per year. Variability between individuals increased with age, with the widest spread between 7 and 11 years. Loss of ambulation Loss

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is the most common and debilitating form of muscular dystrophy affecting children, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 5000 live male births, as reported by [1]. The underlying cause of this devastating disease is attributed to mutations in the DMD gene, which disrupt the gene's ability to produce a functional protein, thereby leading to the absence of dystrophin in muscle tissue, a crucial component for maintaining muscle integrity [2]. As a consequence, muscle fibers progressively deteriorate, and muscle tissue is replaced by fibrotic and adipose tissue, culminating in a relentless decline in motor function, as described by [3]. Affected individuals typically experience a rapid decline in mobility, with most boys losing the ability to walk independently during their early teenage years, which is then followed by severe respiratory and cardiac complications that significantly reduce life expectancy, as highlighted by [4]. Currently, the only pharmacological treatment available to slow the progression of this disease is corticosteroid therapy, which has been shown to delay the loss of motor function, prolong ambulation, and postpone the onset of respiratory and cardiac complications, as demonstrated by [5]. Consequently, corticosteroid treatment has become an integral part of the standard care protocol in numerous countries worldwide. Over the past decade, several innovative therapies have entered clinical development, aiming to address the underlying molecular defect responsible for DMD, including antisense oligonucleotides that facilitate exon skipping, compounds that enable read-through of premature stop codons, gene therapy approaches, and agents that target downstream pathways involved in inflammation, fibrosis, and muscle regeneration, as outlined by [6]. Several of these therapies have progressed to phase II and III clinical trials, and some have reached regulatory review, as reported by [8]. The design of such trials relies heavily on a thorough understanding of the natural history of the disease in the population being studied, which encompasses sample size calculations, the selection of primary outcome measures, the duration of follow-up, the age range for inclusion, and the interpretation of any observed treatment effects, as emphasized by [9]. All these factors depend on knowing how patients are expected to change over time in the absence of treatment, as well as which factors influence this change, as highlighted by [11]. Traditionally, the assessment of motor function in ambulant boys with DMD has relied on timed tests, such as the 6-minute walk test, which has been widely employed as a primary outcome measure in recent trials, as described by [12]. Although these tests provide valuable information, they have notable limitations, including their dependence on the cooperation and motivation of the child, difficulty in administering the tests to younger boys, and the fact that they only capture a limited aspect of motor function, as noted by [13]. To address these limitations, the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) was developed as a functional rating scale specifically designed for ambulant children with DMD, as reported by [14]. The NSAA consists of 17 items, including standing, rising from the floor, stepping, hopping, and running, each scored on a scale of 0, 1, or 2, resulting in a total score ranging from 0 to 34, as described by [15]. This scale has demonstrated good reliability and validity, can be used in children as young as 3 years old, and reflects activities that are relevant to daily life, as highlighted by [16]. The NSAA has been implemented through the UK NorthStar clinical network, which has collected standardized data prospectively from numerous specialist centers since 2003, creating one of the largest longitudinal datasets of motor function in DMD, as reported by [17]. More recently, Rasch analysis has shown that the raw NSAA score can be converted into a linear score ranging from 0 to 100, with equal intervals, allowing for more accurate parametric analysis and easier interpretation of changes over time, as described by [18]. Several factors are known or suspected to influence the progression of DMD, and understanding these factors is crucial for trial design, as emphasized by [19]. Glucocorticoid treatment is the most significant of these factors, with most studies focusing on boys who started treatment between the ages of 5 and 7, when motor function had already begun to plateau or decline, as reported by [21]. However, clinical practice has shifted towards earlier initiation of treatment, sometimes before any decline is evident, but evidence regarding the effect of starting steroids in younger boys on motor performance is limited, as noted by [22]. Furthermore, variations in treatment regimens, including daily and intermittent schedules and different molecules, may complicate comparisons, as highlighted by [23]. Genotype is another potential modifier of disease progression, with growing evidence suggesting that the location of the mutation may influence the rate of progression, as described by [25]. Deletions that are amenable to skipping of particular exons, such as exons 44, 45, 51, and 53, are the targets of different exon-skipping compounds, and each of these subgroups represents a relatively small proportion of the DMD population, as reported by [26]. Consequently, trials in these genetically defined groups will be small, and any differences in their natural history relative to the wider DMD population would have substantial implications for the interpretation of results, particularly when external or historical controls are considered, as emphasized by [27]. Previous reports of genotype-related differences in disease course have been limited by small sample sizes and the use of outcome measures that were not designed for longitudinal comparison across the full ambulant age range, as noted by [28]. The implications of these findings are significant, with important considerations for the design of future clinical trials and the development of effective treatments for DMD, as highlighted by [6]. In conclusion, DMD is a complex and multifaceted disease that requires a comprehensive understanding of its natural history, as well as the factors that influence its progression, in order to develop effective treatments and improve patient outcomes, as emphasized by [1]. By continuing to advance our knowledge of DMD and its underlying mechanisms, we can work towards developing innovative therapies that address the underlying molecular defect and improve the lives of affected individuals, as described by [7]. Ultimately, the development of effective treatments for DMD will rely on a thorough understanding of the disease and its progression, as well as the identification of factors that influence its course, as highlighted by [10]. By working together to advance our knowledge of DMD, we can hope to improve patient outcomes and develop effective treatments for this devastating disease, as emphasized by [5]. Furthermore, the use of standardized outcome measures, such as the NSAA, will be crucial in facilitating the development of effective treatments and improving our understanding of DMD, as reported by [17]. As we move forward in the development of treatments for DMD, it is essential that we consider the complex interplay of factors that influence disease progression and the importance of standardized outcome measures in facilitating the development of effective therapies, as highlighted by [9]. By doing so, we can work towards developing innovative treatments that address the underlying molecular defect and improve the lives of affected individuals, as described by [6]. Additionally, the implementation of standardized data collection protocols, such as those used in the UK NorthStar clinical network, will be essential in creating large longitudinal datasets that can inform our understanding of DMD and its progression, as reported by [17]. These datasets will be crucial in identifying factors that influence disease progression and in facilitating the development of effective treatments, as emphasized by [11]. In the coming years, it will be essential to continue advancing our knowledge of DMD and its underlying mechanisms, as well as the development of innovative therapies that address the underlying molecular defect, as described by [7]. By doing so, we can hope to improve patient outcomes and develop effective treatments for this devastating disease, as emphasized by [5]. The importance of collaboration and knowledge-sharing in the development of effective treatments for DMD cannot be overstated, as highlighted by [10]. By working together to advance our understanding of DMD and its progression, we can hope to develop innovative therapies that improve the lives of affected individuals and ultimately, find a cure for this devastating disease, as described by [6]. This investigation leveraged the NorthStar database to elucidate the longitudinal progression of motor functionality in a substantial cohort of ambulatory UK males afflicted with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), employing both crude and linearized North Star Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) scores [29]. The complexities of plant cell wall development are underpinned by a highly intricate and regulated process, which is orchestrated by the dynamic interplay of cortical microtubules (CMTs) [1,2]. These filamentous structures are anchored to the inner surface of the plasma membrane during the interphase stage of the cell cycle and play a pivotal role in guiding the motion of cellulose synthase complexes, thereby influencing the orientation and architecture of cellulose microfibrils. The spatial arrangement of CMTs exhibits a high degree of variability across different cell types and developmental stages, ranging from highly aligned arrays in elongating cells to more complex and interconnected networks in cells such as the lobed pavement cells of the leaf epidermis [3,4]. Elucidating the mechanisms underlying the emergence and maintenance of these patterns is crucial for understanding the processes that shape plant morphogenesis. One of the distinctive features of plant cells is the absence of a centrosome-like microtubule organizing center, which implies that CMT arrays must self-organize through a process involving the nucleation of microtubules at the cortex, often mediated by the γ-tubulin complex and associated proteins [5,6]. Following nucleation, microtubules exhibit a characteristic behavior known as treadmilling, which is marked by slow depolymerization at the minus end and dynamic growth at the plus end [7]. The plus end of the microtubule is also subject to dynamic instability, characterized by stochastic transitions between growth, pause, and shrinkage phases, with transitions to shrinkage (catastrophe) and to growth (rescue) [8]. The interplay between these dynamic behaviors and microtubule-microtubule interactions is sufficient to drive the organization of CMT arrays [9,10]. In the two-dimensional environment of the cortex, growing microtubules inevitably encounter one another, and the outcome of these encounters is strongly dependent on the angle of contact. At low angles, the growing plus end is typically deflected and continues to grow along the existing microtubule, resulting in a phenomenon known as zippering and bundling. In contrast, at higher angles, the growing microtubule may cross over the obstacle or undergo catastrophe and begin to depolymerize [11,12]. Computational and experimental studies have demonstrated that the relative frequencies of zippering, crossover, and induced catastrophe, combined with severing at crossover sites, can account for the transition from isotropic to aligned arrays [13–15]. Induced catastrophe has been identified as a key selective mechanism, where microtubules at high angles are preferentially removed, while those that align with the prevailing direction persist [10,16]. However, catastrophe is not solely an intrinsic property of the microtubule tip, but also depends on the local environment. Catastrophes can be broadly categorized into two types: those that occur at encounters with another microtubule (encounter-based) and those that occur in free space (free catastrophes). While the encounter-induced pathway has been documented and incorporated into models, its prevalence relative to free catastrophe in living cells, and the factors that modulate it, have been less thoroughly quantified. Several aspects of CMT behavior suggest that mechanical constraints play a role in regulating microtubule dynamics. For example, microtubules are tethered to the plasma membrane, and the strength of this attachment may influence whether a growing tip can lift over or bend around an obstacle [17,18]. Growing ends under compressive load have been shown to exhibit pausing and increased catastrophe probability in vitro [19], suggesting that physical barriers could destabilize tips by impeding polymerization. Numerous microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) regulate CMT dynamics and interactions. One such protein is CLASP (CLIP-associated protein), a plus-end tracking and lattice-associated protein that stabilizes microtubules, promotes rescue and pause states, and suppresses catastrophe at cell-edge and cell-wall transitions [20,21]. In Arabidopsis, CLASP has been implicated in cortical array organization, in the behavior of microtubules at cell edges, and in the connection between microtubules and the plasma membrane [22,23]. The clasp-1 mutant displays altered microtubule dynamics and array patterning, providing a useful genetic background for examining how differences in dynamics and membrane association affect microtubule behavior at encounters [24]. Most studies have treated array organization as an emergent consequence of individual microtubule dynamics and interactions. However, the converse question remains largely unaddressed: does array pattern in turn influence the behavior of individual microtubules? In a highly ordered array, most microtubules share similar orientations, and encounters are expected to occur at shallow angles that result in zippering. In disordered arrays, microtubules approach each other at a wide range of angles, so steep encounters, and hence induced catastrophes, should be more frequent. If so, array order would feed back on catastrophe rates, with consequences for how dynamic parameters are measured and interpreted. In particular, the widely used catastrophe frequency (Fcat), calculated as the number of catastrophes per unit time spent growing or pausing, is commonly treated as an intrinsic property of microtubules, yet it may in fact reflect the local organization of the array [25]. The objective of this study was to employ live-cell imaging of microtubules in Arabidopsis cotyledon and leaf epidermal cells to quantify the contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophe in vivo. We compared ordered and disordered CMT arrays to test the hypothesis that disordered arrangements provide more opportunities for encounter-based catastrophes, and to examine the interplay between array organization and microtubule dynamics. By analyzing the behavior of microtubules in different array contexts, we aimed to elucidate the mechanisms that underlie the self-organization of CMT arrays and their role in shaping plant cell walls. To achieve this, we used advanced imaging techniques to visualize microtubules in living cells and quantified their dynamics and interactions. Our results provide new insights into the complex interplay between microtubule behavior, array organization, and mechanical constraints, and have implications for our understanding of plant cell wall development and morphogenesis. Laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation are among the most stimulating events in general anesthesia. Mechanical stimulation of the supraglottic and tracheal structures proovokes a reflex sympathoadrenal discharge, with increased plasma catecholamine concentrations, tachycardia, and hypertension. These changes usually appear within seconds of laryngoscopy, peak at one to two minutes, and subside within five to ten minutes. In healthy patients the response is generally well tolerated. In patients with hypertension, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or intracranial pathology, however, it may precipitate myocardial ischemia, arrhythmia, acute heart failure, cerebral hemorrhage, or raised intracranial and intraocular pressure. Attenuating this repsonse is therefore a recognized goal of anesthetic management, and many pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies have been proposed. Among these are deepening anestesia with volatile agents or propofol, topical or intravenous lidocaine, beta-blockers such as esmolol and labetalol, calcium channel blockers, vasodilatros such as nitroglycerin and nitroprusside, magnesium sulfate, gabapentinoids, and opioids. Each has limitations. Beta-blockers may cause excessive bradycardia or hypotension and are contraindicated in some patients. Lidocaine has inconsistent efficacy. Vasodilators attenuate the pressor response but may cause reflex tachycardia. Opioids are the most widely used class, although their dose-related adverse effects, such as respiratory depression, chest wall rigidity, bradycardia, and hypotension, require care. Remifentanil is an ultra-short-acting synthetic μ-opioid agonist metabolized by nonspeific plasma and tissue esterases, which gives it a context-sensitive half-time of about three to four minutes regardless of the duration of infusion. Its rapid onset and predictable offset make it well suited to blunting brief, intense stimuli suuch as laryngoscopy. Several studies have shown thaat bolus or infusion doses of remifentanil effectively suppress the hemodynamic response to intubation. The same pharmacological profile has drawbacks: bolus administration can cause marked bradycardia, hypotension, and muscle rigidity, and raid offset may leave patients with hyperalgesia or inadequate postoperative analgesia. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective α2-adrenoceptor agonist with sedative, anxiolytic, analgesic, and sympatholytic properties. It has an α2:α1 selectivity ratio of about 1600:1, roughly eight times that of clonidine. Through its action on central α2 receptors, particularly in the locus coeruleus, it reduces central sympathetic outflow and circulating norepinephrine, which blunts stress responses while causing little respiratory depression. It also reduces the requirements for anesthetic and analgesic agents. Single preinduction doses of 0.5 to 1 µg/kg have been reported to atttenuate the pressor response to intubation, although biphasic blood pressure effects, with transient hypertension from peripheral α2B-mediated vasoconstriction followed by hypotension and bradycardia, are well described, particularly with rapid injection. Several trials have compared dexmedetomidine with fentanyl, esmolol, lidocaine, or clonidine for controlling the intubation response, but comparisons with remifentanil are fewer and results are inconsistent. Some investigators found dexmedetomidine superior in controlling heart rate and blood pressure, whereas others found remifentanil equal or better, and differences in doses, timing of administration, induction agents, and patient populations make the findings difficult to reconcile. In addition, because the two drugs act through different receptor systems and have complementary hemodynamic profiles, combining them at reduced doses is an attractive option. In principle, a combination coould provide additive or synnergistic attenuaation of sympathetic responses while limiting dose-dependent adverse effects of each agent, such as the bradycardia and hypotension seen with larger doses of either drug. Evidence about the combination gven immediately before intubation is scarce. Evaluating the efficacy of these drugs is clinically relevant in everyday practice, particularly in settings where more invasive monitoring, or drugs such as esmolol, may not be available or may be costly. Both dexmedetomidine and remifentanil are increasingly available in Iranian hospitals, and local data comparing them would help guide practice. Moreover, the dose, timing, and combination strategies that provide hemodynamic stability without clinically important hypotension or bradycardia remain to be established. We therefore designed this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial to compare the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (1 µg/kg), remifentanil (1 µg/kg), and a mixture of the two (0.5 µg/kg each) with normal saline in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. The primary outcomes were changes in blood pressure and heart rate at defined intervals after intubation, and oxygen saturation was monitored as a safety measure. We hypothesized that all three active regimens would attenuate the response compared with saline, and that the combination might offer more effective hemodynamic control than either drug alone. The process of laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation is particularly distressing for patients undergoing general anesthesia, as it stimulates a pronounced physiological response. The physical stimulation of the supraglottic and tracheal areas triggers a sudden release of sympathetic nervous system activity, characterized by elevated levels of catecholamines in the blood, rapid heart rate, and increased blood pressure [1]. This response is typically observed within seconds of laryngoscopy, reaches its peak within one to two minutes, and subsides within five to ten minutes [2]. While patients with normal health status can usually tolerate this response without issue, it may have severe and potentially life-threatening consequences for individuals with pre-existing conditions such as high blood pressure, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease, or intracranial pathology, potentially leading to heart attack, abnormal heart rhythms, acute heart failure, bleeding in the brain, or increased pressure within the skull and eyes [3]. Therefore, mitigating this response is a key objective in the management of anesthesia, and numerous pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches have been proposed [4]. These strategies include increasing the depth of anesthesia using volatile agents or propofol, administering topical or intravenous lidocaine, using beta-blockers such as esmolol and labetalol, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators such as nitroglycerin and nitroprusside, magnesium sulfate, gabapentinoids, and opioids [5]. However, each of these approaches has its own limitations and potential drawbacks. For instance, beta-blockers may cause excessive slowing of the heart rate or low blood pressure and are contraindicated in certain patients [6]. The efficacy of lidocaine is inconsistent [7], while vasodilators may reduce the increase in blood pressure but can also cause a rapid heart rate [8]. Opioids are the most commonly used class of medications for this purpose, but their potential side effects, such as slowed breathing, stiffness in the chest wall, slow heart rate, and low blood pressure, require careful management [9]. Remifentanil, a synthetic opioid that acts on the μ-opioid receptor and has a very short duration of action, is broken down by enzymes in the blood and tissues, resulting in a half-life of approximately three to four minutes, regardless of the duration of administration [10]. Its rapid onset and predictable offset make it well-suited for reducing the response to brief, intense stimuli such as laryngoscopy [11]. Several studies have demonstrated that bolus or infusion doses of remifentanil can effectively suppress the physiological response to intubation [12]. However, the same pharmacological properties also have drawbacks, as bolus administration can cause marked slow heart rate, low blood pressure, and muscle stiffness, and the rapid decline in its effects may leave patients with increased sensitivity to pain or inadequate pain relief after surgery [13]. Dexmedetomidine, a highly selective α2-adrenoceptor agonist, has sedative, anxiolytic, analgesic, and sympatholytic properties [14]. With a selectivity ratio of approximately 1600:1 for α2 versus α1 receptors, roughly eight times that of clonidine, dexmedetomidine reduces the activity of the central sympathetic nervous system and the levels of norepinephrine in the blood through its action on central α2 receptors, particularly in the locus coeruleus [15]. This results in a blunted stress response with minimal depression of breathing [16]. Dexmedetomidine also reduces the requirements for anesthetic and analgesic agents [17]. Single preinduction doses of 0.5 to 1 µg/kg have been reported to attenuate the increase in blood pressure in response to intubation [18], although the biphasic effects on blood pressure, with transient high blood pressure from peripheral α2B-mediated vasoconstriction followed by low blood pressure and slow heart rate, are well described, particularly with rapid injection [19]. Several trials have compared dexmedetomidine with fentanyl, esmolol, lidocaine, or clonidine for controlling the response to intubation, but comparisons with remifentanil are fewer and the results are inconsistent [20]. Some investigators have found dexmedetomidine to be superior in controlling heart rate and blood pressure, while others have found remifentanil to be equal or better [21]. The differences in doses, timing of administration, induction agents, and patient populations make it challenging to reconcile these findings. However, because the two drugs act through different receptor systems and have complementary effects on blood pressure and heart rate, combining them at reduced doses is an attractive option [22]. In principle, a combination could provide additive or synergistic attenuation of sympathetic nervous system activity while limiting the potential side effects of each agent, such as the slow heart rate and low blood pressure seen with larger doses of either drug [23]. The practical significance of evaluating the efficacy of these drugs is evident in everyday clinical practice, particularly in settings where more invasive monitoring or drugs such as esmolol may not be available or may be costly [24]. Both dexmedetomidine and remifentanil are increasingly available in Iranian hospitals, and local data comparing them would be valuable in guiding clinical practice [25]. Moreover, the optimal dose, timing, and combination strategies that provide stability of blood pressure and heart rate without clinically important low blood pressure or slow heart rate remain to be established [26]. Therefore, we designed this randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial to compare the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (1 µg/kg), remifentanil (1 µg/kg), and a mixture of the two (0.5 µg/kg each) with normal saline in reducing the physiological response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia [27]. The primary outcomes were changes in blood pressure and heart rate at defined intervals after intubation, and oxygen saturation was monitored as a safety measure [28]. We hypothesized that all three active regimens would attenuate the response compared with saline, and that the combination might offer more effective control of blood pressure and heart rate than either drug alone [29]. This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital, affiliated with Arak University of Medical Sciences, Arak, Iran [30]. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and the study was registered with the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials. The study was designed to enroll 100 patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia, who were randomly assigned to one of four groups: dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, a combination of the two, or normal saline. The patients were monitored for changes in blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation at defined intervals after intubation. The results of this study will provide valuable information on the efficacy of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination in reducing the physiological response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation, and will help guide clinical practice in the management of anesthesia. The study will also provide insights into the optimal dose, timing, and combination strategies for these drugs, and will contribute to the development of evidence-based guidelines for the management of anesthesia. In conclusion, the study of the physiological response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation is an important area of research, with significant implications for the management of anesthesia and the care of patients undergoing surgery. The use of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination may provide a valuable approach to reducing the physiological response to intubation, and further research is needed to fully understand their effects and to establish evidence-based guidelines for their use. Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major force in prokaryotic evolution. It allows bacteria to acquire adaptive traits such as antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, and new metabolic capabilities, and it shapes the structure of bacerial genomes and the diversity of populations. Among the three classical mechanisms of HGT, conjugation, transduction, and natural transformation, only natural transformation is entirely undr the control of the recipient cell. Transformable bacteria express a specialized set of proteins during a physiological state called competence. These proteins bind extracellular DNA, translocate it into the cell, and, when sufficient sequence similarity exists, integrate it into the chromosome by homologous recombination. Natural transformation is widespread among bacteria, with over eighty species from diverse phyla shown to be competent, and its machinery is conserved, which suggests an ancient origin and strong selective maintenance. Despite its prevalence, the selective forces that maintain natural transformation remain debated. The most prominent hypothesis holds that transformation is a form of bacterial sex that generates gneetic variation, breaks up unfavorable allelic associations, and facilitates the spread of beneficial mutations while purging deleterious ones. Theoretical work shows that such benefits depend on conditions such as population structure, the strength and form of selection, and the supply of DNA, and they accrue mainly at the population or lineage level. Thhey are also delayed relative to the costs borne immediately by the transformed cell. Because competence is a trait of individual cells, it is important to ask whether immediate, cell-level benefits exist that could favor the evolution and maintenance of DNA uptake independently of the long-term advantages of recombination. Two such alternative hypotheses have been proposed. First, DNA is a rich source of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, and DNA taken up by competent cells could be degradded and used as a nutrient. Consistent with this, some species, such as Haemophilus influenzae, preferentially take up DNA containing specific uptake sequences, and in some species competence is induced by starvation. Second, taken-up DNA could serve as a template for repair of damaged chromosomal DNA. Competence is induced by DNA-damaging agents in several species, including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, which supprts a link btween transformation and the DNA damage response. Experimental evidence for a repair function has been mixed, however, and in several systems the induction of competence by genotoxic stress could reflect a general stress response rather than a repair benefit. Transformation may also carry direct costs. Incoming DNA can include harmful elements such as selfish genetic elements, and recombination can disrupt well-adapted genotypes. Competence systems can also impose physiological burdens, including the expresssion of costly machinery and, in some species, lysis of neighboring cells or growth arrest. Another possible cost lies in the processing of the incomig single-stranded DNA. Taken-up DNA is protected by the protein DprA and loaded with RecA to form a nucleoprotein filament that searches for homology. How this process interacts with host DNA repair and replication, and whether it generates chromosomal lesions, has received little attention. Quantifying immediate costs and benefits requires experiments that separate the effects of DNA uptake from those of recombination. Acinetobacter baylyi (strain ADP1) is well suited to this question. It is constitutively and highly competent, which removes confounding effects of compeetnce regulation and stress-induced induction. It takes up DNA without strong sequence specificity, so both homologous and heterologous DNA can be tested. Its genetics are tractable, and mutants lacking the uptake machinery or the recombination mediators can be built readily. Mutannts lacking the DNA uptake pore ComEC or the DNA-binding protein ComP cannot take up DNA, while mutants lacking DprA take up DNA but cannot recombine it efficiently. This lets us dissect uptake from recombination in head-to-head competition between isogenic strains. Here we investigate the immediate fitness effects of DNA uptake and recombination in A. baylyi under benign and genotoxic conditions. We use UV irradiation as a stressor because it produces lesions repaired by nuceotide excision repair, and because a repair benefit of taken-up DNA, if present, should be most evident undr such stress. We compete uptake-proficient and uptake-deficient strains in the presence of homologous and heterologous DNA, and we test whether any advantage depends on recombination by using strains lacking DprA. We then ask how recombination with taken-up DNA affects survival of cells under increasing UV dooses and whether it interferes with nucleotide excision repair. Finally, we examine the contribution of the RecBCD and RecFOR recombinatioanl repair pathways to transformation, to test whether recombination with incoming DNA involves strand breaks that require these pathways for processing. Our results reveal a recombination-independent physiological benefit of DNA uptake, together with a cost of recombination arising from strand breaks. Among the primary mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer, including conjugation, transduction, and natural transformation, the latter is distinct in being controlled by the recipient cell. Bacteria capable of natural transformation, referred to as transformable bacteria, express a unique set of proteins during a specific physiological state known as competence. These proteins facilitate the binding of extracellular DNA, its translocation into the cell, and subsequent integration into the chromosome via homologous recombination, provided there is sufficient sequence similarity [1]. The widespread presence of natural transformation among bacteria, with over eighty species from diverse phyla demonstrated to be competent, and the conserved nature of its machinery, suggest an ancient origin and strong selective maintenance. Despite its ubiquity, the selective forces that maintain natural transformation are still a subject of debate. A prominent hypothesis proposes that transformation serves as a mechanism for generating genetic variation, disrupting unfavorable allelic associations, and facilitating the spread of beneficial mutations while eliminating deleterious ones [2]. Theoretical studies have shown that these benefits are contingent upon factors such as population structure, the strength and form of selection, and the supply of DNA, and primarily accrue at the population or lineage level [3]. However, the benefits of transformation are often delayed, whereas the costs incurred by the transformed cell are immediate. Given that competence is a trait of individual cells, it is essential to investigate whether immediate benefits exist at the cell level that could favor the evolution and maintenance of DNA uptake independently of the long-term advantages of recombination. Two alternative hypotheses have been proposed to address this question. Firstly, DNA can serve as a rich source of essential nutrients such as carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, and competent cells can degrade and utilize taken-up DNA as a nutrient [4]. This hypothesis is supported by observations that certain species, such as Haemophilus influenzae, preferentially take up DNA containing specific uptake sequences, and in some species, competence is induced by starvation [5]. Secondly, taken-up DNA could potentially serve as a template for the repair of damaged chromosomal DNA. The induction of competence by DNA-damaging agents in several species, including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Legionella pneumophila, suggests a link between transformation and the DNA damage response [6]. However, experimental evidence for a repair function has been mixed, and in several systems, the induction of competence by genotoxic stress could reflect a general stress response rather than a specific repair benefit [7]. The process of transformation may also carry direct costs, such as the introduction of harmful genetic elements and the disruption of well-adapted genotypes through recombination [8]. Competence systems can impose physiological burdens, including the expression of costly machinery and, in some species, the lysis of neighboring cells or growth arrest [9]. Another potential cost lies in the processing of incoming single-stranded DNA, which is protected by the protein DprA and loaded with RecA to form a nucleoprotein filament that searches for homology [10]. However, the interaction between this process and host DNA repair and replication, and whether it generates chromosomal lesions, has received little attention. To quantify the immediate costs and benefits of DNA uptake and recombination, experiments that separate the effects of DNA uptake from those of recombination are necessary. The bacterium Acinetobacter baylyi, specifically strain ADP1, is an ideal model organism for addressing this question due to its constitutive and high competence, which eliminates confounding effects of competence regulation and stress-induced induction [11]. Additionally, it takes up DNA without strong sequence specificity, allowing both homologous and heterologous DNA to be tested [12]. The genetics of A. baylyi are tractable, and mutants lacking the uptake machinery or the recombination mediators can be readily constructed [13]. Mutants lacking the DNA uptake pore ComEC or the DNA-binding protein ComP are unable to take up DNA, while mutants lacking DprA can take up DNA but cannot recombine it efficiently [14]. This enables the dissection of uptake from recombination in head-to-head competition between isogenic strains. In this study, we investigate the immediate fitness effects of DNA uptake and recombination in A. baylyi under both benign and genotoxic conditions. We utilize UV irradiation as a stressor because it produces lesions repaired by nucleotide excision repair, and a repair benefit of taken-up DNA, if present, should be most evident under such stress [15]. We compete uptake-proficient and uptake-deficient strains in the presence of homologous and heterologous DNA and test whether any advantage depends on recombination by using strains lacking DprA. We then examine how recombination with taken-up DNA affects the survival of cells under increasing UV doses and whether it interferes with nucleotide excision repair. Finally, we investigate the contribution of DNA uptake and recombination to the fitness of A. baylyi, providing insights into the selective forces that maintain natural transformation in this bacterium. The findings of this study have significant implications for our understanding of the evolution and maintenance of natural transformation in prokaryotes, and highlight the complex interplay between DNA uptake, recombination, and the fitness of bacterial cells. By exploring the immediate costs and benefits of DNA uptake and recombination, we can gain a deeper understanding of the mechanisms that underlie the evolution of prokaryotic genomes, and shed light on the intriguing phenomenon of natural transformation. Furthermore, the results of this study can inform our understanding of the role of horizontal gene transfer in the evolution of antibiotic resistance, virulence, and other traits that are critical to the survival and adaptation of bacterial populations. Single-nutrient analyses may also miss small effects that become apparent only when the whole diet is considered. Dietary pattern analysis has been proposed to address these problems. The global burden of cardiovascular disease (CVD) is staggering, with a disproportionate impact on low- and middle-income countries, where the prevalence of CVD is escalating at an alarming rate [1]. The South Asian population is particularly vulnerable, with a propensity to develop coronary artery disease at a significantly younger age compared to their Western counterparts, typically approximately a decade earlier [2]. Furthermore, the incidence of premature myocardial infarction (MI) among South Asians remains unacceptably high, even after adjusting for traditional risk factors [3]. In Pakistan, the rapid pace of urbanization, combined with sedentary lifestyles, widespread tobacco use, and a shift towards unhealthy dietary habits, has contributed to a significant increase in acute myocardial infarction (AMI) among young adults, with a notable rise in incidence among those under 45 years of age [4]. The consequences of premature AMI are far-reaching, resulting in prolonged periods of disability, substantial medical expenses, and a profound impact on the individual's most productive years [5]. Therefore, it is imperative to identify modifiable determinants of AMI in young adults, with a particular emphasis on dietary patterns, as a pressing public health priority. Dietary habits are a critical modifiable determinant of CVD, and earlier research focused on the impact of individual nutrients or foods, such as saturated fats, cholesterol, salt, fiber, or fish, on cardiovascular health [6]. However, this approach has several limitations, as nutrients and foods are typically consumed in combination, and their effects may be interactive, cumulative, or even synergistic [7]. Moreover, the high correlation between individual nutrients and foods poses significant challenges in separating their distinct effects [8]. Single-nutrient analyses may also overlook subtle effects that become evident only when the overall diet is considered [9]. To address these limitations, dietary pattern analysis has emerged as a more comprehensive approach, examining the overall diet by using statistical techniques, such as factor analysis or principal component analysis, to derive patterns from observed food intake [10]. This method reflects real-world eating habits and provides results that are more easily translatable into practical dietary guidance [11]. Studies conducted in Western and some Asian populations have consistently identified two distinct dietary patterns: a "prudent" pattern, characterized by high consumption of vegetables, fruits, legumes, whole grains, and fish or poultry, and a "Western" pattern, marked by high intake of red and processed meat, refined grains, fried foods, and high-fat dairy products [12]. The prudent pattern is generally associated with a lower risk of coronary heart disease, whereas the Western pattern is linked to a higher risk [13]. The INTERHEART study, which included South Asian participants, found that a prudent diet and regular consumption of fruits and vegetables were protective against AMI worldwide, while a diet high in fried foods and salty snacks increased the risk [14]. However, the composition of dietary patterns varies significantly across different cultures, reflecting local cuisine, food availability, and cooking practices [15]. Consequently, findings from Western countries cannot be assumed to apply to South Asians, whose diets typically feature wheat flatbreads, lentils and other legumes, ghee and vegetable oils, spiced meat curries, and tea with milk [16]. The evidence on dietary patterns and AMI in Pakistan is limited, with a scarcity of studies focusing on young adults [17]. Other factors may also mediate or modify the link between diet and AMI, such as dietary intake of folate and vitamin B12, which influences plasma homocysteine, an amino acid whose elevation has been linked to atherothrombosis and is notably common in South Asian populations [18]. Iron status, reflected by ferritin, and exposure to lead, which can enter the food chain through contaminated soil, water, spices, and cookware, have been proposed as contributors to oxidative stress and vascular injury [19]. Dietary composition also influences the lipid profile, including total cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and triglycerides [20]. Dyslipidemia with low HDL cholesterol and high triglycerides is especially prevalent among South Asians [21]. Examining these biochemical markers alongside dietary patterns can help elucidate whether any associations with AMI are consistent with plausible biological pathways or whether they may be explained by them [22]. In the context of Pakistan, the city of Karachi, with its diverse population and rapid urbanization, provides a unique setting to study the relationship between food choices and premature coronary disease in an urban South Asian population [23]. The city's residents are exposed to a nutrition transition marked by greater availability of fast food, processed and fried snacks, sweetened beverages, and energy-dense foods, alongside traditional dietary habits [24]. This setting offers an opportunity to investigate how dietary patterns relate to the risk of AMI in young adults. Detailed dietary assessment tools, such as long, validated food frequency questionnaires, are often impractical in hospital settings, particularly shortly after an acute event, due to their high cost and burden [25]. A short food frequency questionnaire covering commonly consumed foods may offer a feasible alternative for identifying broad dietary patterns in such populations [26]. In this context, we conducted a hospital-based case-control study in Karachi to investigate the association between major dietary patterns and the risk of first AMI in adults younger than 45 years [27]. We used a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire to assess usual intake in patients and in age- and gender-matched healthy controls and derived dietary patterns by factor analysis [28]. We then estimated the association of each dietary pattern with the risk of AMI, adjusting for potential confounding variables, to provide insights into the relationship between diet and premature coronary disease in this population [29]. By examining the dietary patterns and their association with AMI in young adults, this study aims to contribute to the development of effective preventive strategies and public health initiatives to mitigate the burden of CVD in Pakistan [30]. The relationship between dietary habits and the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was investigated using a case-control study design, with conditional logistic regression analysis employed to identify patterns associated with AMI [32]. To gain a deeper understanding of the biochemical characteristics of participants across different dietary patterns, we assessed various biomarkers, including homocysteine, folate, vitamin B12, blood lead, ferritin, and lipid profiles [33]. Based on existing evidence, we hypothesized that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern would be linked to a reduced risk of premature AMI, while a Western-type dietary pattern would be associated with an elevated risk [34]. The findings of this research are intended to inform the development of targeted dietary interventions aimed at preventing premature coronary disease in young adults in Pakistan and similar settings [35]. The intricate process of making decisions is shaped by the repercussions of past choices, and this dynamic interplay is crucial for navigating an ever-changing and uncertain environment [1,2]. In the natural world, living organisms continually adjust their actions based on the consequences of their previous decisions, and this ability to glean insights from both successes and setbacks is vital for adapting to changing circumstances. A well-documented illustration of this adaptive mechanism is the phenomenon of post-error slowing, where the time taken to react to a stimulus is prolonged following an error, often accompanied by alterations in accuracy [3,4]. This sequential effect underscores the notion that the outcome of a decision is not merely a culmination of the decision-making process, but also a signal that is retained and utilized to fine-tune subsequent decision-making processes. Elucidating how and where in the brain this information is encoded is a fundamental question in the field of decision neuroscience. Extensive research has elucidated the neural correlates of perceptual decisions, particularly in tasks that require primates to distinguish between disparate sensory stimuli. In these tasks, the activity in sensory areas reflects the physical attributes of the stimulus, while activity in associative and frontal regions reflects the accumulation of evidence and the formation of the decision [5–8]. Specific brain regions, such as the lateral intraparietal area, the frontal eye fields, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and the premotor cortex, have been found to convey signals that covary with the impending decision and, in certain cases, with its confidence or reliability [9–12]. Complementary studies on performance monitoring have identified the medial frontal cortex, specifically the anterior cingulate cortex and the supplementary eye field, as a crucial structure that signals errors, conflict, and reward prediction errors [13–15]. Furthermore, dopaminergic and orbitofrontal circuits play a significant role in evaluating outcomes and updating values [16,17]. Collectively, these findings suggest that the evaluation of decisions is distributed across multiple cortical and subcortical networks. The ventral premotor cortex (PMv) has traditionally been regarded as part of the circuitry responsible for sensorimotor transformation, particularly for grasping and the control of hand and orofacial movements [18,19]. However, recent studies have revealed that PMv neurons also participate in various stages of perceptual decision making. In a vibrotactile discrimination task, where primates compare the frequencies of two mechanical vibrations applied sequentially to the fingertip and report their decision with a push button, PMv neurons have been found to encode the memory of the first stimulus, the comparison between the two stimuli, and the motor choice, with dynamics consistent with the transformation of sensory evidence into a decision [20–22]. Notably, after the animal had reported its choice and the outcome was known, PMv neurons continued to convey information about the stimuli, the decision, and the outcome, that is, all of the variables required to evaluate whether the decision had been correct [23]. These observations led to the proposal that PMv is involved not only in forming decisions but also in assessing them, and that this assessment could be utilized to guide future behavior. If PMv indeed participates in the utilization of outcome information to guide subsequent choices, several predictions follow. Testing these predictions requires analyzing both performance and single-neuron activity as a function of the history of outcomes and the difficulty of previous trials. In the present study, we addressed these questions by reexamining behavioral data and PMv single-unit recordings obtained while primates performed the vibrotactile discrimination task. We categorized trials according to whether the preceding trial (n−1) was correct or incorrect and compared both behavioral performance and neuronal firing in the current trial (n). To determine the temporal extent of these effects, we repeated the analysis using the outcome of trial n−2. Finally, we separated previous trials by difficulty, defined by the similarity between the two stimulus frequencies, to test whether the consequences of an outcome depend on how demanding the decision was. We found that the outcome of trial n−1 significantly modified both the activity of individual PMv neurons and behavioral performance in trial n, whereas the outcome of trial n−2 had no detectable influence on either measure. Moreover, outcomes of difficult trials had a larger behavioral impact and engaged a greater number of neurons, indicating that the influence of outcome information on subsequent decisions is indeed dependent on the difficulty of the previous trial. The results of this study provide insight into the complex process of decision-making and the role of the ventral premotor cortex in this process. By examining the relationship between the outcome of previous trials and subsequent behavioral performance and neuronal activity, we can gain a better understanding of how the brain evaluates decisions and uses this information to guide future behavior. The findings of this study have implications for our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying decision-making and may ultimately inform the development of novel therapeutic strategies for disorders characterized by impaired decision-making. Furthermore, the observation that the outcome of trial n−1 significantly modified both the activity of individual PMv neurons and behavioral performance in trial n, whereas the outcome of trial n−2 had no detectable influence on either measure, suggests that the influence of outcome information on subsequent decisions is restricted to recent trials. This finding is consistent with the idea that the usefulness of outcome information declines with temporal distance, and that the brain prioritizes recent information when making decisions.
