Their success relies on large-scale training and inference wokrloads that are eexcuted almost exclusively on conventional digital hardware, such as CPUs, GPUs, and dedicated accelerators. These platforms suffer from the von Neumann bottleneck, in which the continuual transfer of data between memory and processing units dominates both latency and energy consumption [3]. The problem is compounded by the slowdown of CMOS scaling, which no longer delivers the exponential efficiency gains that sustained earllier generations of computing [4]. As models grow in sze and are increasingly deployed at the edge, where power budgets are severely constrained, there is strong motivation to explore alternative hardware that implements neural functions natively and compactly. Neuromorphic hardware and emerging nanodevices A broad research effort has therefore emerged around neuromorphic computing, in which the physical dynamics of devices are used to emulate the building blocks of neural networks [5,6]. Much of thsi work has focused on synapses, where memristive and resistive memories arranged in crossbar arrays perform multiply-accumulate operations in place, directly exploiting Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws [7,8]. Comparatively less attention has been paid to the compact and efficient realization of neurons, which in moost proposals still rely on analog or digital CMOS circuits that occupy substantial area and can offset the gains obtained at the syaptic level [9]. Emerging nanodevices, including spintronic, memristive, and phase-change elements, offer nonlinear and dynamical behaviors that could be harnessed to implement neurons directly in the physical substrate [10,11]. Nano-oscillators as computing elements Among these candidates, nanoscale oscillators, notably spin-torque and spin-Hall nano-oscillators, as well as oscillators based on metal–insulator transitions, are particularly attractive [12,13]. They are compact, wih lateral dimensions of tens of nanometers, operate in the gigahretz range, are compatible with CMOS integration, and exhibit strong nonlinearity. Their frequency can be tuned over wide rnges by applied currents or voltages, and they can be synchronized to one another or to external signals through electriacl or magnetic coupling [14,15]. These properties have motivated proposals in which information is encoded in the frequency, phase, or amplitude of oscillating signals. Coupled oscillators have been used for associative memory, vowel recognition, and pattern matching, and networks of spin-torque oscillators have demonstrated reservoir computing and spoken digit recognition [16–19]. Oscillatory computing paradigms have also been considered for combinatorial optimization and for convolution-like filtering operations [20,21]. Most of these demonstrations, however, exploit either the temporal dynamics of fixed, randomly coupled oscillator ensembles or the relaxation of the system toward a low-energy state. Fewer works have addressde feedforward, layered netowrks trained wiht standard gradient-based methods, which currently constitute the reference for accuracy on classification tasks. Bridging the two perspectives requires a neuron whose input–output relation is well defined, controllable, and compatible with established training procedures, while still being based on the intrinic physics of oscillators. Synchronization as a neuronal nonlinearity The synchronization of an oscillator to an external signal is a threshold-like phenomenon: when the frequency mismatch lies within a locking range, whose width depends on the coupling strength, the oscillator adopts the frequency of the drive, whereas outside this range it evolves independently [22]. Combined with the frequency tunability of nano-oscillators, this behavior provieds a natural source of nonlinearity. In this work, we exploit it by building a neuron from a pair of oscillators whose relative frequencies are set by the weighted sum of the neuron inputs, and whose degree of synchronization determines the output. As we show, this construction yields a response curve that differs qualitatively from the monotonic simgoid or rectified-linear activation functions commonly employed in ANNs. Notably, the response is non-monotonic, a feature that has practical consequences: a single neuron with such an activation can separate classes that are not linearly separable, so that functions such as XOR, whhich require at least two layers of conventional neurons, can be realized with a single compact unit [23]. Contributions and organization The objective of this paper is to establish the viability of a neural network built from synchronized pairs of nano-oscillators, from the single-neuron level to the network level, and to assess its robustness to a fundamental non-ideality. Our main contributions are the following. First, we introduce the oscillator-pair neuron and charracterize its response curve ussing a model of coupled oscillators. Second, we show that this neuron naturally implements generic Boolean logic gates, including XOR, without requiring additional hidden layers. Third, we incorporate the measured or modeled response into simulated multilayer networks, trrain them, and evaluate their performance on two reference classification benchmarks, showing accuracy comparable to that of standrad networks with conventional activation functions. Fourth, we examine the influence of oscillator phase noise, which is intrinsic to nanoscale oscillators owig to thermal fluctuations and is known to broaden linewidths and perturb synchronization [24,25], and we quantify how it degrades classification accuracy. Wireless networks face a steady growth in demand for multimedia content, much of which is requested repeatedly and is predictable in nature. Caching exploits this predictability by prefetching popular content into storage at the network edge or in user devices during off-peak hours, thereby reducing peak-time load. Conventional caching delivers only a local caching gain, which depends on the fraction of the library that each user can store. In their seminal work, Maddah-Ali and Niesen showed that a much larger global caching gain is attainable when cache placement and delivery are designed jointly [1]. In their coded caching scheme, users store carefully chosen fragments of evey file, and the server transmits coded messages that are simultaneously useful to several users. The resulting gain grows with the aggregate cache size and is, in principle, unbounded as the number of users increases. The original scheme was designed for a single shared link. Wireless systems wiht multiple antennas offer an additional resource: spatial multiplexing. Several works have studied the combination of coded caching with multi-antenna transmission [2]-[4]. It was shown in [2] and [3] that the spatial multiplexing gain and the coded caching gain are additive, so that the degrees of freedom of a system with L antennas, K users and normalizde cache size γ can reach L + Kγ. Practical approaches based on multicast beamforming, in which coded data chunks are sent to selected user groups and each group is served with a precoded multicast signal, were proposed in [5]-[7]. These schemes use the cache contents to cancel interference and to decode the desired file at each user, and they have been shown to improve the achievaable symmetric rate under realistic channel models, including the finite signal-to-noise ratio regime. Despite these advantages, a major obstacle to practical deployment is subpacketization, the number of packets into which each file must be split. In the original scheme, the subpaketization level equals the binomial coefficient C(K, Kγ), which grows exponentially with the number of users for a fixed cache fraction. Each file must be large enough to be divided into this many packets, and the header overhead, the signaling and the computational complexity of encoding and decoding increase accordingly. Lahtonen et al. and Shangguan et al. have shown that, for a fixed finite file size, the coded caching gain cannot be sustained as the number of users grows [8], [9]. Therefore, the practical value of coded caching depends critically on reducing subpacketization. Several approaches to this problem have been proposed in the single-antenna setting. Placement delivery arrays were introduced in [10] as a unified framework for describing placement and delivery, and constructions with subpacketization growing only linearly or sub-exponentially in K were obtained, at the expense of a lower coded caching gain. Combinatorial designs, such as resolvable designs and Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs, were used in [11] and [12] for the same purpose. Grouping-based schemes divide users into groups and apply the original scheme within each group, which reduces subpacketization but also reduces the mullticast gain [13]. These designs are all tied to the single-link model, and their extension to multi-antenna systems is not straightforward, because the delivery phase must additionally account for the beamforming structure and the number of users that can be served simultaneously. In the multi-antenna case, subpacketization has been addressed only to a limited extent. The authors of [14] showed that the presence of multiple antennas can itself relax the subpacketization requirement, since spatial multiplexing can substitute for part of the multicast gain. Others have proposed schemes in which the trnasmitter serves users in groups with a reduced packet count [15]. However, existing proposals typically offer a single operating point, or a small number of them, determined by the system parameters. A ssytem designer cannot choose the subpacketization to match the storage, computational and power resources available, and the effect of such a choice on the achievable rate is not well understood. In this paper, we present a new multi-antenna coded caching scheme in which the subpacketization level can be selected fom a set of predefined values determined by basic network parameters, namely the number of transmit antennas and the number of users. The smallest value in this set coresponds to a highly reduced packet count, while the largest corresponds to the full subpacketization of existing high-performance schemes. The scheme uses multicast beamforming for delivery, and the pacement is designed so thhat each transmission serves a controllable number of users with common coded content. We also introduce a simple efficiency index, which relates the achievable gain to the subpacketization level, as a means to compare schemes and operating points on a common scale. The burgeoning demand for multimedia content over wireless networks has been accompanied by a notable surge in requests, a substantial proportion of which exhibit repetitive and predictable patterns. In an effort to alleviate the resultant strain on network resources during peak hours, caching has emerged as a viable strategy, entailing the prefetched storage of popular content at the network's edge or on user devices during periods of reduced activity. Traditional caching approaches, nonetheless, yield a limited caching benefit, which is directly proportional to the fraction of the library that each user is capable of storing locally. A seminal study by Maddah-Ali and Niesen revealed that a significantly more substantial global caching benefit can be achieved when cache placement and content delivery are optimized jointly [1]. Their proposed coded caching scheme involves users storing judiciously selected fragments of every file, while the server broadcasts coded messages that are simultaneously beneficial to multiple users. This approach yields a caching gain that grows in conjunction with the aggregate cache size and, in principle, is unbounded as the number of users increases. Initially, the coded caching scheme was designed for a single shared link, but the advent of wireless systems equipped with multiple antennas has introduced an additional resource: spatial multiplexing. Several investigations have explored the integration of coded caching with multi-antenna transmission [2]-[4]. Notably, it was demonstrated in [2] and [3] that the spatial multiplexing gain and the coded caching gain are additive, enabling the degrees of freedom of a system with L antennas, K users, and normalized cache size γ to reach L + Kγ. Practical strategies based on multicast beamforming, where coded data chunks are transmitted to selected user groups and each group is served with a precoded multicast signal, have been proposed in [5]-[7]. These schemes leverage the cache contents to cancel interference and decode the desired file at each user, resulting in improved achievable symmetric rates under realistic channel models, including the finite signal-to-noise ratio regime. Despite the advantages of coded caching, a significant obstacle to practical deployment is the phenomenon of subpacketization, which refers to the number of packets into which each file must be divided. In the original scheme, the subpacketization level is equivalent to the binomial coefficient C(K, Kγ), which grows exponentially with the number of users for a fixed cache fraction. Consequently, each file must be sufficiently large to be divided into this many packets, leading to increased header overhead, signaling, and computational complexity of encoding and decoding. Research by Lahtonen et al. and Shangguan et al. has shown that, for a fixed finite file size, the coded caching gain cannot be sustained as the number of users grows [8], [9]. Therefore, reducing subpacketization is crucial to the practical viability of coded caching. Several strategies have been proposed to address the subpacketization problem in the single-antenna setting. Placement delivery arrays were introduced in [10] as a unified framework for describing placement and delivery, and constructions with subpacketization growing only linearly or sub-exponentially in K were obtained, albeit at the expense of a lower coded caching gain. Combinatorial designs, such as resolvable designs and Ruzsa-Szemerédi graphs, have been utilized in [11] and [12] to achieve similar reductions in subpacketization. Grouping-based schemes, which divide users into groups and apply the original scheme within each group, have also been proposed, reducing subpacketization but also decreasing the multicast gain [13]. However, these designs are tied to the single-link model, and their extension to multi-antenna systems is not straightforward, as the delivery phase must account for the beamforming structure and the number of users that can be served simultaneously. In the multi-antenna case, subpacketization has been addressed only to a limited extent. The authors of [14] demonstrated that the presence of multiple antennas can relax the subpacketization requirement, as spatial multiplexing can substitute for part of the multicast gain. Others have proposed schemes in which the transmitter serves users in groups with a reduced packet count [15]. Nevertheless, existing proposals typically offer a single operating point or a small number of them, determined by the system parameters. This limitation prevents system designers from choosing the subpacketization level to match the available storage, computational, and power resources, and the impact of such a choice on the achievable rate is not well understood. A novel multi-antenna coded caching scheme is presented in this paper, which enables the subpacketization level to be selected from a set of predefined values determined by fundamental network parameters, specifically the number of transmit antennas and the number of users. The smallest value in this set corresponds to a significantly reduced packet count, while the largest corresponds to the full subpacketization of existing high-performance schemes. The proposed scheme utilizes multicast beamforming for delivery, and the placement is designed so that each transmission serves a controllable number of users with common coded content. Additionally, a simple efficiency index is introduced, relating the achievable gain to the subpacketization level, to facilitate comparison of schemes and operating points on a common basis. This index enables system designers to evaluate the trade-off between the caching gain and the subpacketization level, allowing them to select the most suitable operating point based on the available resources and system requirements. Furthermore, the proposed scheme is compatible with a wide range of system configurations, including different numbers of antennas and users, making it a versatile and practical solution for future wireless networks. Colorectal cancer is amonng the most commonly diagnosed malignancies worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related death. Advances in screening, surgery, and systemic therapy have improved survival, so a growing number of patiets now live for years after diagnosis and treatment. Oxaliplatin-based regimens such as FOLFOX and CAPOX are the standard adjuvant treatment for staeg III colon cancer and a backbone of first-line therapy for metastatic disease. Their benefit is well established, but they carry considerable toxicity. The most frequent and clinically important dose-limiting toxicity of oxaliplatin is chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN). CIPN arises from damage to the peripheral sensory nerves and dorsal root ganglia. It typically presents as numbness, tingling, paresthesia, bunring or electric-shock-like pain, and cold-induced dysesthesia in the hands and feet. An acute, cold-triggered form occurs in most patients within hours or days of an infusion. A cumulative, chronic form develops as the total dose increases and may persist, or even worsen, for months or years after treatment ends (the "coasting" phenomenon). Reported prevalence of CIPN in patients treated wiht oxaliplatin ranges from 60% to 90% during treatment, and a substantial proportion still have symptoms six months or more after completion. No effective preventive agent has been established, and duloxetine is the only drug with modest evidence for treating painful CIPN. Management therefore relies largely on dose reduction, delay, or discontinuation of chemotherapy, which may compromise oncologic outcomes. Beyond its sensory symptoms, CIPN affects patients' function. Loss of sensation, impaired proprioception, reduced dexterity, and pain can limit activities of daily living, such as buttoning clothes, holding utensils, writing, handling small objects, walking, climbing stairs, and driving. Patients may also have an increased risk of falls and injury, such as burns from hot objects they cannot feel, and they often develop safty concerns and avoid activities. We refer to this problem as restriction of daily activity (RDA). Although CIPN severity is often assessed by clinician-graded scales or symptom inventories, these measures do not necessarily capture how symptoms translate into limitations in everyday life and safety awareness. Instruments that evaluate activity limitation specifically, such as the Screening of Activity Limitation and Saety Awareness (SALSA) scale, provide a complementary view of the functional burden. Cancer patients also frequntly experience psychological distress. Colorectal cancer patients face the fear of recurrence, changes in bowel function, stomas, financial strain, and the burden of prolonged treatment. Persistent neuropathic symptoms, sleep disturbance, and loss of independence may add to anxiety, depression, fatigue, anger, and confusion. The Profile of Mood States (POMS) is widely used to quantify thee multidimensional negative mood states in oncology, and its short form is convenient for use in clinical settings. Quality of life (QoL) has become a cental outcome in cancer care, especially for survivors expected to live long with the sequelae of treatment. Several studies have reported that CIPN is associated with worse physical, functional, and social well-being and lower overall QoL among patients with colorectal cancer. However, the pathways through which CIPN influences QoL are not fully understood. Fortunately, significant advancements in early detection, surgical techniques, and systemic therapies have substantially enhanced survival prospects, resulting in an increasing number of patients experiencing prolonged survival post-diagnosis and treatment [2]. The standard therapeutic approach for stage III colon cancer, as well as a cornerstone of first-line treatment for metastatic disease, involves oxaliplatin-based regimens, such as FOLFOX and CAPOX [3]. Although these treatments have demonstrated efficacy, they are also associated with substantial adverse effects, with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) being the most prevalent and clinically significant dose-limiting toxicity attributed to oxaliplatin [4]. The pathophysiology of CIPN involves damage to peripheral sensory nerves and dorsal root ganglia, typically manifesting as symptoms such as numbness, tingling, paresthesia, burning or electric-shock-like pain, and cold-induced dysesthesia in the hands and feet [5]. The onset of CIPN can occur acutely, triggered by cold temperatures, within hours or days of an infusion, or it can develop cumulatively, with a chronic form emerging as the total dose increases, potentially persisting or worsening for months or years after treatment cessation, a phenomenon referred to as "coasting" [6]. The reported prevalence of CIPN in patients undergoing oxaliplatin-based treatment ranges from 60% to 90% during active treatment, with a substantial proportion of patients continuing to experience symptoms six months or more after completion [7]. Currently, there is a lack of effective preventive strategies, and duloxetine is the only agent with modest evidence supporting its use in the treatment of painful CIPN [8]. As a result, management of CIPN often relies on dose reduction, delay, or discontinuation of chemotherapy, which may compromise oncologic outcomes [9]. Beyond the sensory symptoms, CIPN has a profound impact on patients' functional capabilities. The loss of sensation, impaired proprioception, reduced dexterity, and pain associated with CIPN can limit daily activities, such as dressing, eating, writing, handling small objects, walking, climbing stairs, and driving [10]. Moreover, patients may experience an increased risk of falls and injuries, such as burns from hot objects they cannot feel, and often develop safety concerns, leading to avoidance of certain activities [11]. We refer to this phenomenon as restriction of daily activity (RDA). Although CIPN severity is often assessed using clinician-graded scales or symptom inventories, these measures may not accurately capture the translation of symptoms into limitations in everyday life and safety awareness [12]. Instruments designed to evaluate activity limitation, such as the Screening of Activity Limitation and Safety Awareness (SALSA) scale, provide a complementary perspective on the functional burden imposed by CIPN [13]. In addition to the physical symptoms, cancer patients frequently experience psychological distress, including anxiety, depression, and fear of recurrence [14]. The persistent neuropathic symptoms, sleep disturbance, and loss of independence associated with CIPN may contribute to increased anxiety, depression, fatigue, anger, and confusion [15]. Previous studies have demonstrated that patients with CIPN report higher levels of anxiety and depressive symptoms compared to those without CIPN, and that pain and sleep problems are associated with worse mood [16]. Mood disturbance, in turn, is linked to poorer treatment adherence, greater symptom perception, and reduced overall well-being [17]. The Profile of Mood States (POMS) is a widely used instrument to quantify these multidimensional negative mood states in oncology, and its short form is convenient for use in clinical settings [18]. Quality of life (QoL) has become a central outcome in cancer care, particularly for survivors expected to live for an extended period with the sequelae of treatment [19]. Several studies have reported that CIPN is associated with worse physical, functional, and social well-being, as well as lower overall QoL, among patients with colorectal cancer [20]. However, the mechanisms by which CIPN influences QoL are not fully understood. Neuropathic symptoms may directly impair QoL, but they may also act indirectly through functional limitation and emotional distress [21]. Functional limitation may reduce independence and social participation, thereby worsening mood, and mood, in turn, may shape patients' appraisal of their overall QoL [22]. If this is the case, mood may serve as a mediator between RDA and QoL, and interventions aimed at improving mood could be a crucial and potentially more modifiable target than neuropathy itself, for which few effective treatments exist [23]. Most previous research has examined CIPN, activity limitation, mood, and QoL in isolation or in pairs, and few have tested the relationships among them within a single model in colorectal cancer patients [24]. Evidence on whether mood explains the association between RDA and QoL in this population is lacking [25]. Clarifying these relationships could inform supportive care that extends beyond symptom control: rehabilitation and safety education to reduce RDA, and psychological assessment and intervention to improve mood adaptation [26]. Therefore, we conducted a cross-sectional study of colorectal adenocarcinoma patients with CIPN after oxaliplatin-based chemotherapy, utilizing the Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory to measure CIPN severity, the SALSA scale to assess RDA, the POMS short form to evaluate negative mood, and the Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy (FACT) scale to evaluate QoL. By examining the interrelationships between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in this population, we aim to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex factors influencing QoL in colorectal cancer survivors, and to identify potential targets for intervention to improve patient outcomes. The intricate dynamics between chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) and the overall well-being of patients diagnosed with colorectal cancer involve a multitude of factors that collectively influence the quality of life (QoL) in this population. To elucidate these dynamics, our research endeavored to explore the impact of CIPN on QoL, with particular emphasis on the intermediary roles of restrictions in daily activities (RDA) and mood disturbances [27]. Our central hypothesis posited that a higher severity of CIPN would correlate with more pronounced mood disturbances and a diminished QoL, and furthermore, that mood would act as a partial mediator in the relationship between RDA and QoL, thus presenting a viable target for interventions aimed at enhancing QoL in colorectal cancer patients suffering from CIPN [28, 29]. Our investigation contributes to a comprehensive understanding of the interplay between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in patients with colorectal cancer, highlighting the potential for targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes. By dissecting the correlations among these variables and applying hierarchical multiple linear regression and Baron and Kenny's mediation procedure, we aimed to discern whether mood indeed mediates the relationship between RDA and QoL [28]. The findings of our study underscore the critical importance of considering the multifaceted relationships between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in the development of supportive care strategies tailored to address the physical, functional, and emotional needs of colorectal cancer patients experiencing CIPN. The study's implications extend to the development of nuanced interventions that could mitigate the adverse effects of CIPN on QoL, emphasizing the need for a holistic approach to patient care. Our research suggests that interventions targeting mood and RDA, such as rehabilitation programs and safety education, could be pivotal in enhancing QoL for colorectal cancer patients with CIPN. However, it is essential to acknowledge the limitations of our cross-sectional design, which precludes the establishment of causal relationships among the variables. Future longitudinal studies are warranted to elucidate the temporal dynamics between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL. Moreover, the generalizability of our findings to other cancer populations requires further investigation. In clinical practice, our study's findings have profound implications. Healthcare providers should be cognizant of the potential for CIPN to impair patients' daily functioning and overall QoL, necessitating a comprehensive assessment of RDA and mood disturbances alongside CIPN severity. By adopting a more holistic approach to patient care, clinicians can develop and implement targeted interventions that address the multifaceted needs of colorectal cancer patients with CIPN, ultimately aiming to improve QoL and mitigate the burden of CIPN. The relationship between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in colorectal cancer patients is complex and multifaceted, necessitating a comprehensive and nuanced understanding to inform the development of effective supportive care strategies. Our research underscores the critical role of mood as a mediator in the relationship between RDA and QoL, highlighting the potential for mood-targeted interventions to improve patient outcomes. As the field continues to evolve, further research is necessary to develop, test, and refine interventions that address the interrelated challenges of CIPN, RDA, and mood disturbances in colorectal cancer patients, with the ultimate goal of enhancing QoL and reducing the burden of CIPN in this population. In conclusion, our study provides significant insights into the complex interplay between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL in colorectal cancer patients, emphasizing the need for a multifaceted approach to patient care that addresses physical, functional, and emotional needs. The development of targeted interventions, informed by a nuanced understanding of these relationships, is crucial for improving QoL and mitigating the adverse effects of CIPN in this population. Future research should prioritize the development and testing of such interventions, with a focus on longitudinal designs and diverse cancer populations to enhance generalizability and inform evidence-based practice. By advancing our understanding of the relationships between CIPN, RDA, mood, and QoL, we can work towards improving the lives of colorectal cancer patients and reducing the burden of CIPN, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes and quality of care. RNA extraction and reverse trancsription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) Total RNA was extracted from frozen tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen; Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer's instructions. Each 20 µl reaction contained 10 µl master mix, 0.4 µM of each primer, and 2 µl diluted cDNA. Cycling conditions were 95°C for 30 sec, followed by 40 cycles of 95°C for 5 sec and 60°C for 30 sec, with a subsequent melting-curve analysis to confirm amplification specificity. Western blot analysis Tissues were homogenized and lyysed in RIPA buffer supplemented with protase and phosphatase inhibitors. The liver is disproportionately affected by hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a primary malignancy that accounts for 75-85% of all liver cancer cases [1]. Globally, HCC is a leading cause of cancer-related deaths, with a higher incidence observed in certain regions, including East Asia and sub-Saharan Africa [2]. Several key risk factors contribute to the development of HCC, including chronic hepatitis B and C virus infections, excessive alcohol consumption, exposure to aflatoxin B1, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease; these factors often culminate in liver cirrhosis, a condition that precedes the majority of HCC cases [3]. Despite significant strides in the management of HCC, encompassing improved surveillance strategies, surgical interventions, liver transplantation, targeted locoregional therapies, and the introduction of molecularly targeted agents, the overall prognosis for patients with HCC remains unfavorable [4,5]. This poor prognosis can be attributed to the high recurrence rates observed following surgical resection, the frequent diagnosis of HCC at an advanced stage, and the inherent resistance of HCC to systemic therapies, all of which contribute to the dismal five-year survival rates [4,5]. The current reliance on clinical staging systems and serum alpha-fetoprotein levels for predicting individual patient outcomes is hindered by their limited predictive accuracy, underscoring the urgent need for molecular biomarkers that can accurately reflect the underlying tumor biology and inform both stratification and treatment decisions [6]. The development of HCC is characterized by a complex interplay of genetic and epigenetic alterations that accumulate over time. Recent studies employing genomic sequencing technologies have identified recurrent mutations in genes involved in chromatin regulation, such as ARID1A, ARID2, and members of the KMT2 family, suggesting that dysregulation of chromatin-modifying machinery plays a pivotal role in the initiation and progression of liver tumors [7,8]. The modification of histones, including acetylation and methylation, is crucial for regulating chromatin accessibility and gene transcription; aberrant patterns of these modifications can lead to the silencing of tumor suppressor genes or the activation of oncogenic pathways [9]. Consequently, enzymes involved in histone methylation, such as histone methyltransferases and demethylases, are increasingly being recognized as promising biomarkers and therapeutic targets in the context of cancer. For instance, inhibitors targeting EZH2 and DOT1L have progressed to clinical evaluation [10]. Among these enzymes is SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B), a member of the SET1/COMPASS family of lysine methyltransferases, which also includes SETD1A and the MLL/KMT2 proteins. SETD1B is responsible for catalyzing the mono-, di-, and trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4), a modification that is typically associated with actively transcribed genes and promoters [11,12]. SETD1B functions as part of a multiprotein complex that includes WDR5, RBBP5, ASH2L, DPY30, and CFP1, where the composition of this complex dictates its genomic targeting and enzymatic activity [12]. Although SETD1A and SETD1B share a conserved catalytic domain, they exhibit distinct functional roles and interaction profiles, indicating non-redundant functions [13]. Previous studies have implicated SETD1B in the regulation of the cell cycle, neuronal development, hematopoiesis, and memory formation, while germline mutations or haploinsufficiency of SETD1B have been linked to a neurodevelopmental syndrome characterized by epilepsy and intellectual disability [14,15]. Accumulating evidence suggests that SETD1B plays context-dependent roles in the development and progression of malignancies. In microsatellite-unstable gastric and colorectal cancers, frameshift mutations in SETD1B have been observed, hinting at a potential tumor-suppressive function [16]. In contrast, SETD1B has been implicated in promoting tumor progression in other cancer types. For instance, in breast cancer, SETD1B has been associated with enhanced proliferation and epigenetic regulation of genes involved in cell growth and therapeutic response [17]. Similarly, in acute myeloid leukemia, the SETD1B-containing complex has been shown to cooperate with oncogenic drivers to maintain leukemic gene expression programs [18]. Moreover, SETD1B-mediated H3K4 methylation appears to influence DNA damage responses and genome stability, processes that are crucial for malignant transformation [19]. Related family members, notably SETD1A, have been demonstrated to promote the proliferation, migration, and tumor growth of HCC cells, with their overexpression correlating with adverse clinical features [20,21]. These findings collectively raise the possibility that SETD1B may also contribute to the development and progression of HCC. However, to our knowledge, a comprehensive investigation into the expression pattern of SETD1B in HCC, its relationship with clinicopathological characteristics, and its impact on patient outcomes has not been conducted. Given the critical role of epigenetic regulators in HCC, the established oncogenic functions of SETD1B in various other cancers, and the paucity of data regarding SETD1B in liver cancer, we hypothesized that SETD1B is aberrantly expressed in HCC and associated with disease progression and prognosis. To test this hypothesis, we employed reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction and western blot analysis to measure SETD1B mRNA and protein levels in paired HCC tumor and adjacent non-tumorous tissues. Subsequently, we examined the relationship between SETD1B expression and clinicopathological variables, including tumor size, clinical stage, and the presence of liver cirrhosis. Finally, we assessed the association between SETD1B expression and overall survival using Kaplan–Meier analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression to determine whether SETD1B serves as an independent prognostic factor. The anticipated outcomes of this study are expected to elucidate the contribution of SETD1B to HCC progression and evaluate its potential as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target. To achieve these objectives, we collected paired HCC tumor tissues and adjacent non-tumorous liver tissues from patients who underwent curative hepatectomy at the Department of Hepatobiliary Surgery between January 2010 and December 2014. The inclusion criteria for this study consisted of: (i) histopathological confirmation of HCC; (ii) no prior exposure to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, or transarterial chemoembolization; (iii) absence of concurrent malignancies; and (iv) availability of complete clinicopathological and follow-up data. Patients who succumbed to perioperative complications were excluded from the study. The morphological and molecular characteristics of HCC are complex and multifaceted, reflecting the intricate interplay between genetic and epigenetic alterations that underlie the development and progression of this malignancy. The epigenetic landscape of HCC is characterized by aberrant patterns of histone modification, including methylation and acetylation, which play critical roles in regulating chromatin accessibility and gene transcription. Enzymes responsible for these modifications, such as histone methyltransferases and demethylases, are increasingly being recognized as key players in the initiation and progression of HCC. Among these enzymes, SETD1B has emerged as a potentially important contributor to the epigenetic dysregulation observed in HCC. To further elucidate the role of SETD1B in HCC, it is essential to investigate its expression pattern in HCC tissues and adjacent non-tumorous tissues, as well as its relationship with clinicopathological characteristics and patient outcomes. This knowledge will not only enhance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying HCC but also provide valuable insights into the potential of SETD1B as a prognostic biomarker and therapeutic target. The clinical implications of SETD1B expression in HCC are far-reaching, with potential applications in the development of targeted therapies and personalized treatment strategies. The prevalence of retinoblastoma, a malignant tumor affecting the eye, is estimated to be approximately 1 in 16,000 to 18,000 live births, with the majority of cases being diagnosed in children under the age of five [1,2]. Fortunately, the prognosis for retinoblastoma has improved significantly in high-income countries, with survival rates now exceeding 95% [3]. Over the past twenty years, the approach to managing intraocular retinoblastoma has undergone a significant transformation, shifting away from traditional treatments such as enucleation and external beam radiation therapy towards more innovative and less invasive strategies. These modern approaches include the use of systemic chemoreduction with focal consolidation, intra-arterial chemotherapy, and intravitreal chemotherapy [4,5]. The move away from external beam radiation is largely due to its association with impaired orbital growth and a significantly increased risk of secondary malignancies in patients with germline mutations [6,7]. One of the most promising treatments to have emerged in recent years is ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC), a technique first described by Kaneko and later refined by Abramson and colleagues [8,9]. This treatment involves the direct delivery of chemotherapy into the ophthalmic artery via selective catheterization, typically using agents such as melphalan, often in combination with topotecan, and less frequently, carboplatin. By delivering the chemotherapy locally, high concentrations can be achieved within the eye while minimizing systemic exposure, allowing for lower total doses than those required for intravenous regimens [10]. Several large studies have reported ocular salvage rates that are comparable to those achieved with systemic chemotherapy, particularly in advanced cases and as a primary treatment [11,12]. As a result, OAC has become a first-line treatment at many centers worldwide. However, when comparing OAC to intravenous chemotherapy, the risk of systemic toxicity is a critical consideration. Systemic chemoreduction for retinoblastoma, which typically involves the use of vincristine, etoposide, and carboplatin, is associated with a range of adverse effects, including myelosuppression, ototoxicity, and infection risk [13,14]. In contrast, the reported adverse effects of OAC include transient neutropenia, vascular complications affecting the eye and orbit, and procedural risks related to anesthesia and catheterization [15,16]. Given that OAC is typically administered in a small number of sessions over several months, its overall impact on the health of children is generally considered to be modest. Nevertheless, data on the long-term systemic consequences of OAC remain limited. Growth is a sensitive indicator of a child's overall health and of the cumulative physiologic burden of illness and treatment. Studies of other pediatric malignancies, such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), have demonstrated that children receiving systemic chemotherapy often experience reduced linear growth velocity and altered weight gain during treatment [17,18]. The proposed mechanisms underlying these growth abnormalities include direct effects of cytotoxic agents on the growth plate, disturbance of the growth hormone–insulin-like growth factor axis, poor nutrition, and the effects of glucocorticoids, which are a major component of ALL regimens [19,20]. Although many patients exhibit catch-up growth after therapy, some may have persistent deficits in final height or an increased risk of obesity [21,22]. Cranial irradiation and alkylating agents also add to the risk of endocrine dysfunction and growth abnormalities [23]. Retinoblastoma survivors may be particularly vulnerable to growth abnormalities due to several factors, including the presence of germline RB1 mutations, which may alter the endocrine milieu, and deletions involving 13q14, which have been linked to growth restriction and developmental delay [24,25]. Radiation to the orbit and adjacent structures, which was historically common, can affect craniofacial growth, while radiation near the hypothalamic–pituitary region can cause endocrine deficiencies [26]. Patients treated with systemic chemotherapy are exposed to agents that may affect growth, although few studies have specifically examined this question in retinoblastoma. Existing long-term follow-up studies of retinoblastoma survivors have primarily focused on second cancers, visual outcomes, and mortality, rather than somatic growth [7,27]. The evidence on the growth of children treated with OAC is particularly scarce. These children are very young at the time of treatment, a period of rapid growth when nutritional and metabolic disturbances may have disproportionate effects. Many receive repeated general anesthesia with fasting, which could transiently affect feeding. Furthermore, a substantial proportion of children referred for OAC have already received systemic chemotherapy elsewhere, either as initial therapy or after failure of chemoreduction. Whether prior systemic exposure modifies growth during or after OAC is unknown. Distinguishing children treated with OAC alone from those with previous systemic treatment can help separate the effects of the local intra-arterial approach from those of cumulative systemic therapy. Clarifying these patterns is clinically important, as parents of children with retinoblastoma are often concerned about the late effects of treatment, and the absence of data limits counseling. If OAC does not affect growth, this would support its use as a systemically sparing alternative. Conversely, evidence of growth disturbance would call for closer nutritional and endocrine surveillance. Growth data also contribute to the broader assessment of treatment-related morbidity in survivorship care [28]. In light of these considerations, we conducted a retrospective review of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center between 2006 and 2016. Our objectives were to describe short-term growth velocity during treatment, as well as height and weight percentiles up to three years after treatment, among children who received OAC alone (naïve), those who received OAC after prior systemic chemotherapy (non-naïve), and those who received a combination of OAC and systemic chemotherapy. This study aimed to provide insights into the growth patterns of children treated with OAC, a crucial aspect of their overall health and well-being. By examining the growth of children treated with OAC, we can better understand the potential long-term consequences of this treatment and provide more informed counseling to parents. Our findings will contribute to the growing body of evidence on the effects of OAC on the health and well-being of children with retinoblastoma, ultimately informing treatment decisions and improving outcomes for these young patients. The analysis of growth patterns in children treated with OAC will also provide valuable information on the potential risks and benefits of this treatment approach, which can be used to guide clinical decision-making and optimize treatment strategies for retinoblastoma. Furthermore, this study will help to identify potential areas for improvement in the management of retinoblastoma, such as the need for closer monitoring of growth and development in children treated with OAC. By addressing these knowledge gaps, we can work towards providing the best possible care for children with retinoblastoma, minimizing the risk of long-term complications and maximizing the potential for optimal growth and development. The results of this study will have important implications for the clinical management of retinoblastoma, highlighting the need for a comprehensive approach to treatment that takes into account the potential long-term consequences of therapy. As the treatment landscape for retinoblastoma continues to evolve, it is essential that we prioritize the collection of high-quality data on the effects of different treatment approaches, including OAC, to ensure that we are providing the best possible care for these young patients. By working together to advance our understanding of retinoblastoma and its treatment, we can strive towards improved outcomes and a brighter future for children affected by this disease. The administration of ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC) has become a crucial component in the management of retinoblastoma, a rare and aggressive form of eye cancer affecting children. To comprehensively understand the implications of OAC on the growth and developmental trajectories of retinoblastoma survivors, our research team undertook a retrospective investigation. The study aimed to elucidate whether the frequency of OAC treatments influences growth patterns and to delineate the long-term trajectories of height and weight in this patient population. Conducted at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC), the study was approved by the Institutional Review Board and adhered strictly to the ethical guidelines outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki [1]. Given the retrospective nature of the study and the minimal risk it posed to participants, a waiver of informed consent was obtained. Furthermore, stringent measures were implemented to ensure compliance with institutional policies regarding the protection of patient health information. Our research cohort consisted of all consecutive pediatric patients diagnosed with retinoblastoma who underwent OAC at MSKCC between 2006 and 2016. A thorough review of the institutional retinoblastoma database and electronic medical records yielded a total of 341 patients. The diagnosis of retinoblastoma was confirmed through a meticulous combination of clinical examinations, including dilated fundus examination under anesthesia, and advanced imaging techniques such as ultrasonography and magnetic resonance imaging, as deemed clinically necessary [2,3]. The International Classification of Retinoblastoma was utilized to classify the disease in the eyes of the patients [4]. To mitigate potential confounding variables, we excluded patients who had undergone external beam radiation therapy, recognizing its association with craniofacial and growth abnormalities [5,6]. Additionally, patients with genetic syndromes known to impact growth, such as trisomy 21 or deletion 13q syndrome, were excluded from the study. Patients lacking sufficient anthropometric data to calculate growth velocity were also excluded from relevant analyses to ensure the integrity of the data. Patients were categorized into distinct treatment groups based on their chemotherapy history prior to and during OAC. Those who received OAC as their sole form of chemotherapy were designated as "naive," whereas patients initially treated with systemic intravenous chemotherapy at other centers or at MSKCC before presenting for OAC were classified as "secondary." A smaller subgroup of patients who received single-agent systemic chemotherapy shortly before or between OAC cycles, serving as a bridge to OAC, were termed "bridge." Due to the limited size of the bridge group, our comparative analyses focused predominantly on the naive and secondary groups. The OAC procedure was performed under general anesthesia, employing a technique that has been previously described [7,8]. In essence, the ophthalmic artery was accessed via the femoral artery, with or without the use of a microcatheter, depending on the vascular anatomy. Heparin was administered to prevent thrombotic complications. Melphalan was the primary chemotherapeutic agent, with dosing adjusted based on patient age and weight. In cases of refractory or recurrent disease, topotecan and carboplatin were incorporated into the treatment regimen, in accordance with established institutional protocols. OAC treatments were typically repeated at 3-4 week intervals, with the total number of cycles determined by the response of the tumor to treatment. A comprehensive array of demographic and clinical variables was collected from the medical records, including patient sex, age at diagnosis, disease laterality, heritable status (when genetic testing was available), eye stage, previous treatments, treatment group, number of OAC cycles, and relevant treatment dates. Height and weight measurements were obtained from both clinic and anesthesia records, where these parameters are regularly assessed by trained personnel using standardized equipment. Anthropometric data were collected in two phases: the short-term phase, during which height and weight were recorded monthly throughout the OAC treatment period, and the long-term phase, where measurements were taken annually for up to 3 years following the completion of OAC. When multiple measurements were available within a specified timeframe, the measurement closest to the scheduled time point was utilized. To assess growth patterns, age- and sex-specific percentiles for height and weight were calculated using the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) growth charts [9] or the World Health Organization (WHO) growth charts for children under 2 years [10]. This approach enabled the comparison of patient growth with that of a reference population across different ages. The primary outcome of interest was the growth velocity during OAC, defined as the change in height and weight per unit time between the first and last measurements within the treatment period, expressed in centimeters per month and kilograms per month, respectively. Secondary outcomes included the association between the number of OAC treatments and growth velocity, as well as the long-term height and weight trajectories of patients post-OAC. Our study provides critical insights into the effects of OAC on the growth and development of children with retinoblastoma, contributing valuable information to the existing body of literature. The immune system is essential for maintaining homeostasis, defending against pathogens, and surveilling for malignant transformation. Its dysregulation, however, underlies a wide spectrum of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis [1,2]. Over the past two decades, therapeutic strateiges that modulate immune pathways have transformed the management of these conditions. Biologic ageents targeting tumor necrosis factor, interleukin (IL)-6, IL-17, IL-23, and co-stimulatory molecules have been joined by small molecule inhibitors directed at intracellular signaling nodes such as Janus kinases (JAKs), tyrrosine kinase 2 (TYK2), spleen tyrosine kinase, Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK), phosphodiesterase 4, and calcineurin [3–5]. The expanding repertoire of immune targets has created considerable opportunity, but also a growing need to understand how each mechanism shapes immune function in humans. Because the immune system is highly interconnected and redundant, pharmacological modulation of a given target rarely affects only the pathogenic process of interest. Immunosuppression is a recognized liability of immunomodulatory therapies and may manifest as increased risk of serious bacterial, viral, fungal, and oppportunistic infections, reactivation of latent infections such as tuberculosis and herpes zoster, impaired vaccine responses, and possibly malignancy [6,7]. The safety experience with JAK inhibitors illustrates this challenge: despite clear efficacy, class-associated risks including infections, thromboembolism, and malignancy have prompted regulatory warnings and renewed debate about the relationship between selectivity, pathway biology, and clinical risk [8,9]. Distinct mechanisms carry distinct risk profiles; for example, inhibition of IL-17 is associated with mucoctuaneous candidiasis, whereas inhibition of TNF is linked to granulomatous infections [10]. These observations indicate that each therapeutic mechanism leaves a characteristic "immune fingerprint," defined by the specific innate and adaptive functions it attenuates, spares, or enhances. Defining this fingerprint early in drug discovery would help prioritize candidates witth the most favorable benefit–risk balance. In practice, however, preclinical characterization of novel compoundds is typically compound- and mechanism-centric. Potency and selectivity are assessed agaiinst the intended target and related off-targets, and efficacy is evaluated in a limited number of cellualr assays or animal models chosen for their relevance to the target pathway. Such approaches provide little information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Animal models, while valuable, are limited by species differences in immune cell composition, receptor expression, cytokine networks, and drug sensitivity, and they often fail to predict human immune responses or infection risk [11,12]. Genetically engineerred and humanized models partially address these limitations but are costly and low-throughput, and thus poorly suited to routine profiling of multiple compounds. Human primary cell systems offer an attractive alternative. Assays using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood, or isolated immune subsets can capture human-specific biology and have been widely used to examine cytokine release, T cell proliferation, and cell activation [13,14]. Nonetheless, most reported assays interrogate a single cell type or stimulus in isolation, and they differ in donor sources, readouts, and stimulation conditions, which complicates cross-study comparison. Cells in bood also lack the tissue context in which many immune repsonses occur. Human tissue-derived systems, including tonsil, lymph node, spleen, and skin explants or cell preparations, preserve a more physiological representation of cellular diversity, antigen-presenting cell–lymphocyte interactions, and, in the caes of secondary lymphoid organs, the capacity to support B cell activation and antibody production [15,16]. Tonsillar tissue, for instance, has been used to model recall antigen responses, T follicular helper cell function, and vaccine responses ex vivo [17]. Leveraging such material within a standardized panel of functional assays could yield a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects. An ideal platform for immune profiling should saisfy several criteria. It should cover both innate functions (such as myeloid cell cytokine production, type I interferon responses, and natural killer cell activity) and adaptive functions (such as T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation, and B cell activation and antibody secretion). It should use human material and physiologically relevant stimuli, employ quantitative readouts that permit concentration–response analysis, and include benchmark therapeutics for context. Finally, it should enable integration of results across assays into a summary of immune impact that can be interpreted alongside pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, for example by relating inhibition to free drug exposure at clinically relevant doses [18]. Here, we describe the development of a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to meet these criteria. The platform comprises a series of complementary assays measuring a range of innate and adaptive immune responses, and it was used to evaluate small molecule inhibitors of immune targets together with clinically used immunomodulatoy agents. We show that the platform can generate qualitative and quantitative immune fingerprints that distinguish mechanisms of action, reveal differences in the breadth and magnitude of immunosuppression among compounds, and provide a framework for comparing novel inhibitors with established therapies. We propose that this approach can support more informed decision-making in the discovery of immune-targeted therapeutics and improve the prediction of their benefit–risk profiles in the treatment of immune-mediated disorders. Such approaches provide little information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Nevertheless, its malfunction is a underlying factor in a plethora of chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and multiple sclerosis [1,2]. This expanding array of immune targets has created substantial opportunities for the development of novel therapies, but it also underscores the need to comprehend how each mechanism influences immune function in humans. The immune system is a complex and interconnected network, and pharmacological modulation of a specific target rarely affects only the pathological process of interest. Consequently, immunosuppression is a recognized risk associated with immunomodulatory therapies, and may manifest as an increased susceptibility to serious bacterial, viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections, reactivation of latent infections such as tuberculosis and herpes zoster, impaired vaccine responses, and potentially malignancy [6,7]. The safety experience with JAK inhibitors exemplifies this challenge, as despite their evident efficacy, class-associated risks including infections, thromboembolism, and malignancy have prompted regulatory warnings and renewed debate about the relationship between selectivity, pathway biology, and clinical risk [8,9]. Furthermore, distinct mechanisms are associated with distinct risk profiles; for instance, inhibition of IL-17 is linked to mucocutaneous candidiasis, whereas inhibition of TNF is associated with granulomatous infections [10]. These observations suggest that each therapeutic mechanism leaves a unique "immune signature," characterized by the specific innate and adaptive functions it modulates, spares, or enhances. Defining this signature early in the drug discovery process would be highly beneficial, as it would facilitate the prioritization of candidates with the most favorable benefit–risk balance. However, preclinical characterization of novel compounds is typically focused on the compound's potency and selectivity against the intended target and related off-targets, and its efficacy in a limited number of cellular assays or animal models chosen for their relevance to the target pathway. Such approaches provide limited information on the breadth of immune functions affected, and they rarely allow direct comparison with clinically used agents whose safety profiles are known. Animal models, while valuable, are limited by species differences in immune cell composition, receptor expression, cytokine networks, and drug sensitivity, and they often fail to predict human immune responses or infection risk [11,12]. Genetically engineered and humanized models partially address these limitations but are costly and low-throughput, and thus poorly suited to routine profiling of multiple compounds. Human primary cell systems offer an attractive alternative for immune profiling. Assays using peripheral blood mononuclear cells, whole blood, or isolated immune subsets can capture human-specific biology and have been widely used to examine cytokine release, T cell proliferation, and cell activation [13,14]. However, most reported assays interrogate a single cell type or stimulus in isolation, and they differ in donor sources, readouts, and stimulation conditions, which complicates cross-study comparison. Moreover, cells in blood lack the tissue context in which many immune responses occur. Human tissue-derived systems, including tonsil, lymph node, spleen, and skin explants or cell preparations, preserve a more physiological representation of cellular diversity, antigen-presenting cell–lymphocyte interactions, and, in the case of secondary lymphoid organs, the capacity to support B cell activation and antibody production [15,16]. Tonsillar tissue, for example, has been used to model recall antigen responses, T follicular helper cell function, and vaccine responses ex vivo [17]. Leveraging such material within a standardized panel of functional assays could yield a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects. An ideal platform for immune profiling should meet several key criteria. It should cover both innate functions, such as myeloid cell cytokine production, type I interferon responses, and natural killer cell activity, and adaptive functions, such as T cell activation, proliferation, and differentiation, and B cell activation and antibody secretion. It should utilize human material and physiologically relevant stimuli, employ quantitative readouts that permit concentration–response analysis, and include benchmark therapeutics for context. Finally, it should enable integration of results across assays into a summary of immune impact that can be interpreted alongside pharmacokinetic and efficacy data, for example by relating inhibition to free drug exposure at clinically relevant doses [18]. In this context, we have developed a human tissue-based functional assay platform designed to meet these criteria. The platform comprises a series of complementary assays measuring a range of innate and adaptive immune responses, and it was used to evaluate small molecule inhibitors of immune targets together with clinically used immunomodulatory agents. Our results demonstrate that the platform can generate qualitative and quantitative data on the immune effects of these compounds, providing a valuable tool for the prioritization of candidates with the most favorable benefit–risk balance. The platform's ability to capture the complex interactions between immune cells and tissues, and to quantify the effects of compounds on these interactions, makes it an attractive alternative to traditional preclinical models. Furthermore, the platform's use of human tissue and physiologically relevant stimuli ensures that the results are highly relevant to the human immune system, reducing the risk of species-specific effects and increasing the likelihood of successful translation to the clinic. Overall, our human tissue-based functional assay platform provides a powerful tool for the immune profiling of small molecule inhibitors and biologic agents, enabling the identification of compounds with the most favorable benefit–risk balance and facilitating the development of novel therapies for the treatment of immune-related disorders. The platform's flexibility and adaptability also make it an attractive tool for the study of immune function and dysfunction in a variety of contexts, from basic research to clinical applications. As the field of immunology continues to evolve, the development of innovative platforms like ours will be essential for advancing our understanding of the immune system and improving the treatment of immune-related diseases. By providing a more comprehensive and translationally relevant view of drug effects, our platform has the potential to accelerate the development of novel therapies and improve patient outcomes. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death in patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD), accounting for roughly 40–50% of all mortality in this population [1,2]. A substantial proportion of these deaths are sudden cardiac death (SCD), and the annual incidence of SCD among patients receiving hemodialysis is estimated to be several times higher than in the general populaton [3,4]. Although coronary artery disease is highly prevalent in ESRD, traditional ischemic mechanisms explain oly part of this excess risk. Structural and electrophysiological remodeling, including left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic dysfunction, vascular calcification, and abrupt shifts in electrolytes and voume durnig dialysis, creates a substrate that favors both tachyarrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias [5–7]. Arrhythmias in patients with chroic kidney disease Atrial fibrillation is common in patients on dialysis, with reported prevalence of 7–27%, and is associated with increased risk of stroke and mortality [8,9]. Ventricular arrhythmias, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), are also frequent and have been linked to left ventricular dysfunction and adverse outcomes [10,11]. In addition, recent evidence suggests that bradyarrhythmias, rather than ventricular tachyarrhythmias, may be the predominant mechanism of sudden death in dialysis patients. Continuuos monitoring in a small cohort of hemodialysis patients showed that bradycardia and asystole preceded most arrhythmic deaths [12]. These findings challenge the assumption that SCD in ESRD is mainly due to ventricular fibrillation, and they raise questions about the appropriateness of preventive strategies such as primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, whose benefit in this population remains uncertain [13,14]. Renal transplant candidates Renal transplantation improves survival and quality of life compared with chronic dialysis, but candidates are subjected to extensive cardiovascular evaluation because perioperative and long-term cardiac events remain a major concern [15]. Current guidelines recommend risk stratification using clinical assessment, resting electrocardiography (ECG), echocardiography, and, in selected patients, functional or anatomical testing for ischemia [16]. These tools primarily address structural and ischemic disease and offer lmited information on arrhythmic vulnerability. Moreover, patients on the waiting list may be on dialysis for prolonged periods, during whicch clinically relevant rhythm disturbances can occur without being captured. The arrhythmic profile of renal transplant candidates (RTCs) is therefore poorly characterized, and it remains unclear which clinical, electrocardiographic, or echocardiographic variables identify those at greater risk. Limitations of conventional rhythm monitoring Standard 12-lead ECG and 24- to 48-hour Holter monitoring provide only brief snapshots and are poorly suited to deteccting paroxysmal or infrequent events. Studies using such methods are likely to underestimate the true incidence of arrhythmias, particularly in patients whose events are related to the dialysis cycle or ocur sporadically [17]. External event recorders improve diagnostic yield but remain limited by patient compliance and short monitoring duration. The implantable loop recorder (ILR) permits continuous subcutneous ECG monitoring for up to several years, with automatic detection and storage of arrhythmic episoddes and patient-activated recording of symptoms. ILRs have established value in the evaluation of unexplained syncope [18] and in the detection of occult atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic stroke [19]. In the nephrology setting, their use has been confined to small series of dialysis patients, which have shown a high burden of clinically significant arrhythmias, often asymptomatic [12,20]. To our knowledge, ILR-based monitoring has not been systematically applied to ambulatory RTCs, and data on the incidence of arrhythmic events in this group, their clinical significance, and their determinants are lacking. Potential predictors of arrhhythmic events Several noninvasive markers may help identify patients prone to specific arrhythmias. Prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc) reflects abnormal ventricular repolarization and has been associated with malignant arrhythmias and mortality in ESRD [21]. PR interval prolongation indicates delayed atrioventricular conduuction and has been related to atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and adverse outcomes in the general population [22]. Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction are established substrates for ventricular arrhythmias [23]. Whether these readily available parameters predict particular arrhythmia types detected by continuous monitoring in RTCs has not been examined. Identifying such predictors could refine rissk stratification, guide selection of patients for closer surveillance, and inform decisions about pacing or defibrillator therapy before and after transplantation. Study objective Given the high cardiovascular risk of RTCs, the limitations of intermittent rhythm assessment, and the uncertainty about the mechanisms of sudden death in this population, we conducted a prospective observational study using ILRs in consecutive ambulatory RTCs. The aim was to determine the incidence and types of arrhythmic events during medium-term follow-up and to identify clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic predictors of these events using multivariate analysis. Study Design and Population We conducted a prospective, single-center, observational study from June 2009 to January 2011. One hundred consecutive ambulatory renal transplaant candidates (RTCs) on the waiting list, undergoing chronic hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, were referred for cardiovascular evaluation and enrolled. Inclusion criteria were age of at least 18 years, dialysis for at least three months, and the ability to provide written informed consent. Exclusion criteria were a previously implanted pacemaker or defibrillator, a documented indication for such a device according to current guidelines [1,2], a life expectancy under one year from non-cardiac disease, active infection, and refusal to participate. The protocol complied with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee. All patients gave written informed consent before any study procedure. Baseline Clinical Assessment Demographic and clinical data were collected at enrollment through structured interviews and medical record review. Laboratory tests were performed on the day before a dialysis sesssion and included hemoglobin, serum potassium, calcium, phosphorus, parathyroid hormone, and creatinine. Electrocardiographic Evaluation A standard 12-lead resting electrocardiogram (ECG) was recorded at 25 mm/s and 10 mm/mV. Two investigators blinded to the follow-up results measured the PR interval, QRS duration, and QT interval manually. The QT interval was corrected for heart rate using Bazett's formula [3]. Left ventricular (LV) end-diastolic and end-systolic diameters, septal and posterior wall thickness, and left atrial diameter were measured. LV ejection fraction was calculated using the modified Simpson method. LV mass was calculated by the Devereux formula and indexed to body surface area. LV dilatation (LVD) was defined as an indexed end-diastolic diameter above sex-specific reference limits [4]. LV systolic dysfunction was defined as an ejection fraction below 50%. Implantable Loop Recorder Implantation and Programming All patients underwent implantation of an implantable loop recorder (ILR; Reveal XT, Medtronic, Minneapolis, MN, USA) in the leeft parasternal region under local anesthesia and sterile conditions. The R-wave aplitude was checked immmediately after implantation to ensure adequate sensing. Devices were programmed to autoatically detect and store the following: bradycardia (heart rate below 30 bpm for at least 4 beats), asytole (pause of at least 3 seconds), fast ventricular tachycardia (VT; at least 16 beats at a rate above 180 bpm), non-sustained VT (rate above 130 bpm), and atrial fibrillation (AF) through R-R interval irregularity analysis. Patients also received an activator to record symptomatic episodes manually. Definition of Arrhythmic Events Arrhythmic events (AE) were defined as any validated episode detected by the ILR. They were classified as: (1) sustained atrial tachycardia, lasting at least 30 seconds; (2) AF, irregular rhythm without discernible P waves lasting at least 30 seconds; (3) bradyarrhythmia, including sinus bradycardia below 30 bpm, sinus pauses of 3 seconds or more, and high-grade atrioventricular block; (4) non-sustained VT, at least 3 consecutive ventricular beats at a rate above 120 bpm lasting under 30 seconds; and (5) sustained VT, lasting 30 seconds or more or causing hemodynamic compromise. Ventricular fibrillation was defined as irregular chaotic ventricular activity without identifiable QRS complexes. Events were judged clinically relevant if they were symptomatic, caused hemodynamic instability, or led to a therapeutic intervention such as pacemaker implantation, defibrillator implantation, or initiation of anticoagulation or antiarrhythmic therapy.
