The mortality rate among individuals with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) is predominantly attributed to cardiovascular disease, which accounts for roughly 40-50% of all deaths within this demographic [1,2]. Notably, a considerable proportion of these fatalities can be ascribed to sudden cardiac death (SCD), with the annual incidence of SCD in patients undergoing hemodialysis being substantially higher than that observed in the general population [3,4]. While coronary artery disease is highly prevalent among ESRD patients, traditional ischemic mechanisms only partially account for the elevated risk of SCD. The intricate interplay between structural and electrophysiological remodeling, including left ventricular hypertrophy, myocardial fibrosis, autonomic dysfunction, vascular calcification, and abrupt shifts in electrolyte and fluid balance during dialysis, creates an environment that predisposes individuals to both tachyarrhythmias and bradyarrhythmias [5–7]. In patients with chronic kidney disease, arrhythmias are a pressing concern, with atrial fibrillation being a common occurrence among those on dialysis, affecting 7-27% of patients and increasing the risk of stroke and mortality [8,9]. Ventricular arrhythmias, including non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (VT), are also frequent and have been linked to left ventricular dysfunction and adverse outcomes [10,11]. Recent studies suggest that bradyarrhythmias, rather than ventricular tachyarrhythmias, may be the primary mechanism underlying sudden death in dialysis patients. Continuous monitoring of a small cohort of hemodialysis patients revealed that bradycardia and asystole preceded most arrhythmic deaths [12]. These findings challenge the prevailing assumption that SCD in ESRD is primarily caused by ventricular fibrillation and raise questions about the efficacy of preventive strategies, such as primary prevention implantable cardioverter-defibrillators, whose benefit in this population remains uncertain [13,14]. Renal transplantation has been shown to improve survival and quality of life compared to chronic dialysis; however, transplant candidates are subject to extensive cardiovascular evaluation due to the high risk of perioperative and long-term cardiac events [15]. Current guidelines recommend risk stratification using clinical assessment, resting electrocardiography (ECG), echocardiography, and functional or anatomical testing for ischemia in selected patients [16]. Nevertheless, these tools primarily focus on structural and ischemic disease, providing limited insight into arrhythmic vulnerability. Furthermore, patients on the waiting list may undergo dialysis for extended periods, during which clinically significant rhythm disturbances can occur without being detected. As a result, the arrhythmic profile of renal transplant candidates (RTCs) is not well characterized, and it remains unclear which clinical, electrocardiographic, or echocardiographic variables identify those at greater risk. Conventional rhythm monitoring methods, such as standard 12-lead ECG and 24- to 48-hour Holter monitoring, provide only brief glimpses into cardiac activity and are poorly suited to detecting paroxysmal or infrequent events. Studies employing these methods are likely to underestimate the true incidence of arrhythmias, particularly in patients whose events are related to the dialysis cycle or occur sporadically [17]. External event recorders offer improved diagnostic yield but are limited by patient compliance and short monitoring duration. In contrast, implantable loop recorders (ILRs) enable continuous subcutaneous ECG monitoring for up to several years, with automatic detection and storage of arrhythmic episodes and patient-activated recording of symptoms. ILRs have established value in the evaluation of unexplained syncope [18] and the detection of occult atrial fibrillation after cryptogenic stroke [19]. In the nephrology setting, their use has been confined to small series of dialysis patients, which have demonstrated a high burden of clinically significant arrhythmias, often asymptomatic [12,20]. However, to our knowledge, ILR-based monitoring has not been systematically applied to ambulatory RTCs, and data on the incidence of arrhythmic events in this group, their clinical significance, and their determinants are lacking. Several noninvasive markers may help identify patients prone to specific arrhythmias. Prolongation of the corrected QT interval (QTc) reflects abnormal ventricular repolarization and has been associated with malignant arrhythmias and mortality in ESRD [21]. PR interval prolongation indicates delayed atrioventricular conduction and has been related to atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and adverse outcomes in the general population [22]. Left ventricular dilatation and systolic dysfunction are established substrates for ventricular arrhythmias [23]. Whether these readily available parameters predict particular arrhythmia types detected by continuous monitoring in RTCs has not been examined. Identifying such predictors could refine risk stratification, guide selection of patients for closer surveillance, and inform decisions about pacing or defibrillator therapy before and after transplantation. Given the high cardiovascular risk of RTCs, the limitations of intermittent rhythm assessment, and the uncertainty about the mechanisms of sudden death in this population, we conducted a prospective observational study using ILRs in consecutive ambulatory RTCs. The objective was to determine the incidence and types of arrhythmic events during medium-term follow-up and to identify clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic predictors of these events using multivariate analysis. We conducted a prospective, single-center, observational study from June 2009 to January 2011. One hundred consecutive ambulatory renal transplant candidates (RTCs) on the waiting list, undergoing chronic hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, were referred for cardiovascular evaluation and enrolled. Inclusion criteria consisted of an age of at least 18 years, dialysis for at least three months, and the ability to provide informed consent. Patients with a history of renal transplantation, those with a known cardiac device (e.g., pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator), and those with a life expectancy of less than one year were excluded. All patients underwent a comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation, including medical history, physical examination, resting ECG, echocardiography, and laboratory tests. ILR devices were implanted in all patients, and they were instructed on how to activate the device in the event of symptoms. The ILR devices were programmed to automatically detect and store arrhythmic episodes, including atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and bradycardia. Patients were followed for a median period of 24 months, during which time they were seen at regular intervals for clinical evaluation and ILR interrogation. The primary outcome measure was the incidence of arrhythmic events, including atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and bradycardia. Secondary outcome measures included the identification of clinical, electrocardiographic, and echocardiographic predictors of arrhythmic events. We also examined the relationship between arrhythmic events and cardiovascular outcomes, including stroke, myocardial infarction, and sudden cardiac death. Our study aimed to provide a comprehensive understanding of the arrhythmic profile of RTCs and to identify potential predictors of arrhythmic events. The findings of this study have important implications for the management of RTCs, including the potential for targeted interventions to reduce the risk of arrhythmic events and improve cardiovascular outcomes. By elucidating the relationship between arrhythmic events and cardiovascular outcomes, our study may inform the development of novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of sudden cardiac death in this high-risk population. The use of ILR-based monitoring in RTCs represents a significant advancement in the field of nephrology, enabling the detection of arrhythmic events that may be asymptomatic or occur sporadically. Our study demonstrates the feasibility and potential benefits of this approach, which may be used to refine risk stratification and guide clinical decision-making in this population. In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of arrhythmic events in RTCs and the need for comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation and monitoring in this population. The findings of this study have significant implications for the management of RTCs and may inform the development of novel strategies for the prevention and treatment of sudden cardiac death in this high-risk population. Further studies are needed to confirm our findings and to explore the potential benefits of ILR-based monitoring in RTCs. Additionally, the development of novel biomarkers and predictive models may help to identify patients at highest risk of arrhythmic events and inform the development of targeted interventions to reduce this risk. Ultimately, our study aims to contribute to the improvement of cardiovascular outcomes in RTCs and to reduce the risk of sudden cardiac death in this population. By advancing our understanding of the arrhythmic profile of RTCs and the predictors of arrhythmic events, we may be able to develop more effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of cardiovascular disease in this high-risk population. Insulin resistance is a state in which insulin-responsive tissues, principally skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, respond inadequately to nomal circulating concentrations of the hormone. It is the central pathological feature of obesity and metabolic syndrome and the core defect that precedes and drives type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) [1,2]. The global prevalence of obesity and T2DM continues to rise, and insulin resistance contributes to related conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty livver disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease [3]. Although lifestyle intervention, metformin, and thiazolidinediones can improve insulin sensitivity, their efficacy is often limited and side effects are common, so there is a need to identify new molecular targets [4]. The mechanisms of insulin resistance are complex and include lipotoxicity, chronic low-grade inflammation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, all of which impair insulin signaling through the insulin receptor, insulin reecptor substrates (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and AKT [5,6]. Cellular energy status is tightly coupled to these processes, and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) has emerged as a key metabolic sensor. Tissue NAD+ levels deecline with aging and in overnutrition, and this decline is associated with metabolic deterioration [7]. The Sirtuins are NAD+-dependent enzymes that link cellular redox and energy state to protein modification and gene expression. The founding member, yeast Sir2, was identified as a regulator of replicative lifespan and transcriptional silencing, and its homologs have been associated with longevity in several model organisms [8,9]. Mammals have seven Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7), which share a conserved catalytic core but differ in their N- and C-terminal domains, substrate specificities, eznymatic activities, and subcellular localization [10]. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are predominantly nuclear, SIRT2 is mainly cytoplasmic, and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside in mitochondria, although several Sirtuins shuttle between compartments in response to physiological cues [11]. Initially characterized as deacetylases, Sirtuins are now known to catalyze a broader range of reactions, including removal of long-chain fatty acyl groups, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation [12,13]. Through these activities tey regulate cell survival, senescence, DNA repair, genome stability, and metabolism [14]. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been studied most etensively in metabolic regulation. SIRT1 deacetylates and moulates PGC-1α, FOXO proteins, LXR, SREBP, PPARγ, and the insulin signaling mediator PTP1B, thereby influencing gluconeogenesis, fatty acd oxidation, cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitivity [15–17]. Transgenic overexpression of SIRT1 and pharmacological activators such as resveratrol and SRT1720 improve glucose tolerance and prtect against diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis in rodents, whereas tissue-specific deletion of SIRT1 exacerbates metabolic dysfunction [18,19]. SIRT6 regulates glycolysis through deacetylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56, represses HIF1α-dependent glucose uptake, and controls hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory signaling; its loss causes severe hypoglycemia in mice, while its overexpression protects against high-fat diet-induced metabolic damage [20,21]. These findings have implicated SIRT1 and SIRT6 in obesity, T2DM, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease, and they have been the subject of severaal comprehensive reviews [22]. By contrast, the contributions of the remaining Sirttuins to insulin resistance are less well defined. Recent work indicates that they also influence processes tightly linked to insulin action. Mitochondrial SIRT3 deacetylates components of the respiratory chain and antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2, and its reduced expression is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance in muscle and liver [23,24]. SIRT4 modulates glutamine metabolism, insulin secretion, and fatty acid oxidation, while SIRT5 regulates ammonia detoxification, glycolysis, and fatty acid oxidation through desuccinylation and demalonylation [25,26]. Cytosolic SIRT2 affects adipocyte differentiation, gluconeogenesis, and insulin signaling via deacetylation of FOXO1, PEPCK, and AKT [27]. SIRT7 has been liked to hepatic lipid homeostasis, ER stress, and mitochondrial function [28]. Furthermore, several of these enzymes modulate inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which are major drivers of obesity-associated insulin resistance [29]. Human genetic and clinical studies have reported altered Sirtuin expression or polymorphisms in individuals with obesity, T2DM, and metabolc syndrome, supporting their translational relevance [30]. Nevertheless, findings are sometimes inconsistent across tissues, models, and species, and the substrate specificity and physiological regulation of smoe Sirtuins remain unclear. In this review, we summarize recent advances in the roles of the Sirtuin faamily in physiological processes associated with insulin resistance, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling, and glucose and lipid metabolism. We emphasize the Sirtuins other than SIRT1 and SIRT6 while discussing the better-characterized members for comparison. We also highight importnat unresolved questions and discuss the prospects and challenges of targetting Sirrtuins therapeutically for metabolic disease. This review was conducted as a structured narrative synthesis of the literature on mammalian Sirtuins (SIRT1–7) and insulin resistance. The aim was to integrate evidence from molecular, animal, and human studies and to identify gaps in current knowledge. The methodology followed the general principles of the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) to promote transparency and reproducibility [1]. Literature Seearch Strategy Electronic searches were performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase. The search covered records from database inception to the most recent update before manuscript preparation. Controlled vocabulary (MeSH and Emttree terms) was combined with free-text keywords using Boolean operators. Terms for the exposure included "sirtuin", "SIRT1", "SIRT2", "SIRT3", "SIRT4", "SIRT5", "SIRT6", "SIRT7", and "NAD-dependent deacetylase". These were combined with tersm for the outcome and related processes: "insulin resistance", "insulin sensitivity", "insulin signaling", "type 2 diabetes", "obesity", "metabolic syndrome", "glucose metabolism", "lipid metabolism", "inflammation", and "mitochondrial dysfunction". Reference lists of retrieved articles and earlier reviews were hand-searched to identify additional relevant publications [2]. Because SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively reviewed, searches for these proteins were restricted to key mechanistic and translational studies, whereas searches for SIRT2–5 and SIRT7 were conducted exhaustively. Eligibility Criteria Studies were eligible if they met at least one of the following criteria: (i) in vitro experiments in insulin-responsive cellls (hepatocytes, adipocytes, skeletal myocytes, cardiomyocytes, pancreatic β-cells, macrophages, or endothelial cells) examining Sirtuin function in relation to insulin signaling, nutrient metabolism, inflammation, or mitochondrial function; (ii) animal studies using genetic (knockout, knockdown, transgenic, tissue-specific) or pharmacological (activators, inhibitors, NAD+ precursors) manipulation of Sirtuins and reporting metabolic phenotypes such as glucose tolerance, insulin tolerance, or hyperinsulinemic–euglycemic clamp outcomes; and (iii) human studies, including observational cohorts, genteic association studies, and clinical trials, that evaluated Sirtuin expression, activity, polymorphisms, or modulators in relation to insulin resistance, T2DM, obesity, or fatty liver disease. Articles were excluded if they were published in languages other than English, were conference abstracts without ful text, were editorials without primary data, or addressed Sirtuins solely in contexts unrelated to metabolism (e.g., purely oncological or neurodegenerative studies without metabolic endpoints). Wherre multiple publications reported overlapping data, the most complete report was retained. Study Selection and Data Extraction Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially eligible articles. Disagreements were resolved by discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For each included study, the following information was extracted into a standardized template: Sirtuin isoform studied; species and model system; tissue or cell type; type of intervention; metaoblic diet or insulin-resistance induction protocol (e.g., high-fat diet, genetic obesity models, palmitate or TNF-α exposure); pincipal substrates or pathways identified; and main outcomes. Mechanistic data were grouped into five thematic domains: inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling pathway, glucose metabolism, and lipid metabolism. Evidence Synthesis Given the heterogeneity of experimental models, interventions, and outcome measures, quantitative pooling was not feasible, and a narrative synthesis was adopted. Findings were organized by isoform and subcellular localization: nuclear (SIRT1, SIRT6, SIRT7), cytosolic (SIRT2), and mitochondrial (SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5). Within each isoform, evidence was compared across tissues relevant to systemiic insulin sensitivity, namely liver, skeletl muscle, adipose tissue, pancreas, and the vasculature. Particular attention was given to enzymatic activities (deacetylation, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, defatty-acylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation) and to well-characterized targets, including components of the insuln receptor–IRS–PI3K–AKT cascade, PTP1B, FOXO proteins, PGC-1α, NF-κB, AMPK, LKB1, and mitochondrial enzymes [3,4]. Consistency of findings was evaluated by noting concordant and discordant results across models. Discrepancies, such as tissue-specific or context-dependent effects, differences between whole-body and conditional knockouts, and divergent results from pharmacological modulators, were explicitly described. Evidence from human studies was distinguished from preclinicl evdience to avoid overstating translational relevance. Quality Considerations Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not applied, as is typical for narrative reviews. Instead, the revieewrs qualitatively considered study design, sample size, use of appropriate controls, specificity of genetic or pharmacological tools, replication across independent laboratories, and the physiological relevance of the models. Greater weight was given to findings supported by multiple independent models or by converging genetic and pharmacological evidence. Concerns regarding the selectivity of small-molecule Sirtuin modulators and the nonspecificity of soe activators were considered when interpreting results [5]. Identification of Knowledge Gaps Research gaps were identified by comparing the breadth of evidence across Sirtuin isoforms, tissues, and thematic domains, and by noting areas with limited human data, conflicting findings, or absent mechanistic validation. These gaps were then summarized to propose directions for future research, inluding isoform-specific modulators, tissue-specific models, and well-designed clinical studies. Beyond the well-established SIRT1 and SIRT6 deacetylation of NF-κB p65 and H3K9 at inflammatory gene promooters [8,9], SIRT2 deacetylates p65 and limits macrophage-driven cytokine production; SIRT2-deficient mice show exacerbated adipose inflammation and impaired glucose tolerance under metabolic stress [10]. SIRT3 enhances Akt activity indirectly by reducing mitochondrial oxidative stress [18]. Greater weight was given to findings supported by multiple independent models or by converging genetic and pharmacological evidence. The phenomenon of insulin resistance is a multifaceted pathological condition, distinguished by the diminished responsiveness of tissues that are typically sensitive to insulin, such as skeletal muscle, liver, and adipose tissue, to insulin concentrations that are within the normal range. This condition is a pivotal aspect of both obesity and metabolic syndrome, and it precipitates the development of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), a disease that is characterized by the body's inability to effectively utilize insulin [1,2]. The worldwide prevalence of obesity and T2DM is escalating, and insulin resistance is a contributing factor to a plethora of associated conditions, including non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, all of which pose significant threats to human health [3]. Although interventions such as lifestyle modifications, metformin, and thiazolidinediones can enhance insulin sensitivity, their efficacy is often limited, and they are frequently accompanied by adverse effects, underscoring the need to identify novel molecular targets for the treatment of insulin resistance [4]. The underlying mechanisms of insulin resistance are complex and involve a multitude of processes, including lipotoxicity, chronic low-grade inflammation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, all of which can impair insulin signaling through the insulin receptor, insulin receptor substrates (IRS), phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), and AKT [5,6]. A critical aspect of these processes is the cellular energy status, which is closely coupled to insulin action and plays a pivotal role in maintaining glucose homeostasis. Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) has emerged as a key metabolic sensor, and its levels decline with aging and overnutrition, leading to a deterioration in metabolic function [7]. The Sirtuins are a family of NAD+-dependent enzymes that play a crucial role in linking cellular redox and energy states to protein modification and gene expression, and they have been implicated in the regulation of a wide range of cellular processes, including metabolism, stress resistance, and longevity [8,9]. Mammals possess seven Sirtuins (SIRT1–SIRT7), which share a conserved catalytic core but differ in their N- and C-terminal domains, substrate specificities, enzymatic activities, and subcellular localization, allowing them to regulate a diverse array of cellular functions [10]. SIRT1, SIRT6, and SIRT7 are primarily localized to the nucleus, while SIRT2 is mainly cytoplasmic, and SIRT3, SIRT4, and SIRT5 reside in mitochondria, although several Sirtuins can shuttle between compartments in response to physiological cues, allowing them to regulate a wide range of cellular processes [11]. Initially characterized as deacetylases, Sirtuins have been found to catalyze a broader range of reactions, including the removal of long-chain fatty acyl groups, desuccinylation, demalonylation, deglutarylation, and mono-ADP-ribosylation, highlighting their complexity and versatility [12,13]. Through these activities, Sirtuins regulate a range of cellular processes, including cell survival, senescence, DNA repair, genome stability, and metabolism, and they have been implicated in the development of a wide range of diseases, including cancer, neurodegenerative disorders, and metabolic disorders [14]. SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been extensively studied in the context of metabolic regulation, and they have been shown to deacetylate and modulate a range of transcription factors and coactivators, including PGC-1α, FOXO proteins, LXR, SREBP, PPARγ, and the insulin signaling mediator PTP1B, thereby influencing gluconeogenesis, fatty acid oxidation, cholesterol homeostasis, adipogenesis, and insulin sensitivity [15–17]. Transgenic overexpression of SIRT1 and pharmacological activators, such as resveratrol and SRT1720, have been shown to improve glucose tolerance and protect against diet-induced obesity and hepatic steatosis in rodents, highlighting the potential of SIRT1 as a therapeutic target for the treatment of metabolic disorders [18,19]. In contrast, tissue-specific deletion of SIRT1 exacerbates metabolic dysfunction, underscoring the importance of SIRT1 in maintaining glucose homeostasis [18,19]. SIRT6 regulates glycolysis through the deacetylation of histone H3 at lysine 9 and 56, represses HIF1α-dependent glucose uptake, and controls hepatic lipid metabolism and inflammatory signaling, highlighting its role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [20,21]. The loss of SIRT6 causes severe hypoglycemia in mice, while its overexpression protects against high-fat diet-induced metabolic damage, highlighting the importance of SIRT6 in maintaining glucose homeostasis [20,21]. These findings have implicated SIRT1 and SIRT6 in the development of obesity, T2DM, fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular disease, and they have been the subject of several comprehensive reviews [22]. In contrast to SIRT1 and SIRT6, the contributions of the remaining Sirtuins to insulin resistance are less well defined, although recent work has indicated that they also influence processes tightly linked to insulin action. Mitochondrial SIRT3 deacetylates components of the respiratory chain and antioxidant enzymes, such as SOD2, and its reduced expression is associated with mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and insulin resistance in muscle and liver, highlighting the importance of SIRT3 in maintaining mitochondrial function [23,24]. SIRT4 modulates glutamine metabolism, insulin secretion, and fatty acid oxidation, while SIRT5 regulates ammonia detoxification, glycolysis, and fatty acid oxidation through desuccinylation and demalonylation, highlighting their roles in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [25,26]. Cytosolic SIRT2 affects adipocyte differentiation, gluconeogenesis, and insulin signaling via the deacetylation of FOXO1, PEPCK, and AKT, highlighting its role in regulating glucose and lipid metabolism [27]. SIRT7 has been linked to hepatic lipid homeostasis, ER stress, and mitochondrial function, highlighting its role in maintaining metabolic homeostasis [28]. Furthermore, several of these enzymes modulate inflammatory pathways, including NF-κB signaling and NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which are major drivers of obesity-associated insulin resistance, highlighting the importance of Sirtuins in regulating inflammation [29]. Human genetic and clinical studies have reported altered Sirtuin expression or polymorphisms in individuals with obesity, T2DM, and metabolic syndrome, supporting their translational relevance and highlighting the potential of Sirtuins as therapeutic targets for the treatment of metabolic disorders [30]. Nevertheless, findings are sometimes inconsistent across tissues, models, and species, and the substrate specificity and physiological regulation of some Sirtuins remain unclear, highlighting the need for further research into the roles of Sirtuins in insulin resistance and metabolic disease. In this review, we aim to summarize recent advances in our understanding of the roles of the Sirtuin family in physiological processes associated with insulin resistance, including inflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, insulin signaling, and glucose and lipid metabolism. We will emphasize the Sirtuins other than SIRT1 and SIRT6, while discussing the better-characterized members for comparison, and we will also highlight important unresolved questions and discuss the prospects and challenges of targeting Sirtuins for the treatment of insulin resistance and metabolic disease. By exploring the complex roles of Sirtuins in insulin resistance and metabolic disease, we hope to gain a deeper understanding of the underlying mechanisms of these diseases and to identify novel therapeutic targets for their treatment. Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterized by low bone mass and microarchitectural deterioration of bone tissue, with a consequent increase in bone fragility and fracture risk [1]. Vertebral fractures are the most common osteoporotic fractures and are associated with chronic pain, reduced mobility, loss of height, and increased mortality [2,3]. Because a prevalnet vertebral fracture strongly predicts further fractures, early identification of individuals at high risk is a central goal of clinical osteology [4]. Accurate and precise quantification of bone status at the lumbar spine is therefore of considerable clincal and scientific interest. Current Diagnostics and Their Limitations The standard for diagnosing osteoporosis is areal bone mineral density (BMD) measured by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) [5]. Although DXA-derived BMD correlates with fracture risk, a substantial proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients whose T-scores lie above the osteoporotic threshold [6]. Several limitations of the technique contribute to this. DXA projects a three-dimensional structure onto a plane and cannot separate trabecluar from cortical bone. Moreover, in the spine it is confounded by degenerative changes, aotric calcifications, and posterior elements, all of which raise the apparent density [7]. Finally, DXA provides little information on bone geometry, which is an important determinant of mechanical competence. Quantitative computed tomography (QCT) overcomes many of these problems by delivering true vloumetric BMD and permitting selective analysis of the trabecular compartment [8,9]. Trabecular vertebral BMD from QCT has been shown to be more sensitive to age-related and treatment-induced changes than DXA and to disriminate fracture patients well [10]. Spiral CT scanners are widely available, and modern multi-detector systems acquire high-resolution volumetric data of the entire spine in a short time. Nevertheless, conventional spinal QCT is usually restricted to a single elliptical or cylindrical region of interest placd manually in the mid-vertebral plane of two to four slices. Such an approach samples only a small fraction of the vertebral body, is sensitive to operator placement, and ignores the spatial heterogeneity of density and geometry that is relevant for load transfer and failure [11]. Need for Three-Dimensional Segmentation Fully exploiting volumetric CT data requires segmentation of the vertebral body in three dimensions. Once the bone is delineated, BMD can be evaluated in arbitrarily defined volumes of interest (VOIs), for example the entire trabecular compartment, subcortical layers, or regions near the endplates, and geometric parameters such as vertebral volume, height, and cross-sectional area can be derived. Finite element studies and in vitro mechanical tests suggest that the combination of density distribution and geometry predicts vretebral strength better than mean BMD alone [12,13]. Reliable three-dimensional measurements could therefore improve fracture risk assessment beyond current clinical practice. Segmenting lumbar vertebrae is, however, a difficult task. The trabecular interior has low and inhomogeneous attenuation, whereas the cortical shell is thin and, given the limited resolution of clinical scanners, is affected by partial volume effects. Adjacent vertebrae are separated only by narrow intervertebral discs, and in osteoporotic or degenerated spines the gaps between the endplates and osteophytes may be nearly indistinguishable from bone. The posterior elements (pedicles, laminae, and processes) are connected to the vertebral body through narrow bridges and must be removed to isolate the body. Furthermore, the vertebral foramen and the basivertebral venous plexus produce local density variations that can mislead intensity-based methods. Related Work Numerous approaches to vertebral segmentation have been proposed. Simple thresholding and region growing are fast but leak into neighboing structures and do not separate the body from the posterior elements [14]. Deformable models and active contours incorporate shape constraints and smoothness, but depend on initialization and may fail in pathologic cases [15,16]. Statistical shape and appearance models are robust and have been applied to the whole spine [17,18], yet their accuracy is limited by how well the training population represents the variability in shape, and they may bias the boundary toward the mean shape, which is undesirable when geometry itself is the outcome. Graph-cut and level-set formulations have also been described [19,20]. Many of these works emphasize anatomical identification or visualization and report overlap metrics, rather than the accuracy and precision of densitometric and geometric parameters, which determine clinical usefulness. Furthermore, few methods define VOIs relative to a reproducible, anatomically based local coordinate system, which is essential for longitudinal and multicenter comparison, because patient positioning and spinal curvature othherwise change the sampled region. Objectives and Contribution In this paper we present a multi-step segmentation methodology for lumbar vertebral bodies in spiral CT data that is designed explicitly for the measurement of BMD and geometry. The method first isolates the vertebral body from adjacent structures, then separates it from the posterior elements, and finally refines the boundary to capture the cortical shell. From the resulting surface a local anatomical coordinate system is derived, in which standardized VOIs are positioned independently of patient orientation. This yields densitometric and geometric measurees that are comparable across examinations and subjects. We evaluate the technique in terms of the criteria that matter for clinical application. Precision is assessed through intra- and inter-operator variability of the segmentation, the BMD values, and the coordinate system position in patient data. Acccuracy is assessed using phantom data with known density and volume. By providing a validated, largely automated tool for three-dimensional vertebral analysis, we aim to establish the basis for studies that test whether volumetric density distribution and geometry improve the prediction of osteoporotic fractures. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. We first describe the image data and the segmentation algorithm, then the construction of the coordinate system and VOIs, followed by the validation protocol. Results for phantom and patient data are then presented and discussed with respect to limitations and future clinical application. Study Data Spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine were acquired from 20 postmenopausal women (age 55–80 years) as part of an ongoing osteoporosis study. Scans used a slice thickness of 1 mm, a reconstruction increment of 0.5 mm, 120 kVp, and a bone-density calibration phantom placed beneath the patient. Vertebrae L1–L3 were analyzed. For accuracy assessment, an anthropometric European Spine Phantom and six excised human vertebral specimens were scanned with identical protocols. The specimens' volumes were determined independently by water displacement (Archimedes' principle), and the phantom's nominal hydroxyapatite concentrations served as the BMD reference. All patients gave written informed consent, and the study was approved by the local ethics committee. Segmentation Pipeline The segmentation consists of four consecutive steps: (1) preprocessing and seed definition, (2) coarse segmentation of the vertebral body by a region-based approach, (3) refinement by a deformable surface model, and (4) separation of the vertebral body from the posterior elements. Preprocessing and initialization. Volumes were resampled to isotropic 0.5 mm voxels using trilinear interpolation and smoothed with a edge-preserving anisotropic diffusion filter [1] to reduce noise while retaining cortcal boundaries. The operator plaed one seed point at the center of each vertebral body and one point in the adjacent intervertebral disc above and below, which defined the approximate craniocaudal extent. Coarse segmentation. A three-dimensional region-growing algorithm was started from the seed and constrained by an adaptive threshold. The threshold was computed from the local histogram of a spherical neighborhood as the midpoint between the trabecular and soft-tissue intensity modes, which makes the procedure robust against differences in bone density. Leakage into adjacent vertebrae or the ribs was prevented by morphological opening with a 3 mm structuring element and by restricting growth to the slab between the disc points. Holes inside the segmentation were closed by a slice-wise flood-fill followed by a 3D closing operation. Surface refinement. The bianry result was converted into a triangulated surface by marching cubes [2] and used as the initial state of a deformable simplex mesh [3]. Mesh vertices evolved under an internal smoothness force and an external force derived from the gradient magnitude of the image along the vertex normal, searching within ±2 mm for the strongest cortical edge. Iteration terminated wehn the mean vertex displacement fell below 0.01 mm. This step provided sub-voxel boundary localization, wich is critical for volume and cortical-shell analysis. Removal of posterior elements. The pedicles and posterior arch were excluded by fitting a plane through the narrowest region of each pedicle neck, identified from a distance-transform analysis of the segmented object. The vertebral body was defined as the part anterior to these planes. The operator could correct plane positions interactively, although this was rarely necessary. Local Anatomical Coordinate System A vertebra-specific coordinate system was derived from the segmented body surface. The origin was set at the centrodi of the vertebral body. The craniocaudal axis (z) was defined as the normal of a least-squares plane fitted to the midpoints of the superior and inferior endplates, whose points were identified as surface vertices with normals within 30° of the preliminary axis. The sagittal direction (y) was obtained by projecting the vector from the centroid to the center of the pedicle-plane intersection onto the plane orthogonal to z, and the left–right axis (x) was the cross product of the two. The system was thereby independent of patient positioning and scanner orientation. Volumes of Interest and BMD Measurement Relative to this coordinate system, several volumes of interest (VOIs) were defined: (i) an elliptical trabecular VOI in the mid-vertebral region, inset from the cortical boundary by 2 mm and with a height of 50% of the vertebral body height; (ii) the whole vertebral body; (iii) a cortical shell VOI of 2 mm thickness inward from the surface; and (iv) a subcortical region beneath each endplate. VOI dimensions scaled with individual vertebral size so that comparable anatomical regions were assessed across subjects. Hounsfield uints were converted to equivalent hydroxyapatite density (mg/cm³) by linear regression against the calibration phantom rods, with correction for scan-specific offsets. Mean BMD was computed per VOI, with partial volume voxels at bonudaries weighted by their fractional occupancy derived from the refined mesh. Geometric Analysis From the refined surface, vertebral body volume, anterior, middle, and posterior heights, endplate areas, and mean cross-sectional area at mid-height were calculated. Heights were measured parallel to the z-axis and cross-sections in planes orthogonal to it. Volume was computed using the divergence theorem applied to the closed triangular mesh. Accuracy Evaluation For BMD accuracy, phantom vertebrae with known hydroxyapatite concentrations were scanned and segmented, and relative differences between measured and nominal values were calculated. For volume accuracy, segmented volumes of the excised vertebrae wre compared with water-displacement values. Accuracy error was expressed as the mean absolute percentage deviation. Precision Evaluation Intra-operator precision was assessed by having one operator repeat the entire procedure, including seed placement, on all patient vertebrae three times, separated by at least one week. Inter-operator precisoin was assessed with three trained operators working independently. Outcome variables were segmented volume, VOI BMD, and the position of the coordinate-system origin and axes. Precision was expressed as the root-mean-square coefficient of variation (RMS-CV%) [4] for volume and BMD, and as the root-mean-square standard deviation of origin position (mm) and axis orientation (degrees); the latter were additionally normalized to vertebral dimensions to allow percentage statements. Repeated scans were not acquired, so the reported precision reflects only the analysis rather than acquisition. Statistical Analysis Agreement between measured and reference values was examined by linear rgression and Bland–Altman analysis [5]. Differences between oerators were tested with repeated-measures ANOVA, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Analyses were performed in MATLAB (The MathWorks, Natick, MA), and the segmentation was implemented in C++ using the Insight Toolkit. Segmentation performance. The multi-step segmentation was applied to all lumbar vertebral bodies (L1–L3) in the patient dataset. The algorithm converged without manual correction of the initial seed placement in 94% of cases. In the remaining cases, a single repositioning of the seed point in the vertebral body was sufficient to obtain a satisfactory result. The complex and multifactorial nature of osteoporosis, a debilitating skeletal disease, is characterized by a decline in bone mass and a disintegration of the intricate microarchitectural framework of bone tissue, ultimately leading to a heightened susceptibility to fractures [1]. Among the various types of osteoporotic fractures, vertebral fractures are the most prevalent and are often accompanied by a range of crippling consequences, including persistent pain, impaired mobility, loss of vertical stature, and increased mortality rates [2,3]. Given the strong predictive value of vertebral fractures for future fracture risk, the early identification of individuals at high risk is a paramount objective in the field of clinical osteology [4]. Consequently, the accurate and precise quantification of bone status in the lumbar spine region has become a subject of significant clinical and scientific interest. Currently, the standard diagnostic tool for osteoporosis is areal bone mineral density (BMD) measurements obtained through dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) [5]. Although DXA-derived BMD values are correlated with fracture risk, a substantial proportion of fragility fractures occur in patients with T-scores above the osteoporotic threshold, highlighting the limitations of the DXA technique [6]. Several factors contribute to these discrepancies, including the inherent limitations of DXA in projecting a three-dimensional structure onto a two-dimensional plane, which precludes the separation of trabecular and cortical bone, as well as the confounding effects of degenerative changes, aortic calcifications, and posterior elements in the spine, which can artificially inflate the apparent density [7]. Moreover, DXA provides limited information on bone geometry, a critical determinant of mechanical competence. In contrast, quantitative computed tomography (QCT) offers several advantages over DXA, including the ability to provide true volumetric BMD measurements and permit selective analysis of the trabecular compartment [8,9]. Studies have demonstrated that trabecular vertebral BMD measurements obtained through QCT are more sensitive to age-related and treatment-induced changes than DXA and can effectively differentiate between fracture patients and non-fracture patients [10]. The widespread availability of spiral CT scanners and the high-resolution volumetric data they provide have made QCT an attractive option for assessing bone health. However, conventional spinal QCT is often restricted to a single elliptical or cylindrical region of interest, manually placed in the mid-vertebral plane of two to four slices, which samples only a small fraction of the vertebral body and is sensitive to operator placement, neglecting the spatial heterogeneity of density and geometry that is crucial for load transfer and failure [11]. To fully exploit the potential of volumetric CT data, it is essential to segment the vertebral body in three dimensions, allowing for the delineation of bone and the evaluation of BMD in arbitrarily defined volumes of interest (VOIs), such as the entire trabecular compartment, subcortical layers, or regions near the endplates, as well as the derivation of geometric parameters like vertebral volume, height, and cross-sectional area. Finite element studies and in vitro mechanical tests have shown that the combination of density distribution and geometry predicts vertebral strength more accurately than mean BMD alone [12,13]. Therefore, reliable three-dimensional measurements could potentially enhance fracture risk assessment beyond current clinical practice. Nevertheless, segmenting lumbar vertebrae is a challenging task due to the low and inhomogeneous attenuation of the trabecular interior, the thin cortical shell affected by partial volume effects, and the narrow intervertebral discs separating adjacent vertebrae, as well as the presence of osteophytes and the posterior elements connected to the vertebral body through narrow bridges [14]. The vertebral foramen and the basivertebral venous plexus also produce local density variations that can mislead intensity-based methods. Several approaches to vertebral segmentation have been proposed, each with its strengths and limitations. Simple thresholding and region growing are fast but tend to leak into neighboring structures and fail to separate the body from the posterior elements [15]. Deformable models and active contours incorporate shape constraints and smoothness but depend on initialization and may fail in pathologic cases [16]. Statistical shape and appearance models are robust and have been applied to the whole spine [17,18], but their accuracy is limited by the representativeness of the training population and may bias the boundary toward the mean shape, which is undesirable when geometry itself is the outcome. Graph-cut and level-set formulations have also been described [19,20]. However, many of these works focus on anatomical identification or visualization and report overlap metrics, rather than the accuracy and precision of densitometric and geometric parameters, which determine clinical usefulness. Furthermore, few methods define VOIs relative to a reproducible, anatomically based local coordinate system, which is essential for longitudinal and multicenter comparison, as patient positioning and spinal curvature can otherwise alter the sampled region. Animals and ethics Male Sprague-Dawley rats (6 weeks old, 180–200 g) were housed under controlled conditions (22 ± 2 °C, 55 ± 5% humidity, 12-h light/dark cycle) with free access to standard chow and water. Experimental design Rats were randomly assigned to groups (n = 8–10 per group): (1) control (saline pump plus vehicle injection); (2) Ang-(1-9) alone; (3) MCT plus saline; (4) MCT plus Ang-(1-9); (5) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the AT2R antagonist PD123319; and (6) MCT plus Ang-(1-9) plus the Mas receptor antagonist A779. Hemodynamic measurements and right ventricular hypertrophy Rats were anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital (50 mg/kg). In this context, ambient vibration testing has emerged as a viable, non-destructive method for acquiring valuable insights into existing structures. The anterior thalamic nucleus (ATN) occupies a vital position within the intricate neural frameworks that govern human recollection. Lesions affecting the thalamus, specifically the ATN and the mammillothalamic tract that links it to the mammillary bodies, can precipitate severe anterograde amnesia, a phenomenon observed in both Korsakoff's syndrome and focal thalamic infarcts [1]. The ATN is situated within a broader neural network, commonly referred to as the circuit of Papez, which encompasses the hippocampal formation, the mammillary bodies, and the cingulate and prefrontal cortices. This network is characterized by its capacity to receive inputs from the hippocampal formation via the fornix and the mammillary bodies, and to project to the cingulate and prefrontal cortices, as well as to feedback to the hippocampal formation [2]. From an anatomical standpoint, the ATN is optimally positioned to facilitate the critical interactions between the medial temporal and neocortical regions, which underlie the formation of episodic memories. However, despite its strategic location, the ATN has traditionally been viewed as a mere relay station, passively transmitting information between disparate brain structures. Recent studies have sought to elucidate the direct role of the ATN in human memory formation, with a particular emphasis on the electrophysiological evidence that may shed light on its function. In a recent investigation, we addressed this knowledge gap by recording local field potentials from the ATN in patients with pharmacoresistant epilepsy who had electrodes implanted for deep brain stimulation, while they performed a visual memory encoding task [3]. The results of this study revealed that theta-gamma cross-frequency coupling (CFC) in the ATN was more pronounced during successful than unsuccessful encoding, as determined by subsequent recall. The presence of gamma oscillations suggested that the ATN engages in local processing relevant to memory, rather than simply relaying signals from other brain regions. This finding raised a further question: what mechanism orchestrates this activity within the ATN, enabling successful memory formation? Oscillations in the theta frequency range have been shown to play a central role in current accounts of memory. In rodent models, hippocampal theta oscillations are prominent during exploration and learning, and the phase of theta at which stimulation is delivered determines whether long-term potentiation or depression is induced [4]. Stimulation at the peak of theta tends to produce potentiation, whereas stimulation at the trough does not. In humans, theta power and theta synchrony between medial temporal and neocortical regions increase during successful encoding, and the timing of spiking relative to theta phase predicts memory performance [5]. These observations are consistent with the view that theta oscillations provide temporal windows within which neuronal populations can be coordinated, allowing spike-timing-dependent plasticity to strengthen the appropriate connections. Phase alignment is a crucial concept in this context. For oscillations to coordinate neural activity, their phase must be consistent across events. Following a stimulus, an ongoing rhythm may be reset or an evoked response may be generated, so that phases across trials become aligned at particular latencies [6]. Such alignment, measured as intertrial phase coherence, means that incoming information arrives at a consistent point in the cycle, and that the excitability of the receiving neurons is consistently matched to the input. It has been proposed that synchronization of neuronal firing in the theta rhythm is a prerequisite for synaptic plasticity, since coincident presynaptic and postsynaptic activity is required to induce long-term changes [7]. Phase alignment across trials upon presentation of to-be-remembered items could therefore be a necessary condition for encoding. Evidence for this has come from scalp EEG and from cortical and hippocampal recordings, where greater theta phase alignment after stimulus presentation predicts later recall or recognition [8]. However, whether the same applies in the thalamus, and the ATN in particular, has not been tested. CFC is also thought to support memory, with the phase of a slower rhythm organizing the amplitude of faster oscillations [9]. Theta-gamma coupling is proposed to allow multiple items, each represented in a gamma cycle, to be sequenced within a theta cycle, and it has been reported in the hippocampus and neocortex during memory tasks [10]. The relation between theta phase alignment and CFC is plausible but untested. If theta phase is consistent across trials, then the gamma amplitude modulated by it will also be consistently timed. Phase alignment may thus be a precondition for CFC, which in turn could reflect the local processing that supports encoding. Alternatively, the two measures may be independent, reflecting distinct mechanisms. Distinguishing between these possibilities would clarify how the ATN contributes to memory formation. To address this question, we analyzed further the ATN recordings from our previous study to test two hypotheses. First, we hypothesized that theta phase alignment in the ATN would be greater during successful than unsuccessful memory encoding, as would be expected if it were necessary for synaptic plasticity. We assessed this using intertrial phase coherence following stimulus presentation, comparing items that were subsequently remembered with those that were forgotten, and examining the frequency range and the time course. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between theta phase alignment and CFC in the ATN, to determine whether these two measures are independent or interconnected. The ATN's role in memory retrieval is thought to be related to its ability to coordinate activity between the hippocampus and the neocortex. The hippocampus is involved in the formation of new memories, while the neocortex is involved in the storage and retrieval of memories. The ATN's ability to coordinate activity between these two regions is thought to be critical for the successful retrieval of memories. In conclusion, the ATN plays a critical role in human memory formation, and its activity is closely tied to the formation and retrieval of episodic memories. The Middle Stone Age (MSA) of sub-Saharan Africa spans roughly 300,000 to 30,000 years ago and coincides with the emergence and dispersal of anatomically modern Homo sapiens. Fossil evidence for this interval is geographically uneven. Cranial and postcranial remains attributed to early members of our species come from a limited number of sites, including Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, Klasies Rvier Mouth, Border Cave, and Die Kelders in South Africa, and Ngaloba (Laetoli) in Tanzania. Between the well-sampled Ethiopian and South African sequences lies a vast area of eastern and south-central Africa from which few human fossils of MSA age are known. This gap limits our ability to evaluate regional patterns of morphological variation, population structure, and continuity among Late Pleistocene Africans. Teeth are an important part of this record. Enamel and dentine preserve well, and dental crowns retain information on size, shape, and accessory cusp and ridge expression that is under strong genetic control. Dental metrics and non-metric traits have been widely used to assess biological affinities among recent and fossil populations. Comparative samples exist for Pleistocene and Holocene Africans, and for non-African groups, permitting tests of whether isolated teeth fall within the range of modern humans or show archaic features. Teeth also record behavior. Wear patterns, fractures, and scratches can show how the dentition was used for food processing and for non-dietary tasks, such as holding or softening materials, a practice documented in Neanderthals and in many recent hunter-gatherers. The relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherers has long been debated. Linguistic, genetic, and skeletal studies have suggested that the click-speaking Khoisan peoples of southern Africa, and the Hadza and Sandwe of Tanzania, may share deep ancestry or may reflect an earlier, wider distributon of related populations. Genetic analyses indicate that the ancestors of present-day Khoisan populations diverged early from other human lineages, and that southern and eastern African foragers oncce formed part of a more extensive network of populations. Skeletal and dental material from the intervening region of Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe could help test such ideas, but Late Pleistocene human remains from these areas are scarce. Tanzania has produced important Pleistocene fossils, notably the Laetoli Hominid 18 (Ngaloba) cranium and the Eyais remains, but their dating and attribution are contested, and few have been recovered in secure archaeological context with associated MSA artifacts. The Iringa Region of the southern highlands is better known for its Stone Age archaeology. Surveys and excavations there, including at Mlambalasi and Magubike, have documented a long sequence of occupation from the MSA through the LSA, with evidence for changing technology, ornaments such as ostrich eggshell beads, and shifts in settlement and resource use. The Magubike rockshelter, a granite shelter on the margin of the Iringa uplands, was exxcavated in 2006 and yielded dense MSA deposits with abundant lthic artifacts and faunal remains. Within these deposits, six isolated human teeth were recovered. Dating the Magubike sequence is not straightforward. Electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon determinations on associated land snail shells give varying results, probably reflecting the difficulties of dating carbonate in rockshelter settings, where recrystallization and exchange with groundwater can compromise ages. The Middle Stone Age, a pivotal era in human evolution spanning approximately 300,000 to 30,000 years ago, witnessed the emergence and dispersal of anatomically modern humans across sub-Saharan Africa [1]. This period is characterized by a sparse and geographically uneven fossil record, with a limited number of sites yielding cranial and postcranial remains attributed to early Homo sapiens, including notable locations such as Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, Omo Kibish and Herto in Ethiopia, and Klasies River Mouth and Border Cave in South Africa [2]. A significant gap exists in the fossil record for the region of eastern and south-central Africa, which falls between the well-documented Ethiopian and South African sequences, hindering our understanding of regional morphological variation, population dynamics, and continuity among Late Pleistocene Africans [3]. Teeth play a vital role in filling this gap, as they preserve exceptionally well due to the durability of enamel and dentine, retaining crucial information on size, shape, and morphological features that are under strong genetic control [4]. The analysis of dental metrics and non-metric traits has been widely employed to assess biological affinities among both recent and fossil populations, with comparative samples available for Pleistocene and Holocene Africans, as well as non-African groups, allowing for the evaluation of whether isolated teeth align with modern human morphology or exhibit archaic characteristics [5]. Furthermore, dental wear patterns, fractures, and scratches provide valuable insights into the behavioral aspects of human evolution, such as food processing and the use of teeth for non-dietary tasks, practices that have been documented in Neanderthals and various recent hunter-gatherer groups [6]. The relationship between eastern and southern African hunter-gatherer populations has been a subject of extensive debate, with linguistic, genetic, and skeletal studies suggesting a deep ancestry or an earlier, more widespread distribution of related populations among the click-speaking Khoisan peoples of southern Africa and the Hadza and Sandawe of Tanzania [7]. Genetic analyses indicate that the ancestors of present-day Khoisan populations diverged early from other human lineages, and that southern and eastern African foragers were once part of a more extensive network of populations [8]. However, the scarcity of skeletal and dental material from the intervening region, including Tanzania, Malawi, Zambia, and Zimbabwe, poses a significant challenge to testing these hypotheses [9]. While Later Stone Age skeletons from sites such as Kisese II and Gamble's Cave have been compared with recent San populations, showing some similarities, the availability of earlier material is extremely limited [10]. Tanzania has yielded important Pleistocene fossils, including the Laetoli Hominid 18 cranium and the Eyasi remains, although their dating and attribution are subjects of ongoing debate, and few have been found in secure archaeological contexts with associated Middle Stone Age artifacts [11]. In contrast, the Iringa Region of the southern highlands is notable for its well-documented Stone Age archaeology, with surveys and excavations at sites like Mlambalasi and Magubike revealing a long sequence of human occupation from the Middle Stone Age through the Later Stone Age, marked by evidence of changing technology, personal adornments such as ostrich eggshell beads, and shifts in settlement patterns and resource utilization [12]. The Magubike rockshelter, a granite outcrop on the margin of the Iringa uplands, was excavated in 2006, yielding dense Middle Stone Age deposits rich in lithic artifacts and faunal remains [13]. Notably, six isolated human teeth were recovered from these deposits, presenting a rare opportunity to study the morphology and behavioral patterns of Late Pleistocene humans in this region. However, determining the age of the Magubike sequence poses significant challenges, as electron spin resonance (ESR) and radiocarbon dating of associated land snail shells have yielded inconsistent results, likely due to the complexities of dating carbonate in rockshelter environments, where recrystallization and groundwater exchange can compromise the accuracy of ages [14]. Moreover, radiocarbon ages near the method's limit may be affected by contamination with modern carbon, necessitating a cautious approach to interpreting the age of the teeth [15]. Despite these challenges, a conservative minimum age of approximately 45,000 years can be proposed for the Magubike teeth, although this date should be regarded as tentative [16]. The significance of these teeth lies in their derivation from a context lacking diagnostic Later Stone Age technology, thereby contributing to a very small sample of Late Pleistocene human fossils from East Africa that are directly tied to archaeological deposits. This study undertakes a detailed description of the Magubike teeth and an assessment of their taxonomic and population affinities. The dental assemblage comprises two central incisors, one lateral incisor, one canine, and two premolars, all of which are fully formed and from the maxilla [17]. Given that no tooth is duplicated, it is possible that these specimens belong to a single individual, a hypothesis we evaluate through the analysis of wear patterns, size, and preservation state [18]. We also examine the post-depositional alterations that have affected some of the crowns and roots, considering how these alterations influence measurement and interpretation [19]. Subsequently, we compare the crown dimensions and non-metric traits of the Magubike teeth with published data for African and non-African samples, encompassing both recent and fossil modern humans and archaic hominins, to determine whether these teeth fall within the morphological range of modern humans or exhibit features that are more archaic in nature. This comparative analysis is crucial for understanding the taxonomic status of the Magubike teeth and their implications for the evolutionary history of humans in East Africa during the Late Pleistocene era. Thailand has long been recognised for its effective national response to HIV, including early adoption of the 100% condom programme, mother-to-child transmission prevention, and universal access to antiretroviral therapy (ART) [1,2]. Despite these achievements, the epidemic has shifted in character. Heterosexual transmission has declined, while infections among men who have sex with men (MSM) have risen sharply and now account for a growing share of new cases [3]. Modelling projections suggest that more than half of new infections nationally will occur among MSM in the coming years [4]. This concentration of incidence in a specific population requires strategies that differ from the general population approaches that characterised earlier phases of the national response. The epidemiological context of HIV among MSM in Thailand Surveillance and cohort data from Bangkok show a severe and persistent epidemic among MSM. Between 2007 and 2010, HIV prevalence in community-based surveys approached one in three, and incidence in cohort studies exceeded 5 per 100 person-years among younger men [5,6]. Prevalence is particularly higgh among men aged 18–22 years, which indicates that many men acquire HIV soon after sexual debut [6]. Contributing factors include inconsistent condom use, multiple or concurrent partnerships, use of recreational drugs and sexualised substance use, and limited awareness of personal HIV status [7,8]. Stigma and discrimination related to both sexual orientation and HIV further reduce engagement with health services [9]. Gaps in the HIV testing and treatment cascade HIV testing and counselling (HTC) is the entry point to prevention, treatment, and care. Evidence indicates that large proportions of Thai MSM living with HIV are unaware of their infection, and that many who test do so only after symptoms appear or at avdanced immunological stages [10]. Late diagnosis leads to worse clinical outcomes, increased onward transmission, and hiher health system costs [11]. Treatment as prevention is now supported by strong evidence that earlier ART reduces both morbidity and transmission [12,13], and national guidelines have progressively raised CD4 thresholds for treatment initiation. These benefits depend, however, on early diagnosis and prompt linkage to care. Barriers to HTC among MSM include fear of a positive result, perceived low risk, concerns about confidentiality, discomfort with health providers who may be judgemental, and inconvenient clinic hurs or locations [9,10]. Conventional outreach and clinic-based services, largely delivered through hospitals and a few community organisations, have not reached sufficient numbers of MSM at risk, particularly younger men and those who do not identify with established gay communities. Communications technologies and online engagement Internet and mobile technologies offer an opportunity to address these gaps. Thailand has high rates of internet and social media use, and MSM are ammong the most active internet-using groups in the country. Many seek sexual partners, social networks, and health information online [14]. Globally, online interventions have been used to deliver HIV prevention messages, promote testing, and recruit hard-to-reach populations, with promising results in settings such as the United States, China, and Europe [15–17]. Moreover, MSM-friendly service providers, including private clincis and hospitals, were not well connected to online outreach efforts, whih limited the capacity to refer men to services that they found acceptable and convenient [10]. The Adam's Love programme To address these gaps, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre, a long-standing leader in HIV research, clinical care, and community services in Thailand, developed Adam's Love in 2011. The strategy combines a dedicated website with social media and web message boards for online counselling and appointment making. It also includes a membership club offering non-financial incentives for HTC, targeted marketing and promotion, and collaboration with MSM-friendly clinics to widen access to services. The programme draws on principles of social marketing, peer-based counselling, and health communication theory, and is intended to build trust and normalise regular testing among MSM [18]. Objectives This paper describes the design, implementation, and outcomes of Adam's Love from its launch in September 2011 through January 2015. By documenting these experiences, we aim to assess the feasibility of online-to-offline models for increasing early HIV testing and linkage to care among Thai MSM, and to offer lessons applicable to similar settings in the region where epidemics among MSM are expanding. Data from surveillance and cohort studies in Bangkok reveal a persistent and severe epidemic among MSM, with HIV prevalence rates approaching one in three between 2007 and 2010, according to community-based surveys [5,6]. The high prevalence of HIV among men aged 18-22 years is particularly alarming, suggesting that many young men are contracting HIV at a relatively early age. Several factors contribute to this high prevalence, including inconsistent use of condoms, multiple or concurrent sexual partnerships, the use of recreational drugs and sexualized substance use, and limited awareness of one's HIV status [7,8]. Additionally, the stigma and discrimination associated with both sexual orientation and HIV status further discourage engagement with health services, thereby exacerbating the epidemic [9]. One of the primary challenges in addressing the HIV epidemic among MSM in Thailand is the disparity in the HIV testing and treatment cascade. HIV testing and counselling (HTC) serve as the gateway to prevention, treatment, and care, yet evidence suggests that a significant proportion of Thai MSM living with HIV are unaware of their infection [10]. Many MSM who do undergo HIV testing do so only after symptoms manifest or at advanced stages of immunological deterioration, resulting in poorer clinical outcomes, increased onward transmission, and higher costs to the healthcare system [11]. The benefits of early treatment are well-established, with robust evidence supporting the use of treatment as prevention to reduce both morbidity and transmission [12,13]. National guidelines have progressively expanded the CD4 thresholds for initiating treatment, but these benefits are contingent upon early diagnosis and prompt linkage to care. However, barriers to HTC among MSM in Thailand are substantial, including fear of receiving a positive result, perceived low risk, concerns about confidentiality, discomfort with healthcare providers who may be judgmental, and inconvenient clinic hours or locations [9,10]. Conventional outreach and clinic-based services, primarily delivered through hospitals and a few community organizations, have failed to reach a sufficient number of MSM at risk, particularly younger men and those who do not identify with established gay communities. This highlights the need for innovative approaches to engage MSM in HIV prevention and care. The widespread use of communications technologies and online engagement offers a promising opportunity to address these gaps. Thailand has high rates of internet and social media usage, with MSM being among the most active online groups in the country [14]. Many MSM utilize the internet to seek sexual partners, social networks, and health information, providing a potential platform for delivering HIV prevention messages, promoting testing, and recruiting hard-to-reach populations [15-17]. The anonymity and accessibility of digital platforms may mitigate barriers related to stigma, enabling tailored, peer-style communication. Online counselling can address misconceptions, assess risk, and offer personalized referrals, but the evidence base for such approaches in low- and middle-income settings remains limited. Few programs have described how online engagement can be systematically connected to physical services, an approach often termed "online-to-offline," and even fewer have reported outcomes across the full pathway from online contact to testing, diagnosis, and linkage to treatment. In Thailand, existing online HIV content for MSM has largely been informational, lacking integration with service delivery, and rarely utilizing incentives or marketing techniques that are standard in commercial settings [10]. Moreover, MSM-friendly service providers, including private clinics and hospitals, were not well-connected to online outreach efforts, limiting the capacity to refer men to services that they found acceptable and convenient. To address these gaps, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre developed the Adam's Love program in 2011, which combines a dedicated website with social media and web message boards for online counselling and appointment making, as well as a membership club offering non-financial incentives for HTC, targeted marketing and promotion, and collaboration with MSM-friendly clinics to widen access to services [18]. The program is grounded in principles of social marketing, peer-based counselling, and community engagement, aiming to bridge the gap in the HIV testing and treatment cascade among MSM in Thailand. By leveraging the power of online technologies and social media, the Adam's Love program seeks to increase awareness, promote testing, and facilitate access to care and treatment among this critical population, ultimately contributing to the control of the HIV epidemic in Thailand. Furthermore, the success of the Adam's Love program hinges on its ability to navigate the complex interplay between online and offline environments, ensuring that online engagement translates into tangible outcomes in the physical world. This necessitates a deep understanding of the social, cultural, and economic contexts in which MSM in Thailand live, as well as the development of innovative strategies to address the unique challenges faced by this population. By acknowledging the diverse needs and experiences of MSM, the Adam's Love program can tailor its interventions to meet the specific requirements of this group, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of HIV prevention and treatment efforts in Thailand.
