Global burden estimates suggest that 1.3 to 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 deaths occur annually, with the greatest burden in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia [3]. Cholera is a marker of inequity: it persists where access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) is inadequate, and it emerges explosively where conflict, displacement, or disasters disrupt these services [4,5]. Transmission and established risk factors The classical transmission pathway is faecal–oral, through contaminated drinking water or food. Epidemiological investigations in diverse settings have identified a recurring set of risk factors. These include consumption of untreated surface or shared water sources, storage of water in open or unclean containers, inadequate handwashing, consumption of food from street vendors or at social gatherings, contact with a cholera patient in the household, and attendance at funerals of cholera victims [6–9]. Protective factors include household water treatment, use of soap, and oral cholera vaccination [10,11]. However, the relative importance of these determinants varies with local ecology, culture, and infrastructure. Locally specific dietary practices, such as the consumption of raw produce or particular foods, may constitute additional, context-dependent vehicles of transmission that are not captured by generic prevention guidance [12]. Case-control studies conducted during outbreaks therefore remain essential for informing targeted interventions. The cholera epidemic in Yemen Yemen has experienced cholera intermittently, but the current epidemic is unprecedented in scale. Following the escalation of armed conflict in 2015, the country's health, water, and sanitation systems deteriorated markedly. Cholera cases were reported from October 2016, and after a first wave, a much larger second wave began in April 2017 [13,14]. By 2018, more than 1.4 million suspected cases and several thousand associated deaths had been reported, making this the largest documented cholera outbreak in modern history [15]. Genomic aanlyses indicate that the outbreak strain belongs to the sevennth pandemic El Tor lineage, closely related to isolates circulating in East Africa, suggesting introduction from outside the country followed by sustained local transmission [16]. The drivers of this epidemic are complex. Fighting has damaged water treatment plants, pumping stations, and sewage networks; fuel shortages limit water pumping and waste disposal; and unpaid public-sector workers, including health and sanitation staff, have curtailed services [14,17]. Millions of people have been displaced, often into crowded settings with limited WASH facilities. Malnutrition, which is highly prevalent among Yemeni children, further increases susceptibility to severe disease [17]. Under these conditions, households rely on alternative water sources such as water trucks, shared tanks, and unprotected wells, which are vulnerable to contamination. Health authorities and humanitarian partners have responded with case management through diarrhoea treatment centres and oral rehydration points, chlorination of water, hygiene promotion, and, from 2018, targeted oral cholera vaccination in selected districts [15,18]. Nevertheless, the epidemic has continued in successive waves. Rationale for the present study Effective prevention requires an understanding of how transmission occurs in the specific circumstances of Yemen. Several feaures of Yemeni society could shape exposure. Khat (Catha edulis), a leafy stimulant chewed daily by a large proportion of the adult population, is typically consumed fresh and unprocessed, often in social gatherings, and is grown with irrigation water of uncertain qulity and handled by multiple intermediaries before sale. Whether khat, like other raw produce, can act as a vehicle for faecal–oral pathogens has received little attention, and washing practices before chewing are variable. In addition, population movement within and between governorates, and visits by relatives from affected areas, may facilitate introduction of infection into communities. Despite the magnitude of the epidemic, published analytical epidemiological evidence from Yemen is scarce. Most available information derives from surveillance reports describing the distribution of suspected cases by time, place, and age, which cannot quantify the contribution of specific exposures [13,15]. Security constraints, liited access, and the overburdened health system have made fiedl investigations difficult. Aden, the temporary capital and a major port city that has received large numbers of displaced persons and has experienced repeated epidemic waves, provides an important settting in which to examine risk factors. Its urban environment, with a mixture of piped and non-piped water supplies, is also representative of many conflict-affected cities. Identifying modifiable behavioural and environmental determinants of cholera in this setting is a prerequisite for evidence-based public health messaging and for prioritising limited resources, such as water chlorination, distribution of soap and household water treatment products, and community hygiene education. We therefore conducted a case-control study in Aden in 2018 to identify risk factors associated with cholera infection during the ongoing outbreak, considering demographic characteristics, travel and contact history, food and water exposures, and household hygiene practices. The findings are intended to guide control measures in Yemen and to inform preparedness in other fragile settings where cholera threatens populations affected by conflict. Study design and setting We conducted an unmatched case-control stdy in Aden Governorate, southern Yemen, between [month] and [month] 2018, during the ongoing cholera epidemic that began in late 2016. Aden is a port city divided into eight districts, with a population of roughly one million. It hosts a large number of internally displaced persons, and its water, sanitation and health infrastructure has been severely damaged by conflict [1,2]. Cholera cases are treated at diarrhoea treatment centres (DTCs) and cholera treatment units run by the Ministry of Public Health and Population and supported by humanitarian partners. The study was nested within routine surveillance and was designed in accordance with World Health Organization (WHO) and Global Task Force on Cholera Control guidance on case-control investigations of cholera [3]. Reporting followed the STROBE guidelines for observational studies [4]. Case definition and selection Cases were identified from the three largest DTCs in Aden. A suspected case was defined using the WHO definition: a person aged two years or older who developed acute waatery diarrhoea, with or without vomiting, during the study period [3]. To improve specificity, we included only patients with a positive rapid diagnostic test (Crystal VC-O1 dipstick) or, when available, culture-confirmed Vibrio cholerae O1 from a stool or rectal swab. Patients were eligible if they had resided in Aden for at least the preceding two weeks, had onset of symptoms within the previous 72 hours, and gave consent (or consent was given by a guardian). Patients who were severely ill and unable to respond, or who had no available proxy respondent, were excluded. Consecutive eligible patients were enrolled until the target sample size was reached. Control selection Two community controls were selected per case. A control was defined as a person living in the same district as the case, aged two years or older, who had not had acute diarrhoea in the preceding four weeks. Controls were recruited from the neighbourhood of each case using a modified random-walk procedure: from the case's household, the intrviewer chose a random direction, selected every third household, and enrolled one eligibe resident. If no eligible person was present, the next household was visited. Where more than one eligible person lived in a household, one was selected by lottery. Controls were frequency-matched to cases by age group (<15 and ≥15 years) to keep the age distribution comparable, and persons from the same houshold as a case were not eligible. Sample size Sample size was calculated for a two-sided significance level of 5% and 80% power, assuming a control-to-case ratio of 2:1, an expected exposure prevalence of 30% among controls to a major risk factor (e.g. use of unsafe water), and a detectable odds ratio of 3.0 [5]. This yielded a minimum of approximately 55 cases and 110 controls. We enrolled 59 cases and 118 controls to allow for incomplete data. Data collection A structured questionnaire in Arabic was developed from published cholera case-control studies and WHO tools [3,6,7]. It was pre-tested on a small group of patients and community members otuside the study sample, and adjusted for clarity and cultural appropriateness. Trained interviewers, who were health workers with experience in epidemiological surveillance, administered the questionnaire face to face at the DTC (cases) or at the home (controls). Interviewers were not blinded to case status. For children, the primary caregiver answered the questions. The questionnaire covered: (i) sociodemographic characteristics (age, sex, education, household size, income, displacement status); (ii) exposure history in the three days before symptom onset for cases, and in the three days before interview for controls; (iii) travel outside Aden Province and visitors from outside the province in the preceding two weeks; (iv) contact with a peerson with diarrhoea; (v) food history, including meals eaten outside the home, consumption of raw vegetables, fruit, seafood, and khat (Catha edulis), and whether these were washed before consumption; (vi) water source (piped network, public tap, water trucking, protected or unprotected well, or bottled water), storage, and treatment; common-source water was defined as water obtained from a shared point used by multiple households; (vii) household hygiene and sanitation, including latrine type, handwashing practices, soap availability, and use of chlorine for water or surface disinfection; and (viii) receipt of oral cholera vaccine, although vaccination campaigns had not been condcuted in Aden at that time. Variables and definitions The outcome was cholera case status. Exposures were coded as binary variables, with the least risky category taken as reference. Continuous variables such as age and household size were categorised using clinically or programmatically meaningful cut-offs. Handwashing and soap use were self-reported, and soap presence was verified by observation where permitted. Data management and statistical analysis Data were double-entered into EpiData 3.1 and analysed with Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX) [8]. Descriptive statistics were used to summarise participant characteristics. Differences between cases and controls were assessed using the chi-square or Fisher's exact tesst for categorical variables and the Student t-test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, as appropriate. In bivariate analysis, crude odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using unconditional logistic regression. Variables with p<0.20 in bivariate analysis, together with those considered biologically relevant a priori, were considered for the multivariable model. We used backward stepwise elimination based on likelihood ratio tests, retaining variables with p<0.05, and adjusted for age group and sex regardless of significance. Collinearity was checked using variance inflation factors and correlation among exposures; where two variables were highly correlated (e.g. soap use and chlorine use), the one with greater plausibility was retained. Model fit was assessed using the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, and discrimination using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Adjusted ORs (aORs) with 95% CIs are reported. All tests were two-sided, wiith a significance leel of 0.05. Missing data were minimal (<5% for any variable) and a complete-case analysis was performed. Participation was voluntary, and confidentiality was maintained through anonymised coding. The global community is grappling with the far-reaching consequences of cholera, a debilitating gastrointestinal illness triggered by the ingestion of contaminated food or water harboring toxigenic strains of Vibrio cholerae, specifically serogroups O1 and O139. This disease poses a formidable challenge to worldwide health security, as it can rapidly progress from asymptomatic or mild infection to severe, life-threatening dehydration and hypovolaemic shock in approximately 5-10% of infected individuals, leading to mortality within a short timeframe if left untreated [1,2]. The substantial global burden of cholera is underscored by estimates suggesting that between 1.3 and 4.0 million cases and 21,000 to 143,000 fatalities occur annually, with the heaviest toll being borne by regions in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia [3]. The persistence of cholera in areas where access to safe water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) facilities is limited, as well as its emergence in areas affected by conflict, displacement, or natural disasters, which disrupt these essential services, highlights the stark inequities in global health [4,5]. Traditionally, the primary route of cholera transmission has been recognized as the faecal-oral pathway, facilitated by the consumption of contaminated water or food. numerous epidemiological investigations conducted across diverse environments have identified a consistent set of risk factors, including the consumption of untreated surface or communal water sources, the storage of water in uncovered or contaminated containers, inadequate hand hygiene practices, the consumption of food from informal vendors or at social gatherings, contact with a cholera patient within the household, and participation in funerals of cholera victims [6-9]. Conversely, various protective factors, such as the treatment of household water, the use of soap, and oral cholera vaccination, have been demonstrated to mitigate the risk of infection [10,11]. Nevertheless, the relative significance of these determinants can vary substantially depending on local ecological, cultural, and infrastructural contexts. For instance, specific dietary practices prevalent in certain regions, such as the consumption of raw produce or particular foods, may constitute additional, context-dependent vehicles of transmission that are not adequately addressed by generic prevention guidelines [12]. Consequently, case-control studies conducted during outbreaks remain indispensable for informing targeted interventions tailored to the local context. A compelling illustration of the devastating consequences of conflict and inadequate WASH infrastructure is the ongoing cholera epidemic in Yemen. Yemen has experienced intermittent cholera outbreaks, but the current epidemic is unprecedented in scale and severity. Following the escalation of armed conflict in 2015, the country's health, water, and sanitation systems underwent significant deterioration, creating a complex interplay of factors conducive to the rapid spread of cholera [13,14]. The initial reports of cholera cases emerged in October 2016, followed by a first wave, and then a much larger second wave commenced in April 2017. By 2018, the epidemic had resulted in over 1.4 million suspected cases and several thousand associated fatalities, rendering it the largest documented cholera outbreak in modern history [15]. Genomic analyses have revealed that the outbreak strain is closely related to isolates circulating in East Africa, belonging to the seventh pandemic El Tor lineage, suggesting an introduction from outside the country followed by sustained local transmission [16]. The drivers of this epidemic are multifaceted and complex. The conflict has inflicted significant damage on water treatment plants, pumping stations, and sewage networks, while fuel shortages have limited water pumping and waste disposal capabilities. Moreover, the crisis has been exacerbated by the cessation of services by unpaid public-sector workers, including health and sanitation staff [14,17]. The displacement of millions of people into crowded settings with limited WASH facilities, coupled with the high prevalence of malnutrition among Yemeni children, which increases their susceptibility to severe disease, has further contributed to the epidemic [17]. Under these challenging conditions, households are compelled to rely on alternative, potentially contaminated water sources, such as water trucks, shared tanks, and unprotected wells. Although health authorities and humanitarian partners have responded with case management through diarrhoea treatment centres and oral rehydration points, water chlorination, hygiene promotion, and targeted oral cholera vaccination in selected districts [15,18], the epidemic continues to unfold in successive waves. The present study is motivated by the need to understand the dynamics of cholera transmission within the specific context of Yemen. Several features of Yemeni society could influence exposure to cholera, including the widespread consumption of khat (Catha edulis), a leafy stimulant commonly chewed by a large proportion of the adult population. Khat is typically consumed fresh, often in social gatherings, and is cultivated using irrigation water of uncertain quality, handled by multiple intermediaries before being sold. The potential for khat to act as a vehicle for faecal-oral pathogens has received limited attention, and washing practices prior to consumption are inconsistent. Furthermore, population movement within and between governorates, as well as visits from relatives from affected areas, may facilitate the introduction of infection into new communities. Despite the magnitude of the epidemic, there is a scarcity of published analytical epidemiological evidence from Yemen, with most available information derived from surveillance reports that describe the distribution of suspected cases by time, place, and age, but fail to quantify the contribution of specific exposures [13,15]. The constraints imposed by security concerns, limited access, and an overburdened health system have hindered field investigations. Aden, the temporary capital and a major port city that has received large numbers of displaced persons and experienced repeated epidemic waves, presents a critical setting in which to examine risk factors. Its urban environment, characterized by a unique combination of factors, offers a valuable opportunity to investigate the complex interplay of variables contributing to the persistence of cholera. The coexistence of piped and non-piped water supply systems in many urban areas affected by conflict is a significant public health concern. To develop effective, evidence-based strategies for mitigating the spread of cholera, it is essential to identify the modifiable behavioural and environmental factors that contribute to the disease's transmission in these settings. This knowledge will enable the efficient allocation of limited resources, such as water chlorination initiatives, soap distribution, household water treatment products, and community-based hygiene education programs. In response to the ongoing cholera outbreak, our research team conducted a case-control study in Aden, Yemen, in 2018, with the objective of determining the risk factors associated with cholera infection. By examining the complex interplay of factors that facilitate the transmission of this disease, we aimed to inform the development of targeted interventions that can help reduce the impact of the epidemic and ultimately alleviate the burden of cholera in Yemen. Our study focused on understanding the demographic, travel, contact, food, water, and hygiene factors that contribute to the spread of cholera, with the goal of informing control measures and enhancing preparedness in regions vulnerable to outbreaks, particularly in fragile settings where conflict has compromised water, sanitation, and health infrastructure. The analysis of high-dimensional data is a central task in machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD). It is also notoriously difficult. Many algorithms degarde as the number of features grows: nearest-neighbor search loses its discriminative power, distance-based clustering bceomes unstable, and the sample sie needed for reliable estimation increases dramatically. These phenomena are collectively known as the curse of dimensionality. Their practical importance has led to a large body of literature that investigates their origins and consequences, using tools from statistics, computer science, and mathematics. A recurring obserrvation is that the nominal dimension of a data set, meaning the number of coordinates used to represent each point, is often a poor predictor of how hard the data are to analyze. Data may lie close to a low-dimensional manifold, may be strongly clustered, or may have rapidly decaiyng variance along most directions. Conversely, data in a low-dimensional ammbient space can exhibit behavior typicaal of high dimension. This motvates the notion of inntrinsic dimension: a quantity meant to capture the effective complexity of the data, independent of the particular representation. Numerous estimators have been proposed, among them PCA-based approaches, fractal and correlation dimensions, and nearest-neighbor-based maximum likelihood estimators. They are often useful in practice, but thye rest on different assumptions and are usually justified heuristically. They may give inconsistent answers on the sae data, and it is rarely clear which properties a reasonable notion of dimension shouuld satisfy. From a mathematical perspective, a particularly illuminating explanation of the dimenson curse is the concenrtation of measure phenomenon. In high-dimensional spaces such as spheres, cubes, or Gaussian spaces, every sufficiently regular function is almost constant on a set of nearly full measure. As a consequence, distances between random points concentrate around a typical value, and the contrast on which many ML algorithms rely vanishes. This link was recognized in the ML/KD literature, and it suggests that intrinsic dimension should be tied to concentration properties. Pestov developed this idea into an axiomatic approach: a dimension function for metric spaecs with measure should, among other requirements, assign the expected dimension to standard objects, behave monotonically under suitablle maps, and reflect the concentration phenomenon through a suitable observable diameter. Gromov's metric measure geometry supplies the framework for this, providing the notoins of observable diameter, concentration function, and the distance between metric measure spaces. Pestov's approach was developped for idealized objects, namely metic spaces with probability measures, whereas data sets are finite, may cary additional structure, and are analyzed by algorithms thhat use only certain features of that structure. The present work aims to bridge this gap. We introduce a model of a geometric datta set that combines a metric measure space, which describes the geometry and distribution of the data, with a family of functions, or features, which describes what a givven ML/KD algorithm can observe. This second ingredient makes the model adaptable: different algorithms, for instance those using onnly linear functionals, Lipshitz functions, or the outputs of a given class of classifiers, correspond to different feature classes and therefore to different notions of intrinsic dimension. We define isomorphism of geometric data sets and study the set of isomorphism classes. Our first main contribution is structural. We introduce a metric on the set of isomorphism classes, inspired by the Gromov–Wasserstein and box distances, which makes it possible to quantify how close two data sets are, including a finite samplle and the underlying distribution from which it is drawn. We also define a partial order, a form of domination, which expresses that one data set is a simplification of another, obtained through feature-preserving maps. We investigate the topological and order-theoretic properties of these objects, including compaibility between the order and the metric. Our second main contribution is an axiomaic treatment of intrinsic dimension for geometric data sets. Building on Pestov's axioms, we formulate requirements for a diemnsion function: monotonicity with respect to the partial order, continuity or stability with respect to the metric, normalization on reference examples, and consisetncy with measure concentration. We show that these requirements are mutually compatible by constructing a concrete dimmension function that satisies them. The function is defined through the concentration behavior of the faeture class, via a notion of separation or observable diameter, and we prove its basic properties, including its behavior under products and its relation to the classical notion of dimension on model spaces. Third, we address computational feasibility. A definition that cannot be evaluated on real data woulld be of limited value to the ML/KD community. We show that our dimension function can be estimated from finite samples and we describe algorithms for doing so. Experimennts on synthetic and real data sets illustrate that the resulting values reflect known intrinsic structure, that they respond sensibly to the choice of feature class, and that they correlae with the performance of specific algorithms, such as nearest-neighbor classification, on the data. The examination of complex, high-dimensional data is a fundamental challenge in the realms of machine learning (ML) and knowledge discovery (KD), posing significant difficulties. As the number of features or dimensions increases, the performance of many algorithms degrades substantially: the ability to distinguish between data points using nearest-neighbor search diminishes, clustering based on distance becomes less stable, and the required sample size for reliable estimation increases exponentially [1]. These challenges are collectively referred to as the curse of dimensionality, a phenomenon that has been extensively studied using tools from statistics, computer science, and mathematics due to its significant practical implications [2]. A common observation in the relevant literature is that the nominal dimension of a dataset, which is defined by the number of coordinates used to represent each data point, often fails to accurately predict the difficulty of analyzing the data [3]. For example, data may be situated close to a manifold of lower dimension, exhibit strong clustering, or display variance that decreases rapidly along most directions, making analysis easier than would be expected based on the nominal dimension [4]. Conversely, data in a space with a lower nominal dimension can exhibit characteristics typical of high-dimensional data, rendering analysis more challenging than anticipated [4]. This discrepancy highlights the importance of the concept of intrinsic dimension, a measure aimed at capturing the effective complexity of the data independently of its representation [5]. Several estimators have been proposed for determining the intrinsic dimension of a dataset, including approaches based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), fractal and correlation dimensions, and maximum likelihood estimators that utilize nearest-neighbor information [6]. Although these estimators are often useful in practice, they are based on different assumptions and are typically justified through heuristic arguments, which can lead to inconsistent results when applied to the same data [7]. Furthermore, it is often unclear what properties a sensible notion of dimension should possess, making the development of a rigorous and broadly applicable theory of intrinsic dimension challenging [8]. From a mathematical standpoint, the concentration of measure phenomenon provides a particularly insightful explanation for the curse of dimensionality [9]. Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, accounting for nearly one third of all deaths each year [1]. Epidemiological studies have consistently shown that premenopausal women have a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, hypertension, and heart failure than age-matched men, and that this relative protection diminishes after menopause [2,3]. The incidence of cardiovascular events in women rises sharply in the decade following the cessation of ovarian function, eventually approaching that of men [4]. These observations have led to the long-standing hypothesis thhat endogenous ovarian hormones, particularly 17β-estradiol (E2), confer protection against cardiac injury and adverse remodeling. E2 is the most abundant and biologically potent estrogen in premenopausal women. Beyond its classical roles in reproductive physiology, E2 exerts pleiotropic effects on the cardiovascular system, including vasodilation, modulation of lipid metabolism, attenuation of inflammation, and inhibition of vascular smooth muscle proliferation [5,6]. In the myocardium, experimental studies indicate that E2 reduces cardiomyocyte apoptosis, limits infarct size after ischemia-reperfusion injury, attenuates pathological hypertrophy, and preseves mitochondrial function [7-9]. Ovariectomy in animal models aggravatse cardiac dysfunction after pressure overload or myocardial infarction, and these deleterious effects are largely reversed by E2 supplementation [10,11]. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of E2 in maintaining cardiac homeostasis in women of reproductive age. The biological actions of E2 are mediated primarily through estrogen receptors (ERs). Three ER subtypes have been identified in cardiomyocytes: the classical nuclear receptors ERα and ERβ, and the membrane-associated G protein-coupled estrogen receptor GPR30 (also known as GPER) [12,13]. ERα and ERβ are ligand-activated transcription factors encoded by separate genes, and they share a conserved structure comprising a DNA-binding domain and a ligand-binding domain. Upon E2 binding, they dimerize and translocate to the nucleus, where they regulate the transcription of target genes by binding to estrogen response elements or by interacting with other transcription factros such as AP-1 and Sp1 (the genomic pathway) [14]. In addition, a subpopulation of ERα and ERβ localizes at the plasma membrane and in caveolae, where it rapidly activates kinase cascades, including PI3K/Akt, MAPK/ERK, and endothelial nitric oxide synthase signaling, within seconds to minutes (the nongenomic pathway) [15,16]. GPR30 further contributes to rapid estrogen signaling through the activation of adenylyl cyclase, transactivation of the epidermal growth faactor receptor, and mobilization of intracellular calcium [17]. The relative contribution of each receptor subtype to cardioprotection is context dependent, and accumulating evidence suggests that the receptors may act cooperatively or in a compensatory manner depending on the type of cardiac insult [18,19]. Given the apparent cardioprotective effects of E2, hormone replacement therapy (HRT) was initially promoted as a strategy for preventing CVD in postmenopausal women. Early observational studies supported this notion, reporting significant reductions in coronary events amnog HRT users [20]. However, large randomized controlld trials, notably the Heart and Estrogen/Progestin Replacement Study and the Women's Health Initiative, failed to demonstrate cardiovascular benefit and instead reported increased risks of thromboembolism, stroke, breast cancer, and endometrial cancer [21,22]. Subsequent analyses have proposed the "timing hypothesis," which suggests that the cardiovascular effects of estrogen depend on the age of the patient and the time elappsed since menopause, with benefit observed when therapy is initiated early [23]. Nevertheless, safety concerns, particularly regarding hormone-dependent malignancies, have substantially limited the clinical use of conventional estrogen therapy and stimulated the search for safer alternatives. Phytoestrogens are plant-derived polyphenolic compounds whose structures resemble that of E2 and which can bind to ERs, with a generally higher affinity for ERβ than for ERα [24]. The major classes include isoflavones (genistein, daidzein), lignans, coumestans, and stilbenes such as resveratrol, which are abundant in soybeans, flaxseed, legumes, and grapes [25]. Populations consuming diets rich in these compounds, such as those in East Asia, display a lower incidence of CVD and fewer menopausal symptoms than Western populations [26]. Experimental studies have shown that phytoestrogens can reduce oxidative stress, improve endothelial function, inhibit cardiomyocyte apoptosis, and attenuate cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis, in part through ER-dependent activation of PI3K/Akt and related survival pathways [27-29]. Because of their selective receptor binding and weaker estrogenic activity, phytoestrogens may behave as natural selective estrogen receptor modulators, potentially providing cardiovascular benefit with a reduced risk of adverse effects on the breast and uterus [30]. Clinical findings, however, remain inconsistent, reflecting variability in compounds, doses, study populations, and individual metabolism, such as the gut microbial conversion of daidzein to equol [31]. A better understanding of ER-mediated signaling in cardiomyocytes is therefore essential for the rational development of phytoestrogen-based therapies. In this review, we summarize current knowledge of estrogen and ER-mediated genomic and nongenomic pathways that underlie cardioprotection against diverse stresses. We further discuss the clinical implications of ERs and phytoestrogens and provide insights into the potential of phytoestrogens as alternatives in estrogen replacement therapy. Literature search strategy A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Google Scholar, and other electronic resources accessible through institutional library services. The search covered articles published from database inception to the date of final search. Boolean operatrs (AND, OR) were used to combine terms; for instance, "recurrent miscarriage AND thyroid" or "recurrent pregnancy loss AND (insulin resistannce OR diabetes)." The phenomenon of pregnancy loss is a pervasive and intricate issue that affects a substantial proportion of human pregnancies, exerting a profound impact on the physical and emotional welfare of those affected. The spontaneous termination of a pregnancy prior to the stage at which the fetus is capable of surviving outside the womb, referred to as miscarriage or spontaneous abortion, occurs in approximately 15-20% of pregnancies that have been clinically confirmed [1,2]. However, when biochemical pregnancies and losses that occur prior to clinical recognition are taken into account, the actual incidence of pregnancy loss is significantly higher, with estimates suggesting that up to 50% of all conceptions may fail to progress to a viable pregnancy [3]. The majority of isolated miscarriages can be attributed to random chromosomal anomalies in the embryo, which are unlikely to recur. Nevertheless, a subset of women experiences repeated pregnancy losses, a condition known as recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), recurrent miscarriage, or habitual abortion. Traditionally, RSA has been defined as the occurrence of three or more consecutive pregnancy losses prior to the twentieth week of gestation [4]. However, certain professional organizations, including the American Society for Reproductive Medicine and the European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology, have proposed a revised threshold of two or more losses as a criterion for initiating evaluation, acknowledging the substantial emotional toll and the clinical value of earlier investigation [5,6]. According to the traditional definition, RSA affects approximately 1% of couples attempting to conceive, whereas around 2-5% experience two or more losses [2,7]. The risk of subsequent miscarriage increases in conjunction with the number of previous losses and advancing maternal age, rendering a history of repeated loss an independent predictor of further pregnancy failure [8]. Beyond the physical risks, RSA is associated with considerable psychological distress, including anxiety, depression, and grief, as well as a significant burden on healthcare resources [9]. The etiology of RSA is multifaceted and, in many cases, remains incompletely understood. Established causes include parental chromosomal abnormalities, uterine anatomical defects such as septa, fibroids, and intrauterine adhesions, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome and other immunological disturbances, infections, thrombophilic states, environmental and lifestyle factors, and endocrine disorders [4,10]. Despite exhaustive evaluation, no underlying cause is identified in approximately half of couples, and this unexplained group continues to pose a significant diagnostic and therapeutic challenge [10]. Endocrine abnormalities are thought to account for roughly 8-12% of cases, making them one of the more common and potentially treatable contributors to RSA [11]. The successful implantation and maintenance of early pregnancy depend on a delicately coordinated hormonal environment. Following ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen, which transform the endometrium into a receptive decidua, suppress uterine contractility, and modulate the maternal immune response toward tolerance of the semi-allogeneic conceptus [12]. Thyroid hormones, insulin, prolactin, and androgens also influence follicular development, oocyte quality, endometrial receptivity, and placental function [13]. Disruption of any component of this regulatory network may compromise implantation, trophoblast invasion, or early embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss. Several endocrine conditions have been implicated in RSA, including polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrinopathy of reproductive-age women, characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and frequently insulin resistance and obesity, which has been associated with an increased risk of early miscarriage [14,15]. Hyperprolactinemia may impair folliculogenesis and corpus luteum function, and dopamine agonist treatment has been reported to improve pregnancy outcome in affected women [16]. Luteal phase defect, an inadequate progesterone-mediated endometrial secretory response, has long been proposed as a cause of implantation failure and early loss, although its diagnostic criteria and clinical significance remain debated [17]. Thyroid dysfunction, both overt and subclinical hypothyroidism as well as thyroid autoimmunity, has been linked to adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage [18,19]. Diabetes mellitus with poor glycemic control during the periconceptional period increases the risk of miscarriage and congenital malformations through metabolic disturbance of the developing embryo [20]. Hyperandrogenism, whether of ovarian or adrenal origin, may adversely affect endometrial receptivity and early placentation [21]. The relationship between these endocrine disorders and RSA is complex and not fully understood, with studies often yielding conflicting results due to differences in diagnostic criteria, sample sizes, and control populations [14]. It is essential to distinguish cause from association, as in the case of PCOS, where obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated luteinizing hormone may each contribute independently [14]. Likewise, the benefit of interventions such as progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists remains controversial in some settings [22,23]. The clinical significance of clarifying the role of endocrine dysfunction in RSA cannot be overstated. Many of these conditions are readily detectable and treatable, and appropriate screening and management could improve the live birth rate in affected couples. In this context, the present article provides a comprehensive review of the role of endocrine dysfunction in patients with recurrent spontaneous abortion. Relevant publications were identified through electronic databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, using key words related to recurrent miscarriage and specific endocrine abnormalities. The findings were then grouped according to the individual disorders, namely PCOS, hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defect, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism. The intricate relationships between these endocrine conditions and RSA are examined in detail, with a focus on the underlying mechanisms, diagnostic challenges, and potential therapeutic strategies. By elucidating the complex interplay between endocrine dysfunction and RSA, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the role of endocrine disorders in recurrent pregnancy loss, ultimately informing the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes for affected couples. The importance ofIFT analysis in the diagnosis of RSA is also highlighted, as well as the need for a multidisciplinary approach to the management of affected couples. Furthermore, the review discusses the potential benefits and limitations of various interventions, including progesterone supplementation, levothyroxine, metformin, and dopamine agonists, and emphasizes the need for further research to clarify their role in the management of RSA. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of the complex relationships between endocrine dysfunction and RSA is essential for the development of effective therapeutic strategies to improve outcomes for affected couples. By providing a comprehensive review of the current literature and highlighting areas for future research, this article aims to contribute to the ongoing efforts to improve our understanding of RSA and to develop effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches to manage this complex and multifaceted condition. Human pose estimation, the task of localizing the body joints of a person in an image or video, is a fundamental problem in computer vision with applications in action recognition, human-computer interaction, surveillance, and animation. Over the past few years, deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have dramatically advanced the accuracy of pose estimation on static images. Among the most successful designs are multi-stage architectures, such as Convolutional Pose Machines and stacked hourglass networks, in which a sequence of CNN stages progressively refines the joint confidence maps predicted by the preceding stage. Each stage takes the image evidence together with the previous belief maps and produces a more accuraet estimate, so that long-range dependencies among joints are implicitly captured through large effective receptive fields. Despite this success on still images, applying these models to vdeos remains unsatisfactory. The most direct approach is to run a single-image model independently on every frame. This has three main drawbacks. First, it is computationally expensive: a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, and the cost grows lineary with the number of stages. Second, frame-wise prediction ignores the temporal structure of video. Adjacent frammes show nearly the same pose, yet independent predictions are not constrained to agree, which produces jittering outputs and visible flicker. Third, video frames frequently suffer from motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints. A model that sees only one frame has no means of recovering from such degradation, whereas a human observer easily infers the hidden or blurred joint position from preceding frames. Together, these problems cause performance degeneration and make the predictions inconsistent over time. Previous attempts to address video pose estimation usually add post-processing or explicit tempporal modeling on top of single-frame networks. Examples include optical flow to propagate predictions between frames, graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness, and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames. These approaches typically require additional components, such as flow estimators, which are expensive and prone to error under exactly the conditions (blur, occlusion) where help is most needed. They also treat temporal reasoning as separate from the pose network itself, which complicates training and inference. In this paper, we propose a different view. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages: each stage applies the same transformation to the previous belief maps and the image features. Under this view, stage-wise refinement is simply a recurrent computation. This observation has two important consequences. First, it decouples the stages from one another. Rather than running every stage on every frame, the recurrence can be unrolled along the time axis of the video, so that eaach new frame needs only one pass through the shared module, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames. This yields a significant speedup when processing video. Second, the recurrent formulation allows us to insert Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units naturally, so that the refinement is performed across vido frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame. We call the resulting model the LSTM Pose Machine. It consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames. At each time step, the network receives the current frame, and the LSTM combines the current image evidence wth its memory of earlier frames and earlier predictions to output the joint confidence maps. The memory cells thus accumulate information about the pose and motion of the person over time. This imposes geometric consistency acrooss frames, because the prediction at one time step is conditioned on the state summarizing the past, and it improves robustness to degraded inputs, since information from clean frames can compensate for blurred or occluded ones. The whole system is trained end to end with supervision on every frame, without optical flow or any other external motion model. We evaluate our approach on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and show that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in accuracy while also being considerably faster than repeatedly invoking a multi-stage CNN on each frame. Qualitative results demonstrate that our predictions are visibly more stable and remain accurate under motion blur and occlusion. Beyond reporting performance, we also look inside the network and analyze the memory cells of the LSTM. Our analysis shows that different cells specialize in encoding information such as the motion direction of paritcular body parts and the spatial configuration of the joints, providing insight into why such a memory mechanism benefits pose estimation in video. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows. (1) We show that a multi-stage CNN with shared weights can be rewritten as an RNN, and exploit this to decouple the stages and greatly reduce the computation for video. (2) We introduce LSTM units between frames, yielding a model that enforces temporal and geoometric consistency and handles quality degradation. (3) We achieve state-of-the-art results on two large-scale video benchmarks. (4) We analyze the learned memory cells to explain the behavior of the model. The task of determining the precise location and orientation of a person's body joints within an image or video sequence, referred to as human pose estimation, poses a significant challenge in the realm of computer vision. This technology has far-reaching implications for various fields, including the recognition of actions, interaction between humans and computers, surveillance, and animation. In recent years, substantial progress has been made in enhancing the accuracy of pose estimation in static images, primarily attributed to the development of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) [1]. Among the most effective architectural designs are those that employ a multi-stage approach, such as Convolutional Pose Machines [2] and stacked hourglass networks [3], which iteratively refine the confidence maps of joints through a series of CNN stages. Each stage takes into consideration the visual evidence from the image, as well as the prior belief maps, to produce a more accurate estimate. This process enables the implicit capture of long-range dependencies between joints through the utilization of large effective receptive fields. However, the application of these models to video sequences has yielded less satisfactory results. The most straightforward approach to video pose estimation involves applying a single-image model independently to each frame, but this method has several significant drawbacks [4]. Firstly, it is computationally intensive, as a multi-stage network must be fully evaluated for each frame, resulting in a computational cost that increases linearly with the number of stages. Secondly, the frame-wise prediction approach neglects the temporal structure of the video, leading to independent predictions that are not constrained to be consistent, thereby resulting in jittering outputs and visible flicker. Furthermore, video frames often suffer from degradation due to motion blur, defocus, self-occlusion, and unusual viewpoints, all of which can cause a model that only considers one frame to struggle with recovering from such degradation. In contrast, human observers can easily infer the position of hidden or blurred joints from preceding frames. Previous attempts to address the challenge of video pose estimation have typically involved incorporating post-processing techniques or explicit temporal modeling on top of single-frame networks [5]. Examples of such approaches include the use of optical flow to propagate predictions between frames [6], graphical models or tracking-by-detection frameworks that enforce smoothness [7], and spatio-temporal convolutions over stacked frames [8]. However, these approaches often require additional components, such as flow estimators, which can be computationally expensive and prone to error under the exact conditions (e.g., blur, occlusion) where they are most needed. Moreover, these methods treat temporal reasoning as a separate entity from the pose network itself, which can complicate both the training and inference processes. In this paper, we propose a novel perspective on this problem. We observe that if the weights of the stages in a multi-stage CNN are shared, the network becomes equivalent to a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) unrolled over stages [9]. Each stage applies the same transformation to the prior belief maps and the image features, effectively rendering the stage-wise refinement a recurrent computation. This observation has two important implications. Firstly, it decouples the stages from one another, allowing us to unroll the recurrence along the temporal axis of the video. As a result, each new frame only needs to pass through the shared module once, with the refinement carried over from earlier frames, yielding a significant speedup when processing video. Secondly, the recurrent formulation enables us to naturally integrate Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) units [10], so that the refinement is performed across video frames instead of across redundant stages of a single frame. We refer to the resulting model as the LSTM Pose Machine, which consists of a fully convolutional feature extractor, an initial prediction module, and a recurrent refinement module with convolutional LSTM units whose parameters are shared across all frames. At each time step, the network receives the current frame, and the LSTM combines the current visual evidence with its memory of earlier frames and earlier predictions to output the joint confidence maps. The memory cells accumulate information about the pose and motion of the person over time, imposing geometric consistency across frames and improving robustness to degraded inputs. The entire system is trained end-to-end with supervision on every frame, without the need for optical flow or any other external motion model [11]. We evaluate our approach on two large-scale video pose estimation benchmarks and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, while also being considerably faster than repeatedly invoking a multi-stage CNN on each frame [12]. Qualitative results show that our predictions are visibly more stable and remain accurate under motion blur and occlusion. Beyond reporting performance, we also analyze the memory cells of the LSTM to gain insight into why such a memory mechanism benefits pose estimation in video [13]. Our analysis reveals that different cells specialize in encoding information such as the motion direction of particular body parts and the spatial configuration of the joints, providing a deeper understanding of the strengths of our approach and highlighting the potential of recurrent neural networks for modeling temporal dependencies. The key to our approach lies in the ability of the LSTM to capture and exploit the temporal structure of the video, allowing for more accurate and robust pose estimation. By leveraging the recurrent nature of the LSTM, we can effectively model the temporal relationships between frames and improve the overall performance of the pose estimation system. Furthermore, the use of convolutional LSTM units enables us to capture spatial and temporal dependencies simultaneously, resulting in a more comprehensive understanding of the pose and motion of the person in the video. The implications of our approach extend beyond the realm of pose estimation, as it demonstrates the potential of recurrent neural networks for modeling complex temporal dependencies in a variety of applications. In conclusion, our proposed approach, the LSTM Pose Machine, offers a novel and effective solution for video pose estimation, leveraging the strengths of recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance and robustness. The processing of video data has been a long-standing challenge in the field of computer vision, with applications in various domains such as surveillance, animation, human-computer interaction, and action recognition. A key aspect of video analysis is pose estimation, which involves identifying the spatial configuration of a person or object in a sequence of images. Recently, significant advances have been made in this area, particularly with the introduction of deep learning-based methods. This paper presents a comprehensive overview of our research, which explores the application of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to pose estimation in video data. Our contributions are multifaceted and can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we demonstrate the equivalence between a multi-stage convolutional neural network (CNN) with shared weights and an RNN, allowing us to exploit this relationship to enhance the efficiency of video data processing. Secondly, we propose a novel architecture, termed the LSTM Pose Machine, which leverages the capabilities of long short-term memory (LSTM) networks to model temporal dependencies and improve pose estimation accuracy in video sequences. Thirdly, we provide an in-depth analysis of the LSTM's memory cells, shedding light on the underlying mechanisms that enable our approach to achieve state-of-the-art performance in video pose estimation [14]. The significance of our work lies in its potential to facilitate the development of more accurate and efficient pose estimation systems, which can be applied to a wide range of fields. For instance, the LSTM Pose Machine has been shown to be effective in scenarios where the video data is corrupted by noise or where the pose of the person is partially occluded [14]. The ability of the LSTM to accumulate information over time and enforce geometric consistency across frames is particularly valuable in such cases. Furthermore, the use of convolutional LSTM units enables the model to capture spatial dependencies in the data, which is essential for accurate pose estimation. In addition to its technical contributions, our work highlights the importance of considering the temporal structure of video data when designing pose estimation systems. By harnessing the strengths of RNNs, we can capture temporal dependencies and improve pose estimation accuracy in video. This has significant implications for the development of more accurate and efficient pose estimation systems, and we believe that our approach will be of interest to researchers and practitioners working in this field. Moreover, the application of RNNs to pose estimation in video is a relatively new area of research, and there are many opportunities for further development and improvement [15]. One potential direction for future work is the development of more advanced recurrent architectures, such as those that employ attention mechanisms or graph convolutional networks. Another potential direction is the application of our approach to other tasks, such as action recognition or object tracking. The devastating consequences of dementia, a complex neurodegenerative disorder, are becoming increasingly evident as the global population ages, with Alzheimer's disease (AD) being the primary cause of this debilitating condition [1]. Despite extensive research spanning several decades, the current therapeutic options for AD are predominantly focused on alleviating symptoms, rather than halting the progression of the disease [2]. The most commonly prescribed medications, including acetylcholinesterase inhibitors such as donepezil, rivastigmine, and galantamine, as well as the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist memantine, often have limited efficacy and are plagued by adverse effects, including gastrointestinal and cardiovascular complications [3]. Consequently, there is a growing interest in exploring safer, naturally derived compounds that can potentially prevent or delay cognitive decline. The cholinergic system plays a pivotal role in regulating learning and memory, and disruptions to this system, particularly in the hippocampus and cortex, are a hallmark of AD [4]. The muscarinic receptor antagonist scopolamine has been shown to induce transient amnesia in both rodents and humans, while also increasing oxidative stress in the brain by promoting lipid peroxidation and diminishing the activity of endogenous antioxidant enzymes [5, 6]. As a result, the scopolamine-induced amnesia model has become a widely accepted paradigm for screening compounds with potential cognitive-enhancing properties [7]. Behavioral assessments, including the Morris water maze, which evaluates spatial learning and memory, and the passive avoidance test, which assesses associative fear memory, are commonly employed to evaluate memory function in this model [8]. At the molecular level, the formation of memories is contingent upon the activation of signaling cascades in the hippocampus, including the extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) pathway, which culminates in the phosphorylation of the cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB), a transcription factor that regulates the expression of genes involved in synaptic plasticity and neuronal survival [9]. One of the primary targets of CREB is brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which supports neuronal growth, differentiation, and long-term potentiation [10]. Notably, reduced levels of p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF have been observed in AD brains and in scopolamine-treated animals, and oxidative stress has been shown to impair this pathway [11]. Antioxidants that mitigate oxidative damage may therefore preserve ERK-CREB-BDNF signaling and protect cognitive function [12]. Spirulina, a filamentous cyanobacterium, has been consumed as a food and dietary supplement for centuries, and is renowned for its exceptional nutritional profile, including high levels of protein, essential fatty acids, vitamins, minerals, and pigments such as phycocyanin, chlorophyll, and carotenoids [13, 14]. Extracts of Spirulina have been reported to exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and neuroprotective effects [15]. Among its constituents, β-carotene is one of the most abundant and well-characterized antioxidants, and epidemiological and experimental studies suggest that carotenoids may be associated with reduced cognitive decline, owing to their ability to quench singlet oxygen and scavenge free radicals [16, 17]. However, direct evidence demonstrating the ability of β-carotene to improve memory in animal models of dementia is scarce, and its contribution to the bioactivity of Spirulina remains unclear [18]. Fermentation with lactic acid bacteria is a traditional and safe bioprocess that can enhance the functional properties of food materials, including the degradation of cell walls and macromolecules, the release of bound phenolics and pigments, and the production of new metabolites such as peptides and organic acids, ultimately increasing bioavailability and bioactivity [19, 20]. Fermented plant and algal materials have been shown to exhibit stronger antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective activities than their unfermented counterparts [21]. Spirulina's rigid cell wall composition and strong characteristic odor limit its use in foods, and fermentation could potentially improve both its sensory qualities and functional value [22]. Lactobacillus plantarum strains are widely used for fermentation purposes due to their robust growth, generally recognized as safe status, and beneficial metabolic capacity [23]. Some L. plantarum strains have been reported to influence brain function through the gut-brain axis, suggesting that fermentation with these organisms may offer additional benefits [24]. Nevertheless, the effect of fermented S. maxima extract on memory impairment has not been investigated. In a previous screening, we found that S. maxima extract fermented with L. plantarum HY-08 exhibited enhanced antioxidant properties and an increased content of bioactive components compared with the unfermented extract [25]. These observations led us to hypothesize that the fermented extract could mitigate cognitive deficits by reducing oxidative stress and activating neurotrophic signaling in the hippocampus. As the practical application of a functional food ingredient depends on both dose efficiency and efficacy, determining a dose that provides substantial benefits at a reasonable cost is also crucial [26]. The objectives of this study were therefore to (i) evaluate the cognitive-enhancing effect of the fermented S. maxima extract in scopolamine-treated mice using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, with donepezil as a positive control; (ii) compare the effects of different doses to identify an economically feasible dose; (iii) examine whether β-carotene, a major bioactive component of S. maxima, has memory-enhancing activity; and (iv) clarify the underlying mechanism by which the fermented extract exerts its cognitive-enhancing effects. Through a comprehensive examination of oxidative stress indicators and the expression of key proteins, including p-ERK, p-CREB, and BDNF, in the hippocampal region [27], the potential of fermented Spirulina as a functional food material for the prevention of memory impairment and dementia can be elucidated. To initiate this investigation, Spirulina maxima powder was first dispersed in distilled water to create a homogeneous mixture, which was then subjected to fermentation by Lactobacillus plantarum HY-08, resulting in the production of a fermented extract [28]. Subsequently, the extract was administered to mice treated with scopolamine at various doses to assess its potential cognitive-enhancing properties [29]. The efficacy of the extract in improving memory function was evaluated using the Morris water maze and passive avoidance tests, with the results compared to those obtained with donepezil, a well-established cognitive enhancer [30]. For a select group of individuals with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy, surgical intervention, specifically resection or ablation of the epileptogenic zone (EZ), offers the most effective treatment option, but its success hinges on the precise identification of the brain regions responsible for seizure generation [3]. In situations where non-invasive diagnostic techniques, including scalp EEG, video monitoring, MRI, PET, and MEG, fail to provide a clear localization of the seizure onset zone, invasive recordings become necessary to determine the exact location of the seizure onset zone. The utilization of stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) has been a cornerstone in the diagnosis and treatment of epilepsy since its introduction by Talairach and Bancaud in the 1950s [4]. This technique involves the stereotactic implantation of multiple depth electrodes, each equipped with several contacts, to sample cortical and subcortical structures in three dimensions. SEEG offers several advantages over subdural grids, including access to deep and sulcal structures, the ability to explore bilateral regions without requiring a craniotomy, and a lower risk of complications [5,6]. Furthermore, SEEG is increasingly being applied in the fields of cognitive and systems neuroscience, where intracranial recordings provide unparalleled spatial and temporal resolution in human subjects [7]. However, the clinical utility of SEEG is contingent upon accurately determining which anatomical structure each contact records from, as electrophysiological data can only be interpreted and used to plan a resection if contact positions are expressed in the patient's anatomical space and, for group studies, in a common reference space [8]. Typically, the trajectories of the electrodes are planned using pre-implant MRI, and the implantation procedure is performed with the aid of a stereotactic frame or robotic assistance. Following implantation, a post-implant CT or Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) is acquired to verify the final positions of the electrodes. Nevertheless, due to factors such as bending of the electrode shaft, brain shift, and inaccuracies in the entry point or insertion depth, the final position of the electrodes often deviates from the planned coordinates [9,10]. Consequently, the planned coordinates cannot be used in place of the true contact locations, which must be recovered from the post-implant image. This process is crucial for accurate SEEG interpretation, as incorrect contact localization can lead to misidentification of the seizure onset zone and suboptimal treatment outcomes. Currently, contact localization is performed using manual or semi-manual procedures, where the post-implant CT is co-registered with the pre-implant MRI, and contacts are identified one by one using 3D visualization tools. This process is time-consuming, requiring several hours per patient, and is susceptible to variability between and within raters. A single implant can comprise 10-20 electrodes and 100-200 contacts, making this task labor-intensive and prone to errors. Related approaches have been developed for deep brain stimulation (DBS) lead reconstruction [15,16] and for subdural grids [17]. However, DBS leads are typically fewer in number, have a distinct geometry, and are usually isolated in space, whereas SEEG implants involve multiple closely spaced electrodes, often crossing or running in proximity, and with variable numbers of contacts. To our knowledge, no fully automatic method has been proposed that leverages the characteristics of SEEG implants to segment contacts without manual intervention. Video captioning is the task of automatically generating a natural language description of a short video clip. It sits at the intersection of computer vision and natural language processing, and it supports applications such as video retrieval, assistive technology for visually impaired users, and human-robot interaction. Compraed with image captioning, the task is harder because a model must capture temporal dynamics, recognize actions and events, and compose them into a fluent sentence. Recent progress has been driven largely by sequence-to-sequence architectures, which encode a sequence of frame-level or clip-level visual features with a recurrent network and decode a caption word by word [Venugopalan et al., 2015; Yao et al., 2015; Pan et al., 2016]. Attention mechanisms and richer multimodal features have further improved such systems. Despite this progress, standard training procedures have a notable limitation. Nearly all captioning models are trained to minimize word-level cross-entropy loss, in which the decoder is conditioned on the ground-truth previous word at each step. This creates two well-documented problems. The firts is exposure bias [Ranzato et al., 2016]: at test time the model must condition on its own, possibly erroneous, predictions, a distribution it never encountered during training. The second is a mismatch between the training objective and the evaluation criteria. Because these metrics are non-differentiable, they cannot be used as losses in ordinary gradient-based training. Reinforcement learning for sentence-level metrics. A natural remedy is to cast caption generation as a sequential deecision problem and apply reinforcement learning, treating the decoder as a stochastic policy and the evaluation metric as a reward. Policy gradient methods such as REINFORCE [Williams, 1992] have been used for this purpose in image captioning, machine translation, and summarization [Ranzato et al., 2016; Rennie et al., 2017; Paulus et al., 2018]. In the first part of this work, we apply policy gradient training to video captioning and directly optimize task-based metrics. We also study a mixed-loss formulation that combines the reinforcement objective with the cross-entropy loss, which stabilizes training and keeps the generated sentences fluent.
