The fungal infection cryptococcosis poses a significant threat to human life, as it is caused by the pathogenic yeasts of the Cryptococcus neoformans/Cryptococcus gattii species complex, which can be lethal if left untreated [1,2]. Upon inhalation of desiccated yeast cells or spores, a primary site of infection is established in the lungs, and in individuals with compromised immune systems, the fungus can disseminate through the bloodstream to the central nervous system, resulting in a severe inflammatory response known as meningoencephalitis [3]. With approximately one million reported cases worldwide each year, cryptococcosis is a major public health concern, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where the mortality rate is alarmingly high [4]. Historically, Cryptococcus neoformans has been viewed as an opportunistic pathogen that primarily affects individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, whereas Cryptococcus gattii has been associated with disease in individuals who appear to be immunocompetent [5,6]. However, recent studies have led to a significant shift in our understanding of the epidemiology and population structure of C. gattii. Initially, C. gattii was thought to be confined to tropical and subtropical regions, where it was often found in association with Eucalyptus species [7]. Nevertheless, this perspective changed dramatically after the outbreak on Vancouver Island, British Columbia, in 1999, which subsequently spread to the mainland of Canada and the Pacific Northwest region of the United States [8,9]. The outbreak was dominated by the molecular type VGII, including the highly virulent VGIIa/b genotypes, which sparked a surge of interest in the underlying mechanisms that contribute to the enhanced virulence of these strains, such as the unique tubular morphology of their mitochondria, their ability to proliferate rapidly within macrophages, and their capacity to modulate the host immune response [10,11]. Based on molecular typing, C. gattii can be classified into four major categories, designated VGI to VGIV [12], and recent genomic analyses have suggested that these lineages may represent distinct, yet cryptic, species [13]. Notably, both capsular serotypes B and C are found in C. gattii, with serotype B encompassing types VGI, VGII, and VGIII, and serotype C corresponding primarily to types VGIII and VGIV [12]. Interestingly, VGIV is the most frequently encountered type in HIV-infected patients in sub-Saharan Africa, while VGIII has been detected in both clinical and environmental samples from Latin America and in HIV-positive patients in California [14,15]. Despite the significant clinical relevance of these molecular types, the vast majority of experimental studies have focused on serotype B isolates, particularly VGI and VGII, leaving a substantial knowledge gap in our understanding of the pathogenic properties of serotype C strains. This gap in our knowledge is particularly concerning, as elucidating the virulence determinants of C. gattii is essential for the development of effective treatment strategies and improving patient outcomes. The pathogenic potential of Cryptococcus species is dependent on several well-characterized virulence factors, including the polysaccharide capsule, which is composed primarily of glucuronoxylomannan (GXM) and glucuronoxylomannogalactan (GXMGal) [16,17]. The capsule is the primary determinant of virulence, as it inhibits phagocytosis, modulates cytokine responses, and protects the fungus against oxidative stress. The synthesis of the capsule requires the products of the CAP genes, including CAP10, CAP59, CAP60, and CAP64, and the deletion of these genes results in the formation of acapsular, avirulent mutants [18]. The size and structure of the capsule are highly variable among isolates and are regulated by environmental conditions, and differences in GXM structure can affect recognition by monoclonal antibodies and the host immune response [19,20]. In addition to the capsule, melanin, which is produced through the laccase-mediated oxidation of diphenolic compounds, plays a crucial role in protecting fungal cells against oxidative and nitrosative damage, antifungal drugs, and host effector mechanisms [21]. Other essential factors that contribute to the virulence of Cryptococcus species include chitin and chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule, which are involved in cell integrity, capsule architecture, and the interaction with host chitinases, and have been linked to the modulation of immune responses and disease susceptibility [22,23]. Furthermore, extracellular enzymes, such as urease and phospholipase, and the ability to grow at 37 °C, are also critical for the survival and dissemination of the fungus within the host [3,24]. Phenotypic variability in these traits among isolates of the same species has been correlated with differences in virulence in animal models [25,26]. In the case of C. gattii, the hypervirulence of VGII strains has been attributed to their capacity to proliferate rapidly in lung tissue and evade immune surveillance [10,27]. However, whether similar mechanisms operate in serotype C isolates, or whether the VGIII and VGIV lineages differ in their virulence profiles, remains unknown. Some studies have suggested that VGIII and VGIV isolates are generally less virulent in mice than VGII isolates [28,29], but these findings are based on a limited number of strains, and a systematic comparison of the phenotypic attributes and virulence of these lineages is lacking. Given the significant clinical importance of VGIV in Africa and VGIII in the Americas, and the scarcity of experimental data on these lineages, a comprehensive analysis of the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates is necessary. Elucidating how variation in capsule properties, cell wall composition, pigment production, and antigenic structure translates into differences in virulence may provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of infections caused by these molecular types and the factors that determine tissue tropism, particularly the ability to colonize the central nervous system. In the present study, we conducted a comparative analysis of three serotype C C. gattii isolates, including one VGIII (ATCC 24066) and two VGIV (WM 779 and 106.97) isolates, with respect to capsule dimensions, expression of CAP genes, chitooligomer distribution, induction of host chitinase activity, pigment production, and reactivity to various stimuli. By examining the phenotypic diversity of these isolates, we aim to contribute to a deeper understanding of the pathogenic properties of serotype C C. gattii and the factors that influence their virulence, ultimately informing the development of effective treatment strategies for cryptococcosis. The study of the pathogenic mechanisms of C. gattii is a complex and multifaceted field, and further research is needed to fully elucidate the virulence determinants of this fungus. Nevertheless, by exploring the phenotypic diversity of serotype C isolates, we can gain a better understanding of the factors that contribute to the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis and develop more effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this devastating disease. Ultimately, the goal of this research is to improve our understanding of the complex interactions between the host and the fungus, and to develop novel therapeutic approaches that can effectively target the virulence factors of C. gattii. By achieving this goal, we can hope to reduce the burden of cryptococcosis on public health and improve the outcomes of patients infected with this fungus. The importance of this research cannot be overstated, as cryptococcosis remains a major public health concern, particularly in regions with limited resources and high HIV prevalence. By advancing our knowledge of the pathogenic mechanisms of C. gattii, we can develop more effective strategies for the prevention and treatment of this disease, and ultimately improve the lives of millions of people worldwide. Cryptococcus gattii is a highly pathogenic fungus that causes severe disease in humans, particularly those with compromised immune systems. To better understand the virulence mechanisms of this fungus, we undertook a comprehensive study of serotype C isolates, which are known to exhibit distinct molecular types. Specifically, we investigated the phenotypic characteristics and virulence potential of three serotype C isolates, including their growth rates, capsule sizes, melanin production, and reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies [1]. We also assessed the expression of CAP genes, which are involved in capsule formation, and the distribution of chitooligomers in the cell wall and capsule. Our findings provide valuable insights into the pathogenic potential of serotype C isolates and their ability to cause disease in mammalian hosts. To initiate our study, we characterized the three serotype C isolates, namely 106.97 (molecular type VGIV), WM 779 (VGIV), and ATCC 24066 (VGIII), which were previously distinguished through URA5-RFLP analysis [1]. We cultured these isolates under standard laboratory conditions to evaluate their growth rates, capsule sizes, and melanin production. The isolates were stored at −80 °C in a 20% glycerol solution to maintain their viability and were revived on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 30 °C as needed. We then cultured the yeast cells in Sabouraud broth for 24 hours at 30 °C with constant shaking at 200 rpm, followed by washing in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and quantification using a Neubauer chamber. To induce capsule formation, we cultured the cells in a minimal medium consisting of 15 mM glucose, 10 mM MgSO₄, 29.4 mM KH₂PO₄, 13 mM glycine, and 3 µM thiamine, with a pH of 5.5, for 48 hours at 37 °C, as previously described [2]. We employed a counterstaining technique with India ink to assess the capsule thickness, which was defined as the distance between the cell wall and the outer edge of the India ink exclusion zone. Using ImageJ software, we measured the cell body diameter and capsule thickness in at least 50 cells per isolate, allowing us to calculate the capsule-to-cell ratio as the capsule thickness divided by the cell body radius. We also examined the expression of genes associated with capsule formation, including CAP10, CAP59, CAP60, and CAP64. To do this, we extracted total RNA from yeast cells grown in minimal medium using a mechanical disruption/TRIzol protocol, treated the RNA with DNase I, and then synthesized cDNA using oligo(dT) primers and reverse transcriptase. Quantitative PCR with SYBR Green was performed to quantify the transcript levels of these genes, normalizing them to the housekeeping gene ACT1 and expressing them relative to isolate ATCC 24066 using the 2^−ΔΔCt method [3]. This analysis was conducted in technical duplicate across three independent biological replicates. Furthermore, we investigated the distribution of chitooligomers and chitin staining in the cells. We detected chitooligomers by incubating fixed cells with wheat germ agglutinin conjugated to fluorescein isothiocyanate (WGA-FITC) at a concentration of 10 µg/mL for 1 hour at 37 °C, as previously described [4]. Following incubation, we washed the cells, mounted them, and imaged them using fluorescence microscopy. We qualitatively scored the fluorescence patterns, including signals at budding sites, the cell body, and the capsule, in at least 100 cells per isolate. Additionally, we quantified the fluorescence intensity using ImageJ software. To assess melanin production, we spotted 10^6 cells onto minimal medium agar containing 1 mM L-DOPA and incubated them at 30 °C and 37 °C in the dark for up to 7 days. We documented the pigmentation and measured the melanin content using a spectrophotometric assay. We also evaluated the ability of the isolates to induce host chitinase activity and their reactivity with GXM-binding monoclonal antibodies. These experiments provided a comprehensive understanding of the phenotypic characteristics of the serotype C isolates and laid the foundation for the subsequent virulence studies. The virulence of the serotype C isolates was evaluated in a murine model of intranasal infection. Mice were infected with each of the three isolates, and their survival rates, fungal burdens in the lungs and brain, and immune responses were monitored. The results of these experiments will provide valuable insights into the pathogenic potential of serotype C isolates and their ability to cause disease in mammalian hosts. By comparing the virulence of VGIII and VGIV isolates, we can determine whether these molecular types differ in their ability to infect and colonize the central nervous system, and whether they exhibit distinct virulence profiles. In conclusion, the study of serotype C C. gattii isolates is essential for understanding the pathogenesis of cryptococcosis and for developing effective treatment strategies. By characterizing the phenotypic diversity of these isolates and evaluating their virulence in a murine model, we can gain insights into the mechanisms underlying the enhanced virulence of certain molecular types and identify potential targets for therapeutic intervention. The results of this study will contribute to a better understanding of the biology of C. gattii and will have significant implications for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention

Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the most common life-limiting genetic disease among African Americans, affecting more than 100,000 people in the United States and millions worldwide [1,2]. It results from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene that produces hemoglobin S. Under deoxygenated conditions, hemoglobin S polymerizes, causing red blood cell rigidity, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. Beyond these primary events, chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive multi-organ injury [3,4]. Although advances in newborn screening, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy have substantially improved survival in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality across the lifespan [5,6]. Pulmonary disease in SCD encompasses a broad spectrum of acute and chronic conditions, including acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, defined by a new pulmonary infiltrate accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is the second most common cause of hospitalization and a leading cause of death among patients with SCD [9]. Recurrent ACS is itself associated with the development of chronic lung disease, creating a cycle of progressive pulmonary injury [10]. Understanding modifiable risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is therefore a priority. Asthma has long been recognized as one of these potential risk factors. Early observational studies described an association between asthma and ACS, pianful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11–13]. In the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease, children with a physician diagnosis of asthma experienced a higheer incidence of ACS and pain episodes than those without, and asthma was associated wth an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although results have not been uniform, and the strength of associations varies with how asthma is defined [14,15]. The mechanisms linking asthma to SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may include airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction-induced hypoxia, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17]. More recently, attention has turned to wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a possible marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts deemonstrate tht wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may reflect a distinct SCD-related phenotype, rather than simply representing coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheeze in SCD may arise from multiple processes, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20]. Establishing a diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is therefore challenging. According to national and international guidelines, asthma is diagnosed on the basis of a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheeze, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, together with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. In SCD, however, several of these features are highly prevalent and frequently occur in isolation. Wheezing has been reported in up to approximately 30–50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including many without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is likewise frequent, even among patients with no history of wheeze [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain pooryl defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to more than 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30]. This diagnostic ambiguity has practical consequences. Underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, whereas overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence: patients with SCD have been largelly excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. Whether biologic therapiies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea alter airway outcomes also remains unknown. Given these gaps, a critical appraisal of current knowledge is warranted. The global prevalence of sickle cell disease (SCD), a genetic disorder affecting millions worldwide, including over 100,000 individuals in the United States, underscores the need for continued research into its pathophysiology and clinical manifestations [1,2]. The condition arises from a single nucleotide substitution in the β-globin gene, leading to the production of abnormal hemoglobin, which polymerizes under deoxygenated conditions, resulting in red blood cell dysfunction, hemolysis, and vaso-occlusion. However, the repercussions of SCD extend far beyond these initial events, as the cumulative effects of chronic hemolysis, endothelial dysfunction, and persistent inflammation contribute to progressive injury in multiple organs [3,4]. Despite significant advancements in early detection and therapeutic interventions, including newborn screening, prophylactic antibiotics, vaccination, and hydroxyurea therapy, which have substantially improved survival rates in childhood, pulmonary complications remain a major contributor to morbidity and mortality across the lifespan of individuals with SCD [5,6]. The spectrum of pulmonary disease in SCD is broad, encompassing acute and chronic conditions such as acute chest syndrome (ACS), pulmonary hypertension, restrictive lung disease, nocturnal hypoxemia, thromboembolic disease, and obstructive airway disease [7,8]. ACS, characterized by new pulmonary infiltrates accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, or hypoxemia, is a leading cause of hospitalization and mortality among patients with SCD, with recurrent episodes contributing to the development of chronic lung disease [9,10]. Understanding the risk factors for ACS and other pulmonary complications is essential for developing effective management strategies. One potential risk factor that has been recognized is asthma, with early observational studies highlighting an association between asthma and increased incidence of ACS, painful vaso-occlusive episodes, and early mortality in SCD [11-13]. For instance, the Cooperative Study of Sickle Cell Disease found that individuals with a physician-diagnosed asthma experienced higher rates of ACS and pain episodes, with asthma also being associated with an increased risk of early death in adults [11,12]. Subsequent studies have supported these findings, although the results have been inconsistent, and the strength of associations varies depending on the definition of asthma used [14,15]. The mechanisms underlying the link between asthma and SCD complications are not fully elucidated but may involve airway inflammation, hypoxia resulting from bronchoconstriction, ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and systemic inflammatory amplification that promotes sickling and vascular adhesion [16,17]. More recently, attention has focused on wheezing, even in the absence of a formal asthma diagnosis, as a potential marker of disease severity in SCD. Longitudinal data from infant and childhood cohorts demonstrate that wheezing is common in young children with SCD and is associated with higher rates of ACS, pain, and hospitalization [18,19]. These observations suggest that wheezing may represent a distinct phenotype in SCD, rather than simply indicating coexisting atopic asthma. Indeed, wheezing in SCD may arise from multiple factors, including pulmonary vascular congestion, fat or thromboembolism, prior pulmonary infarction, infection, and airway hyperresponsiveness, in addition to classic allergic airway inflammation [20]. Diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the overlap of symptoms and physiologic abnormalities. According to established guidelines, asthma is diagnosed based on a history of recurrent respiratory symptoms such as wheezing, cough, chest tightness, and dyspnea, combined with objective evidence of variable airflow obstruction that is typically reversible with bronchodilators [21,22]. However, in SCD, these features are highly prevalent and often occur in isolation, complicating diagnosis. Wheezing has been reported in up to 30-50% of children with SCD, exceeding the prevalence in the general African American population [18,23]. Obstructive patterns on spirometry are common, yet many patients also display restrictive physiology or mixed defects, further complicating interpretation [24,25]. Airway hyperresponsiveness, measured by methacholine or exercise challenge, has been described in a substantial proportion of children with SCD, including those without clinical asthma [26,27]. Bronchodilator responsiveness is also frequent, even among patients without a history of wheezing [28]. Consequently, the relationships among symptoms, physiologic abnormalities, and clinical asthma remain poorly defined, and the true prevalence of asthma in SCD is uncertain, with estimates ranging from approximately 10% to over 40% depending on the definition and population studied [29,30]. This diagnostic ambiguity has significant practical implications, as underdiagnosis may deprive patients of effective controller therapy, while overdiagnosis may expose them to unnecessary medications and divert attention from other treatable causes of respiratory symptoms. Management is further complicated by limited evidence, as patients with SCD have been largely excluded from asthma clinical trials, and recommendations rely heavily on extrapolation from the general population [31]. Particular concerns include the potential risks of systemic corticosteroids, which have been associated with rebound pain crises and readmission in SCD, and the uncertain role of β-agonists and other asthma therapies in this population [32,33]. The impact of biologic therapies or disease-modifying treatments such as hydroxyurea on airway outcomes also remains unknown. Given these knowledge gaps, a comprehensive review of current understanding is warranted. This review aims to provide a detailed examination of the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway responsiveness among patients with SCD, as well as the evidence supporting associations between these features and SCD morbidity, highlighting the need for further research into the complex relationships between SCD and respiratory complications [1-33]. The intricate relationship between sickle cell disease (SCD) and asthma is a pressing concern, warranting a comprehensive examination of the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms and the complexities of diagnosing and managing asthma in patients with SCD [1]. This discussion aims to elucidate the multifaceted nature of asthma in SCD, exploring its epidemiological, pathophysiological, and clinical aspects, as well as the challenges and future directions in its diagnosis and treatment [2]. The coexistence of asthma and SCD presents a formidable challenge, as the symptoms and physiological alterations associated with both conditions can overlap, complicating diagnosis and management [3]. A profound understanding of the interplay between these conditions is crucial for developing effective strategies to improve patient outcomes [4]. SCD, characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin, leads to recurrent episodes of pain, infection, and other complications, with asthma being a significant comorbidity that can significantly alter the disease's course [5]. The presence of asthma in SCD patients can exacerbate symptoms and contribute to the development of complications, underscoring the need for a thorough comprehension of its epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations in this population [6]. The epidemiological landscape of asthma in SCD is complex, with asthma being a common comorbidity that impacts the disease's progression, yet its diagnosis is hindered by overlapping symptoms and physiological abnormalities [7]. Therefore, elucidating the epidemiological aspects of asthma in SCD is essential for providing optimal care to patients with this condition [8]. Furthermore, the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the relationship between asthma and SCD are not fully elucidated, although it is evident that asthma can worsen SCD symptoms and contribute to complications [9]. The airway inflammation seen in asthma can interact with the vascular and hemodynamic alterations characteristic of SCD, potentially leading to increased morbidity [10]. Thus, further research into the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD and the development of effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies is imperative [11]. The clinical presentation of asthma in SCD patients is varied and can include symptoms such as wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath, which can also be attributed to other conditions, making accurate diagnosis challenging [12]. The management of asthma in SCD requires a multifaceted approach, taking into account the unique physiological and pathological characteristics of SCD, as well as the potential interactions between asthma therapies and SCD [14]. Further research is crucial to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the relationship between asthma and SCD and to develop effective diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, ultimately aiming to improve outcomes for patients with SCD [17]. The future of SCD and asthma management lies in the development of targeted therapeutic strategies that address the unique needs of patients with these comorbid conditions, requiring ongoing research and clinical innovation [21]. By shedding light on the intricate relationship between SCD and asthma, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective diagnostic and therapeutic approaches, ultimately enhancing the care provided to patients with these conditions [22]. As our understanding of the relationship between SCD and asthma evolves, so too will our ability to provide tailored, effective care to those who need it most [26]. Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the mean of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditional means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. Our Contributions In this paper, we address these gaps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. New key-value perturbation mechanisms. We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showing improved accuracy over existing approaches. 2. Conditional frequency estimation. We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. 3. Conditional mean estimation. We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. 4. Support for learning tasks. We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities. 5. Extensive evaluation. We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The results show that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. Large-scale data collection from individuals underpins personalized services, public-health surveillance, and the training of modern machien learning models. At the same time, the data that users contriibute are frequently sensitive, and centralized collection exposes them to breaches, misuse, and untrusted curators. Differential privacy (DP) [1] offers a rigorous guarantee that the output of an analysis is insensitive to any single individual's record, but its standard formulation presumes a trusted aggregator. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] removes this assumption: each user perturbs her data on her own device before transmission, so the aggregator never observes raw values. Because of this strong threat model, LDP has been deployed in industrial sysems such as Google's RPAPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6]. Most of the LDP literature considers simple data types. Substantial progress has been made on categorical frequency estimation [4], [7], [8], heavy-hitter identification [9], and mean estimation for numerical attributes [10], [11]. Real-world data, however, are often richer. In particular, key-value data, the basic data model of NoSQL stores, appear in user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records. A key-value pair couples a categorical key (e.g., a poduct or an app) with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage time). Such data arise naturally in applications scuh as estimating how many users own a certain item and what average rating they give it. Challenges of Key-Value Data under LDP Key-value data cannot be handled by applying existing mechanisms independently to keys and values. First, the key and value are correlated: a value is meaningful only if its key is present, and perturbing them separately wastes the privacy budget and yields biased estimates. Second, a user typically holds many keys, so the data are high-dimensional and sparse, and the privacy budget must be split across potentially many coordinates, degrading utility. Third, the value domain is continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation that preserves unbiased aggregates. PrivKV [12] was the first work to formalize LDP for key-value data, perturbing each pair by a sequence of value and key randomization steps and supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, such as interactive variants, reduce estimation error [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is small or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. A further limitation is that current methods deliver only marginal statistics: the frequency of each key and the men of the values of each key. Many downstream tasks require conditional information. Naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems all depend on conditional probabilities or conditionl means, such as the probability that a user holds key B given that she holds key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15]. Estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. Our Contributions In this paper, we address these gapps by designing new perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and by building conditional analysis on top of them. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. New key-value perturbation mechanisms. We propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. The mechanisms are designed so that unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean can be derived in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, showinng improved accuracy over existinng approaches. 2. Conditional frequency estimation. We introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. 3. Conditional mean estimation. We develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated wiht one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis thhan marginal means. 4. Support for learning tasks. We show how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream leanring tasks, and illustrate this with classification based on conditional probabilities. 5. Extensive evaluation. We conduct experiments on synthetic datasets with varied distributions and on real-world rating datasets. The rsults shoow that our mechanisms achieve lowwer error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors acoss a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. Section III presents preliminaries, including the formal definition of LDP and the problem statement. Section IV describes the proposed perturbation mechanisms and their theoreticla analysis. Section V develops conditional frequency and conditional mean estimation. Section VI reports experimental results, and Section VII concludes the paper. (Users holding multiple pairs are handled by sampling one pair uniformly, which is standard in prior work [1].) An untrusted aggregator wishes to estimate (i) the key frequency fk, (ii) the mean value mk of each key, (iii) the cnoditional frequency f{k|c} = Pr[key k | condition c], and (iv) the conditional mean m{k|c} = E[v | key k, cndition c], where c is a predicate on a second key or attribute held by the same user. Eacch user perturbs the pair locally with a randomized mechanism M satisfying ε-LDP [2]: for all inputs x, x′ and outputs y, Pr[M(x)=y] ≤ e^ε Pr[M(x′)=y]. By sequential composition [3], when a user's report is split into components with budgets ε₁ and ε₂, the overall guarantee is (ε₁+ε₂)-LDP. We build on randomized response (RR) [4] for categorical data and on stochastic rounding for numerical data [5]. A value v is discretized to v ∈ {−1,1} with Pr[v=1] = (1+v)/2, which is unbiased, and v is then flipped by RR with keep probability e^{ε₂}/(e^{ε₂}+1). Key-Value Perturbation Mechanism Each user encodes its input as a d-dimensional vector in which a held key k carries the discretized value v ∈ {−1,1} and every other entry is 0. A report is generated by sampling one coordinate j and perturbing only that coordinate, so the output domain is {−1,0,1}. The sampling step is analogous to the one in [6], and the estimator is rescaled by d to correct for it. For the sampled coordinate with true entry x ∈ {−1,0,1}, the mechanism outputs y with probability Pr[y | x] = p if y = x, and q = (1−p)/2 otherwise, with p = e^ε/(e^ε+2). The ratio p/q = 2e^ε/(1−p)… more precisely, p/q = 2e^ε/2 = e^ε after normalization, so the mechanism satisfies ε-LDP, since any two inputs differ only by the ratio p/q. Using a three-way mechanism over the joint key-value domain spends the whole budget once rather than splitting it between key and value, which gives lower variance than sequential perturbation at equal ε. Unbiased Estimators Let ny(j) be the number of reports that sample coordinate j and output y ∈ {−1,0,1}, and let Nj be the number of reports sampling j. Defining the debiased counts ĉ₊ = (n₊ − qNj)/(p−q), ĉ₋ = (n₋ − qNj)/(p−q), where n₊ and n₋ denote the counts of outputs +1 and −1 on coordinate j, we have E[ĉ₊] = c₊ and E[ĉ₋] = c₋, the true counts of users holding key j with discreetized value +1 and −1 respectively. The key frequency estimator is f̂j = (ĉ₊ + ĉ₋)/Nj, and the mean estimator is m̂j = (ĉ₊ − ĉ₋)/(ĉ₊ + ĉ₋). The frequency estimator is unbiased because the sampling is uniform and the debiasing is linear. The mean estimator is a ratio of unbiased quantities and is therefore asymptotically unbiased; a second-order Taylor expansion shows the bias is O(1/(n fj)). Because estimates may fall outside [−1,1] or be negative, we apply a post-processing projection (clipping and normalization), which preserves LDP by the post-processing property [3] and does not increase the expected error. The variance of ĉ₊ is of order d·q(1−q)/(p−q)² per user, so the mean squared error scales as O(d e^ε/(n(e^ε−1)²)). These estimates are broadcast, and in round two the remaining users apply the same mechanism but the aggregator calibrates the estimate by replacing the uninformative prior used in debiasing with m̂j. This is analogous to the iterative scheme in [1] but is applied to the aggregated statistics, so no user is queried twice and the privacy guarantee remains ε. The aggregator obtains f̂{(a,k)} and m̂{(a,k)} directly and computes f̂{k|a} = f̂{(a,k)} / Σ{k′} f̂{(a,k′)}, m̂{k|a} = m̂{(a,k)}. This is simple and asymptotically unbiased, but the variance grows with |A|d. Split-budget encoding. The user spends εa on a (using generalized RR [7]) and εk = ε − εa on the key-value pair. For a pair of reports (ã, ỹ), the joint distribution is related to the true one through the Kronecker product of the two perturbation matrices, P = Pa ⊗ Pkv. The aggregator estimates the joint distribution by inverting this matrix: π̂ = (Pa⁻¹ ⊗ Pkv⁻¹) r, where r is the empirical disttribution of reports. Because the inverse of a Kronecker product factorizes, the computation costs O(|A|² + d²) rather than O(|A|²d²). Conditional frequency is then f̂{k|a} = π̂(a,k)/Σ{k′} π̂(a,k′), and the conditional mean follows by applying the mean estimator to the signed components of π̂. The budget split εa is chosen by minimizing the approximate varance expression derived above, which we do by one-dimensional numerical search. The increasing reliance on individualized services, disease surveillance, and artificial intelligence has fueled the necessity for aggregating vast amounts of personal data. Nevertheless, the confidentiality concerns surrounding user-contributed data make individuals vulnerable to cyber threats, data misuse, and unreliable data handlers. To mitigate these risks, a robust framework known as differential privacy (DP) [1] has been established, ensuring that data analyses are unaffected by any single individual's data entry. However, the conventional DP paradigm presupposes a trustworthy data aggregator, which is not always the case. Local differential privacy (LDP) [2], [3] addresses this limitation by empowering users to distort their data locally before transmitting it, thereby precluding the aggregator from accessing raw data. The robust threat model underlying LDP has led to its integration into various industrial systems, including Google's RAPPOR [4], Apple's iOS and macOS telemetry [5], and Microsoft's telemetry collection [6]. Despite the advancements in LDP, the majority of existing research focuses on simple data structures, such as estimating categorical frequencies [4], [7], [8], identifying high-frequency data points [9], and estimating numerical attribute means [10], [11]. However, real-world data often exhibit complex structures, particularly in the form of key-value pairs, which serve as the fundamental data model for NoSQL databases. Key-value pairs are ubiquitous in various applications, including user-profile databases, e-commerce logs, and smart-device records, where a categorical key (e.g., a product or application) is paired with a numerical value (e.g., a rating or usage duration). Estimating the frequency of a specific item and its average rating are examples of applications that rely on key-value pairs. Handling key-value data under LDP poses significant challenges. Firstly, the correlation between keys and values means that perturbing them independently would not only compromise the privacy budget but also yield biased estimates. Secondly, users typically possess multiple keys, resulting in high-dimensional and sparse data that necessitates dividing the privacy budget across numerous coordinates, ultimately degrading data utility. Thirdly, the value domain is often continuous or ordinal, requiring perturbation methods that preserve unbiased aggregate estimates. The pioneering work on LDP for key-value data, PrivKV [12], perturbs each pair through a sequence of value and key randomization steps, supporting frequency and mean estimation. Subsequent refinements, including interactive variants, have reduced estimation errors [12], [13]. Nevertheless, existing mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance when the privacy budget is limited or the key domain is large, and the correlation between key and value perturbation is not fully exploited. Furthermore, current methods only provide marginal statistics, such as key frequencies and value means, which may not be sufficient for various downstream tasks. Many applications, including naive Bayes classification, decision-tree induction, association-rule mining, and recommendation systems, rely on conditional information, such as conditional probabilities or conditional means. For instance, estimating the probability that a user possesses key B given that they possess key A, or the mean value of key B among users holding key A [14], [15], is essential for these tasks. However, estimating such quantities under LDP is challenging because the conditioning event itself is observed only through noisy reports, and errors in the condition compound errors in the target statistic. In this study, we address these gaps by introducing novel perturbation mechanisms for key-value data and constructing conditional analysis frameworks upon them. Our primary contributions can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we propose a family of LDP mechanisms that jointly perturb the key and value of a pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. These mechanisms enable the derivation of unbiased estimators of key frequency and value mean in closed form, and we analyze their estimation variance, demonstrating improved accuracy over existing approaches. Secondly, we introduce a method for estimating the conditional frequency of one key given another from perturbed reports, enabling the recovery of conditional probabilities and marginal statistics for key analysis. We prove the estimator's unbiasedness and bound its error. Thirdly, we develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. Fourthly, we demonstrate how the released conditional statistics can be used directly in downstream learning tasks, illustrating this with classification based on conditional probabilities. Finally, we conduct extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with diverse distributions and on real-world rating datasets, showing that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes, and that conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful. Section III presents preliminary concepts, including the formal definition of ε-LDP and its application to key-value data. Section IV introduces our proposed LDP mechanisms and conditional analysis frameworks, while Section V presents experimental results and comparisons with existing methods. SECTION II: Related Work. Local differential privacy (LDP) has emerged as a prominent framework for protecting user data in various applications, including data collection and analysis. Several LDP mechanisms have been proposed for simple data types, such as categorical and numerical attributes. However, key-value data pose unique challenges due to the correlation between keys and values and the high dimensionality of the data. Recent studies have addressed these challenges by proposing LDP mechanisms specifically designed for key-value data, such as PrivKV [12] and its variants [13]. Nevertheless, these mechanisms still suffer from considerable variance and limited applicability to downstream tasks. Other studies have explored the application of LDP to related data structures, such as graph data [16] and time-series data [17]. However, these studies do not directly address the challenges posed by key-value data. SECTION III: Preliminaries. Our proposed LDP mechanisms jointly perturb the key and value of each pair while satisfying ε-LDP under a unified privacy budget. Furthermore, we develop an estimator of the mean of the values associated with one key, conditioned on the presence of another key, supporting richer value analysis than marginal means. SECTION V: Experimental Results. We conduct extensive experiments on synthetic datasets with diverse distributions and on real-world rating datasets to evaluate the performance of our proposed mechanisms. Our results show that our mechanisms achieve lower error in frequency and mean estimation than state-of-the-art competitors across a wide range of privacy budgets and key-domain sizes. Additionally, our conditional estimates remain accurate enough to be useful in downstream learning tasks, such as classification based on conditional probabilities. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed mechanisms and conditional analysis frameworks in handling key-value data under LDP. Conclusion. Therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) is an extracorporeal blood purification technique that removes large molecular weight substances from the circulation, such as autoantibodies, immune complexes, paraproteins, and toxins, and replaces the removed plasma with albumin solutions or fresh frozen plasma. It is established as first-line or adjunctive therapy in a wide range of neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated diseases, including thrombotic microangiopathies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic crises, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and humoral rejection after transplantation. Plasma can be separated either by centrifugation or by membrane filtration. In membrane-based TPE, blood is pumped through a hgihly permmeable plasmafilter, and the separated plasma is discarded and replaced. Any extracorporeal circuit exposes blood to artificial surfaces and thereby activates the coagultaion cascade and platelets, with a risk of clotting of the filter and lines. Clotting reduces the efficacy of the procedure, causes blood loss, and increases costs and workload. Anticoagulation is therefore needed. Unfractionated heparin is the most widely used agent in membrane-based TPE, but its use is limited by the risk of bleeding, which is particularly relevant in patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, recent surgery or biopsy, uremic platelet dysfunction, or active vasculitis with hemorrhagic lesions. Heparin may also induce heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and its effect is varialbe and difficult to predict. Moreover, TPE itself removes coagulation factors and may alter the response to heparin. Low molecular weight heparins and other agents such as argatroban or nafamostat have been used, but they share a systemic effect and are costly or not universally available. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) was developed to confine the anticoagulant effect to the extracorporeal circuit. Citrate chelates ionized calcium, a cofactor essential for several steps of the coagulation cascade, so that infuusing citrate at the beginning of the circuit decreases ionized calcium and prevents clotting. Part of the citrate-calcium complex is removed in the effluent, and the remainder returns to the patient, where it is rapidly metabolized by the liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney cortex to bicarbonate, releasnig calcium. RCA has become the preferred anticoagulation strategy in continuous renal replacement therapy, as recommended by the KDIGO guidelines, with lower bleeding rates and longer filter life compared with heparin. Its use has also been described in intermittent hemodialysis, hemodiafiltration, and in apheresis procedures. However, RCA is not free of risk. Excessive citrate delivery can cause systemic hypocalcemia, with paresthesia, cramps, arrhythmias, and hypotension, as well as metabolic alkalosis due to bicarbonate generation. Conversely, citrate accumulation, particularly in patients with impaired hepatic metabolism or poor tissue perfusion, can lead to metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap and a high total to ionized calcium ratio. Insufficient citrate yields inadequate reduction of ionized calcium in the circuit, and thus filter clotting. Safe and effective RCA requires a balance between these limits, and it depends on the target concentration of ionized calcium in the extracorporeal blood, generally considered to lie between 0.25 and 0.35 mmol/l. Protocols for RCA in continuous techniques are well standardized, usually using a fixed ratio of citrate infusion to blood flow, with adaptation based on post-filter ionized calcium measurements and systemic calcium replacement. TPE differs importantly from these techniques. Blood flow rates are higher, sessions are shorter, and the plasma removed contains moost of the citrate-calcium complexes, so that the amount of citrate returned to the patient depends on the plasma fraction removed and replacement fluids. In addition, replacement with fresh fozen plasma brings additional citrate, sincce plasma units are themselves anticoagulated with citrate, whereas albumin solutions contain little calcium. The volume of distribution of calcium and citrate and the proportion of calcium bound to albumin vary with the patient's hematocrit and plasma composition. Since the plasma is separated from blood cells, the hematocrit determines the plasma flow and therefore the amount of citrate needed per unit of blood to reach a given plasma citrate concentration. Despite these particularities, the literature on RCA in TPE is limited to small series and empirical protocols using fixed citrate infusion rates relative to blood flow, often wih calcium infusion adapted from clinical experience. To our knowledge, no individualized presciption has been proposed that takes into account patient characteristics and the physicochemical determinants of calcium chelation. Such a model would help clinicians to start treatment at the appropriate citrate dose, avoid early clotting of the circuit, limit exposure to excess citrate, and reduce the need for repeated measurements. The objective of this study was therefore to identify the determinants of the blood citrate concentration needed to achieve effective regional anticoagulation during membrane-based TPE, and to develop, using a mathematical approach, an individualized prescription algorithm for citrate and calcium supplementation. We alos evaluated the efficacy of the resulting protocol in terms of circuit patency, as well as its safety in terms of systemic ionized calcium and acid–base balance. This was a prospective observational study conducted in the intensive care and nephrology units of a university hospital. The protocol was approved by the local ethics committee, and all patients provided informed consent, or consent was obtained from a relative when the patient was unable to giive it. Adult patients scheduled for TPE for standard clinical indications were eligible. Patients were excluded if they had severe hepatic failure (given the risk of citrate accumulation), if they were pregnant, or if they had a known allergy to the materials used in the circuit. Study population and treatment procedures Fourteen patients underwent a total of 47 TPE sessions. TPE was performed by membrane plasma separation using a hollow-fiber plasmafilter, with blood flow, plasma removal rate and session duration prescribed by the treating physician according to the patient's plasma volume. Vascular access was obtained through a double-lumen dialysis catheter. The replacement fluid was 4% albumin or fresh frozen plasma, according to the clinical indication, and was infused post-plasmafilter. No systemic anticoagulation was given. Sessions in which the circuit clotted were recorded, as were any premature terminations. Citrate anticoagulation Trisodium citrate was infused continuously into the arterial line pre-plasmafilter using a dedicated volumetric pump. Calcium chloride was infused through a separate line into the patient's venous return, using a central venous route distinct from the dialysis catheter, to compensate for citrate-bound calcium loss in the removed plasma and for the citrate returned to the patient. The aim of anticoagulation was to loweer the ionized calcium concentration in the blood entering the plasmafilter to a level that prevents clotting, without exposiing the patient to excess citrate. Sampling and measurements Blood samples were drawn at standardized time points: before the start of the session, at fixed intervals during treatment, and at the end of the session. At each time point, samples were collected from the post-plasmafilter port, representing circuit ionized calcium, and from the patient (systemic). Ionized calcium, pH, bicarbonate, base excess, sodium and lactate were measured on a blood gas analyzer with ion-selective electrodes. Hematocrit, total calcium, magnesium, albumin and coagulation parameters were obtained before treatment from routine laboratory analysis. Hypocalcemia was defined as a systemic ionized calcium below a prespecfiied threshold (<0.9 mmol/l), and was considered significant when it required intervention beyond the protoocl adjustments or was symptomatic. Acid–base disturbances werre defined by deviations in pH and bicarbonate from normal ranges. Calcium supplementation algorithm A calcium supplementation algorithm was defined a priori. The calcium infusion rate was started in proportion to the citrate infusion rate and then adjusted according to systemic ionized calcium measured at each time point. The infusion was increased when systemic ionized calcium fell below the target range and decreased when it rose above it. The aim was to maintain systemic ionized calcium within the physiological range throughout and at the end of the session. Discovery phase In the discovery phase, citrate was infused at a fixed starting rate relative to blood flow. The rate was then adapted according to the post-plasmafilter ionized calcium obtained at the first measurement, with the target range for the post-filter value defined from the literature on regional citrate anticoagulation in continuous renal replacement therapy. Citrate was increased if post-plasmafilter ionized calcium exceeded the target and decreased if it was below. The citrate dose needed to bring plasma ionized calcium from its baseline to the target level was then modeled mathematically, using the chelation relationship between citrate and ionized calcium observed in the discovery data. Variables were retained in the model if they significantly improved the fit. The resulting equation allowed calculation of the citrate infusion rate needed for a given blood flow, hematocrit and baseline ionized calcium, to achieve a prefilter ionized calcium within the target range. Validation phase The equation was then applied prospectively in subsequent sessions to prescribe the initial citrate infusion rate individually. Post-plasmafilter ionizzed calcium was measured to verify that the target was reached, and the agreement between predicted and observed values was assessed. Occurrence of circuit clotting, systemic hypocalcemia and acid–base disturbances was recorded. Statistical analysis Continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median and interquartile range, according to distribution. Because multiple sessions were obtained in the same patient, repeated measures were accounted for by mixed-effects models. Associations between variables and the required citrate rate were tested using linear regression, first univariate and then multivariate. Agreement between predicted and measured values was evaluated with Bland–Altman analysis. Categorical variables are presented as counts and percentages. A two-sided p value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses wree performed with standard statistical software. The application of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) has become a staple in the treatment of various neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated disorders, serving as a primary or supplementary therapy [1]. This extracorporeal blood purification technique operates by extracting high molecular weight substances, including autoantibodies, immune complexes, paraproteins, and toxins, from the bloodstream and subsequently replacing the removed plasma with albumin solutions or fresh frozen plasma. The efficacy of TPE has been demonstrated in the management of conditions such as thrombotic microangiopathies, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myasthenic crises, anti-glomerular basement membrane disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and humoral rejection post-transplantation [2-5]. The separation of plasma from blood can be accomplished through either centrifugation or membrane filtration, with the latter being a commonly employed approach [6]. In this method, blood is pumped through a highly permeable plasma filter, and the separated plasma is discarded and replaced. Nevertheless, the interaction between blood and artificial surfaces within the extracorporeal circuit can trigger the coagulation cascade and activate platelets, leading to a risk of filter and line clotting [7]. Clotting can compromise the efficacy of the procedure, result in blood loss, and increase costs and workload, underscoring the necessity of anticoagulation in TPE [8]. Unfractionated heparin is the most widely used anticoagulant in membrane-based TPE, but its application is limited by the risk of bleeding, which is particularly relevant in patients with thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy, recent surgical or biopsy procedures, uremic platelet dysfunction, or active vasculitis with hemorrhagic lesions [9-11]. Furthermore, heparin may induce heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, and its effect can be unpredictable and variable [12]. Additionally, TPE itself can remove coagulation factors and alter the response to heparin, rendering anticoagulation management challenging in these patients [13]. Alternative anticoagulants, such as low molecular weight heparins and other agents like argatroban or nafamostat, have been utilized, but they share a systemic effect and are often costly or not universally available [14-16]. Regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) was developed as a strategy to localize the anticoagulant effect to the extracorporeal circuit, thereby minimizing the risk of systemic bleeding [17]. Citrate chelates ionized calcium, a cofactor essential for several steps of the coagulation cascade, such that infusing citrate at the beginning of the circuit decreases ionized calcium and prevents clotting [18]. A portion of the citrate-calcium complex is removed in the effluent, and the remainder returns to the patient, where it is rapidly metabolized by the liver, skeletal muscle, and kidney cortex to bicarbonate, releasing calcium [19]. RCA has become the preferred anticoagulation strategy in continuous renal replacement therapy, as recommended by the KDIGO guidelines, with lower bleeding rates and longer filter life compared to heparin [20]. Its application has also been described in intermittent hemodialysis, hemodiafiltration, and apheresis procedures [21-23]. However, RCA is not devoid of risks, as excessive citrate delivery can cause systemic hypocalcemia, with paresthesia, cramps, arrhythmias, and hypotension, as well as metabolic alkalosis due to bicarbonate generation [24]. Conversely, citrate accumulation, particularly in patients with impaired hepatic metabolism or poor tissue perfusion, can lead to metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap and a high total to ionized calcium ratio [25]. Insufficient citrate yields inadequate reduction of ionized calcium in the circuit, resulting in filter clotting. Safe and effective RCA requires a balance between these limits, depending on the target concentration of ionized calcium in the extracorporeal blood, generally considered to lie between 0.25 and 0.35 mmol/l [26]. Protocols for RCA in continuous techniques are well standardized, typically employing a fixed ratio of citrate infusion to blood flow, with adaptation based on post-filter ionized calcium measurements and systemic calcium replacement [27]. However, TPE differs significantly from these techniques, with higher blood flow rates, shorter sessions, and the plasma removed containing most of the citrate-calcium complexes [28]. The amount of citrate returned to the patient depends on the plasma fraction removed and replacement fluids, and the volume of distribution of calcium and citrate varies with the patient's hematocrit and plasma composition [29]. Since the plasma is separated from blood cells, the hematocrit determines the plasma flow and therefore the amount of citrate needed per unit of blood to reach a given plasma citrate concentration [30]. Despite these distinct characteristics, the literature on RCA in TPE is limited to small series and empirical protocols using fixed citrate infusion rates relative to blood flow, often with calcium infusion adapted from clinical experience [31-33]. To our knowledge, no personalized prescription has been proposed that takes into account patient characteristics and the physicochemical determinants of calcium chelation [34]. Such a model would facilitate clinicians in initiating treatment at the appropriate citrate dose, avoiding early circuit clotting, limiting exposure to excess citrate, and reducing the need for repeated measurements. The primary objective of this study was to identify the determinants of the blood citrate concentration required to achieve effective regional anticoagulation during membrane-based TPE and to develop, using a comprehensive approach, a personalized protocol for citrate administration in TPE. This would enable the optimization of anticoagulation therapy, reduction of complications, and improvement of patient outcomes. By elucidating the relationships between patient-specific factors, citrate dosage, and clinical outcomes, this study aims to provide a foundation for the development of evidence-based guidelines for RCA in TPE, ultimately enhancing the safety and efficacy of this therapeutic modality. The development of such a protocol would require a thorough understanding of the physicochemical principles underlying RCA, as well as the clinical factors influencing citrate metabolism and calcium homeostasis in patients undergoing TPE. Furthermore, the study would need to consider the variability in patient responses to citrate and the potential for citrate accumulation or depletion, which can impact the efficacy and safety of the anticoagulation strategy. By addressing these knowledge gaps, this research would contribute to the advancement of TPE as a therapeutic option, enabling clinicians to provide personalized and effective care to patients with complex neurological, hematological, renal, and immune-mediated disorders. The study's findings would have significant implications for the management of these conditions, highlighting the importance of tailored anticoagulation strategies in optimizing patient outcomes and reducing the risk of complications. Our investigation focused on devising a personalized approach to managing citrate and calcium supplementation during therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) procedures, a crucial aspect of patient care in the intensive care and nephrology units [35]. A key objective was to assess the efficacy and safety of our protocol, with particular attention to maintaining circuit patency and ensuring systemic ionized calcium and acid-base balance. These methods are interpretable and come with a growing body of theory [8], [9], but they face practical obstacles. Dictionary learning, the problem of finding a set of atoms in which a collection of sgnals admits sparse representations, is a cornerstone of modern signal processing and machine learning [1], [2]. When the atoms are constrained to be shift-invariant filters, the model is called convolutional dictionary learning (CDL) [3], [4]. Each signal is then expressed as a sum of a small number of translated filters. This model is well suited to data in which a small number of recurring motifs occur at unknown times and wtih unknown amplitudes, as in audio, seismic recordings, naural images, and neural electrophysiology. Learning the filters from daat is thus a form of blind source separation: given only the number of sources and the assumption thhat few of tem overlap at any moment, one seeks to recover the sources and their activation times. Classsical CDL algorithms alternate between two steps: a sparse-coding step, which solves an ℓ1-regularized convolutional least-squares problem (convolutional LASSO) with the dictionary fixed, and a dictionary-update step, which refines the filters with the coodes fixed [5]–[7]. These methods are interpretable and come with a growing body of theory [8], [9], but tey face practical obstacles. Each iteration requires solving a sparse-coding problm over all training signals, which becomes costly for large datasets. The methods are also difficult to parallelize across data and to run on streaming data, and their performance depends on hand-tuned parameters. In parallel, deep learning has produuced powerful architectures, yet they are often opaque, require lrge labeled datasets, and offer few guarantees. A promising bridge is algorithm unrolling [10], which began wiht the Learned ISTA (LISTA) of Gregor and LeCnu [11]. Here the iterations of an optimization algorithm are interpreted as the layers of a recurrent or deep network, whose parameters are then tarined by back-propagation. Unrolled architectures have beeen developed for sparse coding [11], [12], image restoration [13], and dictionary learning [14], and they often reach a given accuracy with far fewer iterations than their classical counterparts. However, most suhc approaches treat the parameteers of the encoder as free variables, decoupled from those of the decoder, and are typically trined in a supervised maanner or for fast approximation of a fixed model. Consequently, the learned weights lose their interpretation as a dictionary, and the guarantees of the underlying optiization problem no longer apply. Contributions In this paper we propose the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), an auto-encoder whose structure is dictated by the alternating-minimization approaach to CDL. The encoder unrolls a fixed nuber of FISTA iterations [15] to comute a sparse code from an input signal and a current dictionary estimate. The deoder applies the samme dictionary to the code to reconstruct the signal. The encoder's filters are the transpose (flipped version) of the decoder's filters, so a single set of weights parameterizes the whole network. This constraint is the key design element. It ensures thaat training the network amounts to learning a dictionary, so that the weights remain interpretable, the number of parameters is minimal, and the network directly mirrors the optimization problem it is meant to solve. To our knowledge, tihs tying of encoder and decoder parameters througgh the unrolled recurrence has not previously been enforced in this setting. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We introduce CRsAE and show that its forward pass corresponnds to the sparse-coding step, and a gradient step on the reconstruction loss with respect to the shared weights corresponds to the dictionary-update step of alternating minimization. 2. We derive the back-propagation algorithm for CRsAE, accounting for the fact that the dictionary appears in both the encdoer and the decodr and at every unrolled iteration. Tihs yields exact gradients, which differ from those obtained by treating the enoder and decoder weights as independent. 3. We show that, because training proceeds in mini-batches with GPU-friendly convolutional operations, CRsE scales to large datasets and long signals where conventional CDL solvers are impractical. It is also trained without labels, and the regularization parameter is the only quantity requiiring tuning. 4. We apply CRsAE to spike sorting, a sourec separation problem in computational neuroscience in which extracellular voltage recordings contin action potentials from several neurons, each with a characteristic waveform, corrupted by noise [16], [17]. Neurons are the sources, their waveforms are the dictionary elements, and spike times are the sparse codes. Overlapping spikes are a well-known difficulty for traditional pipelines based on thresholding, feautre extraction, and clustering, whereas the convolutional model handles superposition natuurally [18]. 5. We evaluate the ability of CRsAE to recover the underlying dictionary on synthetic and real data, and characterize its sensitivity as a function of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR).
