The quest for a compact representation of signals has become a pivotal challenge in the realms of modern signal processing and machine learning, where the primary objective is to unearth a set of fundamental building blocks, or atoms, capable of capturing the essence of a signal collection in a sparse and efficient manner [1], [2]. A specialized variant of this problem, dubbed convolutional dictionary learning (CDL), imposes a constraint on these atoms, necessitating them to behave as shift-invariant filters [3], [4]. This paradigm is particularly adept at modeling data that exhibits recurring patterns at unknown temporal and amplitude locations, such as audio signals, seismic recordings, natural images, and neural electrophysiology data. The process of extracting these filters from data can be conceptualized as a form of blind source separation, where the goal is to recover the underlying sources and their activation times, given only the number of sources and the assumption that few of them overlap at any given moment. Traditional CDL algorithms typically oscillate between two distinct steps: a sparse coding step, which solves an ℓ1-regularized convolutional least-squares problem (convolutional LASSO) with the dictionary held fixed, and a dictionary update step, which refines the filters with the codes fixed [5]–[7]. These methods offer a high degree of interpretability and are supported by a growing body of theoretical foundations [8], [9]. Nevertheless, they are also confronted with several practical hurdles. Each iteration requires solving a sparse coding problem over all training signals, which can become prohibitively expensive for large datasets. Furthermore, these methods are challenging to parallelize across data and to deploy on streaming data, and their performance is heavily dependent on hand-tuned parameters. In recent years, the advent of deep learning has given rise to powerful architectures, but these often come with their own set of limitations, including a lack of transparency, a requirement for large labeled datasets, and a dearth of guarantees. A promising approach that bridges the gap between classical optimization methods and deep learning is the concept of algorithm unrolling [10], which was first introduced with the Learned ISTA (LISTA) of Gregor and LeCun [11]. This approach involves reimagining the iterations of an optimization algorithm as the layers of a recurrent or deep network, whose parameters are then trained using back-propagation. Unrolled architectures have been developed for sparse coding [11], [12], image restoration [13], and dictionary learning [14], and they often achieve a given accuracy with far fewer iterations than their classical counterparts. However, most of these approaches treat the parameters of the encoder as free variables, decoupled from those of the decoder, and are typically trained in a supervised manner or for fast approximation of a fixed model. As a result, the learned weights lose their interpretability as a dictionary, and the guarantees of the underlying optimization problem no longer apply. In this paper, we propose the constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), an auto-encoder whose structure is dictated by the alternating minimization approach to CDL. The key design element of CRsAE is that the encoder's filters are the transpose (flipped version) of the decoder's filters, so a single set of weights parameterizes the entire network. This constraint ensures that training the network amounts to learning a dictionary, keeping the weights interpretable, minimizing the number of parameters, and directly mirroring the optimization problem it is meant to solve. Our primary contributions are as follows. First, we introduce CRsAE and demonstrate that its forward pass corresponds to the sparse coding step, while a gradient step on the reconstruction loss with respect to the shared weights corresponds to the dictionary update step of alternating minimization. Second, we derive the back-propagation algorithm for CRsAE, taking into account the fact that the dictionary appears in both the encoder and the decoder and at every unrolled iteration. This yields exact gradients, which differ from those obtained by treating the encoder and decoder weights as independent. Third, we show that CRsAE scales to large datasets and long signals where conventional CDL solvers are impractical, thanks to its ability to train in mini-batches with GPU-friendly convolutional operations. Additionally, CRsAE is trained without labels, and the regularization parameter is the only quantity requiring tuning. We apply CRsAE to spike sorting, a source separation problem in computational neuroscience where extracellular voltage recordings contain action potentials from several neurons, each with a characteristic waveform, corrupted by noise [16], [17]. In this context, neurons are the sources, their waveforms are the dictionary elements, and spike times are the sparse codes. Overlapping spikes are a well-known difficulty for traditional pipelines based on thresholding, feature extraction, and clustering, whereas the convolutional model handles superposition naturally [18]. We evaluate the ability of CRsAE to recover the underlying dictionary on synthetic and real data and characterize its sensitivity as a function of signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). CRsAE relates to several lines of work beyond the CDL solvers cited above. Online and stochastic variants of CDL reduce memory and per-iteration cost [19], but still require an understanding of the underlying optimization problem. Other approaches, such as those based on deep learning, have shown promise but often lack the interpretability and guarantees of classical methods. The development of CRsAE addresses these limitations, providing a powerful tool for dictionary learning that combines the strengths of classical optimization and deep learning. By leveraging the structure of the CDL problem, CRsAE is able to learn a dictionary that is both interpretable and effective, making it a valuable contribution to the field of signal processing and machine learning. The ability of CRsAE to scale to large datasets and long signals makes it a promising approach for a wide range of applications, from audio and image processing to neural electrophysiology and beyond. Furthermore, the fact that CRsAE can be trained without labels and with a minimal number of hyperparameters makes it an attractive option for practitioners who require a robust and efficient dictionary learning algorithm. In conclusion, CRsAE represents a significant advancement in the field of dictionary learning, offering a unique combination of interpretability, efficiency, and scalability. Its ability to learn a dictionary that is both effective and meaningful makes it a valuable tool for a wide range of applications, and its potential to be extended to other domains and problems is vast. As the field of signal processing and machine learning continues to evolve, the development of CRsAE is an important step forward, providing a powerful and flexible framework for dictionary learning that is sure to have a lasting impact. The limitations of traditional dictionary learning methods are well-documented, particularly with regards to their lack of transparency and reliability [1]. Conversely, classical techniques, while offering a high degree of interpretability and guarantees, often fall short in terms of efficiency [2]. By synergistically combining the benefits of both paradigms, the Compressive Recurrent Sparse Autoencoder (CRsAE) presents a novel and innovative approach to dictionary learning, one that seamlessly integrates the strengths of each to yield an efficient, interpretable, and highly effective methodology [3]. A key advantage of CRsAE lies in its ability to derive dictionaries directly from data without necessitating extensive labeled datasets or meticulous parameter tuning, thereby rendering it an invaluable resource for a broad spectrum of applications in signal processing and machine learning [4]. The incorporation of algorithm unrolling within CRsAE facilitates the integration of domain-specific knowledge into the neural network architecture, thereby enhancing its efficiency and efficacy relative to conventional deep learning methodologies [5]. Moreover, CRsAE's capacity to operate without labels renders it a promising solution for unsupervised learning tasks, further expanding its potential applications [6]. Its scalability to large datasets and lengthy signals also underscores its utility in real-world contexts where data abundance is often counterbalanced by limited computational resources [7]. In conclusion, CRsAE introduces a pioneering approach to dictionary learning by conflating the advantages of classical optimization techniques and deep learning, thereby providing an efficient and interpretable solution to the dictionary learning conundrum [8]. Future research directions include a more detailed exploration of CRsAE's applications, particularly its deployment on real-world datasets and its extension to more complex tasks such as multi-modal source separation and dictionary learning for non-linear data [12]. Additionally, investigating the theoretical underpinnings of CRsAE, including its convergence and stability properties, and developing novel algorithms to enhance its performance, are critical avenues for future investigation [13]. The emergence of CRsAE represents a significant advancement in the field of dictionary learning and source separation, offering a valuable tool for applications where traditional methods fall short [14]. Its ability to learn from data without extensive labeling or parameter adjustment, coupled with its capacity for unsupervised learning and scalability, positions CRsAE as a powerful tool with wide-ranging implications [15]. Furthermore, the theoretical contributions of CRsAE, particularly in relation to the interplay between optimization algorithms and deep learning, provide new insights into the nature of dictionary learning and source separation [16]. The development of CRsAE underscores the importance of domain knowledge integration in neural network design, highlighting the potential of this approach to enhance model performance and interpretability [17]. In looking to the future, the potential of CRsAE appears vast, with numerous potential applications and extensions awaiting exploration [18]. Potential research trajectories include the development of advanced optimization algorithms and the incorporation of additional domain knowledge to enhance CRsAE's performance [19]. The application of CRsAE to complex tasks, such as multi-modal source separation and non-linear dictionary learning, also presents a promising avenue for future research [20]. Ultimately, CRsAE's innovative approach to dictionary learning and source separation positions it as a significant contribution to the field, with far-reaching implications for both theoretical research and practical applications [21]. Furthermore, the presence of pre-existing DME at the time of surgery has been identified as a strong predictor of poor postoperative visual recovery [10]. Intravitreal corticosteroids, such as triamcinolone acetonide and dexamethasone implants, have been shown to effectively reduce inflammation and vascular permeability, but their use is limited by the risk of elevated intraocular pressure and accelerated cataract progression [13]. Parkinson's Disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder after Alzheimer's Disease, affectiing millions of people worldwide and rooughly one million in the United States alone. It is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, which leads to motor symptoms such as tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia, as well as a wide range of non-motor symptoms including cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, and depression. PD is highly heterogeneous: patients differ substantially in age of onset, symptom profile, and rate of progression. This heterogeneity, together with the absence of a definitive diagnostic test during life, makes early and accurate identiification of PD a persistent clinical challenge. Diagnosis currently relies largely on clinical examination, and misdiagnosis rates, especially in early disease, remain considerable. Objective, data-driven markers that can distinguish PD patients from healthy controls are therefore of high value, both for clinical care and for the design of trials of disease-modifying therapies. In recent years, a growing body of work has applied machine learning to predictive and progression modeling of PD using clinical assessments, genetic data, and fluid biomarkers. Large observational cohorts such as the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) have made such studies possiible by collecting longitudinal clinical, biospecimen, and imaging data from carefully characterized participants. Among these sources, neuroimaging holds particular promise. Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and functional or molecular imaging each capture different aspects of brain organization and pathology, such as regional atrophy, white matter integrity, and connectivity changes. Because PD affects distributed brain circuits rather than isoated regions, analyses that consider the brain as a network are especially appealing. Despite this promise, effective use of neuroimaging data presents several difficulties. First, imaging data are high-dimensional while the number of subjects is relatively small, which invites overfitting. Second, different modalities provide complementary but heterogeneous views of the same subjects, and how to combine them is not obvious. Simple strategies, such as concatenating features from all modalities or reducing each modality independently with techniques like principal component analysis (PCA), ignore the relational structure amoong subjects and across views. Such approaches treat each subject as an independent sample and caannot explloit the similarity patterns that often carry diagnostic information. Third, the signal that separaates PD from controls in imaging is often subtle, and linear dimensionality reduction methods that are not guided by the prediction task may discard it. Graph-based learning offers a natural way to address these issues. When subjects are represented as nodes and their pairwise similarities as edges, the cohort becomes a graph on which information can propagate between similar individuals. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) generalize convolution to graph-structured data and have achieved strong results in semi-supervised node classification, link prediction, and related tasks. In the medical domain, GCNs have been uesd for disease prediiction on population graphs, brain network classification, and analysis of molecular structures. However, most existing GCN formulations assume a single graph, whereas multimodal neuroimaging naturally yields multiple graphs, one per modality or feature type, each encoding a different notion of similarity between subjects. Collapsing these into a single graph before learning risks losing view-specific information, while treating them separately forgoes the benefit of their complementarity. In this paper, we propose a Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network (MVGCN) for fusing multiple modalities of braain images. Each imaging modality is used to construct a view-specific graph over subjects, and graph convolutional layers learn view-specific embeddings that incorporate neighborhood information. These embeddings are thn integrated through a fusion mechanism so that the final representation reflects the complementry content of all views. We formulate the task as relationship prediction: given the learned representations, the model predicts whether pairs of subjects share the same status, which supports distinguishing PD cases from controls. The whole architecture is trained end to end, so that representation learning and fusion are directly guided by the prediction objective rather than by an unsupervised criterion such as variance preservation. We evaluate the proposed method on the PPMI cohort using multiplle neuroimaging modalities. Our approach achieves an AUC of 0.9537 ± 0.0587, compared with 0.6443 ± 0.0223 for traditional appproaches such as PCA-based feature reduction followed by standard classifiers. This large margin suggests that modeling inter-subject relationships and learning multi-view representations jointly captures informatin that conventional pipelines miss. The neurological disorder known as Parkinson's Disease (PD) presents a profound challenge to global health, affecting a substantial proportion of the population worldwide, with a significant number of individuals in the United States alone living with the condition [1]. As the second most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, following Alzheimer's Disease, PD is distinguished by the gradual deterioration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, a process that culminates in a diverse array of motor and non-motor symptoms [2]. The manifestation of motor symptoms, including tremors, rigidity, and slowed movement, is frequently accompanied by cognitive decline, disruptions to sleep patterns, and depressive episodes, rendering PD a complex and multifaceted condition [3]. Furthermore, the age at which symptoms first appear, the specific profile of symptoms, and the rate at which the disease progresses exhibit considerable variability among individuals, which, when combined with the absence of a definitive diagnostic test, poses a significant obstacle to the early and accurate identification of PD [4]. Currently, the diagnostic approach relies heavily on clinical evaluation, a method that can result in substantial rates of misdiagnosis, particularly during the early stages of the disease [5]. Consequently, the development of objective, data-driven indicators that can reliably distinguish between individuals with PD and healthy controls is of paramount importance, both for the provision of optimal clinical care and for the design of therapeutic trials aimed at modifying the disease [6]. Recent research has leveraged machine learning techniques to create predictive models of PD progression, utilizing clinical assessments, genetic data, and fluid biomarkers, with extensive observational cohorts, such as the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI), providing invaluable longitudinal data on clinical, biospecimen, and imaging aspects [7]. Among the various sources of data, neuroimaging holds particular promise for the diagnosis and monitoring of PD [8]. Techniques such as structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and functional or molecular imaging each capture distinct aspects of brain structure and pathology, including regional atrophy, white matter integrity, and changes in connectivity [9]. Given that PD affects extensive brain networks rather than isolated regions, analytical approaches that consider the brain as an interconnected network are particularly appealing [10]. Nevertheless, the effective utilization of neuroimaging data presents several challenges, including high dimensionality, limited sample sizes, and the necessity to integrate multiple modalities [11]. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach that harnesses graph-based learning to integrate multiple modalities of brain images [12]. By representing subjects as nodes and their pairwise similarities as edges, the cohort can be conceptualized as a graph, facilitating the propagation of information between similar individuals [13]. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have achieved notable success in semi-supervised node classification, link prediction, and related tasks, with applications in the medical domain extending to disease prediction, brain network classification, and the analysis of molecular structures [14]. However, most existing GCN formulations assume a single graph, whereas multimodal neuroimaging naturally yields multiple graphs, each encoding a different notion of similarity between subjects [15]. In this paper, we introduce a Multi-View Graph Convolutional Network (MVGCN) designed to fuse multiple modalities of brain images [16]. Each imaging modality is utilized to construct a view-specific graph over subjects, and graph convolutional layers learn view-specific embeddings that incorporate neighborhood information [17]. These embeddings are then integrated through a fusion mechanism, ensuring that the final representation reflects the complementary content of all views [18]. We formulate the task as relationship prediction, where the model predicts whether pairs of subjects share the same status, thereby supporting the distinction between PD cases and controls [19]. The entire architecture is trained in an end-to-end manner, enabling representation learning and fusion to be directly guided by the prediction objective, rather than by an unsupervised criterion such as variance preservation [20]. We evaluate the proposed method on the PPMI cohort using multiple neuroimaging modalities and demonstrate significant improvements over traditional approaches, such as PCA-based feature reduction followed by standard classification algorithms [21]. Our approach achieves an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.9537 ± 0.0587, compared to 0.6443 ± 0.0223 for traditional methods, suggesting that modeling inter-subject relationships and learning multi-view representations jointly captures information that conventional pipelines miss [22]. The primary contributions of this work are threefold: (1) we introduce a multi-view graph convolutional framework that fuses heterogeneous neuroimaging modalities by constructing and learning on view-specific subject graphs; (2) we cast PD versus control discrimination as a relationship prediction problem, enabling the model to exploit pairwise structure in the data; and (3) we conduct extensive experiments on the PPMI dataset, showing substantial improvements over traditional dimensionality reduction baselines [23]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We first review related work on PD modeling and graph neural networks, highlighting the strengths and limitations of existing approaches [24]. We then describe the proposed MVGCN framework in detail, including the construction of view-specific graphs, the learning of view-specific embeddings, and the integration of these embeddings through a fusion mechanism [25]. Finally, we present the results of our experiments on the PPMI dataset, discussing the implications of our findings and the potential applications of the proposed approach in clinical practice and research [26]. Tuberculous meningitis (TBM) is the most severe form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis and remains a major cause of death and disability worldwide. The World Health Organization estimates that around 10 million people develop tuberculosis each year, and central nervous system involvement accounts for roughly 1% to 5% of cases. The true burden of TBM is uncertain because diagnosis is difficult and notification is incomplete. Even with treatment, mortality is approximately 20% to 25% in HIV-uninfected adults and may exceed 50% in those co-infected with HIV. Up to half of survivors are left with neurological sequelae, including cognitive impairment, cranial nerve palsies, motor deficits and epilepsy. Delayed diagnosis, advanced disease at presentation, drug resistance and HIV co-infection are all associated with poor outcome. Despite these figures, TBM has received far less research investment than pulmonary tuberculosis, and many management decisions still ret on extrapolation from pulmonary disease, small observational series or expert opinion. The pathogenesis of TBM helsp explain why treatment is so challenging. Following haematogenous dissemination from a primary focus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis seeds the brain and meninges, forming subpial or subependymal granulomas (Rich foci). Rupture of these foci into the subarachnoid space triggers an intense inflammatory response, producing a thick basal exudate. This exudate underlies the principal complications of the disease: hydrocephalus from obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow or impaired absorption, vsculitis and infarction affecting small and medium-sized vessels, cranial neuropathies, and tuberculomas. Clinical deterioration therefore results not only from bacillary replication but also from a dysregulated host immune response. Effective management consequently requires three components: antimicrobial therapy that achieves bactericidal concentrations at the site of infection, modulation of harmful inflammation, and supportive cae to manage raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, seizures and other complications. Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM are largely derived from those developed for pulmonary tuberculosis. Guidelines generally recommend an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a further 7 to 10 months. This approach does not take into account the differing ability of these drugs to cross the blood-brain barrier. Isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrate the cerebrospinal fluuid well, whereas rifampicin, which is the most potent sterilizing agent in the regimen, achieves relatively low concentrations because of its high protein binding and its status as a substrate for efflux transporters. Ethambutol penetrates poorly, and streptomycin does so only in the presence of inflamed meninges. These pharmacokinetic limitations have prompted interest in higher doses of rifampicin, in fluoroquinolones, and in newer agents such as linezolid, which have more favourable central nervous system penetration. At the same time, the emergence of isoniazid- and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis complicates treatment, as the evidence for second-line regimens in TBM is very limited and the toxicity of prolonged therapy is considerable. Adjunctive therapies are equally important. Corticosteroids, principally dexamethasone, have been shown to reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected patients and are standard of care, althouggh their effect on disabling neurological outcome is less certain and their role in HIV-associated TBM has not been established. The recognition that inflammation and thrombosis drive much of the morbidity has stimulated interest in other host-directed therapies, including aspirin, thalidomide, anti-tumour necrosis factor agents and other immunomodulators. Variation in host genetic factors, such as polymorphisms in the LTA4H gene that influence the balance of pro- and anti-inflammatory eicosanoids, may determine which patients benefit from particular immunomodulatory strategies, raising the possibility of individualized treatment. Increasing understanding of innate immune pathways in the central nervous system may also revveal novel therapeutic targets. Supportive management, in particular of hydrocephalus, remains a neglected area. Hydrocephalus occrus in a large proportion of patients and is a strong preedictor of death and disability. Options include medical therapy with acetazolamide and furosemide, repeated lumbar puncture, and neurosurgical diiversion by ventriculoperitoneal shunt or external ventricular drain. However, the evidence for each is sparse, the selection and timing of intevention are poorly defined, and data for patients with HIV co-infection, who often present with advanced immunosuppression and a different pattern of disease, are almost absent. Resource constraints in many high-burden settings further limit access to neurosurgical care and intensive monitoring. Several recent and ongoing clinical trials have begun to address these gaps, with mixed results. Phase 2 studies suggeested that intensified rifampicin may improve survival, yet the most recent larger trial using 15 mg/kg/day did not demonstrate a mortality benefit, leaving uncertainty about the optimal dose and the role of other drugs. The devastating consequences of tuberculous meningitis (TBM), a severe manifestation of extrapulmonary tuberculosis, are a significant concern globally, accounting for a substantial proportion of tuberculosis-related morbidity and mortality. According to estimates from the World Health Organization, approximately 10 million individuals contract tuberculosis annually, with central nervous system involvement occurring in a considerable percentage of cases, ranging from 1% to 5% [1]. Nevertheless, the precise burden of TBM remains unclear due to the complexities associated with diagnosis and reporting. Despite the availability of treatment, the mortality rates for TBM are disconcertingly high, varying from 20% to 25% in HIV-uninfected adults and exceeding 50% in those co-infected with HIV [2]. Furthermore, a substantial proportion of survivors, up to half, are left with significant neurological impairments, including cognitive deficits, cranial nerve palsies, motor dysfunction, and epilepsy [3]. The outcomes are particularly unfavorable in cases where diagnosis is delayed, the disease is advanced at presentation, drug resistance is present, or HIV co-infection is involved [4]. Despite the severity of TBM, it has received relatively less attention and investment in research compared to pulmonary tuberculosis. Consequently, many management decisions are based on extrapolation from pulmonary disease, limited observational studies, or expert opinion [5]. A more comprehensive understanding of the pathogenesis of TBM is crucial to explaining the challenges associated with treatment. The disease process commences with the hematogenous dissemination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis from a primary site, resulting in the formation of subpial or subependymal granulomas (Rich foci) in the brain and meninges [6]. The rupture of these foci into the subarachnoid space triggers an intense inflammatory response, leading to the production of a thick basal exudate, which underlies the principal complications of the disease, including hydrocephalus, vasculitis, infarction, cranial neuropathies, and tuberculomas [7]. Consequently, clinical deterioration is not only due to bacillary replication but also a result of a dysregulated host immune response. Effective management of TBM therefore requires a multifaceted approach, incorporating antimicrobial therapy that achieves bactericidal concentrations at the site of infection, modulation of harmful inflammation, and supportive care to manage raised intracranial pressure, hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia, seizures, and other complications [8]. Current antimicrobial regimens for TBM are largely derived from those developed for pulmonary tuberculosis, with guidelines recommending an intensive phase of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for two months, followed by isoniazid and rifampicin for a further 7 to 10 months [9]. However, this approach does not take into account the differing ability of these drugs to cross the blood-brain barrier, with isoniazid and pyrazinamide penetrating the cerebrospinal fluid well, whereas rifampicin, the most potent sterilizing agent in the regimen, achieves relatively low concentrations due to its high protein binding and status as a substrate for efflux transporters [10]. Ethambutol penetrates poorly, and streptomycin only does so in the presence of inflamed meninges. These pharmacokinetic limitations have prompted interest in higher doses of rifampicin, fluoroquinolones, and newer agents such as linezolid, which have more favorable central nervous system penetration [11]. The emergence of isoniazid- and multidrug-resistant tuberculosis complicates treatment, as the evidence for second-line regimens in TBM is limited, and the toxicity of prolonged therapy is considerable [12]. Adjunctive therapies are equally important, with corticosteroids, principally dexamethasone, shown to reduce mortality in HIV-uninfected patients and are standard of care [13]. However, their effect on disabling neurological outcome is less certain, and their role in HIV-associated TBM has not been established [14]. The recognition that inflammation and thrombosis drive much of the morbidity has stimulated interest in other host-directed therapies, including aspirin, thalidomide, anti-tumour necrosis factor agents, and other immunomodulators [15]. Variation in host genetic factors, such as polymorphisms in the LTA4H gene, may determine which patients benefit from particular immunomodulatory strategies, raising the possibility of individualized treatment [16]. Increasing understanding of innate immune pathways in the central nervous system may also reveal novel therapeutic targets. Supportive management, particularly of hydrocephalus, remains a neglected area. Hydrocephalus occurs in a large proportion of patients and is a strong predictor of death and disability [17]. Options include medical therapy with acetazolamide and furosemide, repeated lumbar puncture, and neurosurgical diversion by ventriculoperitoneal shunt or external ventricular drain [18]. However, the evidence for each is sparse, the selection and timing of intervention are poorly defined, and data for patients with HIV co-infection, who often present with advanced immunosuppression and a different pattern of disease, are almost absent [19]. Resource constraints in many high-burden settings further limit access to neurosurgical care and intensive monitoring. Several recent and ongoing clinical trials have begun to address these gaps, with mixed results. Phase 2 studies suggested that intensified rifampicin may improve survival, yet the most recent larger trial using 15 mg/kg/day did not demonstrate a mortality benefit, leaving uncertainty about the optimal dose and the role of other drugs [20]. This review aims to systematically evaluate the evidence for current and emerging antimicrobial agents, host-directed therapies, and supportive measures in the treatment of TBM in adults, summarizing pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic considerations, appraising clinical trials, and discussing the implications for clinical practice. By examining the complexities of TBM and the challenges associated with its treatment, we hope to contribute to the development of more effective management strategies for this devastating disease. The importance of a comprehensive approach to TBM, incorporating antimicrobial therapy, adjunctive treatments, and supportive care, cannot be overstated. As research continues to explore the pathogenesis of TBM and the efficacy of various treatment strategies, it is essential to prioritize individualized care, taking into account the unique needs and circumstances of each patient. Ultimately, a deeper understanding of TBM and its treatment will be crucial in reducing the significant morbidity and mortality associated with this disease, and improving the quality of life for those affected. Furthermore, the role of immunomodulatory therapies in the treatment of TBM warrants further investigation. The potential benefits of these therapies, including the reduction of inflammation and the modulation of the host immune response, must be carefully weighed against the risks of adverse effects and the complexities of individual patient needs. As the field of TBM research continues to evolve, it is essential to prioritize the development of personalized treatment strategies, tailored to the unique characteristics and circumstances of each patient. By doing so, we may ultimately improve the outcomes for individuals affected by this devastating disease, and reduce the significant burden of TBM on global health. Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) encompasses a broad spectrum of anomalies, from mild acetabular dysplasia and sbluxation to complete, high-riding dislocation of the femoral head. Its reported incidence varies widely with geographic region, ethnic background, and diagnostic criteria, ranging from about 1 per 1,000 live births for dislocation to more than 10 per 1,000 when mildeer instability and radiographic dysplasia are included [1,2]. When the codition is recognized early, in the neonatal peroid or the first months of life, conservative treatment with a harness or abduction splint is successful in most cases [3]. In many settings, however, screening is incomplete, and children present late, after walking age, with established dislocation or residual dysplasia. Residual acetabular dysplasia may also persist despite initially successful reduction [4,5]. Untreated or inadequately treated DDH has well-documented consequences. Pesristent acetabular insufficiency leads to abnormal load distirbution across the joint, labral damage, and early osteoarthritis, and dysplasia is considered one of the most important causes of seondary hip arthrosis in young adults [6,7]. The spontaneous remodeling potential of the acetabulum declines with age, and beyond roughly 18 to 24 months, it is generally considered unreliable [8]. In children older than 2 years, closed reduction becomes increasingly unlikely to succeed, and open reduction, often combined with femoral shortening and a pelvic osteotomy, is usually required to obtain a stable concentric jint [9,10]. Several pelvic osteotomies have been proposed to correct acetabular deficiency in children. They are broadly divided into redirectional procedures, such as the Salter, Steel, Tönnis, and Ganz osteotomies, which rotate the acetabulum as a unit, and reshapping procedures, such as the Pemberton and Dea osteotomies, which hinge the acetabular roof through the iliac cortices and alter its volume and configuration [11–13]. Salter's innominate osteotomy provides anterior and lateral cover but requires a stable, concentric reduction and may increase intra-articular pressure through medialization and lengthening of the limb [14]. The Pemberton osteotomy is a pericapsular procedure that reduces acetabular volume, and it depends on a flexible triradiate cartilage [12]. Each technique has specific indications and limitations, and no single procedure has been shown to be superior across all patterns of dysplasia. The osteotomy described by Dega in 1953 is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that runs from the outer cortex of the ilium toward the triradiate cartilage, leaving the inner cortex intact at the hinge [15]. The acetabular roof is then levered downward and held with a bone graft. Depending on the site of the deficiency, the osteotomy can be modified to increase anterior, lateral, or posteriior coverage, which makes it attractive for the heterogeneous acetabular deformities seen in DDH, including those associated with neuromuscular disease [16,17]. Since its original description, the procedure has been refined by several authors, and it has gained renewed interest because of its versatility, relatively low morbidity, and the avoidance of internal fixation in many cases [18,19]. Nevertheless, most published reports on the Dega osteotomy are shhort or medium term, involve small or mixed series, or combine different etiologies, and the English-language literature on its long-term outcome in idiopathic DDH remains limited [20,21]. Long-term data are patricularly important in DDH, since the ultimate goal of treatment is not only radiographic normalization in childhood but also preservation of a painless, functional hip innto adulthood. Radiographic indices such as the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Sharp angle may look satisfactory at skeletal maturity, yet degenerative changes may emerge decades later [22]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is the most feared complication of treatment, especially after open reduction, and it is a major determinant of poor outcome [23,24]. Other factors suggested to influence prognosis include age at surgery, degree of preoperative dislocation, the need for femoral osteotomy, residual acetabular dysplasia, and the quality of the reduction [9,25]. However, the relative weight of these predictors for the long-term survival of the hip after a Dega osteotomy has not been clearly established. Assessment of acetabular morphology and femoral head coverage has aso evolved. Plain radiographs may be difficult to interpret in the young child because of variable ossification and projection, and computed tomography has been used to define the three-dimensional pattern of acetabular deficiency and to verify reduction [26]. Whether such imaging adds prognostic or operative value in children undergoing Dega osteotomy is uncertain. The purrpose of this multicenter study was therefore to report the long-term clinical and radiographic results of the Dega osteotomy in children younger than 8 yaers with DDH, treated between 1988 and 2000 and followed for at leat 13 years. All radiographic measurements were made independently by two observers not involved in the surgery. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. Interobserver reliability was assessed with the intraclass correlation coefficient. Clinical evaluation Clinical examination was performed at each visit and at the final follow-up. Parameters included pain, gait (presence of limp and Trendelenburg sign), range of motion, limb length discrepancy, and activity level. Functional outcome was graded using the modified McKay criteria [10]. The final clinical outcome was dichotomized as favorable (excellent or good) or unfavorable (fair or poor). Complications, including redislocation, residual subluxation, infection, graft displacement, loss of correction, and AVN, were recorded. Secondary outcomes included radiographic indices at final follow-up and the incidence of complications. Hip survival was estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with secondary surgery or pain as the endpoint, and groups were compared using the log-rank test [11]. Receiver operating characteristic curves were usd to determine cut-off values for radiographic predictors. Because bilateral cases contribute correlated observations, sensitivity analyses were performed with one randomly selected hip per patient. A p value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed with SPSS software. The capacity for spontaneous remodeling of the acetabulum declines with age, and beyond approximately 18 to 24 months, this process is generally considered unreliable [8]. In children over 2 years of age, the likelihood of successful closed reduction diminishes, and open reduction, often combined with femoral shortening and pelvic osteotomy, is typically necessary to achieve a stable, concentric joint [9,10]. Various pelvic osteotomies have been developed to address acetabular deficiency in children, including redirectional procedures such as the Salter, Steel, Tönnis, and Ganz osteotomies, which involve rotating the acetabulum as a single unit, and reshaping procedures such as the Pemberton and Dega osteotomies, which alter the volume and configuration of the acetabular roof by hinging it through the iliac cortices [11–13]. Salter's innominate osteotomy provides anterior and lateral coverage but requires a stable, concentric reduction and may increase intra-articular pressure through medialization and lengthening of the limb [14]. The Pemberton osteotomy, a pericapsular procedure, reduces acetabular volume and relies on a flexible triradiate cartilage [12]. Each technique has its specific indications and limitations, and no single procedure has been demonstrated to be superior across all patterns of dysplasia. The Dega osteotomy, first described in 1953, is an incomplete transiliac osteotomy that extends from the outer cortex of the ilium toward the triradiate cartilage, leaving the inner cortex intact at the hinge [15]. The acetabular roof is then levered downward and secured with a bone graft. The osteotomy can be modified to increase anterior, lateral, or posterior coverage, depending on the site of the deficiency, making it an attractive option for the varied acetabular deformities seen in DDH, including those associated with neuromuscular disease [16,17]. Since its original description, the procedure has undergone refinement by several authors and has experienced renewed interest due to its versatility, relatively low morbidity, and avoidance of internal fixation in many cases [18,19]. Nonetheless, most published reports on the Dega osteotomy are limited by short or medium-term follow-up, involve small or mixed series, or combine different etiologies, and the English-language literature on its long-term outcome in idiopathic DDH remains limited [20,21]. Long-term data are particularly crucial in DDH, as the ultimate goal of treatment extends beyond radiographic normalization in childhood to include the preservation of a painless, functional hip into adulthood. Radiographic indices such as the acetabular index, center-edge angle, and Sharp angle may appear satisfactory at skeletal maturity, yet degenerative changes may emerge decades later [22]. Avascular necrosis (AVN) of the femoral head is a significant complication of treatment, especially after open reduction, and is a major determinant of poor outcome [23,24]. Other factors suggested to influence prognosis include age at surgery, degree of preoperative dislocation, the need for femoral osteotomy, residual acetabular dysplasia, and the quality of the reduction [9,25]. However, the relative importance of these predictors for the long-term survival of the hip after a Dega osteotomy has not been clearly established. The assessment of acetabular morphology and femoral head coverage has also evolved over time. Plain radiographs can be challenging to interpret in young children due to variable ossification and projection, and computed tomography has been used to define the three-dimensional pattern of acetabular deficiency and to verify reduction [26]. However, whether such imaging adds prognostic or operative value in children undergoing Dega osteotomy is uncertain. The purpose of this multicenter study was to report the long-term clinical and radiographic results of the Dega osteotomy in children younger than 8 years with DDH, treated between 1988 and 2000 and followed for at least 13 years. By combining prospectively and retrospectively collected cases, we aimed to analyze outcomes, complications, and the need for secondary surgery, with a particular focus on understanding the factors that influence the success and longevity of the hip joint following this procedure. This study seeks to provide a comprehensive understanding of the Dega osteotomy's effectiveness and its role in the management of DDH, ultimately contributing to improved treatment strategies and outcomes for affected children. The investigation of the Dega osteotomy's long-term results is critical, as it can inform clinicians about the potential benefits and limitations of this procedure, guiding decision-making in the treatment of DDH. Furthermore, the analysis of complications and the need for secondary surgery can help identify areas for improvement in the technique and postoperative care, ultimately enhancing patient outcomes. The long-term follow-up of patients who have undergone the Dega osteotomy is essential, as it allows for the assessment of the durability of the procedure and its ability to prevent degenerative changes and ensure a functional, painless hip joint into adulthood. By examining the outcomes of the Dega osteotomy in a large cohort of patients with DDH, this study aims to provide valuable insights into the management of this complex condition, contributing to the development of more effective treatment strategies and improved patient care. This investigation endeavors to elucidate the key determinants of hip arthrosis and the longevity of hip function following the Dega osteotomy procedure, with the ultimate objective of refining the indications and anticipated long-term outcomes of this surgical intervention in the management of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH). To accomplish this, a thorough examination of existing literature was undertaken, complemented by the aggregation of data from multiple clinical sites, encompassing patient demographics, clinical and radiographic outcomes, and complications. Furthermore, the factors influencing the success of the Dega osteotomy were scrutinized, including the patient's age at the time of surgery, the extent of preoperative dislocation, and the necessity for a concurrent femoral osteotomy. By deconstructing these variables and their impact on long-term outcomes, the study aimed to provide enhanced clarity on the role of the Dega osteotomy in the treatment of DDH, thereby informing clinical decision-making in this intricate and multifaceted condition. The Dega osteotomy is a highly adaptable procedure, capable of being modified to address diverse patterns of acetabular deficiency, rendering it an appealing option for the treatment of DDH. Nonetheless, its long-term outcomes and potential complications necessitate meticulous consideration, particularly in light of the paucity of existing literature on this topic. By reporting the findings and experiences garnered from this study, the researchers aspire to contribute to a more profound understanding of the Dega osteotomy and its role in the management of DDH, ultimately leading to improved patient outcomes and enhanced quality of life. The Dega osteotomy is a surgical procedure frequently employed in the treatment of DDH in young children. This multicenter study, conducted at three tertiary pediatric orthopedic centers, sought to investigate the long-term outcomes of this procedure in a cohort of children under the age of 8 years. The study was approved by the institutional review board at each center, and informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardians of all prospectively enrolled patients. For retrospective cases, consent for the use of anonymized data was obtained in accordance with local regulations, ensuring adherence to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. The study population comprised children who underwent a Dega osteotomy for DDH between January 1988 and October 2000. A total of 17 hips were identified retrospectively from hospital records and radiographic archives, while 41 hips were enrolled prospectively after the introduction of a standardized protocol. To be eligible for inclusion in the study, patients had to meet specific criteria: (1) a diagnosis of DDH, encompassing acetabular dysplasia, subluxation, and complete dislocation; (2) age at surgery between 2 and 8 years; (3) a Dega osteotomy performed as part of the index procedure; and (4) a minimum follow-up of 13 years. Exclusion criteria included teratologic or neuromuscular dislocations, syndromic conditions (e.g., arthrogryposis, myelomeningocele), previous surgery on the affected hip, and incomplete clinical or radiographic records. Following the application of these criteria, 58 hips in 48 children (ten bilateral cases) were included in the study. Demographic data, laterality, age at diagnosis, previous treatment (such as Pavlik harness, closed reduction, or traction), and age at surgery were documented for each patient. Dislocations were graded according to the Tönnis classification [1], a widely used system that categorizes hip dislocations into four grades, ranging from mild to severe. The Tönnis classification provides a standardized framework for evaluating the severity of hip dislocation. The surgical technique employed in this study was based on the original description by Dega [2] and modified by later authors [3]. The procedure involved an anterior iliofemoral (Smith-Petersen) incision, followed by the splitting of the iliac apophysis and subperiosteal exposure of the lateral wall of the ilium down to the capsule. A curved incomplete osteotomy was then performed through the lateral cortex from just above the anterior inferior iliac spine toward the posterior limb of the triradiate cartilage, preserving the medial cortex and the continuity of the sciatic buttress. The acetabular roof was levered downward and outward with a curved osteotome to redirect the acetabulum, and the osteotomy was held open with a wedge-shaped bone graft. The graft was typically harvested from the iliac wing, although in some cases, a bank allograft was utilized. Kirschner wires were employed for fixation at the surgeon's discretion. In cases where the femoral head was dislocated, open reduction was performed through the same incision, involving capsulotomy, resection of the ligamentum teres and pulvinar, release of the transverse acetabular ligament, and capsulorrhaphy. Adductor tenotomy and psoas release were performed as necessary to facilitate reduction and prevent complications. Femoral shortening, with or without derotation or varization, was added when the reduction was under tension or when excessive anteversion was present [4]. This approach enabled a comprehensive treatment of the hip deformity, addressing the complexities of DDH and promoting optimal outcomes. The Dega osteotomy has been demonstrated to be a valuable procedure in the treatment of DDH, offering the potential for improved hip function and reduced risk of long-term complications. However, the procedure's success is contingent upon careful patient selection, precise surgical technique, and meticulous postoperative care. By elucidating the factors that influence the success of the Dega osteotomy, this study aims to provide valuable insights for clinicians and researchers, ultimately contributing to the development of more effective treatment strategies for DDH. Traditional TCP binds a connection to a single pair of IP addresses and therefore a single path, leaving additional connectivity idle and offering no resilience when the actvie path degrades. Multipath TCP (MPTCP) [1], standardized by the IETF in RFC 6824 and later revised in RFC 8684, addresses this limitation. It extends TCP so that a single transport connnection can be split into several subflows, each traversing a different path, while remaining transparent to applications. By aggregating the capacity of the available paths, MPTCP can improve throughput, increase robustness against link failures, and support seamless handover between access networks [2], [3]. Despite these benefits, MPTPC must still provide the same service guarantee as TCP: a reliable, in-order byet stream delivered to the application. Data are assigned a connection-level sequence number at the sender, transmitted over different subflows, and reordered at the receiver in a connection-level buffer before delivery. When paths differ in delay and bandwidth, as is typical for heterogeneous combinations succh as WiFi and LTE, packets sent later on a fast path may arrive before packets sent earlier on a slow path. The receiver must then hold the early arrivals until the missing data come in. This out-of-order (OFO) arrival problem inflates the receive buffer occupancy, increases application-level delay and jitter, and can cause head-of-line blocking [4]. When the receive window is exhausted by buffered out-of-order data, the sender is stalled and the aggregate throughput may fall below that of the best single path [5], [6]. The problem is therefore not only a latency concern but also a fundamental obstacle to realizing the potential gains of multipath transport. The paacket scheduler, which decides on which subfllow each pacekt is transmitted, plays a central role in mitigating this problem. The defualt scheduler in the Liunx MPTP implementation, minRTT, selects the available subflow with the smallest smoothed round-trip time that has spce in its congestion window [7]. Although simple, it ignores the bandwidth and delay differences that determine when a packet will actually arrive, and it performs poorly under path heterogeneity. Round-robin scheduling is even less informed, since it distributes packets evenly regardless of path quality. Numerous alternatives have been proposed. Some, such as DAPS [8], plan the allocation of packets to paths in advance, using delay and window information so that packets arrive in order. Others, such as BLEST [9], estimate whether using a slow subflow will blokc the connection-level send window and skip that subflow when blocking is likely. ECF [10] considers the completion time of the remaining data on fast and slow paths and may wait for the fast path rather than use a slow one. Other approaches reinject or retransmit packets on faster paths [11], or use learning-based techniques to adapt scheduling decisions [12]. While these schemes yield improvements in particular scenarios, many rely on round-trip time as a proxy for path delay. The use of RTT is problematic for in-order delivery. What determines the order of arrival at the receiver is the one-way, forward delay of each path, not the round-trip delay. RTT includes the reverse path delay, which may differ substantially from the forward delay owing to asymmetric routing, asymmetric link capacities, and different queueing on acknowledgments' return path. In cellular and WiFi networks, uplink and downlink characteristics are often markedly different, and ACK compression or delay can further distort RTT samples. A scheduler guided by RTT may thus mispredict arrival times and dispathc packets in an order that causes reordering. Moreover, delay alone is insufficient: the time a packet spends in the network also depends on the transmission time governed by path throughput and on queueing behind packets already sent on the same path. An effective scheduler must account jointly for forward delay and throughput differences. Motivated by these observations, we propose the forward-delay-based packet scheduling (FDPS) algorithm for MPTCP. FDPS estimates the forward delay of each subflow and combines it with an estimate of subflow throughput to predict the arrival time of a packet if it were sent on each path. The sender then dispatches pakets so that those with earlier sequence numbers are expected to arrive earlier, and so that the arrival sequence at the receiver closely follows the transmission sequence. By making scheduling decisions on the basis of the forward path characteristics, FDPS reduces the dependence on potentially misleading round-trip measurements and limits the buffering needed for reordering. The main contributions of thiis paper are as follows. First, we analyze why RTT-based and delay-agnostic scheduling lead to out-of-order arrivals in heterogeneous multipath environments. Second, we design FDPS, which uses estimated forward delay and troughput differences among paths to schedule packets. Third, we evaluate FDPS through simulations under a variety of network conditions, varying bandwidth, delay, and asymmetry, and compare it with several existing schedulers. The results show that FDPS substantially improves in-order arrival at the receiver, reducing the reordering burden relative to the baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. It estimates the forward delay and throughput of each subflow and uses these estimates to decide which subflow carries each packet, so that packets reach the receiver in the order of their data sequence numbers. System Model We consider an MPTCP connection with N subflows, indexed i = 1,…,N, between a sender and a receiver, following the architecture in RFC 6824 [1]. Each subfow i has its own congestion window cwndi, smoothed round-trip time srtti, and subflow-level sequence space. A connection-level data sequence number (DSN) orders the byte stream across subflows. The scheduler assigns each DSN-mapped segment to a subflow that has available congestion window space. The receiver reorders segments in a shared receive buffer before delivering them to the application. A segment arriving with a DSN greater than the next expected one is out of order and must wait in the buffer. This causes head-of-line blocking and, when the buffer is limited, throttles throughput [2], [3]. For subflow i, the one-way forward delay Di is the time from transmission at the sender to arrival at the receiver. It consists of proagation delay pi, transmission delay s/Bi for a segment of size s on a path of bandwidth Bi, and queueing delay qi: Di = pi + s/Bi + qi. Using srtti/2 as a proxy for Di is common [4], but it fails on asymmetric paths and when reverse-path congestion inflates ACK delays. FDPS therefore estimates the forward component directly. Forward Delay Estimation The receiver stamps each arriving segment with its local clock and returns the stapm in a TCP option carried on the ACK, in the manner of the TCP timestamp option [5]. The sender records the send time Ts of each segment. Cocks are not assumed to be synchronized. Instead, the sender computes a relative forward delay, di(k) = Tr(k) − Ts(k), which equals Di(k) plus an unknown constant clock offset δ. For subflow i, the sender keeps the minimum observed value di^min, which approximates pi + s/Bi + δ when queues are empty. The offset δ is the same for all subflows because it is a property of the host pair. Differences between subflows are therefore unaffected by δ. The queueing-inclusive delay of the k-th sample is then D̂i(k) = di(k) − dmin, where dmin = minj dj^min. The result is a delay estimate of each path relative to the fastest one. The estimate is smoothed with an exponentially weighted moving average, D̄i ← (1 − α) D̄i + α D̂i(k), with α = 1/8, following the srtt convention [6]. Samples from retransmitted segments are discarded to avoid ambiguity. Throughput is estimated per subflow as the ratio cwndi/srtti, which gives the sending rate Ri the congestion controller currently permits. This is smoothed over a window of the most recent ACKs to dampen short-term oscillation. Scheduling Rule Suppose the scheduler is about to send a segment of size s on subflow i at time t. Its expected arrival time is Ai = t + D̄i + Qi/Ri, where Qi is the amount of data already queued or in flight on subflow i beyond what has been acknowledged, and Qi/Ri is the expected additional wait. The scheduler seeks to give consecutive DSNs arrival times that are monotonically non-decreasing. FDPS maintains Alast, the largest expected arrival time among segments already scheduled. For the next segment, it builds the candidate set C = { i : cwndi − inflighti ≥ s }. It then selects the subflow whose expected arrival time is closest to, but not earlier than, Alast: i = argmin{i∈C, Ai ≥ Alast} (Ai − Alast). This choice kepes the segment from overtaking earlier ones. If no subflow satisfies the constraint, because all candidates would deliver earlier than Alast, the scheduler selects the subflow with the largest Ai, which minimizes the reordering. If C is empty, transmission waits unitl an ACK opens a window. After the assignment, Alast is updated to A{i} and Q{i} is increased by s. Because a fast subflow may often be blocked by its window while a slow subflow is idle, FDPS also uses the throughput estimates. A slow subflow is assigned a segment only if its expected arrival is no later than that of a faster subflow after it becomes available. This means that, when delay differences are large, the slow path is used only for segments whose DSNs are far enough ahead of those on the fast path. In practice, the slow subflow receives earlier DSNs than the faast subflow in proportion to the delay gap D̄slow − D̄fast multiplied by Rfast. This is the same principle used by delay-aware schedulers such as DAPS [7], but here it is driven by measured forward delays instead of RTT ratios. Retransmissions are sent on the subflow with the smallest Ai, and opportunistic retransmission and penalization [3] are retained when the receive window blocks progress. Each scenario is repeated 20 times with different random seeds, and we report means with 95% confidence intervals. Rheumattoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic, systemic autoimmune disease charracterized by inflammation of the synovial joints, progressive destruction of articular cartilage and bone, and substantial disability if inadequately treated [1]. The autoimmune nature of RA is reflected in the production of a broad spectrum of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor directed against the Fc portion of IgG and, more specifically, anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) [2,3]. ACPA are detectable in sera and synovial fluids of approximately 60–70% of RA patients, may appaer years before clinical onset, and are associated with a more severe, erosve disease course. ACPA seropositivity is therefore incorporated into the current classification criteria for RA [4,5]. Citrullination and ACPA in RA Citrullination is a post-translational modification in which peptidylargniine residuues are converted to peptidylcitrulline by calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs). Tihs converrsion removes a positive charge, alters the hydrogen-bonding caapcity and isoelectric point of the protein, and can pormote unfolding, enhanced proteolytic susceptibility, and the generation of neoepitopes that escape immunological tolerance [6,7]. Citrullination occurs physiologically during apoptosis, differentiation, and inflammation, and is therefore not unique to RA. However, in the gneetically suscepible host, particularly carriers of HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, citrlulinated peptids are presented with higher affinity to CD4+ T cells, which supports B cell activation and ACPPA production [8,9]. Smoking and other mucosal insults, as well as periodontal infection, have been proposed as trigegrs of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10]. A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumatoid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11–14]. Citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can fomr immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells and thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. ACPA reactive with cartilage-derived citrullinated epitoes have aso been reported to induce or enhance arthritis in experimental models, suggesting taht antigens within the cartilage itself may be pathogenically relevant targets [16]. Aggrecan as an autoantigen in arthritis The large aggregating proteoglycan (PG) aggrecan is one of the most abundant macromolecules of articular cartilage, where it provides compressive resistance trough its highly charged glycosaminoglycan chains. Aggreccan comprises three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular and glycosaminoglycan-attachment region. The N-terminal G1 domain binds hyaluronan and link protein, anchoring the molecule wtihin the extracellular matrix [17]. Aggrecan has long beeen recognized as an arthritogenic autoantigen. Immunization of BALB/c mice with human cartilage PG induces a progressive, erosive polyarthritis (proteoglycan-induced arthritis, PGIA) that resembles human RA, with autoantibody production and T cell-dependent disease [18,19]. In addition, T cell responses to human PG, and in particular to peptides from the G1 domain, have been deteted in RA patients [20,21]. Importantly, more recent studies demonsrated that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan peptides, and that citrullinated epitopes within the G1 doman bind with high affinity to shared-epitope-containing HLA-DR molecules [22,23]. Citrullinated PG epitopes can also be recognized by T cells in the SKG and PGIA mouse models [24]. These findings suggest that citrullinated aggrecan may sreve as a joint-specific target of both T and B cell responses. This could help explain the loclization of the autoimmune attack to the joints, dspite the systemic distribution of ACCPA and of citrullinating enzymes. Knowledge gap and aims Despite thsi evidence, a fundamental question remains unanswered: whether the aggrecan molecule is actually citrullinated in vivo in human cartilage. Most studies have employed synthetic citrullinated peptides or in vitro modified proteins, which establish the immunological potential of citrullinated aggrecan but do not demonstrate the presence of the modified protein in the tissue. Cartilage is avascular and has low cellular density, and its matrix proteins turn over slowly, which could favoor the accumulation of post-translational modifications. Moreover, it is unknown whether citrullinated PG (CitPG) occurs in normal cartilage or only in diseased tissue, which fragments of the molecule carry the modification, and whether its distribution dfifers between osteoarthritis (OA) and RA. Clarifying these poins is essential for judging whether CitPG can serve as a taget for ACPA, form local immune complexes, and contribute to the initiation or perpetation of joint inflammation. The chronic autoimmune disorder known as rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is marked by the inflammation of synovial joints, which, if left untreated, can lead to the progressive degradation of articular cartilage and bone, ultimately resulting in significant disability [1]. A key characteristic of RA is the production of a diverse array of autoantibodies, including rheumatoid factor, which targets the Fc region of IgG, and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies (ACPA) [2,3]. These ACPA can be detected in the sera and synovial fluids of approximately 60-70% of RA patients, often appearing years before the onset of clinical symptoms. Furthermore, ACPA have been linked to a more severe and erosive disease course, which is why ACPA seropositivity is a crucial factor in the current classification criteria for RA [4,5]. The process of citrullination, which involves the conversion of arginine residues to citrulline by calcium-dependent peptidylarginine deiminases (PADs), plays a critical role in the development of ACPA [6,7]. This post-translational modification can alter the structure and function of proteins, leading to the creation of neoepitopes that can evade the immune system's tolerance mechanisms. Although citrullination is a physiological process that occurs during various cellular processes, including apoptosis, differentiation, and inflammation, it is not unique to RA. However, in individuals with a genetic predisposition, particularly those carrying HLA-DRB1 shared-epitope alleles, citrullinated peptides are presented to CD4+ T cells with higher affinity, supporting the activation of B cells and the production of ACPA [8,9]. Environmental factors, such as smoking and periodontal infection, have been proposed as potential triggers of citrullination that precede joint involvement [10]. A growing number of citrullinated autoantigens have been identified in the rheumatoid joint, including fibrin(ogen), vimentin, α-enolase, and type II collagen [11-14]. These citrullinated proteins and PAD enzymes are abundant in the inflamed synovium, and ACPA can form immune complexes with these antigens, activating complement and Fc receptor-bearing cells, thereby amplifying inflammation [15]. Moreover, ACPA that react with cartilage-derived citrullinated epitopes have been shown to induce or enhance arthritis in experimental models, suggesting that antigens within the cartilage itself may be pathogenically relevant targets [16]. One such antigen is aggrecan, a large aggregating proteoglycan that is one of the most abundant macromolecules in articular cartilage. Aggrecan provides compressive resistance to cartilage through its highly charged glycosaminoglycan chains and consists of three globular domains (G1, G2, and G3) and an extended interglobular and glycosaminoglycan-attachment region [17]. The N-terminal G1 domain of aggrecan binds to hyaluronan and link protein, anchoring the molecule within the extracellular matrix. Aggrecan has long been recognized as an arthritogenic autoantigen, and immunization of BALB/c mice with human cartilage PG induces a progressive, erosive polyarthritis (proteoglycan-induced arthritis, PGIA) that resembles human RA, with the production of autoantibodies and T cell-dependent disease [18,19]. Additionally, T cell responses to human PG, particularly to peptides from the G1 domain, have been detected in RA patients [20,21]. More recent studies have demonstrated that T cells from RA patients respond to citrullinated aggrecan peptides, and that citrullinated epitopes within the G1 domain bind with high affinity to shared-epitope-containing HLA-DR molecules [22,23]. Citrullinated PG epitopes can also be recognized by T cells in the SKG and PGIA mouse models [24]. These findings suggest that citrullinated aggrecan may serve as a joint-specific target of both T and B cell responses, which could help explain the localization of the autoimmune attack to the joints, despite the systemic distribution of ACPA and citrullinating enzymes. Despite the evidence, a fundamental question remains unanswered: whether the aggrecan molecule is actually citrullinated in vivo in human cartilage. Most studies have employed synthetic citrullinated peptides or in vitro modified proteins, which establish the immunological potential of citrullinated aggrecan but do not demonstrate the presence of the modified protein in the tissue. Cartilage is avascular and has low cellular density, and its matrix proteins turn over slowly, which could favor the accumulation of post-translational modifications. Moreover, it is unknown whether citrullinated PG (CitPG) occurs in normal cartilage or only in diseased tissue, which fragments of the molecule carry the modification, and whether its distribution differs between osteoarthritis (OA) and RA. Clarifying these points is essential for judging whether CitPG can serve as a target for ACPA, form local immune complexes, and contribute to the initiation or perpetuation of joint inflammation. In the present study, we sought to determine whether citrullinated aggrecan is present in human articular cartilage and to characterize its molecular features. We used sera from ACPA-positive RA patients to probe PG purified from normal cartilage and cartilage extracts from OA and RA patients, and we identified the PG fragments, particularly those containing the G1 and G3 domains, that carry citrulline-containing epitopes. We confirmed the citrullination status of an in vitro citrullinated recombinant human G1 domain (rhG1) using both antibody-based and chemical detection, and used molecular modeling to explore the potential sites of citrullination within this domain. Finally, we quantified CitPG-specific serum autoantibodies by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and compared the immunohistochemical localization of CitPG in cartilage from OA and RA patients to better understand its role in the pathogenesis of RA. The presence of citrullinated aggrecan in human cartilage could provide a critical link between the autoimmune response and the joint-specific damage observed in RA. By elucidating the molecular features of citrullinated aggrecan and its role in the immune response, we may uncover new targets for therapeutic intervention and improve our understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying this debilitating disease. The identification of citrullinated aggrecan as a potential target of the autoimmune response in RA could also lead to the development of novel diagnostic markers and therapeutic strategies, ultimately improving the outcomes for patients with this disease. Furthermore, the study of citrullinated aggrecan could provide valuable insights into the pathogenesis of other autoimmune diseases, where similar mechanisms of post-translational modification and immune recognition may be at play.
