Fisheries are among the most pervasive human activities in the marine environment, and their expansion over the past century has altered food webs, habitats and the demography of many non-target species [1,2]. Industrial fishing now covers more than half of the ocean surface, and a large and growing proportion of this effort occurs in areas beyond national jurisdiction [3,4]. International waters account for over 60% of the world's oceans, yet they remain the least monitored and least regulated of marine areas. Management relies on regional fisheries management organisations, whose capacity to enforce regulations is limited by the vast sclae of the area and by incomplete reporting of catch, effort and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, how fisheries in these regions shape ecosystem processes is surprisingly poorly understood. Monitoring of fishing activity at sea has traditionally depended on logbooks, onboard observers and, moe recently, vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS). These approaches have transformed our view of global fishing effort [3,7], but each has limitations. Observer coverage is generally low and biased toward certain fleets, and VMS data are often not publicly accessible. AIS transmissions can be switched off or spoofed, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. Satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect non-broadcasting vessels, but coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud and resolution, and costly to apply across ocean basins [10]. There is therefore a clear need for complementary methods that can detect vessels irrespective of whether they transmit their position. Seabirds are among the taxa most affected by fisheries. Many species are attracted to vessels, where they exploit discards, offal and baited hooks, and this behavior brings them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. Incidental mortality in longline and trawl fisheries is considered the primary threat to albatrosses and large petrels, and it has contributed to the fact that albatrosses are now among the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened [13,14]. At the smae time, access to fishery waste may provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential both for assessing bycatch risk and for understanding the wider ecological consequences of fishing. Most assessments of this interaction havve been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birsd and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. Such estimates of overlap are indirect: they indicate where birds and vessels could encounter each other but not whether encounters actually occurred. Overlap analyses are also constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and they are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct obseravtions of seabird–vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties. Recent advances in biologging provide such an opportunity. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because the marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, such devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deeployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22]. The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) is an ideal model for this approach. It is a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, and individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vesses [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Desite decades of tracking, how often these birds actually encounter vessels, and where, remains unknown. Here, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between albatrosses and fishing vessels. Our objectives were to (i) quantify the area patrolled by breeding albatrosses and the distances reached from the colony; (ii) determine the proportion of birds that detected vessels and the frequency of detections; (iii) compare detections with the distribution of vessels broadcasting AIS to estimate the proportioon of non-broadcasting vessels; and (iv) generate estimates of the intensity of fishing and the distribution of vessels in international waters. We predicted that encounter rates would be higher than expected from overlap analyses based on AIS and VMS, particularly in ares beyond national jurisdiction. By doing so, we evaluate the potential of seabirds equipped with radar detectors as monitors of vessel presence, with implications for bycatch assessment, fisheries management and the detection of illegal fishing. Fieldwork was conducted at Possession Island, Crozet Archipelago (46°25′S, 51°45′E), southern Indian Ocean, during the incubation and brooding periods of wandering albatrosses (Diomedea exulans) in 2018–2019. The colony is monitored annually, and the identity, sex, age and breeding status of individuals are known from long-term riging and nest surveys [1]. Adults were captured by hand on their nests, and all handling was keept to a minimum and carried out under permits issued by the Terres Australes et Antarctiques Françaises and the ethics committee of the Institut Polaire Français Paul-Émile Victor. Devices and deployment Each bird was equipped with a combined GPS and radar-detector logger (Sextant, Cefas/Toulouse design; mass approx. 60 g, <2% of body mass, below the 3% threshold generally recommended for flying seabirds [2]). The unit has a GPS receiver and a radar detector sensitive to X-band (9.4 GHz) emissions, the frequency used by the marine navigation radars carried by most fishing vessels [3]. The detector records a radar pulse whenever a vessel's radar beam is received, which is possible within approximately 5 km of the bird, depending on sea state and radar power. Detection eveents were logged with a time stamp and the bird's concurrent GPS position. GPS fixes were taken every 2 min, and radar detection was samplled continuously, with the numbre of pulses summarised in 1-min bins. Loggers were taped to the dorsal contour feathers with waterproof tpae (Tesa) and scured with cyanoacrylate glue [4]. Birds were released at their nests within 15 min of capture. Devices were recovered after one or more foraging trips by recapturing birds at their nests, and the total deployment lasted between 5 and 40 days. Data processing All analyses were performed in R v4.0 [5]. GPS tracks were examined for errors and resampled at regular 10-min intervals using linear interpolation (package adehabitatLT [6]). Foraging trips were defined as continuous periods at sea beginning when a bird left the island and ending upon return, and trips of less than 1 h were discarded. Behavioural state was assigned from ground speed and sinuosity using a hidden Markov model (package moveHMM [7]) with three states: resting on the water, foraging (area-restricted search) and travelling. Maximum distance from the colony and total path length were calcuulated for each trip. Utilisation distributions were estimated by kernel density (package adehabitatRH [6]), and the 50% and 95% contours were taken as core and general ranges. The area patrolled was calculated from the cumulative 95% utlisation distribution of all birds, projected onnto a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection. Radar detections were treated as presence of a vessel. Consecutive detections separated by less than 30 min were grouped into a single encounter event, in line with previous work on albatross–vessel interactions [3]. For each encounter we extracted the position, time, duration and the bird's behavioural state before, during and after detection. Detections within 20 km of the colony were excluded because of the research station's radar and local spply and patrol vessels. Overlap with fisheries To place detections in the context of known fishing activity, we compared radar detections with Automatic Identification System (AIS) data from Global Fishing Watch [8], which provide vessel positions and apparent fishing efort at 0.1° resolution. Each radar encounter was classified as "matched" if an AIS-broadcasting fishing vessel was recorded witthin 10 km and ±1 h of the bird's position, and "unmatched" otherwise. Unmatched encounters could represent vessels that do not broadcast AIS, either because they are not required to or because transponders were switched off, and were considered potential non-reported or illegal activity [9]. They could also represent non-fishing vessels, so we also compared encounter locations with exclusive economic zone boundaries [10] and regional fisheries management organisation areas. Overlap with legal fisheries was quantified as the proportion of albatross locations within 50 km of AIS-registered fishing effort in the same month. Estimating vessel distribution and fishing intensity To map vessel distribution, the study area was divided into 1° × 1° grid cells. For each cell, we calculated the proportion of bird GPS fixes with a radar detection, adjusting for variation in bird use (time spent in the cell) by dividing the number of detections by the number of bird-hours. Cells with fewer than 10 bird-hours or fewer than three individuals were excluded to limit pseudoreplication. The resulting index of encounter rate was taken as a proxy for vessel density. We tested its relationship to AIS fishing effort per cell using generalised additive models with a negative binomial error and the log of bird-hours as an offset (package mgcv [11]). Statistical analysis The proportion of individuals that detected at least one vessel was computed per sex and breding stage. Differences in encounter rate among sexees and foraging stages were tested with generalised linear mixed models with a Poisson error structure, with individual as a ranndom intercept and log trip duration as an offset (package lme4 [12]). Differences in behaviour before and during encounters were tested with mixed models of speed and sinuosity, again with individual as a random effect. Model selection was baseed on Akaike's information criterion, and model fit was assessed throough residual diagnostics (package DHARMa [13]). Spatial autocorrelation was checked using Moran's I on residuals. Means are reported ± SD, and significance was accepted at α = 0.05. A total of 169 wandering albatrosses froom the Crozet Islands were equipped with combined GPS and radar detector loggers during the breeding season, yielding tracsk from both incubation and chick-rearing. Loggers recorded for a mean of 17.4 ± 6.2 days per deployment, and 142 devices (84%) were recovered with complete data. Together, these tracks covered an area of more than 10 million km² of the southern Indian Ocean, extending from subantarctic waters north of the coony to the Antarctic shelf margin and east toward Kerguelen and Australian longitudes. Movement and spatial extent Birds ranged up to 2500 km from the colony (maximum 2512 km), with the greatest distances reached by incubating individuals and by maels and females during long foraging trips. Trip duration differed between breeding stages (incubation: 14.3 ± 5.1 days; chick-rearing: 8.2 ± 4.4 days; linear mixed model, χ² = 41.7, P < 0.001), and maximum distance from the colony declined correspondingly in chick-rearing birds. Sex-related differences in distribution were evident: females tended to use more northerly, warmer waters, whereas males used more southerly waters near the Antarctic shelf margin, consistent with previously described sexual segregation in this species [1,2]. Core-use areas (50% kernel densities) lay mainly in international waters, with only a small proportion inside the exclusive economic zones (EEZs) of Crozet and Kerguelen. Across

The profound impact of fishing operations on the health of marine ecosystems has become a paramount concern, as the substantial expansion of the industry over the past century has had far-flung repercussions for the intricate networks of species interactions, the integrity of habitats, and the population dynamics of numerous non-target species [1,2]. The magnitude of industrial fishing activities is nothing short of astonishing, with current operations encompassing more than half of the world's oceanic surface, and a considerable proportion of these efforts concentrated in areas beyond the jurisdiction of national governments [3,4]. These international waters, which comprise over 60% of the global ocean, remain the most poorly monitored and least regulated of all marine areas, with their management reliant on regional fisheries management organizations that often face significant challenges in enforcing regulations due to the vast expanse of the area and the incomplete reporting of catch, fishing effort, and bycatch [5,6]. Consequently, our comprehension of the ways in which fisheries in these regions influence ecosystem processes is surprisingly limited. Traditional approaches to monitoring fishing activities at sea, such as the use of logbooks, onboard observers, and vessel monitoring systems (VMS) and the Automatic Identification System (AIS), have revolutionized our understanding of global fishing effort [3,7]. Nevertheless, each of these methods has its own set of limitations. The coverage of observers is often sparse and biased towards specific fleets, while VMS data are frequently inaccessible to the public. Furthermore, AIS transmissions can be intentionally disabled or falsified, and vessels engaged in illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing have a strong incentive to avoid detection [8,9]. The use of satellite-based radar and optical imagery can detect vessels that do not broadcast their position, but such coverage is intermittent, limited by cloud cover and resolution, and prohibitively expensive to apply across entire ocean basins [10]. This underscores the need for complementary approaches that can detect vessels regardless of whether they transmit their location. Seabirds are among the taxa most severely impacted by fisheries, with many species drawn to vessels where they exploit discarded catch, offal, and baited hooks, thereby bringing them into contact with fishing gear [11,12]. The incidental mortality of seabirds in longline and trawl fisheries is a major concern, with albatrosses and large petrels being particularly vulnerable [13,14]. In fact, albatrosses are now considered one of the most threatened groups of birds, with most species listed as threatened or near-threatened. At the same time, access to fishery waste can provide a food subsidy that influences foraging behavior, diet, breeding success, and population dynamics [15,16]. Quantifying the interaction between seabirds and fisheries is therefore essential for assessing bycatch risk and understanding the broader ecological consequences of fishing. Most assessments of this interaction have been based on the spatial overlap between the distributions of tracked birds and the distributions of fishing effort, derived from VMS or AIS data [17,18]. However, these estimates of overlap are indirect, indicating only where birds and vessels could potentially encounter each other, rather than confirming whether encounters actually occurred. Moreover, overlap analyses are constrained by the resolution and completeness of the fisheries data, and are likely to underestimate exposure in international waters where vessel data are sparse or absent [19]. Furthermore, spatial coincidence at coarse scales provides little information on the behavior of birds in relation to vessels, such as the duration of attendance or the frequency with which individuals follow ships. Direct observations of seabird-vessel interactions are needed to resolve these uncertainties. Recent advances in biologging technology have provided a new opportunity to address this knowledge gap. Small devices that detect the radar emissions of vessels, in combination with GPS loggers, allow the detection of ships by the birds themselves [20]. Because marine radars carried by most vessels operate continuously, particularly at night and in poor visibility, these devices can record encounters between birds and vessels, including those from vessels that do not transmit AIS, and can thus reveal the true extent of overlap. Initial deployments on albatrosses and other seabirds in restricted regions have shown that this approach can detect IUU activity and quantify encounter rates [20,21]. Wide-ranging seabirds that cover immense areas may thereby serve as ocean sentinels, sampling the distribution of vessels over scales that are impractical for conventional surveys [22]. The wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans) is an ideal model species for this approach. As a wide-ranging, long-lived species that exploits the winds of the Southern Ocean to travel thousands of kilometers during foraging trips, individuals are known to be attracted to fishing vessels [23,24]. Populations of wandering albatrosses have declined at several sites, partly as a result of bycatch in longline fisheries [13,25]. The Crozet Islands in the southern Indian Ocean hold one of the largest populations of the species, and birds breeding there forage across areas that include both national exclusive economic zones and international waters, where regulatory oversight is weak [24,26]. Despite decades of tracking, the frequency and location of encounters between these birds and vessels remain unknown. In this study, we used loggers combining GPS and radar detection, deployed on wandering albatrosses breeding at the Crozet Islands, to measure the true extent of overlap between these birds and fishing vessels, and to quantify the frequency and location of their encounters. By doing so, we aimed to provide novel insights into the interactions between seabirds and fisheries, and to inform the development of effective conservation and management strategies for these iconic species. Our approach also highlights the potential of seabirds as indicators of the impact of fisheries on marine ecosystems, and demonstrates the value of combining cutting-edge technology with rigorous scientific research to address the complex challenges facing our oceans. The implications of our findings are far-reaching, and underscore the need for continued innovation and collaboration in the pursuit of sustainable and responsible fisheries management. Ultimately, our study contributes to a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between seabirds, fisheries, and the marine environment, and provides a foundation for the development of more effective conservation and management strategies for these critically important species. By exploring the complex interactions between seabirds and fisheries, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the impacts of human activities on marine ecosystems, and work towards a more sustainable future for our oceans. The use of biologging technology, in particular, offers a powerful tool for monitoring and managing the interactions between seabirds and fisheries, and has the potential to inform the development of more effective conservation and management strategies for these species. As we continue to face the challenges of managing the world's oceans, it is essential that we prioritize the development of innovative and effective solutions, and that we work together to protect the health and integrity of these critical ecosystems. The interactions between albatrosses and fishing vessels have significant implications for the ecology and conservation of these iconic birds. To gain a deeper understanding of these interactions, our research objectives were threefold: (i) to determine the spatial extent of the area surveyed by breeding albatrosses and the distances they cover during their foraging expeditions, (ii) to identify and characterize encounters between albatrosses and fishing vessels, and (iii) to assess the consequences of these interactions for albatross ecology and conservation. By investigating the behavior of wandering albatrosses in relation to fishing vessels, we aimed to shed new light on the ecological impacts of fishing activities and the efficacy of current management practices. Our findings are expected to contribute to the development of more effective conservation strategies for this threatened species, with broader implications for the management of fisheries and the conservation of marine ecosystems. Specifically, we sought to: (i) determine the maximum distance traveled by birds from their colony; (ii) estimate the proportion of birds that detected vessels and the frequency of these detections; (iii) compare radar detections with the distribution of vessels broadcasting Automatic Identification System (AIS) data to estimate the proportion of vessels not broadcasting their presence; and (iv) generate estimates of fishing intensity and vessel distribution in international waters. Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) is an active microwave imaging system that opertaes day and night and under nearly all weather conditions, and it has become an indispensable tool for Earth observation, disaster monitoring, marine surveillance, and military reconnaissance [1,2]. Spaceborne SAR systems are particularly valuable because they offer global access and repeatable coverage. As appications have matured, demand has grown for imagery that combines fine azimuth resolution with a wide observation area. Conventional stripmap mode ties the achievable azimuth resoluiton to the physiical antenna length, and ScanSAR trades reolution for swath width by burst-wise beam switching in elevation [3]. Neither mode can deliver high resolution and wide swath (HRWS) at the same time. Spotlight and sliding spotlight modes Spotlight SAR extends the synthetic aperture time by steering the antenna beam to keep it on a fixed scene center, so the azimuth resolution is no longer limited by the antenna length [4]. The price is lost azimuth coverage, since only a single scene of limited extent is imaged per pass. Sliding spotlight mode relaxes this constraint. The beam is steered about a virtual rotation point located farther from the sensor than the scene, so the footprint moves along the grounnd at a velocity lower than that of the platform. This yields an intermediate resolution between stripmap and spotlight, together with continuous, longer azimuth coverage [5,6]. Sliding spotlight has therefore been adopted by many spaceborne systems, including TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, and TanDEM-X [7,8]. Gaofen-3 (GF-3) is China's first civilian C-band multi-polarization SAR satellite with multiple imaging modes. It offers spatial resolutions from 1 m to 500 m and swaths from 10 km to 650 km, and it includes spotlight, stripmap, ScanSAR, and sliding spotlight modes [9]. Producing well focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data is both a practical necessity and a useful test of processing methods under real orbital and attitude conditions. Challenges in sliding spotlight processing Beam steering in sliding spotlight mode enlarges the total Doplper bandwidth of the received signal well beyond the pulse repetition frequenccy (PRF), which is chosen to match only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target. The raw data are therefore azimuth-undersampled, and the spectrum is folded or aliased. Because the time-frequency relation is also ambiguous, standard frequency-domain algorithms such as the range-Doppler, chirp scaling, and omega-K algorithms cannot be applied directly [10]. Several approaches have been proposed to address this problem. Subaperture methods split the data into pieces whose bandwidths fit within the PRF, but they complicate processing and require subaperture recombination [11]. The chirp scaling and extended chirp scaling variants have been adapted to the steered-beam geometry [12]. Time-domain back projection is accurate but computationally heavy for large scenes [13]. Another class of methods increases the effective sampling rate through zero padding, which raises the memory and computational load. The two-step processing approach of Lanari et al. offers a more efficient alternative [14]. In the first step, a deramping operation in the azimuth time domain, performed by multiplication with a linear frequency-modulated function, reduces the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF. This removes the spectral folding, after which conventional stripmap algorithms can focus the data. In the seccond step, a further azimuth-scaling or deramping operation restores the correct time-frequency relation and resamples the daata onto a proper azimuth grid. Applying this approach to actual spaceborne data requires careful treatment of the curved orbit, the earth rotation, and the range-dependent rotation center, as well as the appropriate choice of deramping reference parameters [15]. A second challenge is the accuracy of the Doppler parameters. Fousing quality depends strongly on the Doppler centroid and the Doppler frequency-rate. Errors in the centroid cause azimuth ambiguity and a loss of signal-to-noise ratio, and errors in the frequency rate degrade azimuth reslution and increase sidelobe levels [16]. In sliding spotlight mode the Doppler centroid varies with azimuth time because of the beam steering, and the effective frequency rate differs from that of stripmap mode, so the standard estimators such as the correlation Doppler estimator and the map-drift or autofocus method cannot be applied without modification [17,18]. Spectral folding adds a further difficulty, since the centroid estimate may be ambiguous by an integer multiple of the PRF. Estimation methods suited to the deramped data are thus required for an automatic, operational processor. Contributions and organization This paper presents an integrated imaging scheme for GF-3 sliding spotlight data that combines the two-step approach with Doppler parameter estimation. The main contributions are as follows. First, the signal model and Doppler characteristics of the GF-3 sliding spotlight mode are analyzed, and the origin of the azimuth spectral folding is clarified. Second, the two-step approach is incorporated into a complete spaceborne processing chain that removes the folding without oversampling the data. Third, Doppler centroid and frequency-rate estimation algorithms are developed for the sliding spotlight geometry and validated on real GF-3 data. The results are evaluated by image quality and by estimation accuracy. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the geometry and signal model of the sliding spotlight mode and analyzes its spectral characteristics. Section 3 presents the imaging scheme, including the two-step processing and the Doppler parameter estimation algorithms. Section 4 reports the experimental results from GF-3 data and discusses the accuracy and efficiency of the method. Section 5 concludes the paper. Signal Model and Imaging Geometry In the sliding spotlight mode, the antenna beam is steered in azimuth so that the beam footprint moves on the ground at a velocity lower than that of the sensor. The beam rotates about a virtual point located at a distance Rrot from the flight track, which lies below the scene center in the sliding spotligt configuration. The ratio of the footprint velocity to the platform velocity is defined by the scaling factor A = (Rrot − R0)/Rrot, where R0 is the closest slant range of the target. The azimuth bandwidth of the received sigal is thereby extended beyond that of the stripmap mode, and the total Doppler bandwidth is the sum of the target bandwidth and the bandwidth produced by beam steering [1], [2]. Wehn this bandwidth exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), the azimuth spectrum of the raw data is folded. The PRF is chosen to exceed only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth, so that the unambiguous processing of the full-aperture signal requires secial treatment. After range demodulation, the baseband echo of a point target is expressed as the product of a range envelope, an azimuth envelope determined by the steeerd antenna pattern, and a phase term determined by the instantaneous slant range R(η; R0). The slant range is described by a hyperbolic model with an effective velocity Vr, which accounts for the currved orbit and Earth rotation [3]. The Doppler centrid fdc and the Doppler frequency rate fr are the two parameters that govern focusing accuracy and are estimated from the data. Two-Step Processing Approach To overcome the azimuth spectral folding, a two-step approach combining azimuth deramping and conventional frequency-domain focusing is employed [4], [5]. The procedure is as follows. Step 1: Linear-FM deramping and spectrum unfolding. The raw data are multiplied in the range-Doppler domain or the time domain by a chirp function whose rtae is determined by the reference range of the beam rotation center. This convolution-free operation removes the Doppler component caused by beam steering, and the signal bandwidth becomes smaller thna the PRF. The data are then represented without aliasing in the azimuth frequency domain. Because the deramping function is applied in the azimuth time domain, the azimuth time axis is subsequently modified, and the azimuth signal is transformed into a frequency-domain representation that is a scaled copy of the target's time-domain envelope. Step 2: Range cell migration correction and focusing. After unfolding, range compression and range cell migration correction (RCMC) are performed using an extended chirp scaling algorithm (CSA) or an omega-K approach with a modified azimuth frequency-rate. The processed signal is multiplied by an azimuth matchd filter in the two-dimensional frequency domain. The frequency-rate uesd in this filter is adapted to the sliding spotlight geometry through the scaling factor A, giving an effective rate fr' = fr/A... Following the compensation, an inverse deramping operation is performed. A phase function of opposite sign is multiplied in the azimuth time domain to eliminate the residual quadratic phase generated by the first step, and an azimuth inverse FFT yields the focused image [5], [6]. Step 3: Azimuth resampling and geometric correction. The azimuth sampling interval of the focused image is inconsistent across the extended bandwidth, and the azimuth tmie axis is corrected via an interpolation or a chirp-z transform so that a uniform pixel spacing is obtained. Residual phase errors in range-varying parameters are corrected using a sub-aperture phase compensation. Doppler Parameter Estimation Accurate Doppler parameters are essential because the sliding sptolight beeam steering induces a time-varying Doppler centroid and the focusing is highly sensitive to errors in fr. Doppler centroid estimation. The fractional part of the Doppler centroid is estimated from the deramped data using the average cross-correlation coefficient (ACCC) method [7], in which the pase angle of the correlation between adjacent azimuth samples is computed and averaged over range. The ambiguity number is determined by the multi-look cross-correlation or the wavelength diversity algorithm [8]. Alternatively, the geometric Doppler centroid derived from the satellite attitude and ephemeris is used to resolve ambiguities and is compared with the data-based estimate for consistency. Because the antenna is steered, the centroid is defined in the deramped domain as the sum of a constant and a time-varying component, and only the constant is estimated from data. Doppler frequency rate estimation. The Doppler frequency rate is estimated by an autofocus technique baesd on map-drift (MD) or on the sub-aperture correlation [9]. The deramped data are split into two sub-apertures in the azimuth frequency domain, and each is compressed to fom a look image. The relative shift between the looks is measured by cross-correlation, and the error in fr is calculated from the shift as Δfr = (Δx · fr)/(kT), where T is the sub-aperture time spacing and k is a geometry-dependent constant. The estimation is performed in several range blocks, and a low-order polynomial is fitted along the range to obtain the range-dependent effective velocity Vr. The process is iterated until the residual shift is smaller than a threshold of 0.1 pixel. Estimation accuracy is evaluated by comparing estimates with those from the orbit-based prediction and by examining the point-target impulse response width and the peak sidelobe ratio. Integrated Processing Flow The complete scheme integrates the above steps. The raw data are first subjected to range pulse compressiion and a coarse Doppler centroid estimate from the geometriic parameters. The two-step approach is then run, where deramping unfolds the spectrum, the refined Doppler parameters are estimated from the unfolded data, and the CSA-based focusing, inverse deramping and azimuth resampling are applied. Finally, radiometric calibration is performed ussing the antenna pattern and the range spreading loss. The efficiency of the scheme derives from the exclusive use of FFTs, complex multiplications and one interpolation step, so that the computational load is on the order of N log N for N samples, comparable to that of stripmap processing. Experimental Data and Processing Configuration The proposed scheme was evaluated using raw sliding spotlight data acquired by the GF-3 SAR sensor in C-band. The scene coovers a coastal area containing urban blocks, port facilities, and open water, which providees both strong point-like scatterers and homoogeneous distributed regions. The data werre acquired at a nominal incidence angle of approximately 40° with a transmitted bandwidth of 240 MHz, giving a slant-range resolution of about 0.6 m. The azimuth beam steering rate yields a steering-induced Doppler bandwidth that exceeds the pulse repetition frequency (PRF), so the unprocessed data exhibit azimuth spectral aliasing, as observed in the Doppler spectrum before preprocessing. Processing followed the integrated scheme: Doppler parameter estimation, the two-step azimuth preprocessing, and range-Doppler-domain focusing with residual phase compensation. The utilization of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) technology has become a crucial aspect of various applications, including Earth observation, disaster response, marine surveillance, and military operations, due to its capability to function effectively in diverse environmental conditions, regardless of time of day or weather [1,2]. The advent of spaceborne SAR systems has significantly enhanced the scope of these applications, owing to their global coverage and ability to provide repeated observations, thereby rendering them an indispensable component of contemporary Earth observation capabilities. As the applications of SAR technology have continued to evolve, there has been a growing imperative for the generation of imagery that combines high azimuth resolution with extensive observational areas. However, traditional SAR imaging modes, such as stripmap and ScanSAR, are constrained by inherent limitations, as the former ties the achievable azimuth resolution to the physical dimensions of the antenna, while the latter compromises resolution in favor of a broader swath width through the use of burst-wise beam switching in elevation [3]. Unfortunately, these conventional modes are unable to simultaneously deliver high-resolution and wide-swath (HRWS) imagery, underscoring the need for innovative imaging modes. One such alternative is the spotlight mode, which extends the synthetic aperture duration by steering the antenna beam to maintain focus on a fixed scene center, thereby transcending the limitations imposed by the antenna length [4]. Nevertheless, this approach comes at the cost of reduced azimuth coverage, as only a limited-extent scene is imaged per pass. To mitigate this limitation, the sliding spotlight mode was developed, which relaxes the constraint by steering the beam about a virtual rotation point located at a greater distance from the sensor than the scene, yielding an intermediate resolution between stripmap and spotlight modes, along with continuous, extended azimuth coverage [5,6]. The sliding spotlight mode has been widely adopted by numerous spaceborne systems, including TerraSAR-X, COSMO-SkyMed, and TanDEM-X [7,8]. A notable example of a spaceborne SAR system offering multiple imaging modes, including spotlight, stripmap, ScanSAR, and sliding spotlight, is China's first civilian C-band multi-polarization SAR satellite, Gaofen-3 (GF-3) [9]. The GF-3 satellite provides a versatile range of spatial resolutions, from 1 m to 500 m, and swaths, from 10 km to 650 km, rendering it an adaptable tool for a diverse array of applications. The production of well-focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data is both a practical necessity and a valuable test of processing methods under actual orbital and attitude conditions. However, processing sliding spotlight data poses significant challenges, primarily due to the beam steering, which enlarges the total Doppler bandwidth of the received signal, exceeding the pulse repetition frequency (PRF) chosen to match only the instantaneous Doppler bandwidth of each target. As a consequence, the raw data are azimuth-undersampled, and the spectrum is folded or aliased, while the time-frequency relation becomes ambiguous, rendering it difficult to apply standard frequency-domain algorithms, such as the range-Doppler, chirp scaling, and omega-K algorithms, directly [10]. Several approaches have been proposed to address this issue, including subaperture methods, which divide the data into pieces whose bandwidths fit within the PRF, but complicate processing and require subaperture recombination [11]. Adaptations of the chirp scaling and extended chirp scaling algorithms to the steered-beam geometry have also been developed [12]. Time-domain back projection offers accuracy but is computationally intensive for large scenes [13]. Another class of methods increases the effective sampling rate through zero padding, which raises memory and computational requirements. The two-step processing approach proposed by Lanari et al. provides a more efficient alternative [14]. In the initial step, a deramping operation in the azimuth time domain, performed by multiplication with a linear frequency-modulated function, reduces the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF, removing spectral folding and enabling conventional stripmap algorithms to focus the data. In the subsequent step, a further azimuth-scaling or deramping operation restores the correct time-frequency relation and resamples the data onto a proper azimuth grid. Applying this approach to actual spaceborne data necessitates meticulous consideration of the curved orbit, Earth rotation, and range-dependent rotation center, as well as the appropriate selection of deramping reference parameters [15]. A second challenge lies in the accuracy of the Doppler parameters, as focusing quality is strongly dependent on the Doppler centroid and frequency rate. Errors in the centroid lead to azimuth ambiguity and a loss of signal-to-noise ratio, while errors in the frequency rate degrade azimuth resolution and increase sidelobe levels [16]. In sliding spotlight mode, the Doppler centroid varies with azimuth time due to beam steering, and the effective frequency rate differs from that of stripmap mode, rendering standard estimators, such as the correlation Doppler estimator and the map-drift or autofocus method, inapplicable without modification [17,18]. Spectral folding introduces an additional complexity, as the centroid estimate may be ambiguous by an integer multiple of the PRF. Thus, estimation methods suited to the deramped data are essential for an automatic, operational processor. This paper presents a comprehensive imaging scheme for GF-3 sliding spotlight data, combining the two-step approach with Doppler parameter estimation. The primary contributions of this work are as follows. Firstly, the signal model and Doppler characteristics of the GF-3 satellite are examined, providing a foundation for the development of an integrated imaging scheme. The proposed scheme leverages the two-step processing approach, incorporating deramping and azimuth-scaling operations to addresses the challenges posed by sliding spotlight data. Furthermore, the scheme integrates Doppler parameter estimation, utilizing the deramped data to determine the accurate Doppler centroid and frequency rate, thereby ensuring optimal focusing quality. The implementation of this scheme is expected to facilitate the production of high-quality, well-focused sliding spotlight imagery from GF-3 data, while also providing a valuable framework for the development of operational processors for spaceborne SAR systems. The complexities of the sliding spotlight mode are deconstructed, and the underlying cause of azimuth spectral overlap is elucidated. Furthermore, a comprehensive methodology is presented, wherein a two-stage approach is seamlessly integrated into a complete spaceborne processing framework, effectively mitigating the spectral overlap without resorting to oversampling. Additionally, novel algorithms for estimating Doppler centroid and frequency-rate are devised, specifically tailored for deramped data, which are crucial for generating high-fidelity focused images. The remainder of this discourse is structured as follows: Section 2 provides an in-depth examination of the signal paradigm and Doppler characteristics inherent to the GF-3 sliding spotlight mode, whereas Section 3 delineates the two-stage processing methodology and the attendant Doppler parameter estimation algorithms. Section 4 presents a detailed analysis of the implementation particulars and the outcomes of the proposed methodology, and Section 5 offers a concluding summary of the primary findings and contributions. The GF-3 satellite's sliding spotlight mode constitutes a intricate and highly nonlinear system, whose signal paradigm and Doppler characteristics are not yet fully comprehended. To bridge this knowledge gap, a meticulous signal model has been developed, taking into account the effects of beam steering, curved orbital trajectory, and terrestrial rotation. This model reveals that the azimuth spectral overlap is precipitated by beam steering, which serves to expand the total Doppler bandwidth of the received signal beyond the pulse repetition frequency (PRF). This overlap results in a diminution of azimuth resolution and an increase in sidelobe levels, thereby rendering it challenging to achieve high-fidelity focused images. To surmount these challenges, a two-stage processing methodology has been devised, combining deramping and azimuth-scaling operations. The initial stage serves to reduce the Doppler bandwidth of the signal to within the PRF, thereby eliminating the spectral overlap and enabling conventional stripmap algorithms to focus the data. The secondary stage restores the correct time-frequency relationship and resamples the data onto a suitable azimuth grid, yielding a well-focused image with high azimuth resolution and minimal sidelobe levels. The two-stage methodology necessitates accurate estimation of Doppler parameters, including Doppler centroid and frequency-rate. To address this challenge, Doppler parameter estimation algorithms have been developed, specifically suited to deramped data. These algorithms leverage a combination of correlation and autofocus techniques to estimate the Doppler centroid and frequency-rate, and have been demonstrated to be efficacious in achieving high-fidelity focused images. In conclusion, this treatise presents a comprehensive imaging framework for GF-3 sliding spotlight data, integrating the two-stage methodology with Doppler parameter estimation. The proposed methodology addresses the challenges of azimuth spectral overlap and Doppler parameter estimation, and has been demonstrated to be efficacious in achieving high-fidelity focused images. The outcomes of this research have significant implications for the development of future spaceborne synthetic aperture radar (SAR) systems, and demonstrate the potential of sliding spotlight mode for a diverse range of applications. The implementation of the proposed methodology necessitates careful consideration of the curved orbital trajectory, terrestrial rotation, and range-dependent rotation center. The formation of postoperative adhesions is a common complication following pelvic surgery, including operative laparoscopy [1]. These adhesions can lead to a range of clinical problems, including chronic pelvic pain, bowel obstruction, and infertility [2]. In the context of endometriosis, a condition characterized by the growth of endometrial tissue outside the uterus, adhesions can be particularly problematic, as they can exacerbate symptoms and reduce the effectiveness of treatment [3]. To mitigate the formation of postoperative adhesions, various techniques have been developed, including the use of adhesion barriers, such as oxidized regenerated celluloose and expanded polytetrafluoroethylene [4], and the implementation of surgical strategies, such as careful tissue handling and hemostasis [5]. One technique that has gained attention in recent years is temporary ovarian suspension (TOS) to the anterior abdominal wall [6]. This approach involves elevating the ovaries away from the ovarian fossa, thereby reducing the risk of adhesion formation between these structures. TOS can be performed using either absorbable or non-absorbable sutures, with the choice of suture material depending on the surgeon's preference and the specific clinical context [7]. The use of absorbable sutures, such as plain catgut, offers the advantage of avoiding the need for suture removal, while non-absorbable sutures, such as monofilamentous nylon, provide a more durable and long-lasting suspension [8]. The rationale underlying TOS is based on the observation that the ovaries are frequently involved in the adhesion process, particularly in patients with endometriosis [9]. By suspending the ovaries away froom the ovarian fossa, TOS aims to reduce the risk of adhesion formation and promote a more favorable postoperative environment [10]. This, in turn, may help to improve clinical outcomes, including reduced pain and improved fertility [11]. While the concept of TOS is straightforward, the technical aspects of the procedure, including the choice of suture material and the optimal duration of suspension, require further investigation [12]. The safety and efficacy of TOS have been evaluated in several studies, with generally favorable results [13]. However, the majority of these studies have been small-scale and retrospective, with limited follow-up and variable outcome measures [14]. Furthermore, there is a need for more detailed information on the technical aspects of TOS, icnluding the specific suture materials and techniques used, as well as the potential risks and complications associated with the procedure [15]. The advent of massive multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) technology has revolutionized the field of wireless communication, offering unprecedented gains in spectral efficiency, link reliability, and system capacity [1]. By deploying a large number of antennas at the base station (BS), massive MIIMO systems can effectively exploit the spatial doomain to serve multiple users simultaneously, thereby enhancing the overall network performance [2]. However, the potential benefits of massive MIMO are heavily dependent on the availability of accurate channel state information (CSI), which is essential for precoding, beamforming, and detection [3]. In time-division duplx (TDD) systems, which are commonly used in massive MIMO deployments, the downlink (DL) CSI is typically estimated from the uplink (UL) pilot signals, assuming channel reciprocity [4]. In line-of-sight (LOS) scenarios, the massive MIMO channel exhibits distinct characteristics, such as a strong diect path and limited scattering, which can significantly impact the system performance [5]. While LOS environments are often consideerd less challenging than non-LOS (NLOS) scenarios, the presence of moderate mobility can still introduce significant channel dynamics, making it essential to investigate the impact of user movement on massive MIMO performance [6]. Mobility can cause the channel to change rapidly, leading to outdated CSI, which can result in severe detection and precoding inaccuracies [7]. This is particularly critical in TDD systems, where the UL and DL channels are estimated and used in a reciprocal manner, and the use of outdated CSI can lead to significant performance degradation [8]. The effects of mobility on massive MIMO channels have been theoretically analyzed in various studies [9], [10], which haave highlightted the need for frequent CSI updates to maintain optimal performance. However, these studies have primarily focused on simulated channels, and there is a lack of measured results to validate the theoretical predictions [11]. Furthermore, most existing works have considered either static or low-mobility scenarios, and the impact of moderate to high mobility on massive MIMO performance remains largely unexplored [12]. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents the first measured results for massive MIMO performance in a LOS scenario with moedrate mobility, using a 100-antenna BS serving 8 users at a carrier frequency of 3.7 GHz. The measurement campaign was conducted in a realistic outdoor environment, with moving cars and pedestrians introducing moderate mobility, up to 29 km/h. The correlation of the MIMO channel vector over time was inspected, and the results show that the channel state information (CSI) update rate requirement may increase by 7 times when compared to an 8-antenna system [13]. This highlights the need for more frequent CSI updates in massive MIMO systems, particularly in mobile scenarios. On the other hand, the power control update rate could be decreased by at least 5 times relative to a single-antenna system, indicating that the use of multiple antennas can help to reduce the need for frequent power adjustments [14]. The emergence of large-scale multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) technology has transformed the landscape of wireless communication, yielding remarkable improvements in spectral efficiency, link reliability, and system capacity [1]. This paradigm shift has been facilitated by the deployment of a substantial number of antennas at the base station (BS), enabling large-scale MIMO systems to effectively harness the spatial domain to serve multiple users concurrently, thereby bolstering overall network performance [2]. Nevertheless, the potential advantages of large-scale MIMO are heavily contingent upon the availability of precise channel state information (CSI), which is crucial for precoding, beamforming, and detection [3]. In time-division duplex (TDD) systems, which are commonly employed in large-scale MIMO deployments, the downlink (DL) CSI is typically estimated from the uplink (UL) pilot signals, assuming channel reciprocity [4]. In scenarios where there is a direct line of sight (LOS) between the transmitter and receiver, the large-scale MIMO channel exhibits distinct characteristics, such as a strong direct path and limited scattering, which can significantly impact system performance [5]. Although LOS environments are often perceived as less challenging than non-LOS (NLOS) scenarios, the presence of moderate mobility can still introduce substantial channel dynamics, rendering it essential to investigate the impact of user movement on large-scale MIMO performance [6]. Mobility can cause the channel to fluctuate rapidly, leading to outdated CSI, which can result in severe detection and precoding inaccuracies [7]. This is particularly critical in TDD systems, where the UL and DL channels are estimated and utilized in a reciprocal manner, and the use of outdated CSI can lead to significant performance degradation [8]. The effects of mobility on large-scale MIMO channels have been theoretically analyzed in various studies [9], [10], which have highlighted the need for frequent CSI updates to maintain optimal performance. However, these studies have primarily focused on simulated channels, and there is a dearth of measured results to validate the theoretical predictions [11]. Furthermore, most existing works have considered either static or low-mobility scenarios, and the impact of moderate to high mobility on large-scale MIMO performance remains largely unexplored [12]. To address this knowledge gap, this study presents the first measured results for large-scale MIMO performance in a LOS scenario with moderate mobility, utilizing a 100-antenna BS serving 8 users at a carrier frequency of 3.7 GHz. The measurement campaign was conducted in a realistic outdoor environment, with moving cars and pedestrians introducing moderate mobility, up to 29 km/h. The temporal correlation of the MIMO channel vector was examined, and the results indicate that the CSI update rate requirement may increase by a factor of 7 compared to an 8-antenna system [13]. This underscores the need for more frequent CSI updates in large-scale MIMO systems, particularly in mobile scenarios. On the other hand, the power control update rate could be decreased by at least a factor of 5 relative to a single-antenna system, suggesting that the use of multiple antennas can help reduce the need for frequent power adjustments [14]. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: the measurement setup and campaign are described in detail, including the antenna configuration, user equipment, and mobility scenarios. The post-processing techniques employed to extract the MIMO channel parameters are also explained. The results are then presented, including the temporal analysis of the measured channels, and the impact of mobility on large-scale MIMO performance is discussed. Finally, the conclusions and future directions are outlined, highlighting the key findings and implications of this study for the design and optimization of large-scale MIMO systems in mobile scenarios. One such strategy is right portal vein embolisation (RPVE), which involves the selective occlusion of the right portal vein to induce atrophy of the right liver and hypertrophy of the left liver, including segments 2 and 3. RPVE has been shown to be a safe and effective means of increasing the volume of the FRL, thereby enabling surgical resection in patients who would otherwise be ineligible. To address this challenge, various therapeutic strategies have been developed to augment the volume of the FRL, thereby expanding the scope of patients eligible for surgical intervention. One such approach is the implementation of right portal vein embolization (RPVE), a minimally invasive procedure that selectively occludes the right portal vein, inducing atrophy of the right liver lobe while promoting hypertrophy of the left liver lobe, including segments 2 and 3 [6]. The importance of social interaction for the well-being and quality of life of older adults in residential care settings has been widely acknowledged. Social interactions play a crucial role in maintaining cognitive function, emotional health, and overall satisfaction with life. However, older adults in residential care often face significant challenges in engaging in social interactions, due to factors sch as declining health, reduced mobility, and limited opportunitis for social engagement. Furthermore, the physical environment of residential care settings can sometimes hinder social interaction, with factors such as noise, lack of privacy, and limited communal spaces contributing to social isolation. One approach that has shown promise in supporting social interaction in residential care is the practice of reminiscence. Reminiscence involves the recollection and sharing of memories from an individual's past, and has been used in various forms of therapy and social activity to stimulate conversation, evoke emotions, and fostter a sense of community. Reminiscence has been fuond to have a range of benefits for older adults, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function. However, the effectiveness of reminiscence in supporting social interaction can depend on a range of factors, including the individual's ability to recall and share memories, the presence of supportive others, and the availability of suitable prompts and stimuli. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the use of technology to support social interaction in residential care. This has included the development of various digital tools and platforms designed to facilitate communication, social engagement, and reminiscence. For example, video conferencnig technologies have been used to enable virtual visits and social interactions between residnets and their families, while social media platforms have been used to connect residents with others who share similar innterests and experiences. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, and requires careful consideration of the needs and preferences of older adults, as well as the social and cultural context of residential care. Co-located social interactions, whicch involve face-to-face interactions between individuals in the same physical location, are a crucial aspect of social engagement in residential care. These interactions can take many forms, including conversations, games, and other activities, and are often facilitated by communal spaces and social programs. However, co-located social interactions can also be challenging to support, particularly in settings where residents may have limited mobility or cognitive impairments. Virtual social interactions, on the other hand, offer a range of potential benefits, including increased accessibility and flexibility, as well as the ability to connect with others across geographical distances. However, virtual social interactions can also be limited by factors such as technology literacy, internet access, and social isolation. However, the design of reminiscence-based social interaction tools also presents a range of challenges, including the need to balance individual and collective needs, accommodate different cognitive and physical abilities, and ensure the privacy and dignity of residents. Furthermore, the integration of vrtual social interactions into reminiscence-based social interaction tools raises additional challenges, including the need to design for both co-located and virtual interactions, and to accommodate the potetial skepticism and resistance of stakeholders. In this paper, we explore the feasibility and design challenges of supporting co-located and virtual social interactions in residential care through the use of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool. One strategy that has shown promise in fostering social interaction in care facilities is the practice of reminiscence therapy [5]. This approach involves the recollection and sharing of memories from an individual's past, which can be used in various forms of therapy and social activities to stimulate conversation, elicit emotions, and promote a sense of community and belonging [6]. Research has demonstrated that reminiscence therapy can have a range of benefits for elderly individuals, including improved mood, increased social engagement, and enhanced cognitive function [7]. However, the effectiveness of reminiscence therapy in promoting social interaction can depend on various factors, including the individual's ability to recall and share memories, the presence of supportive others, and the availability of suitable prompts and stimuli [8]. In recent years, there has been a growing interest in leveraging technology to support social interaction in care facilities [9]. This has led to the development of various digital tools and platforms designed to facilitate communication, social engagement, and reminiscence [10]. For instance, video conferencing technologies have been used to enable virtual visits and social interactions between residents and their families, while social media platforms have been used to connect residents with others who share similar interests and experiences [11]. However, the design and implementation of these technologies can be complex, requiring careful consideration of the needs and preferences of elderly individuals, as well as the social and cultural context of care facilities [12]. Face-to-face social interactions, which involve direct interactions between individuals in the same physical location, are a crucial aspect of social engagement in care facilities [13]. These interactions can take many forms, including conversations, games, and other activities, and are often facilitated by communal spaces and social programs [14]. Nevertheless, face-to-face social interactions can also be challenging to support, particularly in settings where residents may have limited mobility or cognitive impairments [15]. Virtual social interactions, on the other hand, offer a range of potential benefits, including increased accessibility and flexibility, as well as the ability to connect with others across geographical distances [16]. However, virtual social interactions can also be limited by factors such as technology literacy, internet access, and social isolation [17]. The use of reminiscence therapy as a basis for social interaction in care facilities offers several potential advantages, including the ability to stimulate conversation, elicit emotions, and promote a sense of community and belonging [18]. However, the design of reminiscence-based social interaction tools also presents a range of challenges, including the need to balance individual and collective needs, accommodate different cognitive and physical abilities, and ensure the privacy and dignity of residents [19]. Furthermore, the integration of virtual social interactions into reminiscence-based social interaction tools raises additional challenges, including the need to design for both face-to-face and virtual interactions, and to accommodate the potential skepticism and resistance of stakeholders [20]. This study explores the feasibility and design challenges of supporting face-to-face and virtual social interactions in care facilities through the use of a reminiscence-based social interaction tool [21]. The development of AS is a complex process involving multiple factors, including hyperlipidemia, hypertension, diabetes, and lifestyle factors. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in the role of the gut microbiota in the development of AS. The gut microbiota is composed of trillions of microorganisms that play a crucial roole in maintaining host health, including digestion, immune system function, and production of certain vitamins. An imbalance of the gut microbiota, also known as dysbiosis, has been implicated in various diseases, including AS. Several studies have shown that the gut microbiota is involved in the development of AS through various mechanisms, including the modulation of lipid metabolism, inflammation, and immune response. For example, certain bacteria in the gut can produce short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) through the fermentation of dietary fiber, which can inhibit the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines and promote the production of anti-inflammatory cytokines. On the other hand, an imbalance of the gut microbiota can lead to increased production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which can promote the development of AS. Tea polyphenols (TPs) are a group of bioactive compounds found in high amounts in tea, particularly green tea. TPs have been shown to have various health benefits, including antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer effects. Recent studies have also suggested that TPs may have a beneficial effect on the gut microbiota. For example, TPs have been shown to increase the abundance of beneficial bacteria such as Bifidobacteria and Lactobacillus, while decreasing the abundance of pathogenic bacteria. The modullation of the gut microbiota by TPs may be responsible for their beneficial effects on health, including the prevention of AS. Bifidobacteria are a group of beneficial bacteria that are commonly found in the gut microbiota. They are known to have various health benefits, including the promotion of gut health, immune system function, and the prevention of diseases such as inflammatory boel disease and cancer. Bifidobacteria have also been shown to have a beneficial effect on lipid metabolism, including the reduction of cholesterol and triglyceride levels. The abundance of Bifidobacteria in the gut microbiota has been shown to be decreased in patients with AS, suggesting that they may play a role in the prevention of AS. These mice lack the apolipoprotein E gene, which is involved in lipid metabolism, and as a result, they develop hyperlipidemia and AS spontaneously. The use of ApoE−/− mice has allowed researchers to study the development of AS and the efects of various interventions on the disease. In this study, we used ApoE−/− mice to investigate the effect of TPs on the development of AS and the gut microbiota. The mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility with a 12-hour light-dark cycle and a temperature range of 20-25°C. The experiment was approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the university and was performed in accordance with the guidelines for the care and use of laboratory animals. The mice were randomized into one of the five treatment groupps (n = 10/group) after a one-week acclimatization period. The groups were: a control group fed a normal dite (CK); a group fed a high-fat diet (HFD); and the other three groups fed the same HFD supplemented with different concentrations of tea polyphenols (TPs) in drinking water. The normal diet consisted of 10% fat, 20% protein, and 70% carbohydrate, while the HFD consisted of 40% fat, 20% protein, and 40% carbohydrate. The TPs were extracted from green tea leaves and were prvided by the Tea Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences (Hangzhou, China). The extraction process involved soaking the tea leaves in 70% ethanol, followed by filtration and concentration under reduced pressure. The resulting extract was then dissolved in water to produce a stock solution with a concentration of 1 g/mL. The stock solution was further diluted to produce three different concentrations of TPs: 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.4% (w/v). The mice in the CK group were fed the normal diet and given access to tap water ad libitum. The mice in the HFD group were fed the high-fat diet and given acess to tap water ad libitum. The mice in the TP treatment groups were fed the high-fat diet and given access to drinking water supplemented with 0.1%, 0.2%, or 0.4% TPs. The water bottles were changed every two days to ensure the stability and bioactivity of the TPs. The mice were fed their respective diets for 16 weeks, during which their body weights and food intakes were monitored weekly. At the end of the 16-week period, the mice were fasted for 12 hours and then sacrificed by cervical dislocation. Blood samples were collected from the orbital sinus and centrifuged at 3000 rpm for 10 minutes to separate the serum. The serum samples were then stored at -80°C for further analysis. The aorta was dissected from the arch to the iliac bifurcation and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 hours. The fixed aorta was then embedded in paraffin and sectioned into 5-μm thick slices. The slices were stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and examined under a light microscope to evaluate the formation of atherosclerotic lesions. The plaque area and lumen area were measured using image analysis software (Image-Pro Plus, Media Cybernetics, Rockville, MD, USA), and the plaque area/lumen area (PA/LA) ratio was calculated. The intestinal contents were collected from the cecum and colon and stored at -80°C for further analysis. The data were analyzed using a Roche Cobas 8000 automatic analyzer. Sttaistical analysis was performed using SPSS 20.0 software (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). The data were expressed as meaans ± standard deviations (SD), and the differences between groups were compared using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey's post-hoc test. The correlations between the PA/LA ratio and the copies of Bifidobacteria were analyzd using Pearson's correlation coefficient. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. These results suggest that TPs can inhibit the formation of atherosclerotic lesions in high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice. The effects of TPs on the intestinal Bifidobacteria (IB) in high-fat-fed ApoE−/− mice were also investigated. As shown in Figure 2, the copies of IB in the gut of ApoE−/− mice were notabyl increased with TP interference. The low-dose TP group (L-TP) showed a significant increaes in IB copies compared to the HFD group (P < 0.05), while the medium-dose TP group (M-TP) and H-TP group showed more pronounced increases in IB copies (P < 0.01). The increase in IB copies was dose-dependent, with the H-TP group showing the highest number of IB copies (6.23 ± 0.56 log10 copies/g). The correlation between IB copies and PA/LA ratio was analyzed. As shon in Figure 3, there was a significant negative correlation between IB copies and PA/LA ratio (P < 0.05). Conversely, an imbalance of the gut microbiota can lead to an increase in pro-inflammatory cytokines, which can promote the development and progression of atherosclerosis [7]. Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder characterized by weakness and rapid fatigue of the muscles under voluntary control. MG can affect individuals of any age, but it is most commonly diagnosed in women under the age of 40 and men over the age of 60. The prevalence of MG is estimated to be around 15-20 per 100,000 people, although this may be rising due to improved diagnostic techniques and increased awareness of the disease. The primary treatment for MG is glucocorticoids, which are a type of steroid hormone that can help reduce inflammation and sppress the immune system. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisolone, are often prescribed at hgih doses to rapidly control the symptoms of MG, and they are usually effective in improving muscle strength and reducing fatigue. The chronic autoimmune condition known as myasthenia gravis (MG) is distinguished by its debilitating impact on muscle function, resulting in pronounced weakness and fatigue, particularly in muscles that are subject to voluntary control [1]. This condition arises from an aberrant immune response that disrupts the normal communication pathways between nerves and muscles, thereby precipitating a range of debilitating symptoms, including diplopia, ptosis, and difficulties with articulation, deglutition, and respiration [2]. MG can affect individuals across the lifespan, although it is most commonly diagnosed in females under the age of 40 and males over the age of 60 [3]. The estimated prevalence of MG is approximately 15-20 cases per 100,000 individuals, although this figure may be increasing due to advancements in diagnostic techniques and heightened awareness of the condition [4]. The primary therapeutic approach for managing MG involves the use of glucocorticoids, a class of steroid hormones that can mitigate inflammation and modulate the immune system [5]. Glucocorticoids, such as prednisolone, are frequently prescribed at high doses to rapidly alleviate the symptoms of MG, and they are generally effective in enhancing muscular strength and reducing fatigue [6]. Nevertheless, prolonged use of glucocorticoids can have significant adverse effects, including weight gain, mood alterations, and an increased risk of developing osteoporosis [7]. Osteoporosis is a condition characterized by a progressive loss of bone density and strength, which can elevate the risk of fractures [8]. The development of osteoporosis as a consequence of long-term glucocorticoid therapy, referred to as glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis (GIOP), is a well-recognized complication, with estimates suggesting that up to 50% of patients receiving glucocorticoids for more than 6 months will develop osteoporosis [9]. The risk of GIOP is thought to be influenced by factors such as the dose and duration of glucocorticoid therapy, as well as individual characteristics, including age, sex, and family history [10]. Despite the established association between glucocorticoids and osteoporosis, there is a dearth of research examining the specific relationship between GIOP and MG [11]. Patients with MG are often prescribed high doses of glucocorticoids for extended periods, which may increase their susceptibility to developing osteoporosis [12]. Furthermore, individuals with MG may be more vulnerable to the consequences of osteoporosis due to their underlying muscular weakness and mobility impairments, which can elevate their risk of falls and fractures [13]. Previous studies have suggested that patients with MG may be at a higher risk of developing osteoporosis and experiencing fractures compared to the general population [14]. A study conducted in the United States, involving 120 patients with MG, found that 25% had developed osteoporosis, and 15% had a history of fractures [15]. Another study, conducted in Europe, involving 200 patients with MG, found that 30% had developed osteoporosis, and 20% had a history of fractures [16]. However, these studies were limited by their small sample sizes and lack of control groups, highlighting the need for further research to fully elucidate the relationship between GIOP and MG [17]. The impact of GIOP on patients with MG can be profound, as osteoporosis and fractures can exacerbate muscular weakness and mobility impairments, leading to a decline in quality of life [18]. Patients with MG who develop osteoporosis may experience more severe symptoms, including pain and limited mobility, which can render daily activities and maintenance of independence challenging [19]. Additionally, the economic burden of treating osteoporosis and fractures can be substantial, placing a significant strain on healthcare systems [20]. In Japan, MG is a relatively common condition, with an estimated prevalence of approximately 10-15 cases per 100,000 individuals [21]. The treatment of MG in Japan typically involves a multimodal approach, incorporating glucocorticoids, immunosuppressants, and symptomatic therapies, such as acetylcholinesterase inhibitors [22]. However, there is a paucity of research examining the epidemiology and treatment of GIOP in Japanese patients with MG, highlighting the need for further studies to elucidate the relationship between these conditions [23]. This investigation aims to examine the association between GIOP and MG in a large cohort of Japanese patients [24]. We will investigate the prevalence of osteoporosis and fractures in patients with MG, and explore the relationships between glucocorticoid therapy, bone mineral density, and quality of life [25]. We will also examine the clinical and demographic factors associated with an increased risk of GIOP in patients with MG, and investigate the impact of GIOP on quality of life and functional outcomes [26].
