Among these proteins, the SET domain-containing 1B (SETD1B) gene has been implicated in various biological processes, including cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival [7]. Several lines of evidence suggest that SETD1B may contribute to the development and progression of HCC. Secondly, SETD1B has been implicated in the regulation of cell cycle progression and apoptosis, two critical processes that are often dysregulated in cancer [12]. One such appproach is ophthalmic artery chemosurgery (OAC), which involves the delivery of chemotherapy directly to the eye through the ophthalmic artery, allowing for high concentrations of the drug to be achieved locally while minimizing systemic exposure [3]. This technqiue has been shown to be effective in treating advanced inraocular retinoblastoma, with reported globe salvage rates ranging from 80% to 100% [4, 5]. Despite the advances in treatment, there is a growing concern about the potential long-term effects of cancer therapy on the health and well-being of survivors [6]. One area of particular interest is the impact of cancer treatment on growth and development, as childhood and adolescence are critical periods for physical growth and maturation [7]. Studies hvae shown that patients with pediatric cancers, such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia, may experience decreased growth velocity during and after treatment, which can be attributed to various factors, including the use of systemic chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and the underlying disease process itself [8, 9]. However, the majority of these studies have focused on patients treated with systemic chemotherapy, and there is a lack of data on the effects of localized treatments, such as OAC, on growth patterns. The use of OAC for retinoblasotma treatment offers a unique opportunity to study the effects of localized chemotherapy on growth and development, as it allows for the delivery of high doses of chemotherapy directly to the tumor site whlie minimizing systemic exposure [10]. However, the potential effects of OAC on growth patterns are not well understood, and there is a need for further research in this area. A few studies have reported on the growth and development of retinoblastoma survivors, but thsee have been limited by small sample sizes, short follow-up periods, and the inclusion of patients treated with a variety of therapies, including systemic chemotherapy and radiation therapy [11, 12]. The purpose of this study is to report on the growth patterns of a large cohort of retinoblastoma patients treated with OAC at a single institution, Memorial Sloan Kettering Caner Center, between 2006 and 2016. We aimed to investigate the effects of OAC on short-term and long-term growth velocity, as well as weight gain, in a group of patients who were treated with this modality as their primary or secondary treatment. We also sought to compare the growth patterns of patients who received OAC as their primary treatment (naive patients) with those who received OAC as a secondary treatment after initial systemic chemotherapy (secondary patients). To achivee this goal, we conducted a retrospective review of the medical records of 341 patients with retinoblastoma who were treated with OAC at our institution between 2006 and 2016. Recent studies hvae suggested that sirtuins may play a crucial role in the regulation of insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key players in this process [9, 10]. The sirtuin protein family, comprising seven distinct members (SIRT1-7) in mammals, has garnered substantial attention in recent years owing to its pivotal role in maintaining cellular equilibrium and its participation in a myriad of physiological processes, including metabolic homeostasis, cellular survival, and genomic stability [1]. As enzymes that rely on NAD+ for their deacylase and mono-ADP-ribosyltransferase activities, these proteins exhibit unique localization patterns within cells and execute a diverse array of functions, thereby enabling them to modulate a broad spectrum of cellular activities [2]. Notably, SIRT1 and SIRT6 have been the subject of extensive investigation, and their involvement in metabolic regulation is well-documented [3]. These two sirtuin family members have been implicated in the pathogenesis of various metabolic disorders, including obesity, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), fatty liver disease, and cardiovascular diseases [4, 5]. However, the functions of the remaining sirtuin family members, namely SIRT2, SIRT3, SIRT4, SIRT5, and SIRT7, are not yet fully comprehended, and their potential roles in metabolic regulation remain to be elucidated [6]. Insulin resistance, a condition characterized by impaired insulin signaling, is a critical pathological feature of obesity and metabolic syndrome, as well as the primary defect underlying T2DM [7]. The development of insulin resistance is a complex process, involving multiple cellular and molecular mechanisms, including inflammatory responses, mitochondrial dysfunction, and alterations in glucose and lipid metabolic pathways [8]. Recent investigations have suggested that sirtuins may play a vital role in regulating insulin resistance, with SIRT1 and SIRT6 emerging as key regulators in this process [9, 10]. Nevertheless, the potential roles of the other sirtuin family members in insulin resistance remain poorly understood, and additional research is necessary to elucidate their functions in this context [11]. The insulin signaling pathway, which plays a central role in maintaining glucose homeostasis, is a complex process involving multiple molecular components, including insulin receptors, insulin receptor substrates, and downstream effectors such as Akt and glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) [12]. Impairments in insulin signaling, which can arise due to various factors, including obesity, inflammation, and genetic predisposition, can lead to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [13]. Sirtuins, particularly SIRT1 and SIRT6, have been shown to modulate insulin signaling, with SIRT1 activating the insulin signaling pathway by deacetylating and activating key components, such as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and Akt [14, 15]. In contrast, SIRT6 has been demonstrated to regulate glucose metabolism by promoting the expression of glucose-6-phosphatase and phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), two key enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis [16]. In addition to their roles in insulin signaling, sirtuins have also been implicated in regulating mitochondrial function and biogenesis, which are critical for maintaining glucose and lipid homeostasis [17]. Mitochondrial dysfunction, which can arise due to various factors, including oxidative stress, inflammation, and genetic mutations, is a hallmark of insulin resistance and T2DM [18]. SIRT1 and SIRT3, in particular, have been shown to regulate mitochondrial biogenesis and function, with SIRT1 promoting the expression of peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1-alpha (PGC-1α) and SIRT3 regulating the activity of mitochondrial enzymes involved in the citric acid cycle and fatty acid oxidation [19, 20]. Furthermore, sirtuins have also been implicated in regulating inflammatory responses, which are a key contributor to the development of insulin resistance and T2DM [21]. Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) is the current gold standard for BMD measurement, but it has limitations, such as being a 2D projection technique, which can lead to inaccuracies in measurements due to overlapping structures and variability in soft tissue composition [4]. Computed tomography (CT) scans, on the other hand, provide a 3D representation of the vertebral bodies, allowing for more accurate measurements of BMD and geeometry [5]. However, extracting the relevant informatiion from CT scans requires sophisticated image processing and analysis techniques. Several segmentation methods have been proposed to extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans, including threshold-based methods [6], edge-based methods [7], and model-based methods [8]. These methods have shown promise, but they often require manual intervention, are sensitive to image noise and artifacts, and may not provide accurate results in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes. To overcome these limitations, a new 3D segmentation methodology is needed that can accurately and precsiely extract the geometry of lumbar vertebral bodies from CT scans. Such a methodology should be able to handle the complexities of the vertebral anatomy, including the presecne of osteophytes, fractures, and other degenerative changes. Additionally, it should be able to provide accurate measurements of BMD and geometry, which are essential for the diagnosis and monitoring of osteoporosis. The development of such a methodology would require a thorough understanding of the anatomy and pathology of the lumbar spine, as welll as expertise in image processing and analysis techniques. The use of local anatomical coordinate systems is crucial for accurate measurements of BMD and geometry [9]. However, the definition of these coordinate systems can be challenging, particularly in cases with complex anatomy or osteoporotic changes. Our approach involves a multi-step process, combining the advatnages of thresholding, edge detection, and model-based segmentation techniques [2]. The first step in our methodology invvolves the acquisition of spiral CT scans of the lumbar spine with a slice thickness of 1-2 mm and an in-plane resolution of 0.5-1 mm [3]. The scans are then imported into a custom-built software platform, which enables the application of our segmentation algorithm. Image Preprocessing Prior to segmentation, the CT scans undergo a series of preprocessing steps to enhance image quality and reduce noise [4]. These steps include the application of a Gaussian filter to reduce pixel noise, followed by a non-uniformity correction to account for variations in X-ray attenuation across the scan field [5]. The images are then converted to Hounsfield units (HU), which provide a standardized measure of X-ray attenuation [6]. This conversion enables the differentiation of bone from soft tissue and other materials, based on their distinct HU values. Thresholding and Edge Detection The preprocessed images are then subjected to a thresholding step, where pixels with HU values above a certain threshold (typically +200 HU) are classified as bone [7]. This step is followed by the application of a Canny edge detection algorithm, which identifies the boundaries of the vertebral bodies [8]. The edge detection step is crucial in defining the outer contours of the vertebrae, while the thresholding step helps to distinguish between bone and soft tissue. Model-Based Segmentation The thresholded and edge-detected images are then used to create a 3D model of the vertebral bodies, using a statistical shape model (SSM) [9]. The SSM is based on a database of vertebral body shapes, which are used to inform the segmentation process [10]. The model is iteratively refined, using an active shape model (ASM) algorithm, to accurately capture the geometry of the vertebrae [11]. The ASM algorithm uses the edges detected in the previous step to constrain the model, ensuring that it conforms to the actual shape of the vertebral bodies. Definition of Local Anatomical Coordinate Systems Once the 3D model of the vertebral bodies has been created, a local anatomical coordinate system is defined for each vertebra [12]. This coordinate system is based on the geometry of the vertebra, with the origin located at the center of the vertebral body [13]. The coordinate system is used to define volumes of interest (VOIs) for BMD measurement, whcih are typically located in the anterior, posterior, and central regions of the vertebra [14]. The VOIs are defined relative to the local anatomical coordinate system, ensuring that they are consistent across different vertebae and patients. BMD Meausrement and Geometric Analysis The segmented vertebral bodies are then used to measure BMD, using a calibrated CT scanner and a phantom-based calibrtaion procedure [15]. The BMD measurements are performed for each VOI, providing a detailed assessment of bone density in different regions of the vertebra [16]. In addition to BMD measurement, the segmented vertebral bodies are also used to analyze their geometry, including parameters such as volume, shape, and cortical thickness [17]. These geometric parameters are important indicators of bone health and can be used to predict fracture risk [18]. Intra- and inter-operator precision were assessed by having multiple operators segment the same datasets, while accuracy was evaluated by comparing the results with gold standard measurements [20]. The results showed that intra- and inter-operator precision were below 1.5% for segmentation, BMD measurement, and position of the coordinate system, while accuracy errors were below 1.5% for BMD and below 4% for volume [21]. These results demonstrate the robustness and accuracy of our methodology, which is essential for clinical applications. Central neurocytoma (CN) is a rare, benign brain tmor that was firts described by Hassoun et al. in 1982 [1]. The incidence of CN is estimated to be approximately 0.2-0.5% of all primary brain tumors [4], with a slight male predominance [5]. Epidemiology and Clinical Presentation The clinical presentation of CN is often non-specific, with patients typically presenting with symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure, such as papilledema, visual disturbances, and cognitive impirment [6]. In some cases, CN may be asymptomatic, and the tumor may be discovered incidentally during imaging studies for unrelated reasonns [7]. The age range of patients with CN is broad, with most cases reported in adults between 20 and 40 years old [8]. However, CN has also been reported in children and adolescents [9], highlighting the need for a high index of suspicion in patients of all ages presenting with symptoms suggestive of a brain tumor. Radiological Features The radiological features of CN are often indistinguishable from those of other brain tumors, such as oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas, and meningiomas [10]. On computed tomography (CT) scans, CNs typically appear as well-circumscribed, lobulated masses with heterogeneous atenuation [11]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is more sensitive than CT in detecting CN, and typically shows a heterogeneous signal intensity on T1- and T2-weighted images [12]. However, these radiological features are not specific, and a definitive diagnosis of CN can only be made based on histopathological examination [13]. Histopathological Features The histopathological features of CN are characterized by a monotonous population of small, round cells with a uniform, neurocytic appearance [14]. The tumor cells are typically arranged in a diffuse or trabecular pattern, and may exhibit a perivascular pseudorosette formation [15]. Immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin, a neuronal marker, is typically positive in CN, and can be useful in distinguishing CN from other brain tumors [16]. Other immunohistochemical markers, such as NeuN and MAP2, may also be positive in CN [17]. The MIB-1 Labeling Index, a measure of cell proliferation, has been shown to be correlated with the prognosis of CN, with higher indices associated with a poorer outcome [18]. Mutations in these gense have been detected in a subset of CNs, and may play a role in the pathogenesis of this tumor [20]. Further studies are needed to fully elucidate the molecular genetics of CN and to identify potential therapeutic targets. The human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) epidemic among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand has been steadily increasing over the past decade, with alarming rates of new infections [1]. According to recent estimates, approximately 54% of new HIV infections in Thailand are expected to occur among MSM, highlighting the urgent need for targeted interventions to address this growing public health concern [2]. Depite the availability of effective antiretroviral therapy (ART) and prevention strategies, many MSM in Thailand remain unaware of their HIV status, and those who are infected often experience delays in diagnosis and treatment initiation [3]. The Thai government has acknowledged the importance of early HIV testing and counselling (HTC) and linkage to care, but the current uptake of these services among MSM remains suboptimal [4]. The widespread use of communications technologies, such as the internet and social media, offers a unique opportunity to engage MSM in early HIV testing and treatment [5]. In Thailand, MSM are the largest demographic group accessing the internet, with over 70% of online users being young men [6]. However, the potential of online platforms to promote HIV prevention and care among MSM has not been fully exploited [7]. Traditional outreach methods, such as peer education and community-based interventions, have been shown to be effective in reaching somme segments of the MSM population, but they often have limited reach and may not be able to enngage harder-to-reach groups [8]. In contrast, online platforms can provide a convenient, anonymous, and accessible means for MSM to access HIV-related information, testing, and care [9]. The use of online technologies to promote HIV preventioon and care among MSM is not without its challenges. Stigma, discrimination, and social norms can all impact the willingness of MSM to engage with online HIV services [10]. Furthermore, the anonymity of online environments can make it difficult to establish trust and ensure the confidentiality of sensitive health information [11]. Nevertheless, a growing body of evidence suggests that well-designed online interventions can be effectiev in promoting HIV testing, linkage to care, and adherence to ART among MSM [12]. For example, a recent systematic review of online HIV interventions found that these programs can increase HIV testing rates, improve knowledge of HIV prevention, and reduce high-risk behaviors among MSM [13]. In Thailand, there is a pressing need for innovative, technology-based strategies to engage MSM in early HIV testing and treatment. The country has made significnat progress in scaling up ART, but the coverage of HTC services remains limited, particularly among high-risk groups [14]. One such program, Adam's Love, has been shown to be effective in engaging MSM in online counselling, testing, and care, and has attracted national and regional recognition as a trusted resource on HIV [16]. By leveraging the popularity of online platfomrs among MSM in Thailand, the Adam's Love program aims to increase awareness of HIV, promote early testing and treatment, and reduce the transmission of HIV among this high-risk population [19]. The devastating cholera epidemic that has gripped Yemen since 2016 has reached unprecedented proportions, with a staggering 1.4 million reported cases, rendering it one of the most catastrophic in recent memory [1]. The ongoing civil war has significantly exacerbated this crisis, precipitating the collapse of the nation's healthcare infrastructure, mass displacement of populations, and widespread contamination of water sources [2]. Cholera, a highly infectious disease caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, is primarily spread through the fecal-oral route, where the consumption of contaminated food or water leads to infection [3]. If left untreated, the disease can rapidly progress to severe diarrhea, dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, and ultimately, death [4]. Yemen, situated on the Arabian Peninsula, has been embroiled in conflict and instability since 2015, resulting in a humanitarian crisis of unprecedented magnitude [5]. The war has led to the destruction of critical infrastructure, including water and sanitation systems, creating an environment that is conducive to the spread of waterborne diseases such as cholera [6]. Furthermore, the displacement of populations and lack of access to basic necessities, including food, water, and healthcare, have further fueled the outbreak [7]. The initial cases of cholera in Yemen were reported in October 2016, in the capital city of Sana'a [8], and the outbreak rapidly spread to other parts of the country, including the southern city of Aden, which has been one of the most severely affected areas [9]. Despite efforts by local and international health authorities to contain the outbreak, cholera continues to spread in Yemen, with new cases reported daily [12]. The response to the outbreak has been hindered by a lack of resources, including funding, personnel, and equipment [13]. The phenomenon of recurrent spontaneous abortion (RSA), also referred to as habitual miscarriage, poses a substantial challenge to reproductive health, affecting a significant proportion of women worldwide, approximately 1-5%, and resulting in the recurrence of three or more pregnancy losses prior to the 20th week of gestation [1]. This experience can be particularly distressing for affected couples, given the high incidence of miscarriage as a complication of early pregnancy, which occurs in 15-20% of all pregnancies [2]. The underlying causes of RSA are complex and multifaceted, involving a range of factors including anatomical, genetic, endocrinological, immunological, and infectious etiologies [3]. Among these, endocrinological disorders have emerged as significant contributors to recurrent pregnancy loss, as they can disrupt the intricate hormonal balance essential for successful implantation, embryonic development, and maintenance of pregnancy [4]. Specific endocrine disorders, such as polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS), hyperprolactinemia, luteal phase defects, thyroid dysfunction, diabetes, and hyperandrogenism, have been linked to an increased risk of RSA [5]. PCOS, a common endocrine disorder affecting women of reproductive age, is characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and the presence of polycystic ovaries [6]. Women with PCOS are at a heightened risk of miscarriage, with studies suggesting that the risk of pregnancy loss is 2-3 times greater compared to women without the condition [7]. Hyperprolactinemia, which refers to elevated levels of prolactin, is another endocrine disorder that has been implicated in RSA, as excessive prolactin levels can interfere with reproductive function and contribute to pregnancy loss [8]. Additionally, luteal phase defects, marked by inadequate progesterone production or action, can lead to recurrent pregnancy loss, as progesterone plays a crucial role in preparing the endometrium for implantation and maintaining pregnancy [9]. Thyroid dysfunction, encompassing both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, has also been associated with RSA, as the thyroid gland plays a vital role in regulating metabolism, and abnormalities in thyroid function can disrupt reproductive function and increase the risk of pregnancy loss [10]. Furthermore, other factors, including genetic and anatomical abnormalities, can also contribute to the development of RSA [11]. Genetic factors, such as chromosomal abnormalities, including balanced translocations, and genetic mutations, can increase the risk of miscarriage [12]. Anatomical abnormalities, such as uterine anomalies, fibroids, and cervical insufficiency, can disrupt implantation and embryonic development, leading to pregnancy loss [13]. Immunological factors, including autoimmune disorders, such as antiphospholipid syndrome, and immune dysregulation, can also play a role in RSA [14]. Moreover, infectious agents, such as bacterial and viral infections, can increase the risk of miscarriage [15]. Despite the complexity of RSA, addressing and managing underlying endocrine disorders can significantly improve pregnancy outcomes [16]. For example, women with PCOS who undergo ovulation induction and receive fertility treatment have improved pregnancy rates and a reduced risk of miscarriage [17]. Similarly, women with hyperprolactinemia who receive dopamine agonist therapy to reduce prolactin levels experience improved reproductive outcomes [18]. The diagnosis and treatment of thyroid dysfunction, luteal phase defects, and other endocrine disorders can also enhance pregnancy outcomes and reduce the risk of RSA [19]. Therefore, it is essential to identify and manage underlying endocrine disorders in women with RSA to optimize their chances of a successful pregnancy. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in this area, with the development of deep learning-based approaches achieving state-of-the-art results on various benchmarks. In particular, multi-stage Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have been widely adopted for single image human pose estimation, demonstrating superior performance in detecting human joints and estimating their positions. However, despite their excellent performance on static images, the application of thee CNN-based models to videos poses significant challenges. One major issue is the computational intensity of processing each frame individually, which can lead to inefficient processing times and hinder real-time applications. Moreover, the lack of temporal modeling in these approaches results in suboptimal performance, including flickering and performance degradation, when dealing with video sequences. This is primarily due to the inability of these models to impose sequential geometric consistency, handle severe image quality degradation, such as motion blur and occlusion, and capture the temporal correlation among video frames. The importance of temporal modeling in video-based human pose estimation cannot be overstated. Human movements are inherently sequential, and the position of joiints in one frame is highly correlated with their positions in adjacent frames. Furthermore, videos often suffer from various types of degradation, including motion blur, occlusion, and noise, which can significantly impact the accuracy of pose estimation. To address thee challenges, there is a need for models that can effectively capture the temporal relationships among frames and impoose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) have been widely used for modeling sequential data, including videos, speech, and text. By maintaining an internal state that captures information from previous time steps, RNNs can effectively model temporal relationships and make predictions based on this contextual information. However, one major limitation of traditional RNNNs is their inability to handle long-term dependencies, which can result in vanishing or exploding gradients during training. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, a tye of RNN, have been designed to address this limitation. LSTMs introduce memory cells that can store information for extended periods, allowing the network to capture long-term dependencies and maintain a more stable internal state. This propery makes LSTMs particularly suitable for modeling complex sequential data, such as videos, where the relationships among frames can span multiple time steps. In the context of human pose estimation, LSTMs can be used to model the temporal relationships among frames and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. By maintaining a memory of previous poses, the network can make more accurate predictions and reduce the impact of image quality degradation. Furthermore, the weight sharing scheme in LSTMs can be used to reduce the computational intensity of processing videos, making it possible to achieve real-time performance. Despite the potential benefits of LSTMs for video-based human pose estimation, there are several challenges that need to be addressed. One major challenge is the design of the network architecture, including the number of layers, the type of recurrent connections, and the way the memory cells are used. Another challenge is the training of the network, includding the choice of loss functions, optimization algorithms, and hyperparameters. However, these approaches have several limitations, including the inability to effectively capture long-term dependencies, handle severe image quality degradation, and impose geometric consistency on the estimated poses. To adapt this architecture for video pose estimation, we first observe that the multi-stage CNN can be rewritten as a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) by imposing a weight sharing scheme across multiple stages. The management of rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic and debilitating autoimmune disorder characterized by joint inflammation and degeneration, has undergone significant transformations in recent years, driven in part by the introduction of biologic therapies [1]. Notably, the advent of biologic disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) has marked a pivotal shift in the treatment paradigm for rheumatoid arthritis, offering improved outcomes for patients by mitigating disease activity, slowing disease progression, and enhancing functional capabilities [2, 3]. bDMARDs, encompassing a broad spectrum of agents including tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, interleukin-1 inhibitors, interleukin-6 inhibitors, as well as modulators of T-cell and B-cell function, have revolutionized patient care [3]. Despite the efficacy of these therapies, a substantial proportion of patients fails to achieve optimal therapeutic responses, and adherence to treatment regimens is often compromised [4]. Indeed, research has indicated that as many as 50% of patients discontinue their initial bDMARD due to inadequate efficacy, adverse effects, or other factors, necessitating the initiation of a second or even third bDMARD treatment [5]. This underscores the critical need for effective strategies to manage rheumatoid arthritis in patients who have not responded adequately to initial bDMARD therapy [6]. The selection of a second bDMARD is typically informed by the mechanism of action of the first bDMARD, as well as the patient's unique clinical profile and treatment history [7]. However, the persistence of treatment with second-line bDMARDs remains poorly understood, and the relationship between the mechanism of action of these treatments and their persistence rates is not well defined [8]. Some analyses have suggested that transitioning to a bDMARD with a disparate mechanism of action may yield superior outcomes compared to switching to another agent with a similar mechanism of action [9], whereas others have found that the choice of second bDMARD does not significantly influence treatment outcomes [10]. In recent times, there has been escalating interest in the use of non-anti-TNF bDMARDs, such as abatacept, rituximab, and tocilizumab, as second-line therapeutic options for rheumatoid arthritis [11]. These agents have demonstrated efficacy in patients who have failed to respond to anti-TNF therapy and may offer advantages in terms of safety and tolerability [12]. Nonetheless, the comparative persistence of treatment with non-anti-TNF bDMARDs versus anti-TNF bDMARDs remains to be elucidated, highlighting the need for further investigation to inform treatment decisions in this context [13]. The examination of real-world data, including claims data and electronic health records, presents a valuable opportunity to investigate the persistence of treatment with bDMARDs in a large and diverse patient population with rheumatoid arthritis [14]. Such data can yield insights into the effectiveness and safety of different bDMARDs in routine clinical practice, facilitating the identification of factors associated with treatment discontinuation and switching [15]. Furthermore, the analysis of real-world data can inform the development of treatment guidelines and healthcare policy, providing critical information for patients, clinicians, and payers [16]. The liver is a vital organ that is susceptible to various diseases, including hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), a primary malignancy that is one of the most common causes of cancer-related mortality globally, resulting in a significant proportion of cancer-related deaths worldwide [1]. The prevalence of HCC is escalating at an alarming rate, with estimates suggesting that it will become a leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the next decade, emphasizing the need for effective therapeutic interventions to combat this disease [2]. Currently, treatment options for HCC include surgical resection, liver transplantation, and locoregional therapies, such as transcatheter hepatic arterial chemoembolization (TACE), which is a minimally invasive procedure that delivers chemotherapeutic agents directly to the tumor via the hepatic artery, followed by embolization to induce tumor necrosis [3]. However, the majority of HCC patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage, and the prognosis remains bleak, with limited treatment options available, highlighting the need for novel therapeutic strategies to improve patient outcomes [4]. Consequently, there is an urgent need to develop effective therapeutic interventions for the treatment of advanced HCC. TACE has been shown to improve survival in patients with advanced HCC, and it is currently considered a standard treatment option for patients with unresectable HCC [5]. Nevertheless, the efficacy of TACE is limited by the development of resistance to chemotherapeutic agents and the potential for tumor recurrence, underscoring the need for combination therapies that can overcome these limitations [6]. To address these challenges, combination therapies that involve the use of TACE with other treatment modalities have been explored. Sorafenib, a multikinase inhibitor, has been shown to improve survival in patients with advanced HCC by inhibiting the activity of various kinases involved in tumor growth and angiogenesis, including vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR), platelet-derived growth factor receptor (PDGFR), and Raf kinase [7]. Sorafenib has been approved for the treatment of advanced HCC and is currently considered a standard treatment option for patients with unresectable HCC [8]. However, the efficacy of sorafenib is limited by the development of resistance and the potential for adverse events, highlighting the need for combination therapies that can enhance its efficacy and minimize its toxicity [9]. The combination of TACE with sorafenib has been explored as a potential therapeutic strategy for the treatment of advanced HCC, with the rationale that TACE can induce tumor necrosis and reduce tumor burden, while sorafenib can inhibit tumor growth and angiogenesis [10]. Several clinical trials have investigated the efficacy and safety of TACE combined with sorafenib in patients with advanced HCC, but the results have been inconsistent, and the efficacy and safety of this combination therapy remain unclear [11]. Meta-analyses are powerful tools that can synthesize the results of multiple clinical trials, providing a more accurate estimate of the efficacy and safety of a particular treatment [12]. Several meta-analyses have been conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of TACE combined with sorafenib in patients with advanced HCC, but these meta-analyses have been limited by the inclusion of non-randomized controlled trials and the lack of standardization in the reporting of outcomes [13]. Therefore, there is a need for a meta-analysis that includes only randomized controlled trials and provides a comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy and safety of TACE combined with sorafenib in patients with advanced HCC. Exclusion criteria were current psychotic episodes, severe substance dependence, or a history of severe brain injury. Measures Body attitude was assessed using the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire (FKB-20) [3], a 20-item self-report instrument that evaluates cognitive and emotional aspects of body experience. The clinical cohort was assessed by a licensed psychologist or psychiatrist using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-5 (SCID-5) [2], while the non-clinical cohort was recruited through online advertisements and social media platforms. Exclusion criteria for the clinical cohort included current psychotic episodes, severe substance dependence, or a history of severe brain injury. In contrast, the non-clinical cohort was characterized by the absence of any psychiatric disorders or trauma, allowing us to investigate the impact of early childhood trauma on bodily experience in a more nuanced manner. To assess bodily experience, we employed a range of well-established measures. Bodily attitude was evaluated using the Dresden Body Image Questionnaire (FKB-20) [3], a 20-item self-report instrument that examines cognitive and emotional aspects of bodily experience. The FKB-20 has demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.85) and test-retest reliability (r = 0.82) [3], making it an ideal tool for our investigation. Bodily satisfaction was measured using the Body Cathexis Scale (BCS) [4], a 30-item self-report questionnaire that assesses the degree of satisfaction with various body parts and aspects of physical appearance. The BCS has shown good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.87) and convergent validity with other body image measures [4]. In addition to bodily attitude and satisfaction, we also investigated bodily awareness using the Somatic Awareness Questionnaire (SAQ) [5], a 25-item self-report instrument that evaluates awareness of bodily sensations, feelings, and needs. The SAQ has demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.83) and discriminant validity with respect to measures of alexithymia and emotional awareness [5]. To assess trauma severity, we used the Davidson Trauma Scale (DTS) [6], a 17-item self-report instrument that evaluates the frequency and severity of post-traumatic stress symptoms. The DTS has demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.89) and test-retest reliability (r = 0.86) [6]. Dissociative symptoms were measured using the Dissociation Experience Scale (DES) [7], a 28-item self-report questionnaire that assesses the frequency and severity of dissociative experiences, including depersonalization, derealization, and amnesia. The DES has shown good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.93) and convergent validity with other measures of dissociation [7]. By employing these measures, we aimed to gain a deeper understanding of the complex interplay between early childhood trauma, bodily experience, and dissociative symptoms, and to inform the development of effective interventions that address the unique needs of trauma survivors. The results of this investigation will contribute to the growing body of research on the impact of early childhood trauma on bodily experience, and will highlight the need for a comprehensive and multifaceted approach to assessing and treating bodily experience in this population. Furthermore, the findings of this study will have significant implications for the treatment and prevention of negative bodily experiences in individuals with a history of childhood trauma, and will inform the development of tailored interventions that address the complex needs of trauma survivors. The congenital disorder known as sickle cell disease (SCD) has a profound impact on the production of hemoglobin, resulting in the formation of aberrant red blood cells that can precipitate a multitude of health issues. As the most prevalent genetically determined condition that limits lifespan among individuals of African descent, it affects a substantial population of over 100,000 individuals in the United States [1]. This condition is marked by recurring episodes of pain, an elevated susceptibility to infections, and damage to various vital organs, including the pulmonary system. Respiratory complications are a major contributor to morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD, and asthma, a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways, is a common comorbidity that can exacerbate the condition [2]. However, the interrelationship between SCD and asthma is intricate, and diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD can be problematic due to the overlapping symptomatology. Asthma is characterized by recurring episodes of wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath, and is a common affliction that affects individuals across all age groups [3]. While its prevalence and severity can vary depending on the population, asthma is typically diagnosed in the general population based on a combination of clinical symptoms, pulmonary function tests, and response to treatment [4]. Nevertheless, in patients with SCD, the diagnosis of asthma can be more complicated due to the frequent occurrence of wheezing, a common symptom of asthma, even in the absence of an asthma diagnosis [5]. This has led to queries regarding the interrelationship between SCD and asthma, and whether wheezing in patients with SCD is a marker of asthma or a distinct entity. The association between asthma and SCD has been recognized for several decades, with early studies reporting a high prevalence of asthma in patients with SCD and suggesting that asthma may be a risk factor for acute chest syndrome (ACS), a life-threatening complication of SCD [6]. ACS is characterized by a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph, often accompanied by fever, respiratory symptoms, and chest pain, and is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with SCD [7]. The interrelationship between asthma and ACS is complex, and it is unclear whether asthma is a cause or a consequence of ACS [8]. However, it is evident that patients with SCD and asthma are at increased risk of developing ACS, and that asthma exacerbations can trigger ACS episodes [9]. In recent years, there has been growing interest in the interrelationship between wheezing and SCD, with several studies reporting that wheezing is a predictor of SCD severity and that patients with SCD who wheeze are at increased risk of developing ACS and other complications [11]. The underlying mechanisms of wheezing in SCD are not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the chronic inflammation and oxidative stress that occur in the disease [12]. Wheezing in SCD may also be related to airway hyperresponsiveness, a characteristic feature of asthma [13]. However, airway hyperresponsiveness can also occur in the absence of asthma, and its significance in SCD is unclear [14]. The diagnosis of asthma in patients with SCD is challenging due to the high prevalence of wheezing and airway obstruction in the disease. Pulmonary function tests, such as spirometry, are often used to diagnose asthma, but they can be abnormal in patients with SCD even in the absence of asthma [15]. Airway obstruction, as measured by forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), is common in patients with SCD and can occur in the absence of asthma symptoms [16]. Similarly, airway hyperresponsiveness, as measured by methacholine challenge, can also occur in patients with SCD without asthma [17]. These findings have led to questions regarding the utility of pulmonary function tests in diagnosing asthma in patients with SCD and highlight the need for a more nuanced approach to diagnosis and management [18]. Despite the challenges, it is evident that asthma and wheezing are important comorbidities in patients with SCD, and their management is crucial to improving patient outcomes. The management of asthma in SCD is similar to that in the general population and involves the use of bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, and other medications to control symptoms and prevent exacerbations [19]. However, the optimal approach to managing asthma in SCD is not clear, and more research is needed to determine the best strategies for diagnosis and treatment [20]. Additionally, the interrelationship between wheezing and SCD severity highlights the need for a better understanding of the pathophysiology of airway inflammation in SCD and the development of new therapies to target this inflammation [21]. This review aims to provide a comprehensive summary of our current understanding of the epidemiology of asthma, wheezing, airway obstruction, and airway hyperresponsiveness in patients with SCD, as well as discuss the evidence supporting associations between these conditions and SCD severity. Furthermore, we will examine the current approaches to diagnosing and managing asthma in SCD, and discuss the need for further research to improve patient outcomes. The complex interplay between SCD and asthma has significant implications for patient care, and a deeper understanding of this relationship is essential to developing effective management strategies. By exploring the epidemiology, pathophysiology, and clinical manifestations of asthma and SCD, we can work towards improving the diagnosis, treatment, and outcomes for patients with these conditions. Ultimately, a comprehensive approach to managing SCD and asthma is necessary to address the complex needs of patients with these conditions and to reduce the significant morbidity and mortality associated with them. The utilization of therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE) as a treatment methodology has become increasingly prevalent across a broad spectrum of medical specialties, encompassing autoimmune disorders, neurological afflictions, and hematological malignancies [1]. This procedure entails the extracorporeal separation of plasma from the bloodstream, followed by its substitution with a suitable replacement solution, such as albumin or fresh frozen plasma [2]. In order to prevent the coagulation of blood during this process, the implementation of anticoagulation measures is imperative. Historically, the administration of systemic anticoagulation via heparin or other anticoagulant agents has been the preferred approach [3]. In recent years, regional citrate anticoagulation (RCA) has emerged as a viable alternative to systemic anticoagulation for various extracorporeal purification techniques, including TPE [5]. The underlying mechanism of RCA involves the introduction of citrate into the blood circuit, which effectively binds to calcium ions, thereby precluding coagulation [6]. In many cases, the observed signals are noisy and corrupted, making it difficult to recover the underlying dictionary. Furthermore, the dictionary is often convolutional in nature, meaning that the basis elements are shifted versions of ecah other. This convolutional structure adds an extra layer of complexity to the dictionary learninng problem. One approach to dictionary learning is to use optimization-based methods, which involve minimizing a cost function that measures the difference between the observed signals and their representation in terms of the dictionary. These methods often rely on alternating-minimization schemes, where the sparse coefficients and the dictionary are updated alternately. While these methods have been shown to be effective in many cases, they can be computationally expensive and may not be scalable to large datasets. Recently, deep learning techniques have been appled to the problem of dictionary learning, with promising results. In particular, auto-encoders have been used to learn dictionaries from observed signals. An auto-encoder is a neural network that consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder maps the input signal to a lower-dimensional representation, while the decoder maaps this representation back to the original signal. By training the auto-encoder to minimize the reconstruction error, the encoder learns to extract the most important features from the input signal, which can be used to learn the dictionary. However, most existing auto-encoder-based dictionary learning methods do not take into account the convolutional structure of the dictionary. Furthermore, they often do not impose any constraints on the prameters of the encoder and decoder, whch can lead to overfitting and poor generalization performance. In this paper, we propose a new auto-encoder architecture, termed constrained recurrent sparse auto-encoder (CRsAE), that addresses these limitations. CRsAE is designed to learn convolutional dictionaries from noisy observed signals, while imposing constraints on the parameters of the encoder and decoder to ensure that tey are not independent. The CRsAE architecture consists of an encoder and a decoder, where the encoder finds a sparse approximation of the input signal using the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (FISTA). Coxiella burnetii is a zoonotic bacterium that causes Q fever, a disease characterized by flu-like symptoms, pneumonia, and hepatitis in humans [1]. The bacterium is widely distributed across the globe and can infect a variety of animals, including cattle, sheep, goats, and wild animals [2]. C. burnetii is typically transmitted to humans through inhalation of contaminated particles or contact with infected animal tissues [3]. The disease is often underdiagnosed and underestimated, partly due to its non-specific symptoms and the lack of awareness among healthcare professionals [4]. In South Korea, there have been limited studies on the prevalence of C. burnetii in livestock, despite the potential risk of transmission to humans [5]. The country has a significant livestock industry, with a large number of cattle, pigs, and chickens being raised on farms across the country [6]. National breeding stock farms, which are government-operated frams that provide high-quality breeding stock to the livestock industry, play a crucial role in maintaining the health and productivity of the national herd [7]. These farms have well-organized biosecurity and management systems in place to prevent the introduction and spread of livestock diseases [8]. However, the risk of C. burnetii transmission to humans from livestock cannot be ignored, particularly in countries where livestock farming is a signifiicant industry [9]. C. burnetii has been detected in various animal species in South Korea, including cattle, sheep, and goats [10], but the prevalence of the bacterium in the national breeding stock farms has not been previously investigated. The serologic and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at these farms is essential to understanding the risk of transmission to humans and to developing effective control strategies [11]. Seveeral studies have investigated the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle worldwide, with varying results [12]. A study in the United States found that 30% of cattle tested positive for C. burnetii antibodes [13], while a study in Japan reported a seroprevalence of 15.6% [14]. In Europe, the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle has been reported to range from 5% to 40% [15]. However, these studies were often conducted on commercial farms or in specific regions, and the results may not be representative of the situation in South Korea. The global health implications of Coxiella burnetii, the zoonotic pathogen responsible for Q fever, are substantial, as it can trigger a range of symptoms in humans, including those akin to influenza, pneumonia, and hepatitis [1]. Given its widespread geographic distribution and capacity to infect various animal species, such as cattle, sheep, goats, and wildlife, C. burnetii poses a significant threat to human health [2]. Human infection primarily occurs through the inhalation of contaminated particles or direct contact with infected animal tissues [3]. However, the underdiagnosis and underestimation of Q fever are issues of concern, largely due to the nonspecific nature of its symptoms and a lack of awareness among healthcare professionals [4]. In the context of South Korea, where the livestock industry plays a pivotal role in the national economy, there is a pressing necessity to examine the prevalence of C. burnetii within the livestock population, particularly in government-operated national breeding stock farms [5]. These farms are critical for maintaining the health and productivity of the national livestock herd, implementing rigorous biosecurity measures and management protocols to mitigate the risk of disease introduction and spread [6, 7]. Nevertheless, despite these stringent controls, the potential for C. burnetii transmission from livestock to humans cannot be overlooked, especially in countries where livestock farming is a major sector [8, 9]. Previous research in South Korea has identified C. burnetii in various animal species, including cattle, sheep, and goats [10], yet the prevalence of this bacterium in national breeding stock farms remains unstudied. Consequently, understanding the serological and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle within these farms is crucial for assessing the risk of human transmission and devising effective mitigation strategies [11]. Various studies globally have investigated the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle, yielding a range of results [12]. For example, research in the United States found that 30% of tested cattle were seropositive for C. burnetii [13], while a study in Japan reported a seroprevalence rate of 15.6% [14]. In Europe, the reported prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle varies widely, from 5% to 40% [15]. However, these studies often focused on commercial farms or specific regions, and their findings may not accurately reflect the situation in South Korea. The advent of molecular techniques, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), has significantly enhanced the detection of C. burnetii in animal tissues and fluids [16]. PCR analysis offers a more precise diagnosis by detecting C. burnetii DNA, surpassing the accuracy of serological tests that identify antibodies against C. burnetii antigens [17]. Furthermore, the sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene is a widely employed method for identifying and characterizing C. burnetii isolates [18]. This approach involves PCR amplification of the 16S rRNA gene, followed by sequencing of the resulting amplicon to determine the genetic identity of the isolate [19]. This study aimed to investigate the serological and molecular prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea, utilizing a combination of serological tests and PCR analysis to detect the bacterium in cattle tissues and fluids. Additionally, 16S rRNA gene sequencing was performed on C. burnetii isolates to ascertain their genetic identity and compare them with isolates from other countries. The outcomes of this research will provide invaluable insights into the prevalence of C. burnetii in cattle at national breeding stock farms in South Korea, informing the development of targeted strategies to prevent human transmission. The estimation of post-mortem interval (PMI) is a crucial aspect of forensic investigations, particularly in cases where the time of death is unknown or disputed [1]. One of the methods used to estimate PMI is forensic entomology, which involves the analysis of insects colonizing human or animal cadavers [2]. Insects such as flies, beetles, and ants are attracted to cadavers and can proviide valuable information about the time of death [3]. The most common approach in forensic entomology is to estimate the age of insects found on a cadaver, usually larvae or pupae, and use this information to calculate the minimum PMI [4]. However, the accuracy of insect age estimates in a forensic context is often redced by large intraspecific variation in insect development time [5]. This variation can arise from various factors, including genetic differences, environmental conditions, and nutrition [6]. As a result, age estimates based on insect development can be uncertain and may lead to incorrect conclusions about the timme of death [7]. To improev the accuracy of age estimates, researchers have explored various methods, including the use of thermal summation models [8] and the analysis of insect growth patterns [9]. Thermal summation models are widely used in forensic entomology to estimate insect age [10]. These models are based on the idea that insect development is temperature-dependent and that the accumulation of thermal units (e.g., degree-days) can be used to predict development time [11]. However, thermal summation models oftten assume a fixed development rate, which can be affected by various factors, including temperature, humidity, and nutrition [12]. As a result, these models may not always provide accurate age estimates, particularly in cases where the environmental conditions are unknown or variable [13]. In recent years, researchers have suggested that insect size at emergence may be used to predict insect physiological age and improve the accuracy of age estimates [14]. This approach is based on the idea that insect size is related to development time and that largeer insects may have required more time to develop [15]. Several studies have explored the relationship between insect size and development time, including studies on flies [16] and beetles [17]. These studies have shown that insect size can be a useful predictor of development time, particularly when combined with other factors, such as temperature and nutrition [18]. The beetle Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is a forensically useful species that is commonly found on human and animal cadavers [19]. This species is known to colonize cadavers in the early stages of decomposition and can provide valuable information about the time of death [20]. However, the development time of C. maxillosus can be variable, and accurate age estimates are essential for reliable PMI estimation [21]. In this study, we investigate the relationship between inseect size at emergence and physiological age in C. maxillosus, with the aim of improving the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic context. The concept of physiological age is important in forensic entomology, as it refers to the cumulative effect of temperature on insect development [22]. Physiological age is often estimated using thermal summation models, which assume a fixed development rate [23]. However, physiological age can also be influenced by other factors, including nutrition and humidity [24]. In this study, we use the thermal summation value (K) as a measure of physiological age, which represents the cumulative effect of temperature on insect development [25]. We hypothesize that insect size at emergence is related to physiological age and that larger insects may have required more time to develop. To test this hypothesis, we conducted a laboratory study on the development of C. maxillosus, in which we measured the size of emerging adults and estimated their physiological age using thermal summation models [26]. We also conducted a validation study, in which we compared the estimated physiological age with the true age of the insects [27]. Our results show that insect size at emergence is a useful predictor of physiological age in C. maxillosus and that larger insects may have requred more time to develop. We also demonstrate that using insect size as a predictor variable can improve the accuracy of age estimates in a forensic context. The use of insect size as a predictor of physiological age has several advantages in forensic entomology [28]. First, it provides a more direct measure of development time, which can be less affected by environmental faactors [29]. Second, it allows for more accurate age estimates, particularly in cases where the environmental conditions are unknnown or variable [30]. Finally, it provides a usefuul tool for forensic entomologists, who can use insect size to estimate the minimum PMI and provide more accurate information about the time of death [31]. Overall, our study demonstrates the potential of using insect size at emergence to improve the accuracy of age estimates in forensic entomology and provides a new tool for forensic investigators. Forensic investigations often hinge on the precise determination of the post-mortem interval (PMI), a crucial aspect particularly when the time of death is either unknown or contested [1]. A key methodology utilized in PMI estimation involves forensic entomology, the scientific analysis of insects that infest human or animal remains [2]. Insects, such as flies, beetles, and ants, are naturally attracted to cadavers and can offer invaluable insights into the time elapsed since death [3]. The predominant approach in forensic entomology entails estimating the age of the insects found on a cadaver, typically at the larval or pupal stages, and leveraging this information to calculate the minimum PMI [4]. However, the reliability of insect age estimates in forensic contexts is frequently compromised by substantial variation within species regarding insect development time [5]. This variability can stem from a multitude of factors, including genetic disparities, environmental conditions, and nutritional intake [6]. Consequently, age estimates derived from insect development can be uncertain, potentially leading to erroneous conclusions about the time of death [7]. To enhance the accuracy of these estimates, researchers have explored diverse methodologies, including the application of thermal summation models [8] and the analysis of growth patterns in insects [9]. Thermal summation models are extensively used in forensic entomology to estimate insect age [10], based on the premise that insect development is temperature-dependent, and the accumulation of thermal units can predict development time [11]. Nonetheless, these models often assume a constant development rate, which can be influenced by various factors, including temperature fluctuations, humidity levels, and nutritional availability [12]. As a result, the accuracy of age estimates provided by these models can be compromised, especially in scenarios where environmental conditions are either unknown or highly variable [13]. Recently, there has been a suggestion that the size of insects at emergence could be a predictive factor for their physiological age, thereby improving the accuracy of age estimates [14]. This approach is grounded in the idea that insect size is correlated with development time, with larger insects potentially requiring more time to reach maturity [15]. Several studies have investigated the relationship between insect size and development time, encompassing research on flies [16] and beetles [17]. These investigations have demonstrated that insect size can be a useful predictor of development time, particularly when considered in conjunction with other factors, such as temperature and nutritional intake [18]. The beetle species Creophilus maxillosus (Linnaeus, 1758) (Staphylinidae) is of particular forensic utility, as it is commonly found on both human and animal cadavers [19]. This species is known to colonize cadavers during the early stages of decomposition, thereby providing critical information regarding the time of death [20]. However, the development time of C. maxillosus can exhibit significant variability, underscoring the need for accurate age estimates to reliably determine PMI [21]. Crowdsourcing, the practice of soliciting contributions from a large, often anonymous group of individuals, has emerged as a promising alternative for exploring and analyzing large networks [4]. By leveragging the collective efforts of many individuals, crowdsourcing can provide a fast, cheap, and scalable means of gathering data and insights about complex networks [5]. Despitte its potential, crowdsourcing complex, open-ended tasks can be challenging [6]. Crowd participants often favor short, repetitive "microtasks" that can be completed quickly and with minimal effort [7]. These microtasks can be useful for simple, well-defined tassks such as data labeling or content moderation [8], but they can be less effective for more complex tasks that require creativity, critical thinking, or domain expertise [9]. Explosions are a major cause of injury in combat and other high-risk environments, accounting for 79% of combat-related injuries [1]. The resultinng polytrauma often includes blast-induced traumatic brain injuries (bTBI), which can lead to long-term neurological deficits and other complications [2]. Internal bleeding in multiple organs is a common consequence of such injuries, and current treatment options are limited to fluid resuscitation and surgery [3]. Furthermore, there is a dearth of effective treatments for traumatic brain injuries, which can result in significant morbidity and mortality [4]. The development of novel therapeutic approaches is therefore crucial to improve outcomes for individuals affected by blast trauma. Blast-induced traumatic brain injuries are a complex and multifaceted condition, involving both primary and secondary injury mechanisms [5]. Primary injury occurs as a result of the initial blast wave, which can cause direct damage to brain tissue and disrupt the blood-brain barrier [6]. Secondary injury mechanisms, including inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, can exacerbate the initial damage and contribute to long-term neurological deficits [7]. The amygdala, a region critical for emotional processing, is particularly vulnerable to blast-induced injury [8]. Damage to this region can lead to anxiety, depression, and other emotional deficits, which are common among individuals with a history of traumatic brain injury [9]. Curretn treatment options for bTBI are largely focused on managing symptoms and supporting recovery, rather than addressing the underlying causes of the injury [10]. Fluid resuscitation and surgery are commonly used to manage internal bleeding and other acute complications, but these approaches do not address the long-term neurological consequences of the injury [11]. There is a need for novel therapeutic approaches that can mitigate the primary and secondary injury mechanisms underlying bTBI, and improve long-term functional outcomes for affected individuals. Nanoparticle-based therapies have shown promise in preclinical models of traumatic brain injury, offering a potential means of delivering targeted treatments to the brain [12]. Hemostatic nanoparticles, which are designed to promote bleeding cessation and reduce inflammation, may be particularly useful in the context of blast trauma [13]. By encapsulating anti-inflammatory agents, such as dexamethasone, these nanoparticles can help to mitigate the secondary injury mechanisms thaat contribute to long-term neurological deficits [14]. The use of biodegradable materials, such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid), can also help to minimize the risk of adverse effects and promote safe, tareted delivery of the therapeutic payload [15]. Animal models of blast trauma have been dveeloped to simulate the complex injury mechanisms associated with explosions [16]. These models typically involve exposure to a blast wave, which can be generated using a variety of methods, including advanced blast simulators [17]. Rats are commonly used as subjects in these models, due to their relatively low cost, ease of handling, and well-characterized neuroanatomy [18]. By using these models, researchers can investigate the effects of blast trauma on the brain and other organs, and evaluate the efficacy of novel therapeutic approaches, such as hemostatic nanoparticles. Our results demonstrate that hDNPs can increase survival, reduce anxiety, and mitigate neuropatholoy in this model, offering a promising new approach for the treatment of blast-induced traumatic brain injuries. The aftermath of explosions in high-stakes environments can have a profound impact, with a considerable proportion of combat-related injuries being attributed to these events, totaling 79% [1]. The resulting complex injuries, often involving blast-induced brain trauma, can lead to lasting neurological damage, significant health complications, and a heightened risk of mortality [2]. A major challenge in treating blast-induced brain trauma is managing internal bleeding in multiple organs, which currently relies on replenishing fluids and surgical intervention [3]. However, these methods have limitations in addressing the intricate and multifaceted nature of blast-induced brain trauma, and there is a scarcity of effective treatments for this condition [4]. Consequently, developing innovative therapeutic strategies is crucial to improving outcomes for individuals affected by blast trauma. Blast-induced brain injuries are a complex phenomenon, involving both immediate and delayed injury mechanisms [5]. The initial blast wave can cause direct damage to brain tissue and disrupt the protective barrier surrounding the brain [6]. This initial insult can trigger a cascade of secondary mechanisms, including inflammation, oxidative damage, and programmed cell death, which can exacerbate the initial damage and contribute to long-term neurological damage [7]. The amygdala, a critical region for emotional regulation, is particularly susceptible to blast-induced damage [8]. Damage to this region can lead to anxiety, depression, and other emotional disturbances, which are common among individuals with a history of brain trauma [9]. Current treatment options for blast-induced brain trauma are primarily focused on managing symptoms and supporting recovery, rather than addressing the underlying causes of the injury [10]. Replenishing fluids and surgery are commonly used to manage internal bleeding and other acute complications, but these methods do not address the long-term neurological consequences of the injury [11]. There is a need for innovative therapeutic strategies that can mitigate the immediate and delayed injury mechanisms underlying blast-induced brain trauma, and improve long-term functional outcomes for affected individuals. In recent years, therapies based on nanoparticles have shown promise in preclinical models of brain trauma, offering a potential means of delivering targeted treatments to the brain [12]. Nanoparticles designed to promote bleeding cessation and reduce inflammation, such as hemostatic nanoparticles, may be particularly useful in the context of blast trauma [13]. By encapsulating anti-inflammatory agents, such as dexamethasone, these nanoparticles can help to mitigate the secondary injury mechanisms that contribute to long-term neurological damage [14]. The use of biodegradable materials, such as poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid), can also help to minimize the risk of adverse effects and promote safe, targeted delivery of the therapeutic payload [15]. Researchers have developed animal models of blast trauma to simulate the complex injury mechanisms associated with explosions [16]. These models typically involve exposure to a blast wave, which can be generated using advanced technology [17]. Rodents, such as rats, are commonly used as subjects in these models due to their relatively low cost, ease of handling, and well-characterized brain anatomy [18]. By using these models, researchers can investigate the effects of blast trauma on the brain and other organs, and evaluate the efficacy of innovative therapeutic approaches, such as hemostatic nanoparticles. The present study hypothesized that hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone would improve survival and mitigate long-term neurological damage in a rodent model of blast trauma. The results demonstrate that these nanoparticles can increase survival, reduce anxiety, and mitigate neurological damage in this model, offering a promising new approach for the treatment of blast-induced brain injuries. The yeast centrosome, also known as the spindle pole boddy (SPB), is a crucial organelle responsible for organizing microtubules during cell division [1]. The duplication of the SPB is a complex process that is essential for the proper segregation of genetic material during mitosis [2]. While significant progress has been made in understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying SPB duplication, many aspects of this process remain poorly understood [4]. Recent advances in super-resolution microscopy, such as structured illumination microscopy (SIM), have begun to address this limitation, allowing for the visualization of cellular structures at the nanoscale [6]. However, the application of SIM to study SPB duplication has been limited by the difficulty in obtaining quantitative information on protein localization and abundance [7]. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel two-color SIM approach combined with single-particle averaging (SPA-SIM), which enables the quantitative analysis of protein localization and intensity at the nanoscale [8]. This approach allows for the simultaneous imaging of multiple fluorescent proteins, enabling the study of the spatial relationships between different SPB components during duplication. However, the precise mechanism by which these components interact to regulatte SPB duplication remians unclear. In addition to the Sfi1 filaament and the Spc29- and Spc42-dependent complex, several other poteins have been implicated in SPB duplication, including those involved in membrane insertion, such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1 [12]. Voltage-gated sodium channels are pivotal for the initiation and propagation of action potentials in excitable tissues, including neurons, muscle cells, and endocrine cells [1]. These channels are responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential, allowing for the transmission of electrical signals throughout the body [2]. The channels are composed of a pore-forming α-subunit and auxiliary β-subunits, which modulate the channel's biophysical properties and cellular localization [3]. The α-subunit is sufficient for channel function, and it is generally accepted that a single α-subunit forms a functional channel [4]. However, recent studis have suggested that sodium channel α-subunits may not function as solitary monomers, but rather interact with each other to form dimers [5]. The idea that sodium channels function as monomers is based on early biochemical and electrophysiological studies, which demonstrated that a single α-subunit is capable of forming a functional channel [6]. This concept has been widly accepted and has shaped our understanding of sodium channel structure and function [7]. However, several lines of evidence have emerged to challenge this traditional view. For example, studies have shown that sodium channel α-subunits can interact with each otehr through specific domains, suggesting a potential for dimerization [8]. Additionally, biochemical and biophysical analyses have revealed that sodium channels can exist as dimers or higher-order oligomers in native tissues [9]. The possibility that sodium channels function as dimmers has significant implications for our understanding of channel assembly, structure, and function. Dimerization could provide a mechanism for cooperative gating, where the activity of one channel influences the activity of its dimeric partner [10]. This could allow for more complex and nuanced regulation of channel function, enabling the fine-tuning of electrical signaling in excitable tissues [11]. Furthermore, dimerization could also influence the biophysical properties of the channel, such as its voltage dependence, kinetics, and pharmacology [12]. Despite the growing evidence for sodium channel dimerization, the mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. The regions of the α-subunit involved in dimerization, as well as the molecular interactions that mediate this process, are not well defined [13]. Additionally, the functional consequences of dimerization, including its effects on channel gating and biophysical properties, require further investigation [14]. The identification of proteins that interact with sodium channels and influence their dimerization and function could also provide important insights into the regulation of channel activity [15]. In recent years, several proteins have been identified that interact with sodium channels and modulate their function, including the 14-3-3 protein family [16]. The 14-3-3 proteins are a group of regulatory molecules that bind to specific phosphorylation sites on target proteins, influencing their activity, localization, and interactions [17]. These proteins have been implicated in the regulation of various ion channels, including potassium and calcium channels [18]. However, their role in regulating sodium channel function, particularly in the context of dimerization, is not well understood [19]. The conservation of sodium channel structure and function across different species is a notable feature of these channels [20]. Mammalian sodium channels, in particular, exhibit a high degree of sequence homology and functional similarity [21]. This conservation suggests that the mechanisms underlying sodium channel function, including dimerization, may also be conserved across species [22]. Investigating the conservation of sodium channel dimerization and its undrelying mechanisms could provide important insights into the evolution of channel function and the devleopment of channelopathies [23]. This notion challenges the long-standing understanding of sodium channel structure and function, which has been largely based on early biochemical and electrophysiological investigations demonstrating the capacity of a single α-subunit to form a functional channel [6]. The concept of sodium channels functioning as solitary monomers has been deeply ingrained and has significantly influenced our comprehension of sodium channel structure and function [7]. Nevertheless, a multitude of evidence has emerged to contest this traditional viewpoint. For instance, research has shown that sodium channel α-subunits can interact with each other through specific domains, implying a potential for dimerization [8]. The possibility that sodium channels function as dimers has profound implications for our understanding of channel assembly, structure, and function. Dimerization could facilitate a mechanism for cooperative gating, where the activity of one channel influences the activity of its dimeric partner, allowing for more intricate and nuanced regulation of channel function [10]. This, in turn, could enable the fine-tuning of electrical signaling in excitable tissues, thereby contributing to the complex and highly regulated processes that underlie various physiological functions [11]. Additionally, dimerization could also impact the biophysical properties of the channel, such as its voltage dependence, kinetics, and pharmacological profile [12]. Despite the accumulating evidence supporting sodium channel dimerization, the underlying mechanisms governing this process remain poorly understood. The cells were incubated at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO2. The BMMSCs were characterized by flow cytometry using a panel of cell surace markers, including CD73, CD90, CD105, CD14, CD19, CD34, and HLA-DR. The cells were also tested for their abliity to differentiate into osteogenic and adipogenic lineages. For osteogenic differentiation, the cells were cultured in osteogenic medium consisting of α-MEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate, 0.1 μM dexamethasone, and 50 μM ascorbic acid. The cells were stained witth Alizarin Red S (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) after 21 days of culture. These programs typically provide incoming students with academic preparation, social support, and professional development opportunities during the summer preceding their freshman year [4]. Despite their growing popularity, the effectiveness of STEM summer bridge programs in acheiving their intendde goals is not well understood [5].
